en: Aṅguttara Nikāya 5.1 1.

Saṅkhittavagga (The Chapter on the Brief) Saṅkhittasutta (The Brief Discourse) "Bhikkhus, there are these five powers of one in training. What five? The power of faith, the power of energy, the power of mindfulness, the power of concentration, and the power of wisdom. These, bhikkhus, are the five powers of one in training."
Thus have I heard—
on one occasion the Blessed One was dwelling at Sāvatthī in Jeta’s Grove, Anāthapiṇḍika’s monastery.
There the Blessed One addressed the bhikkhus: “Bhikkhus.
“Venerable sir,” those bhikkhus replied to the Blessed One.
The Blessed One said this:
“Monks, there are these five powers of one in training.
Which five?
The power of faith, the power of moral shame, the power of moral dread, the power of energy,
and the power of wisdom— these, monks, are the five powers of one in training.
Therefore, monks, you should train yourselves thus:
‘We shall be endowed with the power of faith, the power of a trainee; we shall be endowed with the power of moral shame, the power of a trainee;
we shall be endowed with the power of moral dread, the power of a trainee; we shall be endowed with the power of energy, the power of a trainee;
we shall be endowed with the power of wisdom, the power of a trainee.’
"Thus, monks, should you train yourselves.
This is what the Blessed One said.
Elated, those monks rejoiced in the words of the Blessed One.
First. Aṅguttara Nikāya 5.2 1.
The Chapter on the Powers of a Trainee (Sekhabalavagga)
Vitthatasutta: “Bhikkhus,
there are these five powers of one in training.”
What are the five?
The power of faith, the power of moral shame, the power of moral dread, the power of energy, and the power of wisdom.
And what, monks, is the power of faith?
“Here, monks, a noble disciple is endowed with faith; he has faith in the enlightenment of the Tathāgata:

‘Thus indeed is the Blessed One: worthy, perfectly enlightened, perfect in knowledge and conduct, sublime, knower of the worlds, unsurpassed leader of persons to be tamed, teacher of gods and humans, the Buddha, the Blessed One.
This, monks, is called the power of faith.”
And what, monks, is the power of moral shame?
Here, monks, a noble disciple possesses moral shame; he feels shame at bodily misconduct, verbal misconduct, and mental misconduct; he feels shame at the undertaking of evil, unwholesome states.
This, monks, is called the power of moral shame.
And what, monks, is the power of moral dread?
Here, monks, a noble disciple is morally dreading; he dreads misconduct of body, misconduct of speech, and misconduct of mind; he dreads the undertaking of evil, unwholesome states.
This, monks, is called the power of moral dread.
And what, monks, is the power of energy?

Here, monks, a noble disciple dwells with energy aroused for the abandoning of unwholesome states and for the acquisition of wholesome states; he is steadfast, firm in his exertion, and does not lay down the burden regarding wholesome states.
This, monks, is called the power of energy.
And what, monks, is the power of wisdom? Here, monks, a noble disciple is wise;
he is endowed with the wisdom that discerns arising and passing away, which is noble, penetrative, and leads to the complete destruction of suffering.
This, monks, is called the power of wisdom.
“Monks, these are the five powers of one in training.
Therefore, monks, you should train yourselves thus:

‘We shall be endowed with the power of faith as a power of one in training; we shall be endowed with the power of moral shame… the power of moral dread… the power of energy… the power of wisdom as a power of one in training.’”
“In this way indeed, bhikkhus, should you train yourselves.
The second [discourse]. Aṅguttara Nikāya 5.3

1. Sekhabalavagga Dukkhasutta (AN 5.3, PTS AN iii 3) “Bhikkhus, there are these five powers of one in training (*sekha*). What five? The power of faith, the power of energy, the power of mindfulness, the power of concentration, and the power of wisdom. These, bhikkhus, are the five powers of one in training. When, bhikkhus, a noble disciple possesses these five powers of one in training, he is capable of breaking through the mass of suffering. Just as, bhikkhus, when a great rain cloud has arisen, it is capable of breaking through the mass of darkness; even so, bhikkhus, when a noble disciple possesses these five powers of one in training, he is capable of breaking through the mass of suffering. When, bhikkhus, a noble disciple possesses these five powers of one in training, he is capable of realizing the fruit of stream-entry. When he possesses them, he is capable of realizing the fruit of once-returning. When he possesses them, he is capable of realizing the fruit of non-returning. When he possesses them, he is capable of realizing the fruit of arahantship. Therefore, bhikkhus, you should train yourselves thus: ‘We shall possess the power of faith, the power of energy, the power of mindfulness, the power of concentration, and the power of wisdom. Thus, bhikkhus, should you train yourselves.”

“Bhikkhus, possessed of five qualities, a bhikkhu dwells in suffering in this very life—with vexation, despair, and fever—and after the breakup of the body, after death, a bad destination is to be expected for him.
What are the five?
Here, bhikkhus, a bhikkhu is devoid of faith, shameless, unafraid of wrongdoing, lazy, and lacking wisdom.”

“Monks, a monk endowed with these five qualities dwells in suffering in this very life—with vexation, despair, and fever—and after the breakup of the body, after death, a bad destination is to be expected.

Monks, a monk endowed with five qualities dwells in happiness in this very life—without vexation, despair, or fever—and after the breakup of the body, after death, a good destination is to be expected.
Which five?”
“Here, monks, a monk is endowed with faith, he is possessed of a sense of shame, he is possessed of moral dread, he is energetic, and he is wise.

Endowed with these five qualities, monks, a monk dwells in happiness in this very life—without vexation, without despair, and without fever—and after the breakup of the body, after death, a happy destination is to be expected for him.
This is the third [sutta].
Aṅguttara Nikāya 5.4 1. Sekhabalavagga Yathābhatasutta “Bhikkhus, there are these five powers of one in training (*sekha*). What five?

The power of faith, the power of energy, the power of mindfulness, the power of concentration, and the power of wisdom. These, bhikkhus, are the five powers of one in training. When, bhikkhus, a noble disciple possesses these five powers of one in training, he is capable of breaking through the mass of suffering. Just as, bhikkhus, when a great rain cloud has gathered, it pours down rain upon a mountain peak, and that water, flowing down from the mountain peak, fills the mountain clefts, gullies, and creeks; when the mountain clefts, gullies, and creeks are filled, they fill the pools; when the pools are filled, they fill the lakes; when the lakes are filled, they fill the rivers; and when the rivers are filled, they fill the great ocean—so too, bhikkhus, when a noble disciple possesses these five powers of one in training, he is capable of breaking through the mass of suffering.”
“Bhikkhus, possessed of five qualities, a bhikkhu is deposited in hell as if carried there. Which five? [The Sutta continues with the list.]”
"Here, monks, a monk is faithless, shameless, unafraid of wrongdoing, lazy, and lacking wisdom.
Possessing these five qualities, monks, a monk is placed in hell as if carried there.
Possessing five qualities, monks, a monk is placed in heaven as if carried there."
"By which five?
Here, monks, a monk is endowed with faith, he is possessed of a sense of shame, he is possessed of moral dread, he is energetic, and he is wise.
Endowed with these five qualities, monks, a monk is placed in heaven as if carried there."
The Fourth.
Aṅguttara Nikāya 5.5 1.
Sekhabalavagga (The Chapter on the Powers of a Trainee)

The Discourse on Training (Sikkhāsutta): “Bhikkhus, whatever bhikkhu or bhikkhunī, having renounced the training, reverts to the lower life, for that person there arise in this very life five grounds for censure and reproach consistent with the Dhamma. [The Buddha then enumerates these five: 1. ‘He was able, yet he was not able. 2. ‘He was capable, yet he was not capable. 3. ‘He was competent, yet he was not competent. 4. ‘He was fit, yet he was not fit. 5. ‘He was worthy, yet he was not worthy.’”
Which five?
You had no faith indeed in wholesome states; you had no sense of shame indeed in wholesome states;
you had no dread of wrongdoing indeed in wholesome states; you had no energy indeed in wholesome states.
Indeed, you lacked wisdom regarding wholesome states.
For whatever monk or nun, bhikkhus, having renounced the training, reverts to the lower life, five legitimate grounds for censure arise for them in this very life.
For whatever monk or nun, bhikkhus, [acts] even with pain and even with mental distress...
Facing forward and weeping, he leads the perfect and pure holy life;
in this very life, five grounds for praise from his fellow practitioners come to him.
What are the five?
You indeed possessed faith in wholesome states; you indeed possessed a sense of shame in wholesome states;
you indeed possessed a sense of moral dread in wholesome states; you indeed possessed energy in wholesome states;
and you indeed possessed wisdom in wholesome states.
“Monks, whatever monk or nun, even with suffering and even with dejection,
weeping with tearful face, leads the complete and pure holy life— for such a person,
five grounds for praise according to the Dhamma arise in this very life.”
The Fifth. Aṅguttara Nikāya 5.6 1.
The Chapter on the Powers of a Trainee (Sekhabalavagga)
The Discourse on Attainment (Samāpattisutta; AN 5.6, PTS AN iii 5):
“Monks, as long as faith is not established toward wholesome states, there is no attainment of the unwholesome.”
But when faith has disappeared, bhikkhus, and lack of faith remains as an obsession,
then there is the attainment of the unwholesome.
As long as moral shame is established regarding wholesome states, bhikkhus, there is no attainment of the unwholesome.
But when, monks, moral shame has disappeared and moral shamelessness remains as an obsession,
then there is the attainment of the unwholesome.
Monks, as long as moral dread is present regarding wholesome states, there is no attainment of the unwholesome.
But when, monks, moral dread has disappeared and lack of moral dread persists as an obsession,
then there is the attainment of the unwholesome.
Monks, as long as energy is established in regard to wholesome states, there is no attainment of the unwholesome.
But when, monks, energy has disappeared and laziness persists as an obsession,
then there is the attainment of the unwholesome.
As long as wisdom is established regarding wholesome states, monks, there is no attainment of the unwholesome.
"But when wisdom has disappeared, bhikkhus, and unwise obsession persists,
then there is the attainment of the unwholesome.
Thus ends the sixth [sutta].
Aṅguttara Nikāya 5.7 1.

Sekhabalavagga Kāmasutta “Bhikkhus, there are these five powers of one in training. What five? The power of faith, the power of energy, the power of mindfulness, the power of concentration, and the power of wisdom. These, bhikkhus, are the five powers of one in training.”
“Bhikkhus, for the most part, beings dally in sensual pleasures.

When a clansman has abandoned the life of a householder and gone forth from the home into homelessness, it is sufficient to say of him: ‘This clansman has gone forth out of faith. (AN 5.7, PTS AN iii 5)
For what reason?
Because, monks, it is possible to obtain sensual pleasures through youth—whether they be of such a kind or that kind.
And whatever sensual pleasures there are, whether low, middling, or refined, all sensual pleasures are reckoned simply as "sensual pleasures."
“Bhikkhus, suppose a young, tender infant lying on its back were to put a stick or a pebble in its mouth because of the negligence of its nurse.
The nurse would very quickly pay attention to this;
having very quickly paid attention, she would very quickly remove it.
If he were unable to bring it out quickly, he would grasp the head with his left hand and, making a hook with his right hand, pull it out even if it were bloody.
Why is that? "Because, monks, this would cause pain to the boy."
"I say that it is not impossible.
However, monks, this is what ought to be done by a nurse who desires his welfare, seeks his benefit, and is compassionate, out of compassion for him.
But when that boy has grown up and is capable of understanding, monks, the nurse no longer has any concern for that boy."
‘Now that the prince is self-guarded,
he is no longer capable of negligence. In the same way, monks, as long as a bhikkhu has not yet established faith in wholesome qualities,
has not established a sense of shame in wholesome qualities, has not established moral dread in wholesome qualities, and has not established energy in wholesome qualities...
If, monks, wholesome qualities have not been performed by a bhikkhu, and wholesome qualities have not been performed by him through wisdom,
then that bhikkhu must still be protected by me. But when, monks,
wholesome qualities have been performed by a bhikkhu through faith, and wholesome qualities have been performed through a sense of shame...
There is shame regarding wholesome states; there is moral dread regarding wholesome states;
there is energy applied toward wholesome states; there is wisdom regarding wholesome states.
Monks, I am indifferent toward that monk when he gives a gift.
“Now, a bhikkhu who guards himself is not subject to negligence.
Thus [ends] the seventh [sutta]. Aṅguttara Nikāya 5.8.

1. Sekhabalavagga Cavana Sutta (The Discourse on Passing Away) “Bhikkhus, there are these five powers of one in training (*sekha*). What five? The power of faith, the power of energy, the power of mindfulness, the power of concentration, and the power of wisdom. These, bhikkhus, are the five powers of one in training. When, bhikkhus, a noble disciple possesses these five powers of one in training, it is impossible for him to fall away from the fruit of stream-entry, or from the fruit of once-returning, or from the fruit of non-returning, or from the fruit of arahantship. It is impossible that he would pass away without having realized the fruit of arahantship. Just as, bhikkhus, when a tree possesses five kinds of strength—strength of roots, strength of trunk, strength of heartwood, strength of branches, and strength of leaves—it is impossible for it to fall over, or to be blown over by the wind, or to be uprooted; it is impossible that it would not stand firm: even so, bhikkhus, when a noble disciple possesses these five powers of one in training, it is impossible for him to fall away from the fruit of stream-entry, or from the fruit of once-returning, or from the fruit of non-returning, or from the fruit of arahantship. It is impossible that he would pass away without having realized the fruit of arahantship.”
“Bhikkhus, possessed of five qualities, a bhikkhu falls away and does not become established in the true Dhamma.
Which five?
A bhikkhu who lacks faith falls away and does not become established in the true Dhamma.”
“Bhikkhus, a bhikkhu who lacks moral shame falls away and does not become established in the true Dhamma.
A bhikkhu who lacks moral dread falls away and does not become established in the true Dhamma.
A bhikkhu who is lazy falls away and does not become established in the true Dhamma.”
“Bhikkhus, a bhikkhu who lacks wisdom falls away and does not become established in the true Dhamma.
Possessing these five qualities, bhikkhus, a bhikkhu falls away and does not become established in the true Dhamma.
Possessing five other qualities, bhikkhus, a bhikkhu does not fall away and becomes established in the true Dhamma.”
By which five?
A bhikkhu who is endowed with faith, monks, does not fall away; he is established in the true Dhamma.
A bhikkhu who possesses a sense of shame, monks, does not fall away; he is established in the true Dhamma.
“Bhikkhus, a bhikkhu who possesses moral dread does not fall away; he is established in the true Dhamma.
Bhikkhus, a bhikkhu who has aroused energy does not fall away; he is established in the true Dhamma.
Bhikkhus, a bhikkhu who possesses wisdom does not fall away; he is established in the true Dhamma.”
“Bhikkhus, a bhikkhu endowed with these five qualities does not fall away; he is established in the true Dhamma.
Thus was the eighth [sutta]. Aṅguttara Nikāya 5.9
1. The Chapter on the Powers of a Trainee First Discourse on Lack of Respect (AN 5.9, PTS AN iii 7)
“Bhikkhus, possessing five qualities, a bhikkhu who is disrespectful and undeferential falls away and does not become established in the true Dhamma.
What are the five?
Bhikkhus, a bhikkhu who lacks faith, being disrespectful and undeferential, falls away and does not become established in the true Dhamma.”
“Bhikkhus, a bhikkhu who lacks moral shame, being disrespectful and lacking deference, falls away and does not become established in the true Dhamma.
Bhikkhus, a bhikkhu who lacks moral dread, being disrespectful and lacking deference, falls away and does not become established in the true Dhamma.
Bhikkhus, a bhikkhu who is lazy, being disrespectful and lacking deference, falls away and does not become established in the true Dhamma.”
“Bhikkhus, a bhikkhu who is lacking wisdom, disrespectful, and undeferential falls away and does not become established in the true Dhamma.
Possessing these five qualities, bhikkhus, a bhikkhu who is disrespectful and undeferential falls away and does not become established in the true Dhamma.
Possessing five other qualities, bhikkhus, a bhikkhu who is respectful and deferential does not fall away and becomes established in the true Dhamma.”
By which five?
A bhikkhu who is endowed with faith, O bhikkhus, being respectful and deferential, does not fall away but is established in the True Dhamma.
A bhikkhu who possesses a sense of shame, O bhikkhus, being respectful and deferential, does not fall away but is established in the True Dhamma.
“Bhikkhus, a bhikkhu who possesses moral dread, who is respectful and deferential, does not fall away but is established in the true Dhamma.
Bhikkhus, a bhikkhu who has aroused energy, who is respectful and deferential, does not fall away but is established in the true Dhamma.
Bhikkhus, a bhikkhu who possesses wisdom, who is respectful and deferential, does not fall away but is established in the true Dhamma.”
“Bhikkhus, a bhikkhu who possesses these five qualities—being respectful and deferential—does not fall away but is established in the true Dhamma.
Thus was the ninth [discourse]. Aṅguttara Nikāya 5.10
1. The Chapter on the Powers of a Trainee The Second Discourse on Lack of Reverence (AN 5.10, PTS AN iii 8)
“Bhikkhus, a bhikkhu who possesses five qualities—being disrespectful and lacking deference—is incapable of attaining growth, increase, and maturity in this Dhamma and Discipline.
What are the five?
Bhikkhus, a bhikkhu who lacks faith, being disrespectful and lacking deference, is incapable of attaining growth, increase, and maturity in this Dhamma and Discipline.”
“Bhikkhus, a bhikkhu who lacks moral shame, who is disrespectful and lacking in deference, is incapable of attaining growth, increase, and fulfillment in this Dhamma and Discipline.
Bhikkhus, a bhikkhu who lacks moral dread, who is disrespectful and lacking in deference, is incapable of attaining growth, increase, and fulfillment in this Dhamma and Discipline.
Bhikkhus, a bhikkhu who is lazy, who is disrespectful and lacking in deference, is incapable of attaining growth, increase, and fulfillment in this Dhamma and Discipline.”
“Monks, a monk who is lacking wisdom, disrespectful, and lacking deference is incapable of attaining growth, increase, and maturity in this Dhamma and Discipline.
Monks, a monk endowed with these five qualities—being disrespectful and lacking deference—is incapable of attaining growth, increase, and maturity in this Dhamma and Discipline.
Monks, a monk endowed with five qualities—possessing respect and deference—is capable of attaining growth, increase, and maturity in this Dhamma and Discipline.”
By which five?
A bhikkhu who is endowed with faith, bhikkhus, being respectful and deferential, is capable of attaining growth, increase, and fulfillment in this Dhamma and Vinaya.
A bhikkhu who possesses a sense of shame, bhikkhus... [and] a bhikkhu who possesses moral dread, bhikkhus... [and] a bhikkhu who has aroused energy, bhikkhus...
“A bhikkhu who is wise, bhikkhus, being respectful and deferential, is capable of attaining growth, increase, and fulfillment in this Dhamma and Vinaya.
Possessing these five qualities, bhikkhus, a bhikkhu who is respectful and deferential is capable of attaining growth, increase, and fulfillment in this Dhamma and Vinaya.”
The tenth.
The first section, on the Powers of the Trainee.
Its summary:
The concise, the detailed, suffering,
supported by training as the fifth;
attainment and [attachment] to sensual pleasures.
"Two types of passing away are without fear.
— Aṅguttara Nikāya 5.11, Chapter 2: Powers (Balavagga)
The Discourse on What Has Not Been Heard (Ananussutasutta): “Bhikkhus,
I claim to have reached the perfection of direct knowledge regarding things unheard before.”
“Bhikkhus, there are these five powers of a Tathāgata, possessed of which the Tathāgata claims his place as the leader, roars his lion’s roar in the assemblies, and sets in motion the Brahma-wheel.
What are the five?
The power of faith, the power of moral shame, the power of moral dread, the power of energy, and the power of wisdom.”
“Monks, these are the five powers of a Tathāgata, endowed with which the Tathāgata claims his place as a leader, roars his lion’s roar in the assemblies, and sets in motion the Brahma-wheel.
Thus was the first [discourse]. Aṅguttara Nikāya 5.12

2. Balavagga Kūṭasutta (AN 5.12, PTS AN iii 10) “Monks, there are these four kinds of persons found existing in the world. What four? The person who is like a peak, the person who is like a slope, the person who is like a plateau, and the person who is like a mountain crag. And how, monks, is a person like a peak? Here, monks, a certain person is reborn in a high family—whether a family of Khattiyas, Brahmins, or householders—one that is rich, with great wealth and property, with abundant gold and silver, abundant treasures and commodities, abundant wealth and grain. He is handsome, attractive, graceful, possessing supreme beauty of complexion; he is well-born on both his maternal and paternal sides, of pure descent back through seven generations, unblemished and impeccable in respect of birth. He acquires wealth by means of violence and oppression, and having acquired it, he enjoys it himself and gives it away, and performs no meritorious deeds. This, monks, is called a person who is like a peak. And how, monks, is a person like a slope? Here, monks, a certain person is reborn in a high family... [as above] ...of pure descent... He acquires wealth not by means of violence and oppression, but by means of right effort, and having acquired it, he enjoys it himself and gives it away, and performs meritorious deeds. This, monks, is called a person who is like a slope. And how, monks, is a person like a plateau? Here, monks, a certain person is reborn in a high family... [as above] ...of pure descent... He acquires wealth not by means of violence and oppression, nor by means of right effort, but rather by means of inheritance, and having acquired it, he enjoys it himself and gives it away, and performs meritorious deeds. This, monks, is called a person who is like a plateau. And how, monks, is a person like a mountain crag? Here, monks, a certain person is reborn in a low family—whether a family of beggars, outcastes, wicker-workers, or bamboo-workers—one that is poor, with little wealth and property, lacking in food and clothing. He is ugly, unattractive, ill-favored, possessing an inferior complexion; he is ill-born on both his maternal and paternal sides, of impure descent back through seven generations, blemished and not impeccable in respect of birth. He acquires wealth not by means of violence and oppression, nor by means of right effort, nor by means of inheritance, but rather through some craft or trade, and having acquired it, he enjoys it himself and gives it away, and performs meritorious deeds. This, monks, is called a person who is like a mountain crag. These, monks, are the four kinds of persons found existing in the world.”
“Bhikkhus, there are these five powers of one in training.
Which five?
The power of faith, the power of moral shame, the power of moral dread, the power of energy, and the power of wisdom.”
“Monks, these are the five powers of one in training.
Of these five powers of one in training, monks, this is the foremost, this is the cohesive, this is the unifying factor: namely, the power of wisdom.
Just as, monks, for a gabled house, the roof-peak is the foremost, the cohesive, and the unifying factor.”
"In the same way, monks, among these five powers of a trainee, this is the foremost, this is the cohesive, this is that which binds them together: namely, the power of wisdom.
Therefore, monks, you should train yourselves thus:

‘We shall be endowed with the power of faith as a power of a trainee; we shall be endowed with the power of moral shame … the power of moral dread … the power of energy … the power of wisdom as a power of a trainee.’"
“In this way, monks, you should train yourselves.
The second [sutta].
Aṅguttara Nikāya 5.13

2. Balavagga Saṅkhittasutta (AN 5.13, PTS AN iii 10) "Bhikkhus, when a bhikkhu is possessed of five qualities, he is capable of quickly understanding the Dhamma in brief. What five? Here, a bhikkhu is possessed of faith, possessed of virtuous behavior, possessed of learning, possessed of energy, and possessed of wisdom. When a bhikkhu is possessed of these five qualities, he is capable of quickly understanding the Dhamma in brief."
“Bhikkhus, there are these five powers. What five?
The power of faith, the power of energy, the power of mindfulness, the power of concentration, and the power of wisdom.”
“These, monks, are the five powers.
The third [discourse]. Aṅguttara Nikāya 5.14

2. Balavagga Vitthatasutta (AN 5.14, PTS AN iii 10) “Monks, there are these four powers. What four? The power of wisdom, the power of energy, the power of concentration, and the power of virtue. These, monks, are the four powers. “Monks, for one who possesses these four powers, four fruits and four benefits may be expected. What four? For one possessing the power of wisdom, the fruit and benefit of abandoning unwholesome states and cultivating wholesome states may be expected; for one possessing the power of energy, the fruit and benefit of not falling away from wholesome states once they have arisen may be expected; for one possessing the power of concentration, the fruit and benefit of attaining the cessation of the mental fermentations once they have arisen may be expected; and for one possessing the power of virtue, the fruit and benefit of being dear, beloved, and esteemed by noble ones may be expected. Monks, for one who possesses these four powers, these four fruits and four benefits may be expected. “Monks, there are these four powers. What four? The power of wisdom, the power of energy, the power of concentration, and the power of virtue. And what, monks, is the power of wisdom? Here, monks, a noble disciple possesses wisdom that is noble, penetrative, leading to the complete destruction of suffering; he discerns as it really is: ‘This is suffering’; he discerns as it really is: ‘This is the origin of suffering’; he discerns as it really is: ‘This is the cessation of suffering’; he discerns as it really is: ‘This is the way leading to the cessation of suffering. This, monks, is called the power of wisdom. And what, monks, is the power of energy? Here, monks, a noble disciple dwells with energy aroused for the abandoning of unwholesome states and the cultivation of wholesome states; he is steadfast, firm in effort, not relinquishing his duty regarding wholesome states. This, monks, is called the power of energy. And what, monks, is the power of concentration? Here, monks, a noble disciple, withdrawn from sensual pleasures, withdrawn from unwholesome states, enters and dwells in the first jhāna, which is accompanied by thought and examination, with rapture and happiness born of seclusion; with the subsiding of thought and examination, he enters and dwells in the second jhāna, which has internal composure and mental unification, is free from thought and examination, and has rapture and happiness born of concentration; with the fading away of rapture, he dwells equanimous, mindful, and clearly comprehending, experiencing happiness with the body; he enters and dwells in the third jhāna, of which the noble ones declare: ‘He is equanimous, mindful, and dwelling happily’; with the abandoning of pleasure and pain, and with the previous disappearance of joy and grief, he enters and dwells in the fourth jhāna, which is beyond pleasure and pain, and has purity of mindfulness due to equanimity. This, monks, is called the power of concentration. And what, monks, is the power of virtue? Here, monks, a noble disciple is possessed of virtue; he dwells restrained by the restraint of the Pātimokkha, perfect in conduct and resort, seeing danger in the slightest faults; having undertaken the training rules, he trains in them. This, monks, is called the power of virtue. These, monks, are the four powers.”
“Monks, there are these five powers.
What are the five?
The power of faith, the power of energy, the power of mindfulness, the power of concentration, and the power of wisdom.”
And what, monks, is the power of faith?
Here, monks, a noble disciple is endowed with faith; he has faith in the enlightenment of the Tathāgata:

“Thus indeed is that Blessed One: an arahant, perfectly enlightened, accomplished in true knowledge and conduct, sublime, knower of the worlds, unsurpassed leader of persons to be tamed, teacher of gods and humans, the Buddha, the Blessed One.”
This, monks, is called the power of faith.
And what, monks, is the power of energy?

Here, monks, a noble disciple dwells with energy aroused for the abandoning of unwholesome states and for the acquisition of wholesome states; he is steadfast, firm in effort, and does not relinquish his burden regarding wholesome states.
This, monks, is called the power of energy.
And what, monks, is the power of mindfulness?
Here, monks, a noble disciple is mindful, endowed with supreme mindfulness and circumspection; he remembers and recollects even what was done long ago and spoken long ago.
This, monks, is called the power of mindfulness.
And what, monks, is the power of concentration?

Here, monks, a noble disciple, quite secluded from sensual pleasures, secluded from unwholesome states, enters and dwells in the first jhāna, which is accompanied by applied and sustained thought, and possesses the rapture and happiness born of seclusion.

With the subsiding of applied and sustained thought, he enters and dwells in the second jhāna, which has internal tranquility and singleness of mind, is free from applied and sustained thought, and possesses rapture and happiness born of concentration.
And with the fading away of rapture, he dwells in equanimity, mindful and clearly comprehending, experiencing happiness with the body;
he enters and dwells in the third jhāna, of which the Noble Ones declare: "He dwells happily, mindful and in equanimity."

With the abandoning of pleasure and the abandoning of pain, and with the previous disappearance of joy and grief, he enters and dwells in the fourth jhāna, which is neither-painful-nor-pleasant and possesses purity of mindfulness through equanimity.
This, monks, is called the power of concentration.
And what, monks, is the power of wisdom?
“Here, monks, a noble disciple is wise; he possesses the wisdom that discerns arising and passing away, which is noble, penetrative, and leads to the complete destruction of suffering.
This, monks, is called the power of wisdom.
These, monks, are the five powers.”
The Fourth.
Aṅguttara Nikāya 5.15 2. Balavagga (The Chapter on Powers)
Daṭṭhabbasutta: “Bhikkhus,
there are these five powers.”
Which five?
The power of faith, the power of energy, the power of mindfulness, the power of concentration, and the power of wisdom.
And where, monks, is the power of faith to be seen?
In the four factors of stream-entry.
Herein, the power of faith is to be seen.
And where, monks, is the power of energy to be seen?
In the four right endeavors.
Herein, the power of energy is to be seen.
And where, monks, is the power of mindfulness to be seen?
In the four foundations of mindfulness.
Herein, the power of mindfulness is to be seen.
And where, monks, is the power of concentration to be seen?
In the four jhānas.
Herein, the power of concentration is to be seen.
And where, monks, is the power of wisdom to be seen?
"In the four noble truths.
Herein, the power of wisdom is to be seen.
These, monks, are the five powers."
Fifth. Aṅguttara Nikāya 5.16 2.
Balavagga (The Chapter on Powers)
The Discourse on the Heap of Punas (Punakūṭasutta):
“Monks, there are these five powers.”
Which five? The power of faith, the power of energy, the power of mindfulness, the power of concentration,
and the power of wisdom— these, monks, are the five powers.
“Monks, among these five powers, this is the foremost, the unifying factor, and the cohesive element: namely, the power of wisdom (*paññābala*).

Just as, monks, for a gabled house, the roof-peak is the foremost, the unifying factor, and the cohesive element, even so, monks, among these five powers, this is the foremost, the unifying factor, and the cohesive element: namely, the power of wisdom.”
The Sixth. Aṅguttara Nikāya 5.17 2.
Balavagga (The Chapter on Powers)
The Discourse on One’s Own Welfare (Paṭhamahitasutta).
“Bhikkhus, possessed of five qualities, a bhikkhu is practicing for his own welfare, but not for the welfare of others.
Which five?
Here, monks, a monk is himself accomplished in virtue, but does not encourage others in the accomplishment of virtue;
he is himself accomplished in concentration, but does not encourage others in the accomplishment of concentration.
He himself is endowed with wisdom, but does not encourage others in the attainment of wisdom;
he himself is endowed with liberation, but does not encourage others in the attainment of liberation;
he himself is endowed with the knowledge and vision of liberation, but does not encourage others in the attainment of the knowledge and vision of liberation.
“Bhikkhus, a bhikkhu endowed with these five factors is practicing for his own welfare, but not for the welfare of others.
The seventh. *Aṅguttara Nikāya* 5.18

2. Balavagga The Second Discourse on What is Beneficial (Dutiyahitasutta) “Monks, there are these four things that are beneficial, helpful, and conducive to welfare. What four? Association with superior persons is beneficial, helpful, and conducive to welfare. Hearing the true Dhamma is beneficial, helpful, and conducive to welfare. Careful attention to the true Dhamma is beneficial, helpful, and conducive to welfare. Practice in accordance with the true Dhamma is beneficial, helpful, and conducive to welfare. These, monks, are the four things that are beneficial, helpful, and conducive to welfare.”
“Bhikkhus, possessing five qualities, a bhikkhu is practicing for the benefit of others, not for his own benefit.
What are the five?
Here, bhikkhus, a bhikkhu is himself not accomplished in virtue, yet he encourages others in the accomplishment of virtue.
One is not oneself accomplished in concentration, yet one encourages others in the accomplishment of concentration;
one is not oneself accomplished in wisdom, yet one encourages others in the accomplishment of wisdom;
one is not oneself accomplished in liberation, yet one encourages others in the accomplishment of liberation.
“He himself is not possessed of the knowledge and vision of liberation, yet he encourages others in the attainment of the knowledge and vision of liberation.
Possessed of these five qualities, monks, a bhikkhu practices for the benefit of others, but not for his own benefit.
The eighth.

Aṅguttara Nikāya 5.19 Chapter 2: On Powers (Balavagga) Discourse on the Third Kind of Beneficial Advice (Tatiyahitasutta) “Monks, there are these five powers. What five? The power of faith, the power of energy, the power of mindfulness, the power of concentration, and the power of wisdom.

These, monks, are the five powers. “Monks, there are these five powers. What five? The power of faith, the power of energy, the power of mindfulness, the power of concentration, and the power of wisdom. And what, monks, is the power of faith? Here, monks, a noble disciple possesses faith; he places faith in the enlightenment of the Tathāgata thus: ‘The Blessed One is an arahant, perfectly enlightened, accomplished in true knowledge and conduct, fortunate, knower of the world, unsurpassed leader of persons to be tamed, teacher of devas and humans, the Buddha, the Blessed One. This, monks, is called the power of faith. And what, monks, is the power of energy? Here, monks, a noble disciple dwells with energy aroused for the abandoning of unwholesome states and the acquisition of wholesome states; he is steadfast, firm in exertion, not shirking the burden of wholesome qualities. This, monks, is called the power of energy. And what, monks, is the power of mindfulness? Here, monks, a noble disciple possesses mindfulness and clear comprehension; he remembers and recollects what was done and said long ago. This, monks, is called the power of mindfulness. And what, monks, is the power of concentration? Here, monks, a noble disciple, having secluded himself from sensual pleasures, secluded himself from unwholesome states, enters and dwells in the first jhāna, which is accompanied by thought and examination, with rapture and happiness born of seclusion. With the subsiding of thought and examination, he enters and dwells in the second jhāna, which has internal composure and mental unification, is free from thought and examination, and has rapture and happiness born of concentration. With the fading away of rapture, he dwells equanimous, mindful, and clearly comprehending, and experiences happiness with the body; he enters and dwells in the third jhāna, of which the noble ones declare: ‘He is equanimous, mindful, and dwells happily. With the abandoning of pleasure and pain, and with the previous disappearance of joy and grief, he enters and dwells in the fourth jhāna, which is neither painful nor pleasant and includes the purification of mindfulness through equanimity. This, monks, is called the power of concentration. And what, monks, is the power of wisdom? Here, monks, a noble disciple possesses wisdom; he is endowed with wisdom regarding arising and passing away, which is noble and penetrative, leading to the complete destruction of suffering. This, monks, is called the power of wisdom. These, monks, are the five powers.”
“Bhikkhus, possessing five qualities, a bhikkhu is practicing neither for his own benefit nor for the benefit of others.
Which five? [Text follows]”
In this case, monks, a monk is himself not accomplished in virtue, nor does he encourage others in the accomplishment of virtue;
he is himself not accomplished in concentration, nor does he encourage others in the accomplishment of concentration;
he is himself not accomplished in wisdom, nor does he encourage others in the accomplishment of wisdom.
“He himself is not accomplished in liberation, nor does he encourage others in the accomplishment of liberation;
he himself is not accomplished in the knowledge and vision of liberation, nor does he encourage others in the accomplishment of the knowledge and vision of liberation.
Possessing these five qualities, monks, a monk is practicing neither for his own benefit nor for the benefit of others.”
The Ninth. Aṅguttara Nikāya 5.20 2.
The Chapter on Powers (Balavagga)
The Fourth Discourse on Benefit (Catutthahitasutta).
“Bhikkhus, endowed with five qualities, a bhikkhu is practicing for his own benefit and for the benefit of others.”
By which five?
Here, monks, a monk is himself accomplished in virtue and encourages others in the accomplishment of virtue;
he is himself accomplished in concentration and encourages others in the accomplishment of concentration; he is himself accomplished in wisdom and encourages others in the accomplishment of wisdom.
“He himself is accomplished in liberation, and he encourages others in the accomplishment of liberation;
he himself is accomplished in the knowledge and vision of liberation, and he encourages others in the accomplishment of the knowledge and vision of liberation.
Possessing these five qualities, monks, a bhikkhu is practicing for his own welfare and for the welfare of others.”
The tenth.
The second chapter on strength.
Its summary verse:
The peak of what has not been heard,
the concise and the detailed,
and again the peak that is to be seen.
"And the four with benefit.
Aṅguttara Nikāya 5.21, Chapter 3: The Section on Fivefold Groups.
Paṭhamaagāravasutta:

“Bhikkhus, it is simply not possible that a bhikkhu who is disrespectful, lacking in deference, and of undisciplined conduct will fulfill the Dhamma of proper behavior toward his fellow practitioners in the holy life.”
"It is impossible that one who has not fulfilled the Dhamma of proper conduct will fulfill the Dhamma of a trainee.
It is impossible that one who has not fulfilled the Dhamma of a trainee will fulfill the precepts.
It is impossible that one who has not fulfilled the precepts will fulfill right view."
"It is impossible that one who has not fulfilled right view will fulfill right concentration—such a case does not exist.

But, monks, it is possible that a monk who is respectful, deferential, and conducts himself in accordance with his fellows will fulfill the Dhamma of proper conduct toward his companions in the holy life.
It is possible that, having fulfilled the Dhamma of proper conduct, he will fulfill the Dhamma of a trainee."
"It is possible that, having fulfilled the state of training, one will fulfill virtuous conduct.
It is possible that, having fulfilled virtuous conduct, one will fulfill right view.
It is possible that, having fulfilled right view, one will fulfill right concentration."
First.
Aṅguttara Nikāya 5.22 3.
Pañcaṅgika-vagga (The Chapter on the Five-Fold)
The Second Discourse on Respect (Dutiya-āgaravasutta):

“Bhikkhus, it is simply not possible that a bhikkhu who lacks respect, lacks deference, and does not live in accordance with his companions in the holy life will fulfill the Dhamma of proper conduct toward his fellow practitioners. This is impossible.”
‘Without fulfilling the Dhamma of proper conduct, one will fulfill the Dhamma of a trainee’—this is impossible.
‘Without fulfilling the Dhamma of a trainee, one will fulfill the aggregate of virtue’—this is impossible.
‘Without fulfilling the aggregate of virtue, one will fulfill the aggregate of concentration’—this is impossible.
"It is impossible that one who has not fulfilled the aggregate of concentration will fulfill the aggregate of wisdom;

such a thing cannot occur. But, monks, it is possible that a monk who is respectful, deferential, and conducts himself in accordance with his peers will fulfill the quality of right conduct toward his fellow celibates.
It is possible that, having fulfilled the quality of right conduct, he will fulfill the quality of a trainee."
"It is possible that, having fulfilled the state of a trainee, he will fulfill the aggregate of virtue.
It is possible that, having fulfilled the aggregate of virtue, he will fulfill the aggregate of concentration.
It is possible that, having fulfilled the aggregate of concentration, he will fulfill the aggregate of wisdom."
The Second [Discourse]. Aṅguttara Nikāya 5.23 3.
Pañcaṅgika-vagga (The Chapter on the Five Factors)
Upakkilesasutta (AN 5.23,
PTS AN iii 16): “Bhikkhus,
there are these five impurities of gold, by which impurities being defiled, gold is neither soft nor workable nor radiant, but brittle and not fit for work.
Which five? Tin, copper, brass, lead, and silver—
these, monks, are the five impurities of gold, by which it is defiled.
“Gold, monks, is neither soft, nor workable, nor radiant; it is brittle and does not properly serve its purpose.
But when gold, monks, is freed from these five impurities, that gold becomes soft, workable, and radiant, and being no longer brittle, it properly serves its purpose.”
Whatever kind of ornament one desires—whether a ring, an earring, a neck-ornament, or a golden garland—one achieves that purpose.
In the same way, monks, there are these five defilements of the mind;
when the mind is defiled by these defilements, it is neither pliant nor wieldy, nor is it luminous and malleable, and it does not rightly [concentrate].
One becomes concentrated for the destruction of the taints.
Which five?
Sensual desire, ill will, sloth and torpor, restlessness and remorse, and doubt.
“Monks, these five are the defilements of the mind.
When the mind is defiled by these defilements, it is neither pliant nor wieldy, nor is it luminous and stable; it does not rightly concentrate for the destruction of the taints.
But when, monks, the mind is freed from these five defilements, that mind becomes pliant, wieldy, and luminous, and being stable, it rightly concentrates for the destruction of the taints.”

Whatever state realizable by direct knowledge his mind inclines toward for the sake of realizing through direct knowledge, he attains the capability of being a witness therein, in each and every case where there is a suitable basis.
If he so desires: "May I exercise the various kinds of psychic power—being one, may I become many;
being many, may I become one; may I appear and vanish; may I pass through walls, fences, and mountains as if through space;"
I could go unhindered as if through space; I could dive in and out of the earth as if it were water;
I could walk on water without breaking the surface as if on earth; I could travel cross-legged through the air like a winged bird;
and I could even touch these sun and moon, so powerful and majestic, with my hand.

‘I would touch and stroke it with my hand, and I would wield power with my body even as far as the Brahma-world,’ he attains the capacity to realize this, in each and every instance where there is a suitable basis.

If he should wish: ‘With the divine ear-element, purified and surpassing that of humans, may I hear both kinds of sounds—the divine and the human, whether far or near’—he attains the capacity to realize this, in each and every instance where there is a suitable basis.”
In each and every instance, he attains the capacity for direct realization whenever there is a suitable occasion.
If he so desires: "May I, by encompassing the minds of other beings and other persons with my own mind, understand a mind affected by lust as a mind affected by lust," he understands it thus.
One should know a mind free from lust as a mind free from lust;
one should know a mind with hatred as a mind with hatred;
or one should know a mind free from hatred as a mind free from hatred.
One should know a mind with delusion as "a mind with delusion," one should know a mind free from delusion as "a mind free from delusion," and one should know a contracted mind as "a contracted mind."
One should know a distracted mind as "a distracted mind";
one should know an exalted mind as "an exalted mind";
and one should know a non-exalted mind as "a non-exalted mind."
One should understand a surpassable mind as a surpassable mind;
one should understand an unsurpassable mind as an unsurpassable mind;
one should understand a concentrated mind as a concentrated mind.
‘May I know an unconcentrated mind as an unconcentrated mind;
may I know a liberated mind as a liberated mind;
may I know an unliberated mind as an unliberated mind.’”
In each and every case, he attains the state of being capable of realization whenever there is a suitable basis.
If he so desires: "May I recollect my manifold past lives, that is to say, one birth, two births, three births, four births, five births, ten births, twenty births..."
"Thirty births, forty births, fifty births, a hundred births, a thousand births, a hundred thousand births;
many aeons of world-contraction, many aeons of world-expansion, many aeons of both world-contraction and expansion:
'There I was, with such a name, such a clan, such an appearance, such food, such experience of pleasure and pain, and such a limit to my lifespan.'"
‘Having passed away from there, I arose there; there I was with such a name, such a clan, such an appearance, such food, such an experience of pleasure and pain, and such a limit to my lifespan;
having passed away from there, I have reappeared here’—thus would he recollect his manifold past lives in their modes and details.’
In each and every case, he attains the state of being capable of realization whenever there is a suitable occasion.

If he so desires: "May I, with the divine eye, purified and surpassing that of humans, see beings passing away and being reborn—lowly and exalted, beautiful and ugly, fortunate and unfortunate, according to their kamma"—he can do so.
May I understand beings thus: "These worthy beings, indeed, were possessed of misconduct in body, possessed of misconduct in speech, possessed of misconduct in mind;
they were revilers of the noble ones, held wrong views, and undertook actions based on wrong views.
With the breakup of the body, after death, they have reappeared in a state of deprivation, a bad destination, a lower realm, even in hell. Or these...
But these worthy beings, who were endowed with good conduct of body, good conduct of speech, and good conduct of mind,
who did not revile the noble ones, who held right view, and undertook actions based on right view— these, with the breakup of the body, after death,
have been reborn in a happy destination, in a heavenly world; thus [he sees] with the purified divine eye.
‘May I, with the divine eye, purified and surpassing that of humans, see beings passing away and being reborn— inferior and superior, beautiful and ugly,
fortunate and unfortunate— and may I understand how beings fare according to their kamma,’ in each and every case,
he attains the capability of realization whenever there is a suitable occasion.

Thus, if he should wish: “May I, through the destruction of the taints, dwell in this very life having realized for myself with direct knowledge the taintless liberation of mind and liberation by wisdom, and having attained it,” he attains the capability of being a witness in each and every case, in whatever sphere there may be.
This is the third.

Aṅguttara Nikāya 5.24 3. Pañcaṅgika-vagga Dussīla-sutta (The Immoral One) "Bhikkhus, there are these five qualities of an immoral person. What five? He destroys his own welfare; he destroys the welfare of others; he destroys the welfare of both; he incurs a bad reputation; at the dissolution of the body, after death, he is reborn in a state of misery, a bad destination, a state of ruin, or in hell. These, bhikkhus, are the five qualities of an immoral person. Bhikkhus, there are these five qualities of a virtuous person. What five? He promotes his own welfare; he promotes the welfare of others; he promotes the welfare of both; he acquires a good reputation; at the dissolution of the body, after death, he is reborn in a happy destination, in a heavenly world. These, bhikkhus, are the five qualities of a virtuous person."
“Monks, for one who is immoral,
for one deficient in virtue, right concentration lacks its proximate cause. When right concentration is absent,
for one deficient in right concentration, the knowledge and vision of things as they truly are lacks its proximate cause.”

When there is no knowledge and vision of things as they really are, for one who has failed in knowledge and vision of things as they really are, the proximate cause for disenchantment and dispassion is destroyed.
When there is no disenchantment and dispassion, for one who has failed in disenchantment and dispassion, the proximate cause for the knowledge and vision of liberation is destroyed.
It is just as if, monks, a tree were deprived of its branches and foliage.
Its outer bark does not reach full development, its inner bark does not reach full development, its softwood does not reach full development, and its heartwood does not reach full development.
In the same way, monks, for one who is immoral and deficient in virtue, right concentration lacks its proximate cause.
When there is no right concentration, for one who is deficient in right concentration, the knowledge and vision of things as they truly are lacks its proximate cause.

When there is no knowledge and vision of things as they really are, for one who has failed in knowledge and vision of things as they really are, the proximate cause for disenchantment and dispassion is destroyed.
When there is no disenchantment and dispassion, for one who has failed in disenchantment and dispassion, the proximate cause for the knowledge and vision of liberation is destroyed.
Monks, for one who is virtuous and endowed with virtue, right concentration is endowed with its proximate cause.
When right concentration exists, for one endowed with right concentration, the knowledge and vision of things as they really are is possessed of its proximate cause.

When the knowledge and vision of things as they really are exists, for one endowed with the knowledge and vision of things as they really are, disenchantment and dispassion are possessed of their proximate cause.
When disenchantment and dispassion exist, for one endowed with disenchantment and dispassion, the knowledge and vision of liberation is possessed of its proximate cause.

“Just as, monks, when a tree is possessed of branches and foliage, its bark reaches full development, its inner bark reaches full development, its softwood reaches full development, and its heartwood reaches full development;
even so, monks, for one who is virtuous and perfected in virtue, right concentration has its supporting conditions fulfilled.
When there is right concentration, for one perfected in right concentration, the knowledge and vision of things as they truly are has its supporting conditions fulfilled.”

"When there is knowledge and vision of things as they really are, for one endowed with knowledge and vision of things as they really are, disenchantment and dispassion are fully supported by that condition.
When there is disenchantment and dispassion, for one endowed with disenchantment and dispassion, the knowledge and vision of liberation is fully supported by that condition.
This is the fourth.

Aṅguttara Nikāya 5.25 3. Pañcaṅgika-vagga Anuggahita-sutta (The Supported) "Bhikkhus, when five factors are supported by five other factors, they lead to great fruit and great benefit. What five? When faith is supported by wisdom, it leads to great fruit and great benefit. When wisdom is supported by faith, it leads to great fruit and great benefit. When energy is supported by concentration, it leads to great fruit and great benefit. When concentration is supported by energy, it leads to great fruit and great benefit. When mindfulness is supported by equanimity, it leads to great fruit and great benefit. When equanimity is supported by mindfulness, it leads to great fruit and great benefit. Bhikkhus, when these five factors are supported by these five other factors, they lead to great fruit and great benefit."

“Monks, right view supported by five factors has the fruit of liberation of mind and the benefit of liberation of mind; it has the fruit of liberation by wisdom and the benefit of liberation by wisdom. By which five? [The text continues with the list of five factors.]”
“Here, bhikkhus, right view is supported by virtue, supported by learning, supported by discussion, supported by serenity, and supported by insight.

When right view is supported by these five factors, bhikkhus, it has liberation of mind as its fruit and liberation of mind as its benefit; it has liberation by wisdom as its fruit and liberation by wisdom as its benefit.
Thus was the fifth [discourse].

Aṅguttara Nikāya 5.26 3. Pañcaṅgika-vagga Vimuttāyatana-sutta “Bhikkhus, there are these five bases for liberation. What five? Here, bhikkhus, a bhikkhu has faith in the Tathāgata’s enlightenment thus:

‘The Blessed One is an arahant, perfectly enlightened, accomplished in true knowledge and conduct, fortunate, knower of the world, unsurpassed leader of persons to be tamed, teacher of devas and humans, the Buddha, the Blessed One. This is the first base for liberation. Furthermore, bhikkhus, a bhikkhu possesses the virtues dear to the noble ones: untorn, unbroken, unspotted, unsplattered, liberating, praised by the wise, untarnished, leading to concentration. This is the second base for liberation. Furthermore, bhikkhus, a bhikkhu has heard much, has retained what he has heard, stored what he has heard. Whatever teachings are admirable in the beginning, admirable in the middle, and admirable in the end, that is, in their meaning and expression, proclaim the holy life that is utterly perfect and pure—such teachings he has listened to often, retained, discussed, accumulated, examined with his mind, and well-penetrated by view. This is the third base for liberation. Furthermore, bhikkhus, a bhikkhu is content with any kind of robe, almsfood, lodging, and medicinal requisites for the sick. This is the fourth base for liberation. Furthermore, bhikkhus, a bhikkhu dwells with energy aroused for the abandoning of unwholesome states and the acquisition of wholesome states; he is steadfast, firm in exertion, not shirking the burden of wholesome qualities. This is the fifth base for liberation. These, bhikkhus, are the five bases for liberation.”
“Bhikkhus, there are these five bases of liberation wherein, for a bhikkhu who dwells diligent, ardent, and resolute,
the unliberated mind becomes liberated, or the unabandoned taints reach their total destruction.
Or he attains the unsurpassed security from bondage that has not yet been attained.
What are the five?
Here, monks, the Teacher teaches the Dhamma to a monk, or some other venerable fellow practitioner of the holy life.

In whatever way, monks, the Teacher teaches the Dhamma to that bhikkhu, or another venerable companion in the holy life, in just that way he becomes one who experiences the meaning and experiences the Dhamma in that teaching.
As he experiences the meaning and experiences the Dhamma, gladness arises in him.
For one who is gladdened, rapture arises.
The body of one who is joyful becomes tranquil.
One whose body is tranquil experiences happiness.
The mind of one who is happy becomes concentrated.
This, monks, is the first base for liberation, wherein for a monk who dwells diligent, ardent, and resolute,
the unliberated mind becomes liberated, the unabandoned taints go to their destruction,
or he attains the unsurpassed security from bondage that has not yet been attained.
Furthermore, monks, it may be that neither the Teacher nor another venerable companion in the holy life teaches the Dhamma to a monk.
However, he himself teaches the Dhamma in detail to others exactly as he has heard it and mastered it.

To the extent, monks, that a monk teaches the Dhamma in detail to others exactly as he has heard it and mastered it, to that same extent he becomes one who experiences the meaning and experiences the Dhamma in regard to that teaching.
In him who experiences the meaning and experiences the Dhamma, gladness arises.
In one who is gladdened, rapture arises.
In one whose mind is rapturous, the body becomes tranquil.
With a tranquil body, one feels happiness.
For one who is happy, the mind becomes concentrated.
This, monks, is the second basis for liberation, wherein a monk who is diligent, ardent, and resolute [attains it].
While he is dwelling [in that state], his unliberated mind becomes liberated, his unabated taints reach their exhaustion,
or he attains the unsurpassed security from bondage not yet attained.
Furthermore, monks, it may be that the Teacher does not teach the Dhamma to a monk, nor does another [teacher].
He does not teach the Dhamma in detail to others as he has heard it and mastered it;
rather, he recites the Dhamma in detail as he has heard it and mastered it.

To whatever extent, monks, a bhikkhu recites the Dhamma in detail as he has heard it and mastered it, to that same extent he becomes one who experiences the meaning and experiences the Dhamma in that teaching.
In one who experiences the meaning and experiences the Dhamma, gladness arises.
In one who is glad, rapture arises.
In one whose mind is rapturous, the body becomes tranquil.
With a tranquil body, one experiences happiness.
For one who is happy, the mind becomes concentrated.
This, monks, is the third basis for liberation, wherein a monk who is diligent and ardent... [as before] ...attains the security from bondage.
Furthermore, monks, it may be that a monk neither has the Teacher teach him the Dhamma,
nor does another venerable companion in the holy life teach him the Dhamma, nor does he himself teach the Dhamma in detail to others as he has heard and mastered it,
nor does he himself recite it in detail as he has heard and mastered it.
Moreover, he reflects upon, examines, and contemplates with his mind the Dhamma as it has been heard and mastered.
To whatever extent, monks, a monk reflects upon, examines, and contemplates with his mind the Dhamma as it has been heard and mastered,
to that same extent he becomes one who experiences the meaning within that Dhamma.
And he experiences the Dhamma.
As he experiences the meaning and experiences the Dhamma, gladness arises in him.
In one who is gladdened, rapture arises.
The body of one whose mind is joyful becomes tranquil.
One whose body is tranquil experiences happiness.
The mind of one who is happy becomes concentrated.
This, monks, is the fourth base for liberation, wherein for a monk who dwells diligent, ardent, and resolute,
the unliberated mind is liberated, the unabandoned taints go to their destruction,
or he attains the unsurpassed security from bondage not yet attained.
Furthermore, monks, it may be that neither does the Teacher teach the Dhamma to a monk,
nor does some other venerable fellow-celibate, nor does he himself teach the Dhamma in detail to others as he has heard and mastered it,
nor does he himself recite it in detail as he has heard and mastered it.
He reflects upon, examines, and contemplates with the mind the Dhamma as he has heard it and mastered it;
moreover, he has grasped a certain object of concentration well, attended to it well, retained it well, and penetrated it well with wisdom.
To whatever extent, monks, a monk has grasped a certain object of concentration well, attended to it well...
When that [teaching] has been well grasped and well penetrated by wisdom in such and such a way,
he comes to experience the meaning and experience the Dhamma within that teaching. In one who experiences the meaning and experiences the Dhamma, gladness arises.
In one who is joyful, rapture arises.
For one whose mind is rapturous, the body becomes tranquil.
With a tranquil body, one experiences happiness.
The mind of one who is happy becomes concentrated.
This, monks, is the fifth base for liberation, wherein the mind of a bhikkhu who dwells diligent, ardent, and resolute—
whether his mind was unliberated— becomes liberated, or his unabandoned taints go to their destruction.
Or he attains the unsurpassed security from bondage that has not yet been attained.
These, monks, are the five bases for liberation, wherein the mind of a monk who dwells diligent, ardent,
and resolute becomes liberated if it was not yet liberated, or his unabated taints reach their exhaustion.
They go forth, or they attain the unsurpassed security from bondage that has not yet been attained.
The sixth. Aṅguttara Nikāya 5.27

3. Pañcaṅgika-vagga: Samādhi Sutta (AN 5.27, PTS AN iii 24) “Monks, there are these five factors of concentration. What five? Here, monks, a bhikkhu is possessed of faith, trust in the Tathāgata’s enlightenment thus: ‘The Blessed One is an arahant, perfectly enlightened, accomplished in true knowledge and conduct, fortunate, knower of the world, unsurpassed leader of persons to be tamed, teacher of devas and humans, the Buddha, the Blessed One. “He dwells with his mind firmly established in the four foundations of mindfulness; he possesses the four right strivings; he possesses the four bases for psychic power; he possesses the five spiritual faculties; he possesses the five powers; he possesses the seven factors of enlightenment; he possesses the Noble Eightfold Path. “This, monks, is called the five-factored concentration.”
“Monks, develop concentration that is immeasurable, being wise and mindful.
Monks, for those who develop concentration that is immeasurable, being wise and mindful, five kinds of knowledge arise within themselves.
What are the five?
‘This concentration is pleasant in the present and has a pleasant result in the future’—such personal knowledge arises within him;
‘This concentration is noble and spiritual’—such personal knowledge arises within him;
‘This concentration is not practiced by base men’—such personal knowledge arises within him.
‘This concentration is peaceful, sublime, gained through tranquility, attained to unification, and is not constrained by forced suppression’—such personal knowledge arises within him.
Furthermore, the personal knowledge arises: ‘Mindful indeed I enter this attainment; mindful I emerge from it.
“Monks, develop concentration that is immeasurable, being wise and mindful.”
“Monks, for those who develop immeasurable concentration, being prudent and mindful, these five kinds of knowledge arise within themselves.
Thus was the seventh [sutta]. Aṅguttara Nikāya 5.28
3. Pañcaṅgika-vagga: Pañcaṅgika-sutta (AN 5.28, PTS AN iii 25)
“Monks, I will teach you the development of noble five-factored right concentration.
Listen to it and attend closely; I will speak.
“Yes, venerable sir,” those monks replied to the Blessed One.
The Blessed One said this:
“And what, bhikkhus, is the development of noble five-factored right concentration?
Here, bhikkhus, a bhikkhu, quite secluded from sensual pleasures … [as before] … enters and dwells in the first jhāna.”

He drenches, steeps, fills, and suffuses this very body with the rapture and happiness born of seclusion; there is no part of his entire body that is not suffused with the rapture and happiness born of seclusion.

Just as, monks, a skilled bath attendant or a bath attendant’s apprentice, having poured bath-powder into a bronze basin, would knead it together with water until the ball of bath-powder is saturated with moisture and clings to it.
Saturated with oil, both inside and out, it is filled with oil but does not overflow.
In the same way, monks, a bhikkhu drenches, steeps, fills, and suffuses this very body with the rapture and happiness born of seclusion;
there is no part of his entire body that is not suffused with the rapture and happiness born of seclusion.
Monks, this is the first development of noble five-factored right concentration.
Furthermore, monks, with the stilling of applied and sustained thought, a bhikkhu enters and dwells in the second jhāna...
He drenches, steeps, fills, and pervades this very body with the rapture and happiness born of concentration.
There is no part of his entire body that is not suffused with the rapture and happiness born of concentration.
Just as, monks, there is a deep pool of water with a spring bubbling up from within it,
which has no inlet of water from the eastern direction, none from the western direction, and none from the northern direction.
There would be no source of water from the eastern direction, nor any source of water from the southern direction, and the rain-god would not send down showers properly from time to time.
Yet, from that very lake, a cool stream of water would well up and [fill] that same lake with cool water.
It would drench, steep, fill, and suffuse it so that there would be no part of that entire pool of water untouched by the cool water.
In the same way, monks, a bhikkhu drenches, steeps, fills, and suffuses this very body with the rapture and happiness born of concentration.
There is no part of his entire body that is not suffused with the rapture and happiness born of concentration.
Monks, this is the second development of noble five-factored right concentration.
Furthermore, monks, with the fading away of rapture... [as before] ...he enters and dwells in the third jhāna.
Thus he drenches, steeps, fills, and pervades this very body with raptureless happiness;
there is no part of his entire body that is not suffused with raptureless happiness.
Just as, monks, in a bed of blue lotuses, or red lotuses, or white lotuses, some of them...
It is like blue lotuses, or pink lotuses, or white lotuses, born in the water, grown in the water, not rising above the water, but nourished while submerged within it;
from their tips down to their roots, they are completely saturated, steeped, filled, and suffused with cold water,
such that there is no part of those blue, pink, or white lotuses untouched by the cold water.
In the same way, monks, a monk drenches, steeps, fills, and pervades this very body with a happiness devoid of rapture;
there is no part of his entire body that is not touched by that happiness devoid of rapture.
Monks, this is the third development of noble five-factored right concentration.
Furthermore, monks, with the abandoning of pleasure... [as before] ...a monk enters and dwells in the fourth jhāna.
He sits pervading this very body with a pure and bright mind;
there is no part of his entire body that is not suffused by that pure and bright mind.
“Just as if, monks, a man were sitting down having covered himself head and all with a white cloth,
such that no part of his entire body was untouched by the white cloth;
even so, monks, a monk sits having pervaded this very body with a mind that is pure and radiant.”
There is no part of his entire body that is not pervaded by a mind that is pure and bright.
Monks, this is the fourth development of noble five-factored right concentration.
Furthermore, monks, a monk has well-grasped the sign for review, well-attended to it, well-retained it, and well-penetrated it with wisdom.
“Just as, bhikkhus, one person might review another— one standing reviewing one who is sitting, or one sitting reviewing one who is lying down— so too, bhikkhus,
a bhikkhu’s sign for reviewing is well grasped, well attended to, well remembered, and well penetrated by wisdom. This, bhikkhus,
is the fifth development of noble five-factored right concentration.”
“Monks, when noble five-factored right concentration has been thus developed and cultivated by a monk,
then for whatever state realizable through direct knowledge he inclines his mind toward realizing through direct knowledge,
he attains the capacity to be a witness therein, in each and every case where there is a suitable basis.”
“Bhikkhus, suppose there were a water jar placed on a stand, full of water, brimming to the top so that a crow could drink from it.
If a strong man were to tip it in any direction, would the water come out?”— “Yes, venerable sir.”
“In the same way, monks, when noble five-factored right concentration has been thus developed and cultivated by a monk,
he attains the capacity for realization in whatever state that is to be realized through direct knowledge,
whenever there is a suitable basis for such realization.
“Bhikkhus, suppose there were a square pond on level ground, lined with embankments, full of water right up to the brim so that a crow could drink from it.
If a strong man were to release the embankment from any side, would water come out?”— “Yes, Bhante.”

“In the same way, monks, when noble five-factored right concentration has been thus developed and cultivated by a bhikkhu, whatever state realizable through direct knowledge there may be... in each and every case, he is capable of realizing it, provided there is a suitable basis.
Just as, monks, a chariot harnessed to thoroughbred horses might stand at a crossroads on level ground, with the goad lowered.”

Just as a skilled horse trainer, a charioteer of horses to be tamed, having mounted it, takes the reins in his left hand and the whip in his right hand, and can drive it wherever he wishes, back and forth; even so, monks,
when noble five-factored right concentration has been thus developed and cultivated by a monk,
he directs his mind toward whatever state is to be realized through direct knowledge, for the sake of realizing that state through direct knowledge.
In each and every case, he attains the state of being capable of realization whenever there is a suitable occasion.

If he should wish: "May I exercise the various kinds of psychic power—being one, may I become many... [as far as] may I wield mastery with my body as far as the Brahma-world"—in each and every case, he attains the state of being capable of realization whenever there is a suitable occasion.

Thus, if he wishes: “With the divine ear-element, purified and surpassing that of humans, may I hear both kinds of sounds—the divine and the human, whether far or near”—he attains the capacity for realization in each respective instance, in whatever sphere it exists.
If he wishes: “May I, by encompassing the mind with my own mind, understand the minds of other beings and other persons...”
One should know a mind with lust as "a mind with lust," and one should know a mind free from lust as "a mind free from lust"; likewise,
one should know a mind with hatred...
A mind free from hatred...
a mind with delusion...
or a mind free from delusion...
Whether the mind is contracted … or whether the mind is distracted … or whether the mind is exalted …
...a mind that is not sublime ...
a surpassable mind ...
or an unsurpassable mind ...
Whether the mind is concentrated or unconcentrated,
whether the mind is liberated or unliberated...
‘I shall understand an unliberated mind as an unliberated mind,’ he attains the capacity for realization in each respective case, whenever there is an appropriate basis.

If he so desires: ‘May I recollect my manifold past lives, that is to say, one birth, two births … [and so on] … thus may I recollect my manifold past lives with their aspects and particulars,’ he attains the capacity for realization in each respective case, whenever there is an appropriate basis.
In each and every case, he attains the state of being capable of realization whenever there is an appropriate occasion.

If he should wish: “May I, with the divine eye, purified and surpassing that of humans, understand how beings pass away according to their kamma,” then in each and every case, he attains the state of being capable of realization whenever there is an appropriate occasion.

Thus, if he should wish: “May I, through the destruction of the taints, dwell in this very life having realized for myself with direct knowledge the taintless liberation of mind and liberation by wisdom, and having entered upon them,” he attains the capability of being a witness in each and every case, provided there is a suitable basis.
The eighth.

Aṅguttara Nikāya 5.29 3. Pañcaṅgika-vagga Caṅkama-sutta (The Walking Meditation) “Bhikkhus, there are these five factors for the cultivation of the walking meditation. What five? First, bhikkhus, a bhikkhu dwells contemplating the body in the body, ardent, clearly comprehending, and mindful, having removed covetousness and displeasure regarding the world. This is the first factor for the cultivation of the walking meditation. Second, bhikkhus, a bhikkhu dwells contemplating feelings in feelings, ardent, clearly comprehending, and mindful, having removed covetousness and displeasure regarding the world. This is the second factor for the cultivation of the walking meditation. Third, bhikkhus, a bhikkhu dwells contemplating mind in the mind, ardent, clearly comprehending, and mindful, having removed covetousness and displeasure regarding the world. This is the third factor for the cultivation of the walking meditation. Fourth, bhikkhus, a bhikkhu dwells contemplating phenomena in phenomena, ardent, clearly comprehending, and mindful, having removed covetousness and displeasure regarding the world. This is the fourth factor for the cultivation of the walking meditation. Fifth, bhikkhus, a bhikkhu develops the perception of light, maintains the perception of day, with a mind that is open and unconfined, as by day so by night, and as by night so by day. Thus, with a mind that is open and unconfined, he develops a mind imbued with luminosity. This is the fifth factor for the cultivation of the walking meditation. These, bhikkhus, are the five factors for the cultivation of the walking meditation.”
“Bhikkhus, there are these five benefits in walking meditation.
What five?

“He is able to endure walking; he is able to endure striving; he has little illness; what is eaten, drunk, chewed, and tasted is properly digested; and the concentration attained while walking endures for a long time.
These, monks, are the five benefits of walking.
The ninth.

Aṅguttara Nikāya 5.30 3. Pañcaṅgika-vagga Nāgitasutta “Monks, there are these five factors that lead to the decline of a lay follower who has gone for refuge. What five? Here, monks, a lay follower dwells with a mind obsessed by sensual lust, without having abandoned sensual lust; he dwells with a mind obsessed by ill will, without having abandoned ill will; he dwells with a mind obsessed by dullness and drowsiness, without having abandoned dullness and drowsiness; he dwells with a mind obsessed by restlessness and remorse, without having abandoned restlessness and remorse; and he dwells with a mind obsessed by doubt, without having abandoned doubt. These, monks, are the five factors that lead to the decline of a lay follower who has gone for refuge. There are, monks, these five factors that lead to the non-decline of a lay follower who has gone for refuge. What five? Here, monks, a lay follower dwells with a mind not obsessed by sensual lust, having abandoned sensual lust; he dwells with a mind not obsessed by ill will, having abandoned ill will; he dwells with a mind not obsessed by dullness and drowsiness, having abandoned dullness and drowsiness; he dwells with a mind not obsessed by restlessness and remorse, having abandoned restlessness and remorse; and he dwells with a mind not obsessed by doubt, having abandoned doubt. These, monks, are the five factors that lead to the non-decline of a lay follower who has gone for refuge.”
(AN 5.30, PTS AN iii 30) Thus have I heard:
on one occasion the Blessed One, while wandering on tour among the Kosalans with a large community of monks, arrived at a brahmin village of the Kosalans named Icchānaṅgala.
There the Blessed One was staying at Icchānaṅgala, in the grove of Icchānaṅgala.
The brahmin householders of Icchānaṅgala heard:
