"The ascetic Gotama, the son of the Sakyans who went forth from a Sakyan clan, has arrived at Icchānaṅgala; he is staying at Icchānaṅgala, in the grove of Icchānaṅgala."
Furthermore, this excellent report of Master Gotama’s fame has spread abroad:

“Indeed, that Blessed One is an arahant, perfectly enlightened, accomplished in true knowledge and conduct, fortunate, knower of the world, unsurpassed leader of persons to be tamed, teacher of devas and humans, the Buddha, the Blessed One.

Having personally realized this world with its devas, Māras, and Brahmās, this generation with its ascetics and brahmins, its devas and humans, by means of his own direct knowledge, he makes it known.
He teaches the Dhamma that is good in the beginning, good in the middle, and good in the end, with the right meaning and phrasing; he reveals the holy life, entirely complete and pure.
It is indeed good to see such Arahants.
Then, when that night had passed, the brahmin householders of Icchānaṅgala prepared abundant solid food...
Taking their food, they went to the Icchānaṅgala forest grove. Having arrived, they stood outside the gatehouse, making a loud noise and a great clamor.
Now at that time, the Venerable Nāgita was the Blessed One’s attendant.
Then the Blessed One addressed the Venerable Nāgita:
“Nāgita, who are these making such a loud noise, such a great clamor? They sound like fishermen over a haul of fish!

“Venerable sir, these brahmin householders from Icchānaṅgala have brought abundant hard food and soft food and are standing outside the gatehouse, having brought it specifically for the Blessed One and the Saṅgha of bhikkhus.”
“Nāgita, let there be no meeting with me for the sake of fame,

nor fame for my sake. For whoever, Nāgita, should not obtain at will, without difficulty, and without hardship this happiness of renunciation, this happiness of seclusion, this happiness of peace, this happiness of awakening— which is the happiness of renunciation and the happiness of seclusion that I [possess]— ”

"One who is a recipient of the bliss of tranquility and the bliss of enlightenment at will, without difficulty, and without hardship—would such a person consent to that base pleasure, the pleasure of sloth, the pleasure of gain, honor, and fame?
"Venerable sir, may the Blessed One now consent; may the Sugata now consent."
"Venerable sir, this is now the time for the Blessed One’s acceptance.
Whichever way the Blessed One goes from now on, the brahmins and householders, both those of the towns and the countryside, will incline in that very direction.
Venerable sir, it is just as when rain falls in thick drops, the waters flow along according to the slope."
"In this very way, Bhante, wherever the Blessed One goes now, the brahmins and householders, both those from the towns and those from the countryside, will incline toward that very place.
And for what reason?
Because, Bhante, of the Blessed One’s virtue and wisdom."
“Nāgita, let there be no meeting with me for the sake of fame,

nor fame for my sake. For whoever, Nāgita, would not obtain at will, without difficulty, and without hardship this happiness of renunciation, this happiness of seclusion, this happiness of peace, this happiness of awakening— which is the happiness of renunciation and the happiness of seclusion that I [possess]— ”
One who obtains at will, without difficulty, and without trouble, the happiness of tranquility and the happiness of enlightenment,
might yet accept that dross-like pleasure, that slothful pleasure, the pleasure of gain, honor, and fame. For, Nāgita,
from what one has eaten, drunk, chewed, and tasted, there arise excrement and urine.
This is its result. Nāgita,
from the change and alteration of those who are dear, sorrow, lamentation, pain, grief, and despair arise—
this is its result.
For one devoted to the practice of the sign of the foul, Nāgita, a sense of revulsion toward the sign of the beautiful becomes established—
this is its outcome.
For one dwelling contemplating impermanence in the six bases of contact, Nāgita, a sense of revulsion toward contact becomes established.
This is its result.
Nāgita, for one who dwells contemplating the arising and passing away in the five aggregates of clinging, revulsion toward clinging becomes established—
this is its result.”
The tenth.
The third chapter, the Chapter on the Five Factors.
Its summary verse:
The two stains of lack of reverence,
and that which is supported by the immoral; the five factors of liberation and concentration.
"And by Nāgita on the walking path.
Aṅguttara Nikāya 5.31 4.
Sumanavagga (The Chapter on Sumanā)
Sumanasutta.
On one occasion... [at] Jeta’s Grove, Anāthapiṇḍika’s monastery.
Then Princess Sumanā, surrounded by five hundred chariots and five hundred royal maidens, approached the Blessed One;
having approached and paid homage to the Blessed One, she sat down to one side.
Sitting to one side, Princess Sumanā said this to the Blessed One:
“Suppose, Bhante, there were two disciples of the Blessed One who were equal in faith,
equal in virtue, and equal in wisdom— one a giver,
the other a non-giver. Upon the breakup of the body, after death, they might both be reborn in a happy destination, a heavenly world.”
“But, Bhante, when they have become devas, could there be any distinction or difference between them?
“There could be, Sumana,” the Blessed One said.
“Sumana, that donor, having become a deva, surpasses that non-donor in five respects:”
“With divine life-span, divine beauty, divine happiness, divine fame, and divine sovereignty.
That donor, Sumanā, being reborn as a deity, surpasses that non-donor in these five respects.
“But if, venerable sir, having passed away from there, they come back to this state of existence, would there be any distinction, any difference between them when they have become human beings?”
“It may be so, Sumanā,” the Blessed One said.
“Sumanā, that donor, being a human being, surpasses that non-donor in five respects:
in human lifespan, in human beauty, in human happiness, in human fame, and in human sovereignty.”
“Sumana, that donor, being a human being, surpasses that non-donor by these five grounds.
“But if, Bhante, both of them go forth from the household life into homelessness, would there, Bhante, be any distinction or difference between them once they have gone forth?
“There might be, Sumana,” the Blessed One said.
“Sumana, when that donor, having gone forth, surpasses that non-donor in five respects:
he mostly uses robes only when asked and seldom without being asked; he mostly consumes almsfood only when asked and seldom without being asked;
he mostly uses lodgings only when asked and seldom without being asked.”
He mostly uses requisites for the sick and medicinal supplies only when asked, seldom without being asked.
Furthermore, with regard to those fellow celibates with whom he dwells, they mostly approach him with agreeable bodily actions and seldom with disagreeable ones;
they mostly approach him with agreeable verbal actions and seldom with disagreeable ones.
They treat him mostly with agreeable mental actions and only rarely with disagreeable ones;
they offer him mostly agreeable gifts and only rarely disagreeable ones.
Sumana, that donor, having gone forth as a renunciant, surpasses that non-donor in these five respects.”
“But if, venerable sir, both of them attain arahantship, would there be any distinction or difference between them once they have attained arahantship?
“In this matter, Sumana, I say there is no distinction whatsoever between their liberation and liberation.
“It is wonderful, venerable sir! It is marvelous, venerable sir!”
“To this extent, Bhante, it is indeed enough to give gifts and enough to perform meritorious deeds;

for there are meritorious deeds that are beneficial even when one has become a deva, meritorious deeds that are beneficial when one has become a human, and meritorious deeds that are beneficial when one has gone forth.
“It is so, Sumanā.”
“Indeed, Sumanā, it is enough to give gifts; it is enough to perform meritorious deeds.
Meritorious deeds are beneficial even when one has become a deva, they are beneficial when one has become a human, and they are beneficial even when one has gone forth.
Thus spoke the Blessed One.
Having said this, the Sugata, the Teacher, further spoke as follows:
“Just as the stainless moon,
moving through the expanse of space;”
He outshines all the hosts of stars in the world with his radiance;
even so does one perfected in virtue.
A person endowed with faith outshines all the stingy people in the world through their generosity.
Just as a cloud, thundering and garlanded with lightning,
fills both the highlands and the lowlands;
Raining down upon the earth.
Thus, one endowed with vision,
a disciple of the Perfectly Enlightened One;
The wise person overcomes the miser in five ways:
by longevity and by fame as well.
In beauty and in happiness;
indeed, enriched by wealth,
he rejoices in heaven after passing away.”
First.
Aṅguttara Nikāya 5.32 4.
Sumanavagga (The Chapter on Sumanā)
The Cundī Sutta (AN 5.32, PTS AN iii 35):
On one occasion the Blessed One was dwelling at Rājagaha in the Bamboo Grove, the Squirrels’ Feeding Place.
Then Princess Cundī, surrounded by five hundred chariots and five hundred young women, approached the Blessed One;
having approached and paid homage to the Blessed One, she sat down to one side.
Seated to one side, Princess Cundī said this to the Blessed One:
“Venerable sir, we have a younger brother, a prince named Cunda, who says this:
‘Whatever woman or man has gone for refuge to the Buddha, gone for refuge to the Dhamma, and gone for refuge to the Saṅgha;
who abstains from taking life, abstains from taking what is not given, and abstains from sexual misconduct;’”
"Abstaining from false speech, abstaining from fermented and distilled liquors and intoxicants which are the basis for negligence— he, upon the breakup of the body, after death,
is reborn only in a happy destination,
not in a miserable one. This, venerable sir, I ask of the Blessed One:
“In what kind of teacher, venerable sir, does one have confidence so that, with the breakup of the body, after death, one is reborn only in a good destination, not in a bad destination?
In what kind of Dhamma does one have confidence so that, with the breakup of the body, after death, one is reborn only in a good destination, not in a bad destination?
In what kind of Saṅgha does one have confidence so that, with the breakup of the body, after death, one is reborn only in a good destination, not in a bad destination?”
“What kind of virtues must one fulfill to be reborn in a happy destination after the breakup of the body, after death, and not in a miserable destination?
“Cundi, to whatever extent there are beings—whether footless, two-footed, four-footed, or many-footed; whether with form or formless;
whether percipient, non-percipient, or neither percipient nor non-percipient—the Tathāgata, the Arahant, the Perfectly Enlightened One, is declared to be the foremost among them.”
"Cundi, those who have confidence in the Buddha have confidence in the foremost.
And for those with confidence in the foremost, the result is foremost.
Cundi, among all conditioned phenomena, the Noble Eightfold Path is declared to be the foremost."
Cundi, those who have confidence in the Noble Eightfold Path have confidence in the foremost; and for those with confidence in the foremost, the result is foremost.

Cundi, to whatever extent there are phenomena, whether conditioned or unconditioned, dispassion is declared to be the foremost among them—that is to say, the crushing of intoxication, the removal of thirst, the uprooting of attachment, the cutting off of the cycle of existence, the destruction of craving, dispassion, cessation, and Nibbāna.
"Cundi, those who have confidence in the Dhamma that is dispassionate have confidence in the foremost.
For those with confidence in the foremost, there is a foremost result.
To whatever extent there are assemblies or groups, Cundi, the Saṅgha of the Tathāgata’s disciples is declared the foremost among them, namely:"

There are four pairs of persons, eight individual types of persons; this is the Saṅgha of the Blessed One’s disciples, worthy of offerings, worthy of hospitality, worthy of gifts, worthy of reverential salutation, an unsurpassed field of merit for the world.
Cundi, those who have faith in the Saṅgha have faith in the foremost.
And for those who have faith in the foremost, the result is foremost.
To whatever extent there are virtues, Cundi, those virtues beloved by the noble ones are declared the foremost, namely:
unbroken, flawless, unspotted, untarnished, liberating, praised by the wise, ungrasped, and conducive to concentration.
Those who fulfill the virtues beloved by the noble ones, Cundi, fulfill the foremost.
But for those who act pre-eminently toward the foremost, the result is foremost.
Indeed, for those who have confidence in what is foremost and who understand the foremost Dhamma—
For those with faith in the Supreme Buddha,
the unsurpassed one worthy of offerings;
for those with faith in the Supreme Dhamma...
In the bliss of the pacification of dispassion,
for those with faith in the supreme Saṅgha,
the unsurpassed field of merit.
For those giving the best gift,
the highest merit increases;
the highest lifespan and the highest beauty [arise].
Fame, renown, happiness, and strength belong to the wise giver of the best,
who is established in the supreme Dhamma.
Whether become a god or a human,
having reached the summit, he rejoices. Thus ends the second [verse].

Aṅguttara Nikāya 5.33 4. Sumanavagga Uggahasutta Thus have I heard. On one occasion the Blessed One was dwelling at Sāvatthī in Jeta’s Grove, Anāthapiṇḍika’s Park. There the Venerable Ānanda approached the Blessed One, paid homage to him, sat down to one side, and said: “Venerable sir, it would be good if the Blessed One would teach me the Dhamma in brief, so that, having heard the Dhamma from the Blessed One, I might dwell alone, withdrawn, diligent, ardent, and resolute. “Ānanda, if you would dwell alone, withdrawn, diligent, ardent, and resolute, it is for this purpose that the Dhamma has been taught by me in brief. “A second time, venerable sir, it would be good if the Blessed One would teach me the Dhamma in brief…” “A third time, venerable sir, it would be good if the Blessed One would teach me the Dhamma in brief…” “Ānanda, if you would dwell alone, withdrawn, diligent, ardent, and resolute, it is for this purpose that the Dhamma has been taught by me in brief. “Venerable sir, how should one know, how should one see, so that, having seen that, one might dwell alone, withdrawn, diligent, ardent, and resolute? “Ānanda, when one knows and sees the five aggregates subject to clinging as they really are, one dwells alone, withdrawn, diligent, ardent, and resolute. What five? The aggregate of material form subject to clinging, the aggregate of feeling subject to clinging, the aggregate of perception subject to clinging, the aggregate of volitional formations subject to clinging, and the aggregate of consciousness subject to clinging. When one knows and sees these five aggregates subject to clinging as they really are—impermanent as impermanent, suffering as suffering, and non-self as non-self—one dwells alone, withdrawn, diligent, ardent, and resolute.

Then the Venerable Uggaha approached the Blessed One, paid homage to him, sat down to one side, and said: “Venerable sir, it would be good if the Blessed One would teach me the Dhamma in brief, so that, having heard the Dhamma from the Blessed One, I might dwell alone, withdrawn, diligent, ardent, and resolute. “Uggaha, if you would dwell alone, withdrawn, diligent, ardent, and resolute, it is for this purpose that the Dhamma has been taught by me in brief. “A second time, venerable sir, it would be good if the Blessed One would teach me the Dhamma in brief…” “A third time, venerable sir, it would be good if the Blessed One would teach me the Dhamma in brief…” “Uggaha, if you would dwell alone, withdrawn, diligent, ardent, and resolute, it is for this purpose that the Dhamma has been taught by me in brief. “Venerable sir, how should one know, how should one see, so that, having seen that, one might dwell alone, withdrawn, diligent, ardent, and resolute? “Uggaha, when one knows and sees the six bases of contact as they really are—arising and passing away—one dwells alone, withdrawn, diligent, ardent, and resolute. What six? The eye-base, the ear-base, the nose-base, the tongue-base, the body-base, and the mind-base. When one knows and sees these six bases of contact as they really are—arising and passing away—one dwells alone, withdrawn, diligent, ardent, and resolute. Then the Venerable Sumanas approached the Blessed One, paid homage to him, sat down to one side, and said: “Venerable sir, it would be good if the Blessed One would teach me the Dhamma in brief, so that, having heard the Dhamma from the Blessed One, I might dwell alone, withdrawn, diligent, ardent, and resolute. “Sumanas, if you would dwell alone, withdrawn, diligent, ardent, and resolute, it is for this purpose that the Dhamma has been taught by me in brief. “A second time, venerable sir, it would be good if the Blessed One would teach me the Dhamma in brief…” “A third time, venerable sir, it would be good if the Blessed One would teach me the Dhamma in brief…” “Sumanas, if you would dwell alone, withdrawn, diligent, ardent, and resolute, it is for this purpose that the Dhamma has been taught by me in brief. “Venerable sir, how should one know, how should one see, so that, having seen that, one might dwell alone, withdrawn, diligent, ardent, and resolute? “Sumanas, when one knows and sees the seven stations of consciousness as they really are—arising and passing away—one dwells alone, withdrawn, diligent, ardent, and resolute. What seven? There are beings with diversity of body and diversity of perception; there are beings with diversity of body and unity of perception; there are beings with unity of body and diversity of perception; there are beings with unity of body and unity of perception; there are beings who are formless, percipient; there are beings who are formless, non-percipient; and there are beings who are formless, neither-percipient-nor-non-percipient. When one knows and sees these seven stations of consciousness as they really are—arising and passing away—one dwells alone, withdrawn, diligent, ardent, and resolute. Then the Venerable Puṇṇa approached the Blessed One, paid homage to him, sat down to one side, and said: “Venerable sir, it would be good if the Blessed One would teach me the Dhamma in brief, so that, having heard the Dhamma from the Blessed One, I might dwell alone, withdrawn, diligent, ardent, and resolute. “Puṇṇa, if you would dwell alone, withdrawn, diligent, ardent, and resolute, it is for this purpose that the Dhamma has been taught by me in brief. “A second time, venerable sir, it would be good if the Blessed One would teach me the Dhamma in brief…” “A third time, venerable sir, it would be good if the Blessed One would teach me the Dhamma in brief…” “Puṇṇa, if you would dwell alone, withdrawn, diligent, ardent, and resolute, it is for this purpose that the Dhamma has been taught by me in brief. “Venerable sir, how should one know, how should one see, so that, having seen that, one might dwell alone, withdrawn, diligent, ardent, and resolute? “Puṇṇa, when one knows and sees the eight worldly conditions as they really are—arising and passing away—one dwells alone, withdrawn, diligent, ardent, and resolute. What eight? Gain and loss, fame and disrepute, praise and blame, pleasure and pain. When one knows and sees these eight worldly conditions as they really are—arising and passing away—one dwells alone, withdrawn, diligent, ardent, and resolute. Then the Venerable Mahākoṭṭhita approached the Blessed One, paid homage to him, sat down to one side, and said: “Venerable sir, it would be good if the Blessed One would teach me the Dhamma in brief, so that, having heard the Dhamma from the Blessed One, I might dwell alone, withdrawn, diligent, ardent, and resolute. “Koṭṭhita, if you would dwell alone, withdrawn, diligent, ardent, and resolute, it is for this purpose that the Dhamma has been taught by me in brief. “A second time, venerable sir, it would be good if the Blessed One would teach me the Dhamma in brief…” “A third time, venerable sir, it would be good if the Blessed One would teach me the Dhamma in brief…” “Koṭṭhita, if you would dwell alone, withdrawn, diligent, ardent, and resolute, it is for this purpose that the Dhamma has been taught by me in brief. “Venerable sir, how should one know, how should one see, so that, having seen that, one might dwell alone, withdrawn, diligent, ardent, and resolute? “Koṭṭhita, when one knows and sees the nine progressive dwellings of a bhikkhu as they really are—arising and passing away—one dwells alone, withdrawn, diligent, ardent, and resolute. What nine? Here, a bhikkhu dwells contemplating the body in the body internally, ardent, clearly comprehending, and mindful, having removed covetousness and displeasure in regard to the world. He dwells contemplating the body in the body externally… He dwells contemplating the body in the body internally and externally… He dwells contemplating feelings in feelings
(AN 5.33, PTS AN iii 36) On one occasion the Blessed One was dwelling at Bhaddiya in the Jātiyā Grove.

Then Uggaha, the grandson of Meṇḍaka, approached the Blessed One; having approached, he paid homage to the Blessed One and sat down to one side. As he was sitting there, Uggaha, the grandson of Meṇḍaka, said this to the Blessed One:
“Venerable sir, may the Blessed One accept my meal tomorrow together with three others.
The Blessed One consented by remaining silent.
Then Uggaha Meṇḍakanattā, understanding the Blessed One’s consent, rose from his seat, paid homage to the Blessed One, and keeping him to his right, departed.
Then, when that night had passed, the Blessed One dressed in the morning and, taking his bowl and robe, went to the residence of Uggaha Meṇḍakanattā. Having arrived, he sat down on the prepared seat.
Then Uggaha Meṇḍakanattā, with his own hands, served and satisfied the Blessed One with excellent hard and soft foods.
When the Blessed One had finished eating and had withdrawn his hand from the bowl, Uggaha Meṇḍakanattā sat down to one side.
Seated to one side, Uggaha Meṇḍakanattā said this to the Blessed One:
“Bhante, these young women of mine will go to their husbands’ families.
May the Blessed One exhort them.”
“Venerable sir, may the Blessed One instruct them so that it may lead to their welfare and happiness for a long time.
Then the Blessed One said this to those girls:
“Therefore, girls, you should train yourselves thus:”
‘Whomever your parents may give you to as a husband— being desirous of your welfare, seeking your benefit, and compassionate, out of compassion— they, for his sake,
shall be those who rise before him and retire after him, who respond to whatever needs to be done, who conduct themselves agreeably,
and who speak kindly. Thus, young women, should you train yourselves.
Therefore, young women, you should train yourselves thus:

"Those who will be respected by our husband—whether they be his mother or father, or recluses and brahmins—we will honor, revere, esteem, and worship them; and when they arrive, we will pay our respects with a seat and water.
Thus, young women, should you train yourselves.
Therefore, young women, you should train yourselves thus:

"In whatever internal household duties there may be—whether involving wool or cotton—we shall be skillful and diligent therein; we shall possess the appropriate means of inquiry, being capable of doing and capable of arranging.
In this way, young women, you should train yourselves.
Therefore, young women, you should train yourselves thus:

"Regarding those who are the internal members of our husband's household—whether they be slaves, messengers, or laborers—we shall recognize what has been done by them as done, and what has not been done as not done;
we shall know the strength and weakness of those who are ill; [and we shall provide] hard food..."
‘And we shall share out the food to him according to our means.
In this way, young women, you should train yourselves.
Therefore, young women, you should train yourselves thus:

‘Whatever wealth, grain, silver, or gold our husband brings home, we shall ensure it is preserved through protection and guarded; and therein we shall be non-thieving, non-stealing, non-drunkardly, and non-destructive.
Thus, young women, should you train yourselves.
Endowed with these five qualities, young women, upon the dissolution of the body after death, are reborn in the company of the Manāpakāyika devas.
He who always supports him— ever diligent and zealous— the one who provides all that is desired,
[is truly a father].
She does not despise her husband,
nor does she provoke her husband with jealous behavior.
The wise person honors all their husbands and elders;
they are diligent and free from laziness.
She keeps her attendants restrained;
she acts agreeably to her husband and protects his earnings.
The woman who conducts herself in this way,
following the will and desires of her husband—
those gods are indeed called "the Pleasant Ones."
“Where she is reborn. The third [sutta].
Aṅguttara Nikāya 5.34

4. Sumanavagga: Sīhasenāpati Sutta (AN 5.34, PTS AN iii 38) [The Blessed One said: “Sīha, there are these four kinds of persons found existing in the world. What four? The person who is like a bull; the person who is like a ram; the person who is like a goat; and the person who is like a lion. And how, Sīha, is one a person like a bull? Here, Sīha, some person dwells with his mind obsessed by sensual lust, overwhelmed by sensual lust, and he does not understand as it really is the escape from the arisen sensual lust. When he encounters an object that provokes aversion, his mind becomes full of hate... [and so on]... He does not understand as it really is the escape from the arisen ill will. This, Sīha, is called a person like a bull. And how, Sīha, is one a person like a ram? Here, Sīha, some person dwells with his mind obsessed by ill will... obsessed by dullness and torpor... obsessed by restlessness and remorse... obsessed by doubt, overwhelmed by doubt, and he does not understand as it really is the escape from the arisen doubt. When he encounters an object that provokes sensual lust, his mind becomes full of lust... [and so on]... He does not understand as it really is the escape from the arisen sensual lust. This, Sīha, is called a person like a ram. And how, Sīha, is one a person like a goat? Here, Sīha, some person dwells with his mind obsessed by sensual lust... obsessed by ill will... obsessed by dullness and torpor... obsessed by restlessness and remorse... obsessed by doubt, overwhelmed by doubt, and he does not understand as it really is the escape from the arisen doubt. When he encounters an object that provokes sensual lust, his mind becomes full of lust... [and so on]... He does not understand as it really is the escape from the arisen sensual lust. This, Sīha, is called a person like a goat. And how, Sīha, is one a person like a lion? Here, Sīha, some person dwells with his mind unobsessed by sensual lust, undeluded regarding sensual lust, and he understands as it really is the escape from the arisen sensual lust. When he encounters an object that provokes aversion, his mind does not become full of hate... [and so on]... He understands as it really is the escape from the arisen ill will. This, Sīha, is called a person like a lion. These, Sīha, are the four kinds of persons found existing in the world. [Then the Venerable Sāriputta said to the Venerable Ānanda: “Friend Ānanda, when the Blessed One was teaching the Dhamma to the Licchavi Sīha, did he not speak in praise of the person like a lion? “Yes, friend, when the Blessed One was teaching the Dhamma to the Licchavi Sīha, he spoke in praise of the person like a lion. “Friend Ānanda, just as the Blessed One has spoken in praise of the person like a lion, so too, when the Tathāgata teaches the Dhamma to others, he speaks in praise of the person like a lion. For what reason? Because the Tathāgata himself is a person like a lion. [Then the Venerable Sāriputta said to the Venerable Ānanda: “Friend Ānanda, when the Blessed One was teaching the Dhamma to the Licchavi Sīha, did he not speak in praise of the person like a lion? “Yes, friend, when the Blessed One was teaching the Dhamma to the Licchavi Sīha, he spoke in praise of the person like a lion. “Friend Ānanda, just as the Blessed One has spoken in praise of the person like a lion, so too, when the Tathāgata teaches the Dhamma to others, he speaks in praise of the person like a lion. For what reason? Because the Tathāgata himself is a person like a lion. [Then the Venerable Sāriputta said to the Venerable Ānanda:

“Friend Ānanda, when the Blessed One was teaching the Dhamma to the Licchavi Sīha, did he not speak in praise of the person like a lion? “Yes, friend, when the Blessed One was teaching the Dhamma to the Licchavi Sīha, he spoke in praise of the person like a lion. “Friend Ānanda, just as the Blessed One has spoken in praise of the person like a lion, so too, when the Tathāgata teaches the Dhamma to others, he speaks in praise of the person like a lion. For what reason? Because the Tathāgata himself is a person like a lion. For what reason? Because the Tathāgata himself is a person like a lion. For what reason? Because the Tathāgata himself is a person like a lion.
