For what reason? Because the Tathāgata himself is a person like a lion. [Then the Venerable Sāriputta said to the Venerable Ānanda: “Friend Ānanda, when the Blessed One was teaching the Dhamma to the Licchavi Sīha, did he not speak in praise of the person like a lion? “Yes, friend, when the Blessed One was teaching the Dhamma to the Licchavi Sīha, he spoke in praise of the person like a lion. “Friend Ānanda, just as the Blessed One has spoken in praise of the person like a lion, so too, when the Tathāgata teaches the Dhamma to others, he speaks in praise of the person like a lion. For what reason? Because the Tathāgata himself is a person like a lion. [Then the Venerable Sāriputta said to the Venerable Ānanda: “Friend Ānanda, when the Blessed One was teaching the Dhamma to the Licchavi Sīha, did he not speak in praise of the person like a lion? “Yes, friend, when the Blessed One was teaching the Dhamma to the Licchavi Sīha, he spoke in praise of the person like a lion. “Friend Ān
On one occasion the Blessed One was dwelling at Vesālī in the Great Wood, in the Gabled Hall.

Then Sīha the general approached the Blessed One; having approached, he paid homage to the Blessed One and sat down to one side. As he was sitting there, Sīha the general said this to the Blessed One:
“Is it possible, Bhante, for the Blessed One to point out the visible fruit of giving?”
“It is possible, Sīha,” the Blessed One said.
“A donor, Sīha, a master of giving, is dear and pleasing to many people.
That a donor, Sīha, a master of giving, is dear and pleasing to many people—this too is a visible fruit of giving.”
Furthermore, Sīha, virtuous and noble persons associate with a donor, a master of giving. That, Sīha, is a visible fruit of giving.
Furthermore, Sīha, a good reputation for the donor, the master of giving, spreads abroad.
Furthermore, Sīha, that a good reputation for the donor, the master of giving, spreads abroad— this too is a visible fruit of giving.
Furthermore, Sīha, whatever assembly a donor, a master of giving, approaches— whether an assembly of kṣatriyas,
or an assembly of brahmins, or an assembly of householders, or an assembly of ascetics— he approaches it confident and self-assured.
Furthermore, Sīha, when a donor, a master of giving, approaches whatever assembly—
whether an assembly of kṣatriyas, brahmins, householders, or ascetics—
he approaches it confidently and without timidity; this too is a visible fruit of giving.
"Furthermore, Sīha, a donor, a master of giving, with the breakup of the body, after death, reappears in a happy destination, in a heavenly world.
That a donor, a master of giving, with the breakup of the body, after death, reappears in a happy destination, in a heavenly world—this, Sīha, is the fruit of giving pertaining to the future life.
When this was said, the general Sīha said this to the Blessed One:

“Venerable sir, regarding these four fruits of giving that are visible here and now which have been declared by the Blessed One, I do not proceed there by faith in the Blessed One; I know them myself.
Venerable sir, I am a donor, a master of generosity, dear and pleasing to many people.
Venerable sir, I am a donor, a master of generosity; virtuous true persons associate with me.”
“Venerable sir, I am a donor, a master of giving; a fine reputation for me has spread abroad: ‘Sīha the general is a donor, a benefactor, and an attendant upon the Saṅgha.
Venerable sir, as a donor and master of giving, whenever I approach any assembly—whether an assembly of kṣatriyas, brahmins, householders, or ascetics—I approach it confident and self-assured.”

“Venerable sir, regarding these four fruits of giving that are visible here and now which have been declared by the Blessed One, I do not follow them out of faith in the Blessed One; I know them for myself.
But as for what the Blessed One said to me:

‘Sīha, a donor, a master of giving, with the breakup of the body, after death, reappears in a happy destination, in a heavenly world’—this I do not know; it is in this regard that I follow the Blessed One out of faith.”
“So it is, Sīha; so it is, Sīha.
A donor, a master of giving, with the breakup of the body, after death, is reborn in a good destination, a heavenly world.
By giving, he becomes dear and many people resort to him.”
He attains fame and his reputation increases;
unconfused, he enters the assembly,
and the man who is free from stinginess becomes confident.
Therefore, indeed, the wise give gifts,
having removed the stain of stinginess and seeking happiness;
they are established for a long time in the realm of the Thirty-three.
Having made an opportunity for themselves and performed wholesome deeds, they rejoice upon reaching the company of the devas. Passing away from here,
self-luminous, they roam through the Nandana grove.
There they rejoice, delight, and exult,
fully endowed with the five strands of sensual pleasure,
having followed the word of the Unattached One, the Neutral One.
“The disciples of the Sugata rejoice in heaven.
Thus was the fourth [discourse]. Aṅguttara Nikāya 5.35.

4. Sumanavagga Dānānisaṁsasutta (AN 5.35, PTS AN iii 41) "Bhikkhus, there are these five benefits of giving. What five? One acquires wealth; one is dear and agreeable to many people; one has a good reputation; one dies unconfused; and after death, upon the dissolution of the body, one is reborn in a happy destination, in a heavenly world. These, bhikkhus, are the five benefits of giving."
“Bhikkhus, there are these five benefits of giving.
What are the five?
One becomes dear and agreeable to many people.”
One associates with noble and virtuous persons;
a fine reputation spreads abroad;
and one does not fall away from the duties of a householder.
With the breakup of the body, after death, one is reborn in a happy destination, a heavenly world.
These, monks, are the five benefits of giving.
One who gives becomes dear.
The sequence of the Dhamma of the virtuous;
the virtuous, self-restrained, and celibate ones always resort to it.
They teach him that Dhamma which dispels all suffering,
by knowing which Dhamma here—
“...attains final Nibbāna, free from taints.
The fifth. Aṅguttara Nikāya 5.36

4. Sumanavagga Kāladānasutta (AN 5.36, PTS AN iii 41) “Bhikkhus, there are these five timely gifts. What five? The gift to one who is suffering; the gift to one who is on a journey; the gift to one who is sick; the gift when about to die; and the gift given at the time of the Buddha’s appearance. These, bhikkhus, are the five timely gifts.”
“Bhikkhus, there are these five timely gifts.
What are the five?
One gives a gift to a newcomer;”
One gives a gift to one who is traveling;
one gives a gift to one who is ill;
one gives a gift during a famine.
Those very first-fruits and new crops, he establishes first among those who possess virtue.
"These, monks, are the five timely gifts.
The wise give at the proper time.
Generous and free from stinginess,
giving at the proper time to such noble ones who have become upright.
The merit of one who gives with a serene mind becomes vast;
so too for those who there rejoice in it.
Or perform services;
by that the offering is not deficient,
and they too partake in the merit.
Therefore, one should give with an unrelenting mind to where a gift yields great fruit;
for merits in the world beyond—
“They are a support for living beings.
The sixth [sutta]. Aṅguttara Nikāya 5.37

4. Sumanavagga Bhojanasutta (AN 5.37, PTS AN iii 42) “Monks, there are these five kinds of nutriment for beings who have come to be and for those seeking rebirth. What five? They are: physical food as nutriment, gross or subtle; contact as the second; mental volition as the third; consciousness as the fourth; and intellectual intention as the fifth. These, monks, are the five kinds of nutriment for beings who have come to be and for those seeking rebirth.”
“Monks, when a donor gives food, he gives five things to the recipients.
What are the five?
He gives life; he gives beauty; he gives happiness; he gives strength; he gives eloquence.”
Furthermore, by giving long life, one becomes a partaker of long life, whether divine or human;
by giving beauty, one becomes a partaker of beauty, whether divine or human;
by giving happiness, one becomes a partaker of happiness, whether divine or human.
"By giving strength, one becomes a partaker of strength, whether divine or human;
by giving inspired eloquence, one becomes a partaker of inspired eloquence, whether divine or human.
Monks, when a donor gives food, they give these five things to the recipients."
The wise one is a giver of life, a giver of strength,
a giver of beauty, and a giver of eloquence;
the intelligent one is a giver of happiness.
He attains happiness.
Having bestowed longevity, strength,
beauty, happiness, and eloquence;
“He becomes long-lived and famous wherever he is reborn.
Thus ends the seventh [sutta].

Aṅguttara Nikāya 5.38 4. Sumanavagga Saddha Sutta: To Saddha “Bhikkhus, there are these five kinds of persons found existing in the world. What five? The person who is intent on his own welfare but not on the welfare of others; the person who is intent on the welfare of others but not on his own welfare; the person who is intent neither on his own welfare nor on the welfare of others; and the person who is intent both on his own welfare and on the welfare of others. And how, bhikkhus, is a person intent on his own welfare but not on the welfare of others? Here, someone practices for his own affliction and does not practice for the affliction of others; he experiences suffering and does not cause others to experience suffering; he is harmed and does not harm others; he grieves and does not cause others to grieve. This is called a person intent on his own welfare but not on the welfare of others. And how, bhikkhus, is a person intent on the welfare of others but not on his own welfare? Here, someone practices for the affliction of others and does not practice for his own affliction; he causes others to experience suffering and does not experience suffering himself; he harms others and is not harmed himself; he causes others to grieve and does not grieve himself. This is called a person intent on the welfare of others but not on his own welfare. And how, bhikkhus, is a person intent neither on his own welfare nor on the welfare of others? Here, someone practices for his own affliction and practices for the affliction of others; he experiences suffering and causes others to experience suffering; he is harmed and harms others; he grieves and causes others to grieve. This is called a person intent neither on his own welfare nor on the welfare of others. And how, bhikkhus, is a person intent both on his own welfare and on the welfare of others? Here, someone practices neither for his own affliction nor for the affliction of others; he does not experience suffering and does not cause others to experience suffering; he is not harmed and does not harm others; he does not grieve and does not cause others to grieve. This is called a person intent both on his own welfare and on the welfare of others. These, bhikkhus, are the five kinds of persons found existing in the world.”
“Bhikkhus, there are these five benefits for a clansman who has faith. What are the five? [AN 5.38, PTS AN iii 42]”
"Bhikkhus, those who are the good persons existing in the world first show compassion toward the person of faith, not so toward the person lacking faith;
they first approach the person of faith, not so the person lacking faith;
they first accept gifts from the person of faith, not so from the person lacking faith."
When teaching the Dhamma, they teach it first to one who has faith, not to one who lacks faith;
for the faithful person, with the breakup of the body after death, is reborn in a happy destination, in a heavenly world.
These, monks, are the five benefits for a clansman who has faith.
"Just as, monks, a great banyan tree on level ground at a crossroads is a refuge for birds from all sides,
even so, monks, a clansman endowed with faith is a refuge for many people— monks, nuns, laymen, and laywomen.
Endowed with branches, leaves, and fruit..."
Just as a great tree with a sturdy trunk,
possessing roots and abundant fruit,
becomes a refuge for birds.
In that delightful abode,
birds resort to it;
those seeking shade go to its shade.
Those who seek the fruit and subsist on the fruit—
just so is the person endowed with virtue and possessed of faith.
One who is humble in conduct, free from arrogance,
gentle, kindly, and mild—
such a person is free from lust and free from hatred.
Free from delusion and without taints—
such a person as this, a field of merit in the world,
the wise attend upon.
They teach him that Dhamma which dispels all suffering, that Dhamma which he,
having understood here in this world, [realizes].
“...attains final Nibbāna, free from taints.
Thus was the eighth [discourse]. Aṅguttara Nikāya 5.39.

4. Sumanavagga Puttasutta (AN 5.39, PTS AN iii 43) “Monks, there are these five benefits for a mother and father in having a son. What five? ‘May he support us when we are old,’ this is the first benefit for a mother and father in having a son. ‘May he perform meritorious deeds on our behalf after we have passed away,’ this is the second benefit for a mother and father in having a son. ‘When we are deceased, may he cause offerings to be made in our name,’ this is the third benefit for a mother and father in having a son. ‘May his lineage endure long,’ this is the fourth benefit for a mother and father in having a son. ‘May he, being well-established in virtue, attain heaven,’ this is the fifth benefit for a mother and father in having a son. These, monks, are the five benefits for a mother and father in having a son.”
“Bhikkhus, seeing five grounds, parents desire a son to be born into their family.
What are the five?
‘He will support us when we are supported by him;”
He will perform his duty;
the family lineage will endure for a long time;
he will take up his inheritance.
Or else, "he will provide offerings for the deceased ancestors who have passed away.
Monks, it is seeing these five conditions that parents desire a son to be born into their family.
Seeing these five conditions—
The wise desire a son, thinking:
"He will support us when we are supported by him,
or he will perform our duties."
May the family lineage endure for long,
may it receive its inheritance;
or else, for the sake of the departed—
They will provide the sacrificial fee.
Seeing these grounds,
the wise desire a son.
Therefore, the virtuous and true persons,
grateful and appreciative of what has been done for them,
support their mother and father.
Recalling what was done in the past,
they perform services for them,
just as one would for those who have previously rendered service.
One who follows advice, supports those who maintain him,
and does not let the family lineage perish—
being faithful and endowed with virtue.
“Is a praiseworthy son. Thus [ends] the ninth [sutta].
Aṅguttara Nikāya 5.40

4. Sumanavagga Mahāsālaputtasutta (AN 5.40, PTS AN iii 44) “Bhikkhus, there are these five kinds of sons found existing in the world. What five? The son who is a burden-bearer; the son who is a destroyer of wealth; the son who is a continuer of the family line; the son who is a benefactor; and the son who is a doer of good deeds. And how, bhikkhus, is a son a burden-bearer? Here, bhikkhus, a mother and father have provided for a son, thinking: ‘May he provide for us when we are old, decrepit, and past our prime. But when that son, having been provided for by his parents, does not provide for them when they are old, decrepit, and past their prime, he is called a son who is a burden-bearer. And how, bhikkhus, is a son a destroyer of wealth? Here, bhikkhus, a mother and father have acquired wealth through great effort and exertion. But that son squanders that wealth and does not preserve it. He is called a son who is a destroyer of wealth. And how, bhikkhus, is a son a continuer of the family line? Here, bhikkhus, a mother and father have acquired wealth through great effort and exertion. That son preserves that wealth and does not squander it. He is called a son who is a continuer of the family line. And how, bhikkhus, is a son a benefactor? Here, bhikkhus, a mother and father have done much that is unwholesome, harmful, and blameworthy. But that son establishes them in wholesome states, saying: ‘Do this; do not do that. He is called a son who is a benefactor. And how, bhikkhus, is a son a doer of good deeds? Here, bhikkhus, a mother and father have done much that is unwholesome, harmful, and blameworthy. But that son, having established them in wholesome states, leads them to a state of heavenly rebirth after death. He is called a son who is a doer of good deeds. These, bhikkhus, are the five kinds of sons found existing in the world.”
“Bhikkhus, depending on Himavanta, the king of mountains, great sāl trees grow by way of five kinds of growth.
By what five?
They grow by way of branches, leaves, and foliage;”
They grow by the heartwood; they grow by the inner bark;
they grow by the softwood.
They grow by means of the heartwood.
Monks, depending on the Himalayas, the king of mountains, great sal trees grow by these five kinds of growth.
In the same way, monks, depending on a clansman endowed with faith, the members of his household grow by five kinds of growth.
By which five?
He grows in faith;
he grows in virtue;
One grows through learning;
one grows through generosity;
one grows through wisdom.
“Bhikkhus, it is by depending on a clansman endowed with faith that the household members grow through these five kinds of growth.
For just as a rocky mountain in the wilderness, in a vast forest,”
Those forest trees grow by depending on that tree; even so,
those endowed with virtue [grow].
By relying upon this faithful son of noble family,
his children, wife, and kinsmen all flourish.
The ministers, the circle of kinsmen, and those who depend upon him—
all these follow the virtue of that virtuous man.
Seeing generosity and good conduct,
those who possess true insight practice them accordingly.
Having practiced the Dhamma here,
the path leading to a happy destination,
they rejoice in the world of the gods.
“Those who desire sensual pleasures rejoice.
Tenth. The fourth chapter, the Sumanavagga.
Its summary verse (uddāna) is:
Sumanā, Cundī, Uggaha,
Sīha, and Dānānisamsaka.
Faith in eating at the proper time—
these ten, O son, are your salaries.
(Aṅguttara Nikāya 5.41)

5. Muṇḍarājavagga Ādiyasutta (The Discourse on the Sun) At Sāvatthī. “Bhikkhus, suppose there were a man who, having gone to the Himalayas, the king of mountains, would cut down a great tree standing at its very peak. Having cut it down, he would split it into logs. Having split it into logs, he would carry them away on his head. Having carried them away on his head, he would dry them in the wind and sun. Having dried them in the wind and sun, he would burn them in a fire. Having burned them in a fire, he would reduce them to ashes. Having reduced them to ashes, he would winnow them in a high wind or let them be carried away by a swift current of water. “Now, bhikkhus, do you see that great tree standing at the very peak of the Himalayas, the king of mountains? “Yes, venerable sir. “That great tree, bhikkhus, has been completely destroyed, cut off at the root, made like a palm stump, obliterated so that it is no more subject to future arising. Even so, bhikkhus, when a noble disciple has abandoned ignorance, severed it at the root, made it like a palm stump, obliterated it so that it is no more subject to future arising; and when he has acquired knowledge, he is said to be one who has ‘risen above,’ one who has ‘gone beyond,’ one who has ‘surpassed’ the world. (This is the first sutta in the Muṇḍarājavagga.)
On one occasion the Blessed One was dwelling at Sāvatthī in Jeta’s Grove, Anāthapiṇḍika’s monastery.
Then the householder Anāthapiṇḍika approached the Blessed One;
having approached, he paid homage to the Blessed One and sat down to one side. As the householder Anāthapiṇḍika was sitting to one side, the Blessed One said this to him:
“Householder, there are these five ways of acquiring wealth.
What are the five?

Here, householder, with wealth acquired by energetic striving, amassed by the strength of his arms, earned by the sweat of his brow—righteous wealth, righteously gained—a noble disciple makes himself happy and pleased, and maintains himself in comfort;”
He comforts, satisfies, and properly provides for the well-being of his mother and father;
he comforts, satisfies, and properly provides for the well-being of his children, wife, slaves, laborers, and servants.
This is the first source of wealth.

Furthermore, householder, with wealth acquired through exertion and energy, gathered by the strength of his arms, earned by sweat, righteous, and righteously obtained, the noble disciple comforts, gladdens, and properly maintains his friends and companions in happiness.
This is the second source of wealth.
Furthermore, householder, with wealth acquired through exertion and energy, gathered by the strength of his arms, earned by sweat, righteous, and righteously obtained, there may be those calamities—
From fire, or from water, or from kings, or from thieves, or from unloved heirs—
from such calamities as these, he conducts himself by safeguarding his wealth and ensures his own safety.
This is the third source of wealth.

Furthermore, householder, with wealth acquired by energetic striving, amassed by the strength of his arms, earned by the sweat of his brow, righteous wealth righteously gained, the noble disciple makes the five offerings:
the offering to relatives, the offering to guests, the offering to the departed, the offering to the king, and the offering to the deities.
This is the fourth source of wealth.
Furthermore, householder, with wealth acquired by energetic striving,

amassed by the strength of his arms, earned by the sweat of his brow— righteous wealth, righteously gained— the noble disciple supports those ascetics and brahmins who abstain from intoxication and negligence,
who are established in patience and gentleness, and who tame themselves alone, calm themselves alone, and bring themselves alone to final Nibbāna.
In such ascetics and brahmins, one establishes an uplifting offering that leads to heaven, has a pleasant result, and conduces to rebirth in the celestial realms.
This is the fifth source of wealth.
These, householder, are the five sources of wealth.
If, householder, these five ways of acquiring wealth are pursued by that noble disciple and his wealth comes to exhaustion, it occurs to him:
"Those ways of acquiring wealth that I have pursued, those very ways I am pursuing, and my wealth is coming to exhaustion.
Thus, he is without remorse.
If, householder, these five ways of acquiring wealth are adopted by that noble disciple and his wealth increases, it occurs to him:
"Indeed, those ways of acquiring wealth that I have adopted have resulted in my wealth increasing.
Thus, he is free from remorse in both respects.
Wealth has been enjoyed, servants have been supported,
and I have overcome all calamities;
lofty sacrificial gifts have been bestowed by me.
Furthermore, they have performed the fivefold offerings;
they are established in virtue,
self-restrained, and living the holy life.
Whatever purpose for wealth a wise person living at home might desire—
that purpose has been attained by me.
Having done what causes no regret,
a mortal man, standing firm in the Dhamma of the Noble Ones, should keep this in mind.
"Right here they praise him,
and after passing away, he rejoices in heaven.
Thus ends the first [verse].

Aṅguttara Nikāya 5.42 5. Muṇḍarājavagga Sappurisasutta — The True Person “Monks, there are these five qualities of a true person. What five? Here, monks, a true person is virtuous, endowed with virtuous conduct; he dwells restrained by the restraint of the Pātimokkha, possessed of proper behavior and resort, seeing danger in even the slightest faults; having undertaken the training rules, he trains in them. Furthermore, monks, a true person is learned, possessing the Dhamma; he has retained the teachings in mind, accumulated them through recitation, and investigated them with his mind, even those teachings that are deep, profound, transcendent, and connected with the fundamentals of the holy life. Furthermore, monks, a true person is one who has entered the stream, not subject to perdition, fixed in destiny, and assured of enlightenment. Furthermore, monks, a true person is an attainer of the four jhānas—states of sublime happiness in the present life, which are realized by oneself through direct knowledge and dwell therein. Furthermore, monks, a true person, with the destruction of the taints, realizes for himself with direct knowledge, in this very life, the taintless liberation of mind and liberation by wisdom, and having attained it, dwells therein. These, monks, are the five qualities of a true person.”
“Monks, when a true person is born into a family, he is for the welfare, benefit, and happiness of many people;
he is for the welfare, benefit, and happiness of his mother and father.”
It leads to the welfare, benefit, and happiness of one's children and spouse;
it leads to the welfare, benefit, and happiness of one's slaves, laborers, and servants;
it leads to the welfare, benefit, and happiness of one's friends and colleagues.
It leads to the welfare, benefit, and happiness of recluses and brahmins.
Just as, monks, a great rain cloud, bringing all crops to fruition, leads to the welfare, benefit, and happiness of many people;
even so, monks, a true person, being born into a family, leads to the welfare, benefit, and happiness of many people.
It leads to the welfare, benefit, and happiness of one's mother and father;
it leads to the welfare, benefit, and happiness of one's wife and children;
it leads to the welfare, benefit, and happiness of one's slaves, laborers, and servants.
"It leads to the welfare, benefit, and happiness of friends and companions;
it leads to the welfare, benefit, and happiness of ascetics and brahmins.
Having practiced for the benefit of many, he acquired wealth.
The deities protect him who is guarded by the Dhamma;
fame does not desert the one of great learning, endowed with virtue and conduct,
who stands firm in the Dhamma.
One who stands firm in the Dhamma, endowed with virtue,
truthful in speech, and possessed of a sense of shame—
like a gem from the Jambu River—
Who is worthy to censure him?
Even the gods praise him;
he has been praised even by Brahmā.
The Second.
Aṅguttara Nikāya 5.43 5.
Muṇḍarājavagga (The Chapter on King Muṇḍa)
The Discourse on the Desired (Iṭṭhasutta).
Then the householder Anāthapiṇḍika approached the Blessed One; having approached, he [approached] the Blessed One.
Having paid homage, he sat down to one side. As the householder Anāthapiṇḍika was sitting there, the Blessed One said this to him:
"Householder, there are these five things that are desirable, lovely, pleasing, and rare in the world.
Which five?"
"Householder Āyu, life is desirable, lovely, and pleasing, yet it is rare in the world;
beauty is desirable, lovely, and pleasing, yet it is rare in the world;
happiness is desirable, lovely, and pleasing, yet it is rare in the world."
Fame is desirable, lovely, pleasing, and rare in the world;
heavenly realms are desirable, lovely, pleasing, and rare in the world.
These, householder, are the five things that are desirable, lovely, pleasing, and rare in the world.
“Householder, I do not say that the acquisition of these five things—desirable, lovely, and agreeable, yet difficult to obtain in the world—is due to prayer or aspiration.

Householder, if the acquisition of these five things—desirable, lovely, and agreeable, yet difficult to obtain in the world—were indeed due to prayer or aspiration, who here would be deprived by whom?”
"Householder, it is not fitting for a noble disciple to pray for life or to delight in life, nor even for the sake of life.
Householder, a noble disciple who desires long life should practice the way that leads to long life;
for when one has practiced the way that leads to long life, it conduces to the attainment of long life."
Thus he becomes a recipient of long life, whether divine or human.
But, householder, a noble disciple who desires beauty should not pray for beauty, nor should he delight in it, nor even for the sake of beauty itself.
A noble disciple who desires beauty, householder, should practice the way that leads to beauty.
For the practice he has undertaken leads to the acquisition of beauty;
he becomes a possessor of beauty, whether divine or human.
But, householder, a noble disciple who desires happiness ought not to pray for happiness, nor rejoice in it, nor even for the sake of happiness.
Householder, a noble disciple who desires happiness should practice the way that leads to happiness;
for when one has practiced the way that leads to happiness, it conduces to the attainment of happiness.
Such a person becomes a recipient of happiness, whether divine or human.
“Householder, a noble disciple who desires fame should not entreat for fame, nor should he rejoice in it, nor should he act for the sake of fame.
Householder, a noble disciple who desires fame should practice the way that leads to fame.
For when one has practiced the way that leads to fame, it conduces to the attainment of fame.”
Thus he becomes a recipient of fame, whether divine or human.
But, householder, a noble disciple who desires heaven should not pray for heaven, nor should he rejoice in it, nor even for the sake of heavens.
A noble disciple who desires heaven, householder, should practice the path that leads to heaven.
For the practice he has undertaken leads to the attainment of heaven;
thus he becomes a winner of heavenly realms.
Longevity, beauty, fame, and renown—
Seeking heaven, birth in a high-born family,
and successive, sublime delights.
The wise praise heedfulness in the performance of meritorious deeds;
being heedful, one achieves both goals.
The wise person grasps that which is beneficial both in this present life and that which is beneficial for the future life.
The steadfast one who has realized the goal is called "wise. Thus ends the third [verse].

Aṅguttara Nikāya 5.44 5. Muṇḍarājavagga Manāpadāyīsutta The Discourse on the Giver of What is Dear “Monks, there are these five kinds of persons found existing in the world. What five? The one who gives what is dear; the one who gives what is not dear; the one who gives both what is dear and what is not dear; the one who gives neither what is dear nor what is not dear;

and the one who gives what is dear and what is not dear, and who, when asked, speaks thus: ‘Give this to me; give that to me. And how, monks, is one a person who gives what is dear? Here, monks, someone gives to a bhikkhu robes, almsfood, lodgings, and medicinal requisites for the sick. But he does not give these things to him because he is virtuous, of good character, learned, an observer of the training, one who has entered the stream, or one who has attained the fruit of stream-entry; nor does he give them because he is a once-returner, a non-returner, an arahant, or one who has attained the fruit of arahantship. Rather, it is because of affection, endearment, love, and intimacy that he gives these things to him. This, monks, is called a person who gives what is dear. And how, monks, is one a person who gives what is not dear? Here, monks, someone gives to a bhikkhu robes, almsfood, lodgings, and medicinal requisites for the sick. But he does not give these things to him because of affection, endearment, love, or intimacy; rather, it is because he is angry, displeased, resentful, or malicious toward him that he gives these things to him. This, monks, is called a person who gives what is not dear. And how, monks, is one a person who gives both what is dear and what is not dear? Here, monks, someone gives to a bhikkhu robes, almsfood, lodgings, and medicinal requisites for the sick. He gives some of these things because of affection, endearment, love, and intimacy, and he gives other things because he is angry, displeased, resentful, or malicious toward him. This, monks, is called a person who gives both what is dear and what is not dear. And how, monks, is one a person who gives neither what is dear nor what is not dear? Here, monks, someone gives to a bhikkhu robes, almsfood, lodgings, and medicinal requisites for the sick. He gives these things neither because of affection, endearment, love, and intimacy, nor because he is angry, displeased, resentful, or malicious toward him. Rather, it is with the thought: ‘This bhikkhu is worthy of gifts, worthy of hospitality, worthy of offerings, worthy of reverential salutation, an unsurpassed field of merit for the world,’ that he gives these things to him. This, monks, is called a person who gives neither what is dear nor what is not dear. And how, monks, is one a person who gives what is dear and what is not dear, and who, when asked, speaks thus: ‘Give this to me; give that to me’? Here, monks, someone gives to a bhikkhu robes, almsfood, lodgings, and medicinal requisites for the sick. He gives some of these things because of affection, endearment, love, and intimacy, and he gives other things because he is angry, displeased, resentful, or malicious toward him. And when asked, he speaks thus: ‘Give this to me; give that to me. This, monks, is called a person who gives what is dear and what is not dear, and who, when asked, speaks thus: ‘Give this to me; give that to me. These, monks, are the five kinds of persons found existing in the world.”
(AN 5.44, PTS AN iii 49) On one occasion the Blessed One was dwelling at Vesālī in the Great Wood, in the Gabled Hall. Then,
having dressed in the morning and taken his bowl and robe, the Blessed One went to the residence of the householder Ugga of Vesālī and, having arrived, sat down on the prepared seat.
Then the householder Ugga of Vesālī approached the Blessed One;
having approached and paid homage to the Blessed One, he sat down to one side. As he was sitting there, the householder Ugga of Vesālī said this to the Blessed One:

"Venerable sir, I have heard this in the presence of the Blessed One; I have received it directly from the Blessed One: [that the Tathāgata does not predict the future destiny of those who die while his teaching is being spoken]."
“One who gives what is pleasing receives what is pleasing.
Venerable sir, I have this pleasing *sālapupphaka* food;
may the Blessed One accept it out of compassion for me.
The Blessed One accepted it out of compassion.
"Bhante, I have heard this directly from the Blessed One; I have received it directly from the Blessed One:
'One who gives what is pleasing receives what is pleasing.'"
“Venerable sir, I have some pleasant pork with well-prepared jujube fruits;
may the Blessed One accept it out of compassion.
The Blessed One accepted it out of compassion.
“Bhante, I have heard this directly from the Blessed One and received it directly from him:
‘One who gives what is pleasing receives what is pleasing. Bhante, this oil-cake and nāḷika-vegetable that has appeared to me is indeed pleasing.”
“May the Blessed One accept it from me out of compassion.
The Blessed One accepted it out of compassion.
“Venerable sir, I have heard this directly from the Blessed One; I have received it directly from him:”
“One who gives what is pleasing receives what is pleasing.
“Venerable sir, I have rice porridge that is pleasing to me—free of black grains and served with many soups and many curries.
May the Blessed One accept it out of compassion for me.”
The Blessed One accepted it out of compassion.
"Venerable sir, I have heard this directly from the Blessed One, I have received it directly from him:
'One who gives what is pleasing receives what is pleasing.'"
“Venerable sir, these lovely Kāsī garments are mine;
may the Blessed One accept them out of compassion.
The Blessed One accepted them out of compassion.
“Venerable sir, I have heard this directly from the Blessed One, I have received it directly from the Blessed One:
‘One who gives what is pleasing receives what is pleasing.

Venerable sir, my couch is pleasing, spread with a woolen coverlet embroidered with flowers, spread with a white woolen coverlet, covered with an excellent antelope-hide rug, provided with a canopy above, and with red cushions at both ends.”
Moreover, venerable sir, we also know this:
"This is not permissible for the Blessed One.
Venerable sir, this sandalwood plank of mine is worth more than one hundred thousand [pieces of gold].
“May the Blessed One accept it from me out of compassion.
The Blessed One accepted it out of compassion.
Then the Blessed One expressed his appreciation to Ugga the householder of Vesālī with this verse of thanksgiving:
“One who gives what is pleasing obtains what is pleasing,
he who gives with devotion to those who have become upright:
clothing, bedding, food, and drink.”
Having understood that the Arahants are like a field— wherein various kinds of requisites, whether given up, released, or not yet accepted— are like seeds sown in fertile soil.
“Thus, having given what is difficult to give, the person of integrity receives what is pleasing.
Then the Blessed One, having expressed this thanksgiving to Ugga the householder of Vesālī, rose from his seat and departed.
Then, after some time, the householder Ugga of Vesālī passed away.
Having passed away, the householder Ugga of Vesālī was reborn in a certain mind-made body.
At that time, the Blessed One was dwelling at Sāvatthī in Jeta’s Grove, Anāthapiṇḍika’s monastery.
Then, when the night had advanced, the young deva Ugga, of surpassing beauty, illuminating the entire Jeta’s Grove, approached the Blessed One.
Having approached, he paid homage to the Blessed One and stood to one side.
As he was standing there, the Blessed One said this to the young deva Ugga:
“Is it as you intended, Uggata?
“Truly, Blessed One, it is as I intended.
Then the Blessed One addressed the young deva Uggata with verses:
“One who gives what is pleasing receives what is pleasing;
one who gives the best receives the best in turn;
one who gives what is excellent becomes a recipient of excellence.”
The giver of the best attains the best state.
That man who is a giver of the foremost, a giver of the excellent, and a giver of the best—
"He becomes long-lived and renowned wherever he is reborn. Thus ends the fourth [sutta].

Aṅguttara Nikāya 5.45 5. Muṇḍarājavagga Puññābhisanda Sutta: The Overflowing of Merit “Monks, there are these five kinds of overflowing of merit, overflowing of the wholesome, which bring great fruit and great benefit, lead to what is wished for, desired, and agreeable, and result in happiness. What five? First, monks, a noble disciple possesses unwavering confidence in the Buddha: ‘The Blessed One is an arahant, perfectly enlightened, accomplished in true knowledge and conduct, fortunate, knower of the world, unsurpassed leader of persons to be tamed, teacher of devas and humans, the Buddha, the Blessed One. Second, monks, a noble disciple possesses unwavering confidence in the Dhamma: ‘The Dhamma is well-expounded by the Blessed One, directly visible, immediate, inviting one to come and see, applicable, to be personally realized by the wise. Third, monks, a noble disciple possesses unwavering confidence in the Saṅgha: ‘The Saṅgha of the Blessed One’s disciples is practicing the good way, practicing the straight way, practicing the true way, practicing the proper way; that is, the four pairs of persons, the eight types of individuals. This Saṅgha of the Blessed One’s disciples is worthy of gifts, worthy of hospitality, worthy of offerings, worthy of reverential salutation, the unsurpassed field of merit for the world. Fourth, monks, a noble disciple possesses the virtues dear to the noble ones—virtues that are untorn, unbroken, unspotted, unsplattered, liberating, praised by the wise, not clung to, leading to concentration. Fifth, monks, a noble disciple possesses wisdom regarding rise and fall, which is noble and penetrative, leading to the complete destruction of suffering. These, monks, are the five kinds of overflowing of merit, overflowing of the wholesome, which bring great fruit and great benefit, lead to what is wished for, desired, and agreeable, and result in happiness.”

“Bhikkhus, there are these five outflows of merit, outflows of the wholesome, nutriments of happiness, leading to heaven, ripening in happiness, conducive to heaven; they lead to what is desirable, beloved, agreeable, beneficial, and pleasant. What are the five? [The text continues with the five specific meritorious actions.]”
“Monks, when a monk, while using a robe, enters and dwells in a measureless concentration of mind,
for him there is a measureless outflow of merit, an outflow of the wholesome, a nourishment of happiness— conducive to heaven,
with a happy result, leading to heaven; it conduces to what is desired, liked, agreeable, beneficial, and pleasant.”
“Monks, when a monk, while consuming almsfood... [and so on] ...when a monk, while consuming a dwelling... [and so on] ...when a monk, while consuming a bed and chair...

[and so on] ...when a monk, while consuming medicinal requisites for the sick, enters and dwells in a measureless concentration of mind, his influx of merit, his influx of the wholesome, is measureless; it is a source of happiness.”
It leads to heaven, has a pleasant result, and conduces to heaven; it leads to what is desirable, lovely, agreeable, beneficial, and pleasant.

These, monks, are the five outflows of merit, outflows of the wholesome, nourishments of happiness—leading to heaven, having a pleasant result, conducive to heaven—that lead to what is desirable, lovely, agreeable, beneficial, and pleasant.
And for a noble disciple endowed with these five outflows of merit, outflows of the wholesome, it is not easy to grasp the measure of his merit: [it is so vast that it cannot be measured].

‘So much is this mass of merit, this mass of the wholesome, a nourishment for happiness, leading to heaven, ripening in happiness, conducive to heaven; it leads to what is desirable, lovely, agreeable, beneficial, and pleasant.
Yet, monks, it is reckoned simply as an incalculable, immeasurable, great mass of merit.
Just as, monks, it is not easy to take the measure of the water in the great ocean:

‘So many *āḷhaka* measures of water, or so many hundreds of *āḷhaka* measures of water, or so many thousands of *āḷhaka* measures of water, or so many hundreds of thousands of *āḷhaka* measures of water’—rather, it is reckoned simply as an incalculable, immeasurable, great mass of water. Even so, monks, for a noble disciple endowed with these five floods of merit, floods of the wholesome, it is not easy to grasp the measure of his merit: [“So much merit has been produced by this noble disciple,” or “so much merit has been produced by that noble disciple. Rather, it is reckoned simply as an incalculable, immeasurable, great flood of merit. It is just like the great ocean, monks, which cannot be measured by saying, “It has so many *yojana* of length, so many *yojana* of width, so many *yojana* of depth,” or “it contains so many *āḷhaka* measures of water, so many hundreds of *āḷhaka* measures of water, so many thousands of *āḷhaka* measures of water, or so many hundreds of thousands of *āḷhaka* measures of water”—rather, it is reckoned simply as an incalculable, immeasurable, great mass of water.

Even so, monks, for a noble disciple endowed with these five floods of merit, floods of the wholesome, it is not easy to grasp the measure of his merit: [“So much merit has been produced by this noble disciple,” or “so much merit has been produced by that noble disciple. Rather, it is reckoned simply as an incalculable, immeasurable, great flood of merit. Why is that? Because, monks, the fruit of giving is great, the fruit of self-restraint is great, and the fruit of self-mastery is great.’”
‘Such an outflow of merit, an outflow of the wholesome— a nutriment for happiness, leading to heaven, ripening as happiness, conducive to heaven— that leads to what is desirable, lovely, agreeable,
beneficial, and pleasant’— this, indeed, is reckoned as an incalculable, immeasurable, great mass of merit.
It is like the great ocean, immeasurable, a vast lake.
Just as many rivers frequented by throngs of people flow toward the ocean— the source of many jewels and full of terrors— so do they enter it from all sides.
Thus, for a wise person who gives food, drink, and clothing,
and who is a donor of beds, seats, and coverlets,
streams of merit flow toward them.
"Just as rivers carrying water flow toward the ocean.
(The Fifth) Aṅguttara Nikāya 5.46

5. Muṇḍarājavagga Sampadāsutta (The Discourse on Accomplishment) “Monks, there are these four accomplishments. What four? The accomplishment of faith, the accomplishment of virtue, the accomplishment of learning, and the accomplishment of generosity. These, monks, are the four accomplishments.”
“Monks, there are these five accomplishments. What five?
Accomplishment in faith, accomplishment in virtue, accomplishment in learning, accomplishment in generosity, and accomplishment in wisdom.”
“Monks, these are the five accomplishments.
The sixth. *Aṅguttara Nikāya* 5.47
5. Muṇḍarājavagga Dhanasutta (AN 5.47, PTS AN iii 53) “Monks, there are these four kinds of wealth. What four?
The wealth of the noble, the wealth of the Dhamma, the wealth of merit, and the wealth of wisdom. These, monks, are the four kinds of wealth.”
“Monks, there are these five treasures. Which five?
The treasure of faith, the treasure of virtue, the treasure of learning, the treasure of generosity, and the treasure of wisdom.”
And what, monks, is the wealth of faith?
Here, monks, the noble disciple is endowed with faith; he has faith in the enlightenment of the Tathāgata:

"Thus indeed is that Blessed One: worthy, perfectly enlightened, accomplished in true knowledge and conduct, sublime, knower of the worlds, unsurpassed leader of persons to be tamed, teacher of gods and humans, the Buddha, the Blessed One."
This, monks, is called the wealth of faith.
And what, monks, is the wealth of virtue?
Here, monks, a noble disciple abstains from the destruction of life … [as before] … he abstains from the occasion for negligence consisting in fermented liquor, spirits, and intoxicants.
This, monks, is called the wealth of virtue.
And what, monks, is the wealth of learning?
Here, monks, a noble disciple is one of great learning... [as above] ...one who has well penetrated the view.
This, monks, is called the wealth of learning.
And what, monks, is the wealth of generosity?
Here, monks, a noble disciple dwells at home with a mind free from the stain of stinginess, open-handed, pure-palmed, delighting in relinquishment, devoted to giving, and fond of sharing.
This, monks, is called the wealth of generosity.
And what, monks, is the wealth of wisdom? Here, monks, a noble disciple is wise;
he possesses the wisdom that discerns arising and passing away, which is noble, penetrative, and leads to the complete destruction of suffering.
This, monks, is called the wealth of wisdom.
These, monks, are the five kinds of wealth.
For one who has faith in the Tathāgata...
It is immovable and well-established for one whose virtue is beautiful,
beloved by the noble ones, and praised.
He who has faith in the Saṅgha and whose vision is upright—
him they call "not poor."
His life is not in vain.
Therefore, faith and virtue,
serenity and the vision of the Dhamma—
The wise person should apply themselves,
remembering the teaching of the Buddhas.
Thus ends the seventh [verse].

Aṅguttara Nikāya 5.48 5. Muṇḍarājavagga Alabbhanīyaṭhānasutta (The Discourse on Impossibilities) “Monks, these five things are impossible and unattainable by a person who has gone forth. What five? ‘I shall live the holy life under the Blessed One, and I shall not attain final knowledge until I have reached the end of suffering’—this is impossible and unattainable for one who has great lust, great hatred, and great delusion. ‘I shall live the holy life under the Blessed One, and I shall not attain final knowledge until I have reached the end of suffering’—this is impossible and unattainable for one who is lazy, lacking in energy, and indolent. ‘I shall live the holy life under the Blessed One, and I shall not attain final knowledge until I have reached the end of suffering’—this is impossible and unattainable for one who is unmindful, lacking in clear comprehension, and with a wandering mind. ‘I shall live the holy life under the Blessed One, and I shall not attain final knowledge until I have reached the end of suffering’—this is impossible and unattainable for one who is unwise, lacking in discernment, and devoid of noble insight. ‘I shall live the holy life under the Blessed One, and I shall not attain final knowledge until I have reached the end of suffering’—this is impossible and unattainable for one who does not apply himself to the higher training in virtue, the higher training in concentration, and the higher training in wisdom. But, monks, it is possible and attainable for a person who has gone forth to live the holy life under the Blessed One and to attain final knowledge upon reaching the end of suffering, provided they are not possessed of great lust, great hatred, and great delusion; provided they are not lazy, lacking in energy, and indolent; provided they are not unmindful, lacking in clear comprehension, and with a wandering mind; provided they are not unwise, lacking in discernment, and devoid of noble insight; and provided they do apply themselves to the higher training in virtue, the higher training in concentration, and the higher training in wisdom.”

“Bhikkhus, there are these five things that cannot be obtained by a recluse or a brahmin, by a deva, by Māra, by Brahmā, or by anyone in the world. What are the five? [The text continues with the list.]”
‘May that which is subject to aging not age’— this is an impossible position for a recluse, or a brahmin, or a deva, or Māra, or Brahmā, or anyone in the world.

‘May that which is subject to illness not fall ill’ …pe… ‘May that which is subject to death not die’ … ‘May that which is subject to exhaustion not be exhausted’ … ‘May that which is subject to destruction not be destroyed’—
this is an impossible position for a recluse, or a brahmin, or a deva … [or anyone in the world].
or by Māra, or by Brahmā, or by anyone in the world.
For the uninstructed worldling, bhikkhus, that which is subject to aging grows old.
When that which is subject to aging has grown old, he does not reflect thus:
‘It is not only for me alone that what is subject to aging grows old; rather, for all beings—however far their coming and going, their passing away and rebirth—what is subject to aging grows old.

If I were to grieve, weary myself, lament, beat my breast, weep, fall into confusion, lose my appetite, and undergo physical disfigurement because of this aging that has come upon me, my work would also [be neglected].’
‘May they not prevail; may even my enemies be glad at heart, and may my friends be dejected.
Thus, when one who is subject to aging has grown old, he sorrows, languishes, and laments; he beats his breast and falls into confusion.
This, monks, is called:
“The uninstructed worldling, pierced by the poisonous arrow of sorrow, torments only himself.

Furthermore, monks, for the uninstructed worldling, that which is subject to sickness becomes sick; … [and so on] … that which is subject to death dies; … that which is subject to decay decays; … that which is subject to destruction is destroyed.
When that which is subject to destruction has been destroyed, he does not reflect thus:

‘It is not only for me alone that what is subject to destruction is destroyed; rather, for all beings—however far their coming and going, their passing away and reappearing—what is subject to destruction is destroyed.

If, when what is subject to destruction has been destroyed, I were to grieve, be weary, lament, beat my breast and weep, and fall into confusion, I would lose my appetite for food, and discoloration would come over my body.’
“Business affairs would not proceed; enemies would be elated, and friends would be dejected.
When that which is subject to destruction has perished, he sorrows, languishes, and laments; he beats his breast and falls into confusion.
This, monks, is called:
“The uninstructed worldling, pierced by the poisonous dart of sorrow, torments only himself.
But for the instructed noble disciple, monks, that which is subject to aging does indeed age.
When that which is subject to aging has aged, he reflects thus:”
‘It is not only for me alone that what is subject to aging grows old; rather, for all beings—however far their coming and going, their passing away and rebirth—what is subject to aging grows old.

If I were to grieve, become weary, lament, beat my breast, weep, fall into confusion, lose my appetite, and undergo physical disfigurement because of this aging that has come upon me, my work would also [come to naught].’
‘May they not prevail; may even my enemies be glad and my friends be sorrowful.
Thus, when one who is subject to aging has grown old, he does not grieve, does not weary, does not lament, does not beat his breast, and does not fall into confusion.
This, monks, is called:
‘The learned noble disciple has pulled out the poisonous arrow of sorrow, pierced by which the uninstructed worldling torments himself.
Free from sorrow and free from the arrow, the learned noble disciple brings himself to final Nibbāna.

Furthermore, monks, for the learned noble disciple, that which is subject to sickness becomes sick; ... [and so on] ... that which is subject to death dies; ... that which is subject to exhaustion is exhausted; ... that which is subject to destruction is destroyed.
Thus, when that which is subject to destruction has perished, he reflects:

"It is not only for me alone that what is subject to destruction has perished; rather, for all beings—however far their coming and going, their passing away and rebirth—what is subject to destruction has perished.
If I were to grieve, weary myself, lament, beat my breast, and weep over that which is subject to destruction having perished..."

‘I would weep, I would fall into confusion, my food would not agree with me, discoloration would come over my body, my work would not proceed, my enemies would be delighted, and my friends would be dejected.
Yet, when that which is subject to destruction has perished, he does not grieve, he does not waste away, he does not lament; he does not beat his breast and cry out, nor does he fall into confusion.
“Monks, this is called:
‘The learned noble disciple has pulled out the poisoned arrow of sorrow, by which the uninstructed worldling, when pierced, torments himself alone.
Free from sorrow and free from the arrow, the noble disciple causes himself to attain final Nibbāna.’”
“Monks, these five things are unobtainable by a recluse or a brahmin, by a deva, by Māra, by Brahmā, or by anyone in the world.
There is no gain here, even the slightest, through grieving or lamenting.”
Seeing him anxious and suffering,
his enemies become joyful;
but when the wise man, in times of calamity...
One who knows how to discern the meaning is not shaken;
seeing his face unchanged as before, his adversaries become distressed.
By means of prayer, incantation, well-spoken words,
by making offerings, or by tradition—
whenever and wherever one may obtain benefit through these means.
In such and such a way one should strive therein.
If one should understand that this goal is unattainable,
whether by oneself or by another;
“Without grieving, one should endure it, thinking:
‘What can I do now? Karma is firm.
(The eighth.)

Aṅguttara Nikāya 5.49 5. Muṇḍarājavagga Kosalasutta Thus have I heard. At one time the Blessed One was dwelling at Sāvatthī in Jeta’s Grove, Anāthapiṇḍika’s Park. Then King Pasenadi of Kosala approached the Blessed One, paid homage to him, and sat down to one side. As he was sitting there, King Pasenadi said to the Blessed One: “Venerable sir, I have heard this: ‘The ascetic Gotama does not acknowledge any recluse or brahmin as his equal. It would be good, venerable sir, if the Blessed One would clarify the meaning of this statement. “Great king, I do not say that all recluses and brahmins are my equals, nor do I say that none are my equals. I say that those recluses and brahmins who are similar in training to me are my equals; those who train differently from me are not my equals. “But how, venerable sir, are they similar in training to the Blessed One? “Great king, here a Tathāgata appears in the world, an arahant, perfectly enlightened... [the standard description of a Buddha] ...he teaches the Dhamma that is good in the beginning, good in the middle, and good in the end, with the right meaning and phrasing, and reveals the holy life in its fulfillment and purity.

“A householder or a householder’s son, having heard that Dhamma, acquires faith in the Tathāgata. Possessing that faith, he considers thus: ‘Household life is crowded and dusty; life gone forth is wide open. It is not easy, while living in a home, to lead the holy life utterly perfect and pure as a polished shell. Suppose I shave off my hair and beard, put on the yellow robe, and go forth from the home life into homelessness. “On a later occasion, abandoning a small or a large fortune, abandoning a small or a large circle of relatives, he shaves off his hair and beard, puts on the yellow robe, and goes forth from the home life into homelessness. “When he has thus gone forth, possessing the bhikkhu’s training and way of life, abandoning the killing of living beings, he abstains from killing living beings; with rod and weapon laid aside, gentle and kindly, he dwells compassionate toward all living beings. Abandoning the taking of what is not given, he abstains from taking what is not given; taking only what is given, expecting only what is given, by not stealing he dwells in purity. Abandoning unchastity, he lives a life of chastity, living apart, avoiding the village. Abandoning false speech, he abstains from false speech; he speaks truth, adheres to truth, is trustworthy and reliable, one who does not deceive the world. Abandoning divisive speech, he abstains from divisive speech; he does not repeat elsewhere what he has heard here in order to divide [those people] from these, nor does he repeat here what he has heard elsewhere in order to divide [these people] from those; thus he is one who reunites those who are divided, a promoter of unity, who enjoys concord, rejoices in concord, and delights in concord; he speaks words that promote concord. Abandoning harsh speech, he abstains from harsh speech; he speaks such words as are gentle, pleasing to the ear, and loveable, as go to the heart, are courteous, desired by many, and agreeable to many. Abandoning idle chatter, he abstains from idle chatter; he speaks at the right time, speaks what is true, speaks what is beneficial, speaks on the Dhamma and the discipline; at the right time he speaks such words as are worth recording, reasonable, moderate, and beneficial. “He abstains from injuring seeds and plants. He eats only once a day, abstaining from eating at night and outside the proper time. He avoids dancing, singing, music, and theatrical shows. He abstains from using garlands, scents, cosmetics, and adornments. He abstains from using high and luxurious beds and seats. He abstains from accepting gold and silver. He abstains from accepting raw grain. He abstains from accepting raw meat. He abstains from accepting women and girls. He abstains from accepting men and women slaves. He abstains from accepting goats and sheep. He abstains from accepting fowl and pigs. He abstains from accepting elephants, cattle, horses, and mares. He abstains from accepting fields and lands. He abstains from going on errands and running messages. He abstains from buying and selling. He abstains from false weights, false metals, and false measures. He abstains from cheating, deceiving, defrauding, and trickery. He abstains from wounding, murdering, binding, brigandage, plunder, and violence. “He becomes content with robes to protect his body and almsfood to sustain his belly. Wherever he goes, he takes only these with him. Just as a bird, wherever it flies, carries only its wings with it, so too, a bhikkhu becomes content with robes to protect his body and almsfood to sustain his belly. Wherever he goes, he takes only these with him. “Possessing this aggregate of virtue, he experiences within himself a blameless bliss that is born of virtue. “With the mind well-restrained by mindfulness, he abandons covetousness for the property of others and dwells with a heart free from covetousness; he purifies his mind from covetousness. Abandoning ill will and hatred, he dwells with a mind free from ill will, compassionate for the welfare of all living beings; he purifies his mind from ill will and hatred. Abandoning sloth and torpor, he dwells free from sloth and torpor, percipient of light, mindful and clearly comprehending; he purifies his mind from sloth and torpor. Abandoning restlessness and remorse, he dwells undisturbed, with a mind inwardly peaceful; he purifies his mind from restlessness and remorse. Abandoning doubt, he dwells having gone beyond doubt, unperplexed about wholesome states; he purifies his mind from doubt. “Having abandoned these five hindrances, defilements of the mind that weaken wisdom, secluded from sensual pleasures, secluded from unwholesome states, he enters upon and dwells in the first jhāna, which is accompanied by applied and sustained thought, with rapture and pleasure born of seclusion. With the stilling of applied and sustained thought, he enters upon and dwells in the second jhāna, which has self-confidence and singleness of mind without applied and sustained thought, with rapture and pleasure born of concentration. With the fading away as well of rapture, he dwells equanimous and, mindful and clearly comprehending, he experiences pleasure with the body; he enters upon and dwells in the third jhāna, of which the noble ones declare: ‘He is equanimous, mindful, one who dwells happily. With the abandoning of pleasure and pain, and with the previous disappearance of joy and grief, he enters upon and dwells in the fourth jhāna, which has neither-pain-nor-pleasure and purity of mindfulness due to equanimity. “When his mind is concentrated in this way, purified, cleansed, bright, flawless, rid of corruptions, pliable, workable, steady, and imperturbable, he directs and inclines it to the knowledge of the recollection of past lives. He recollects his manifold past lives, that is, one birth, two births, three births, four births, five births, ten births, twenty births, thirty births, forty births, fifty births, a hundred births, a thousand births, a hundred thousand births, many eons of world-dissolution, many eons of world-evolution, many eons of world-dissolution and world-evolution: ‘There I had such a name, belonged to such a clan, had such an appearance; such was my food, such my experience of pleasure and pain, such my span of life. Passing away from that state, I reappeared in another state; there too I had such a name, belonged to such a clan, had such an appearance;

such was my food, such my experience of pleasure and pain, such my span of life. Passing away from that state, I reappeared here. Thus he recollects his manifold past lives in their modes and details. “This, great king, is the first knowledge he attains. Ignorance is dispelled, knowledge arises; darkness is dispelled, light arises—just as if one were to draw back a curtain. This, great king, is the first of the Tathāgata’s noble attainments, through the development of which he claims the place of the Teacher among teachers, the place of the Charioteer among charioteers, and the place of the Unsurpassed One among unsurpassed beings. “When his mind is concentrated in this way, purified, cleansed, bright, flawless, rid of corruptions, pliable, workable, steady, and imperturbable, he directs and inclines it to the knowledge of the passing away and reappearance of beings. With the divine eye, which is purified and surpasses the human, he sees beings passing away and reappearing, inferior and superior, fair and ugly,

(AN 5.50, PTS AN iii 57) On one occasion the Venerable Nārada was dwelling at Pāṭaliputta in the Kukkuṭa Monastery.
Now at that time King Muṇḍa’s Queen Bhaddā, who was dear and beloved to him, had passed away.
When Queen Bhaddā had passed away—she who was dear and beloved—he neither bathed nor anointed himself, nor did he eat his meals, nor attend to his affairs;
day and night he remained utterly absorbed in the body of Queen Bhaddā.
Then King Muṇḍa addressed Piya, the treasurer-guardian:
“In that case, dear Piyaka, place Queen Bhaddā’s body in an iron oil-vat and cover it with another iron vat, so that we may preserve Queen Bhaddā’s body for a longer time.
“Very well, Your Majesty,” the treasurer Piyaka replied to King Muṇḍa, and having placed Queen Bhaddā’s body in an iron oil-vat, he covered it with another iron vat.
Then, this thought occurred to the treasurer Piyaka:
“Indeed, King Muṇḍa’s Queen Bhaddā has died, beloved and dear to him.
Since Queen Bhaddā, beloved and dear, has passed away, he neither bathes nor anoints himself, nor does he eat his meals, nor does he attend to his affairs;
day and night he remains utterly absorbed in the body of Queen Bhaddā.”
“Who indeed might King Muṇḍa attend upon—a śramaṇa or a brahmin—so that, having heard his Dhamma, he might abandon the dart of sorrow?
Then it occurred to Piya, the treasurer-guardian:
“This venerable Nārada is staying at Pāṭaliputta in the Kukkuṭa Monastery.”
Now, this good report concerning the Venerable Nārada had spread abroad:
“He is wise, learned, intelligent, erudite, eloquent, possessed of ready wit, an elder, and an arahant.
What if King Muṇḍa were to wait upon the Venerable Nārada; perhaps, having heard the Dhamma from the Venerable Nārada, King Muṇḍa might abandon the dart of sorrow.
Then Piyaka, the treasurer-guardian, approached King Muṇḍa; having approached, he said this to King Muṇḍa:
“Sire, this venerable Nārada is staying at Pāṭaliputta in the Kukkuṭa Monastery.
Regarding that venerable Nārada, such a fine report has spread abroad:”
“He is wise, learned, intelligent, erudite, eloquent, possessed of ready wit, and both aged and an arahant.
If Your Majesty were to wait upon the Venerable Nārada, perhaps after hearing the Dhamma from the Venerable Nārada, Your Majesty might abandon the dart of sorrow.
“In that case, my dear Piyaka, inform the Venerable Nārada.”
“How could one such as I think it right to approach a recluse or a brahmin living within my realm without first having informed him?
“Very well, Your Majesty,” Piyaka the treasurer replied to King Muṇḍa. Having assented, he approached the Venerable Nārada;
having approached, he paid homage to the Venerable Nārada and sat down to one side. Seated to one side...
Then Piyaka, the treasurer, said this to the Venerable Nārada:
“Venerable sir, King Muṇḍa’s Queen Bhaddā, who was dear and beloved to him, has passed away.
Because Queen Bhaddā, his dear and beloved wife, has passed away, he neither bathes nor anoints himself, nor does he eat food, nor does he attend to his affairs.”
“Day and night King Bhadda has been utterly infatuated with the queen’s body.

It would be well, venerable sir, if the Venerable Nārada would teach the Dhamma to King Muṇḍa in such a way that, having heard the Venerable Nārada’s Dhamma, King Muṇḍa might abandon the dart of sorrow.
“Now, Piyaṅka, let it be as King Muṇḍa deems fit.”
Then Piyaka, the treasurer, rose from his seat, paid homage to the Venerable Nārada, and keeping him to his right, approached King Muṇḍa. Having approached, he said this to King Muṇḍa:
“The Venerable Nārada has granted you leave, sire.
Now it is for the King to decide the time.”
“In that case, dear Piyaka, have the finest carriages harnessed.
“Very well, Your Majesty,” Piyaka the treasurer replied to King Muṇḍa. Having had the finest carriages harnessed, he said to King Muṇḍa:
“The finest carriages have been harnessed for you, Your Majesty.”
“Now, let the King do as he deems fit.
Then King Muṇḍa mounted a noble carriage and, with a magnificent royal retinue, set out for the Kukkuṭa Monastery in order to see the Venerable Nārada.
He proceeded by carriage as far as the ground would allow for a vehicle; then, alighting from the carriage, he entered the monastery on foot.

Then King Muṇḍa approached the Venerable Nārada; having approached, he paid homage to the Venerable Nārada and sat down to one side. As King Muṇḍa was sitting there, the Venerable Nārada said this to him:
"Great King, there are these five things that cannot be obtained by a recluse or a brahmin, or by a deva, or by Māra, or by Brahmā, or by anyone in the world.
What are the five?"
‘May that which is subject to aging not age’— this is an impossible position for a recluse, a brahmin, a deva, Māra, Brahmā, or anyone in the world.

‘May that which is subject to illness not fall ill’ …pe… ‘May that which is subject to death not die’ … ‘May that which is subject to exhaustion not be exhausted’ … ‘May that which is subject to destruction not be destroyed’—
this is an impossible position for a recluse, a brahmin, a deva, or anyone in the world.
or by Māra, or by Brahmā, or by anyone in the world.
For the uninstructed worldling, O Great King, that which is subject to aging does grow old.
When that which is subject to aging has grown old, he does not reflect thus:
‘It is not only for me alone that what is subject to aging grows old; rather, for all beings as far as their coming and going, their passing away and reappearing, what is subject to aging grows old.

If I were to grieve, weary myself, lament, beat my breast, weep, fall into confusion, lose my appetite, and undergo physical disfigurement because of this thing subject to aging having grown old, my work would come to naught.’
‘May they not prevail; may even my enemies be glad at heart, and may even my friends be dejected.
Thus, when one who is subject to aging has grown old, he sorrows, languishes, and laments; he beats his breast and falls into confusion.
This, Great King, is called:
“The uninstructed worldling, pierced by the poisonous dart of sorrow, torments only himself.

Furthermore, Great King, for the uninstructed worldling, that which is subject to sickness falls ill; … [and so on] … that which is subject to death dies; … that which is subject to decay decays; … that which is subject to destruction is destroyed.
When that which is subject to destruction has been destroyed, he does not reflect thus:

‘It is not only for me alone that what is subject to destruction is destroyed; rather, for all beings—however far their coming and going, their passing away and rebirth—what is subject to destruction is destroyed.

If, when what is subject to destruction has been destroyed, I were to grieve, be exhausted, lament, beat my breast and weep, and fall into confusion, I would lose my appetite for food, and discoloration would come over my body.’
“Businesses would not proceed; enemies would be delighted, and friends would be dejected.
Thus, when that which is subject to destruction has perished, he sorrows, languishes, and laments; he beats his breast and falls into confusion.
This, O Great King, is called:
“The uninstructed worldling, pierced by the poisonous dart of sorrow, torments himself alone.
But for the instructed noble disciple, O Great King, that which is subject to aging does indeed age.
When that which is subject to aging has aged, he reflects thus:”
‘It is not only for me alone that what is subject to aging grows old; rather, for all beings—however far their coming and going, their passing away and reappearing—what is subject to aging grows old.

If I were to grieve, weary myself, lament, beat my breast, weep, fall into confusion, lose my appetite, and undergo physical disfigurement because of this aging that has come upon me, my work would also [be neglected].’
‘May they not prevail; may even my enemies be glad at heart, and may my friends be sorrowful.
Thus, when one who is subject to old age has grown old, he does not grieve, does not weary, does not lament, does not beat his breast, and does not fall into delusion.
This, O Great King, is called:
‘The learned noble disciple has pulled out the poisoned arrow of sorrow, pierced by which the uninstructed worldling torments himself alone.
Free from sorrow and without the arrow, the learned noble disciple brings himself to final Nibbāna.

Furthermore, Great King, when that which is subject to sickness sickens, the learned noble disciple is not [tormented]; when that which is subject to death dies, he is not [tormented]; when that which is subject to exhaustion comes to exhaustion, he is not [tormented]; when that which is subject to destruction is destroyed, he is not [tormented].’
Thus, when that which is subject to destruction has perished, he reflects:

"It is not only for me alone that what is subject to destruction has perished; rather, for all beings—however far their coming and going, their passing away and reappearing—for all those beings, that which is subject to destruction has perished.
If I were to grieve, weary myself, lament, beat my breast, and weep over what is subject to destruction having perished..."

‘I would weep, I would fall into confusion, my food would not agree with me, ugliness would come over my body, my work would not proceed, my enemies would be delighted, and my friends would be grieved.
Thus, when that which is subject to destruction has been destroyed, he does not sorrow, does not waste away, does not lament; he does not beat his breast and cry out, nor does he fall into confusion.
“This, great king, is called:
‘The learned noble disciple has pulled out the poisoned arrow of sorrow, by which the uninstructed worldling, when pierced, torments himself alone.
Free from sorrow and free from the arrow, the noble disciple causes himself to attain final Nibbāna.’”
"These, O Great King, are the five things that cannot be obtained by a recluse or a brahmin, by a deva, by Māra, by Brahmā, or by anyone in the world.
No purpose whatsoever, however small, can be achieved here through grieving and lamenting.
Seeing him anxious and suffering,
his enemies become joyful;
but when a wise man, in times of calamity...
One who knows how to discern the meaning is not shaken;
seeing his face unchanged as before, his adversaries become distressed.
By means of prayer, incantation, well-spoken words,
by way of gifts, or through tradition—
whenever and wherever one may obtain benefit by such means.
In such and such a way one should strive therein.
If one should understand that this goal is unattainable—
whether by oneself or by another— then [one should let go].
“Without grieving, one should endure it, thinking:
‘What can I do now? Karma is firm.
When this was said, King Muṇḍa said this to the Venerable Nārada:
“What is the name, venerable sir, of this discourse on the Dhamma?
“This discourse on the Dhamma, great king, is named ‘The Extraction of the Arrow of Sorrow.
“Truly, venerable sir, it is ‘The Extraction of the Arrow of Sorrow.’”
“Indeed, Bhante, having heard this discourse on the Dhamma, the arrow of sorrow has been removed from me.
Then King Muṇḍa addressed Piyaka, the treasurer-guardian:
“In that case, my dear Piyaka, cremate the body of Queen Bhaddā and erect a stupa for her.”
“From this day forward, we shall bathe, anoint ourselves, eat our meals, and engage in our work.
Tenth. The Fifth Chapter: The Section on King Muṇḍa.
Its summary verse:
The beginning, the true person, the desired,
the giver of what is pleasing, and the outflow.
"Success, wealth, the proper place,
and skilled means, O Nārada"—
thus ends the first fifty.
Aṅguttara Nikāya 5.51 6.

Nīvaraṇavagga Āvaraṇasutta (The Obstruction) "Bhikkhus, there are these five obstructions. What five? The obstruction of sensual desire, the obstruction of ill will, the obstruction of sloth and torpor, the obstruction of restlessness and remorse, and the obstruction of doubt. These, bhikkhus, are the five obstructions."
(AN 5.51, PTS AN iii 63) Thus have I heard—
on one occasion the Blessed One was dwelling at Sāvatthī in Jeta’s Grove, Anāthapiṇḍika’s monastery.
There the Blessed One addressed the bhikkhus: “Bhikkhus.
“Venerable sir,” those bhikkhus replied to the Blessed One.
The Blessed One said this:
“Bhikkhus, there are these five hindrances, obstructions, mental obsessions that weaken wisdom.
Which five?”
Sensual desire, monks, is an obstruction, a hindrance, a mental encumbrance, and a debilitator of wisdom.
Ill will, monks, is an obstruction, a hindrance, a mental encumbrance, and a debilitator of wisdom.
Sloth and torpor, monks, are an obstruction, a hindrance, a mental encumbrance, and a debilitator of wisdom.
Restlessness and remorse, monks, are an obstruction, a hindrance, an encroachment upon the mind, and a weakening of wisdom.
Doubt, monks, is an obstruction, a hindrance, an encroachment upon the mind, and a weakening of wisdom.
These, monks, are the five obstructions, hindrances, encroachments upon the mind, and weakeners of wisdom.
"Indeed, monks, if a bhikkhu does not abandon these five hindrances, these obstructions that invade the mind and weaken wisdom,
then with his weak and feeble wisdom, he will not know his own welfare, nor know the welfare of others, nor know the welfare of both;
nor will he realize the distinction of superior human states, the noble knowledge and vision."
This is impossible.
Monks, it is just as if there were a mountain river, far-reaching, swift-flowing, and carrying away all that it meets;
and a man were to open plow-mouths on both its banks.
For in this way, monks, that stream in the middle of a river— disturbed, spread out, and dispersed— would neither travel far, nor have a swift current, nor carry away its burden. Even so, monks,
that bhikkhu who has not abandoned these five hindrances and obstructions which invade the mind and weaken wisdom,
with his feeble and weak wisdom, would not know his own welfare or the welfare of others.
"Or he will know both [this world and the next], or he will realize a superhuman state, a distinction in knowledge and vision worthy of the noble ones—
this is impossible. For, monks,
that monk who has these five hindrances, these obstructions, these encumbrances of the mind that weaken wisdom..."
Having abandoned [these], it is possible that through powerful wisdom he will know his own welfare, or know the welfare of others, or know the welfare of both,
or realize a superhuman distinction in knowledge and vision worthy of the noble ones.
Just as, monks, there is a mountain river flowing far, swift in its current, and carrying away all that is in its path.
A man would close both ends of that furrow.
In this way, monks, the current of the river in the middle would be undisturbed, not scattered, not dispersed, far-reaching, swift-flowing, and capable of carrying away everything.
Even so, monks, that bhikkhu who has these five hindrances and obstructions, which have crept into his mind...
