"Having abandoned the weakening of wisdom, it is possible that through powerful wisdom one will know one's own welfare,
or know the welfare of others, or know the welfare of both, or realize a superhuman distinction in knowledge and vision worthy of the noble ones."
First.
Aṅguttara Nikāya 5.52 6.
The Chapter on Hindrances (Nīvaraṇavagga)
The Discourse on the Heap of the Unwholesome (Akusalarāsisutta): “Bhikkhus,
one who would speak of a ‘heap of the unwholesome’ would be speaking rightly if they were to speak of the five hindrances.”
"Monks, this alone is a heap of unwholesomeness, namely, the five hindrances.
Which five?
The hindrance of sensual desire, the hindrance of ill will, the hindrance of sloth and torpor, the hindrance of restlessness and remorse, and the hindrance of doubt."
“Monks, one who would speak of a mass of unwholesomeness would be speaking rightly of these five hindrances.
For this, monks, is an entirely unwholesome mass, namely, the five hindrances.
The second [sutta].
Aṅguttara Nikāya 5.53 6. Nīvaraṇavagga Padhāniyaṅgasutta (The Factors of Exertion) “Monks, there are these five factors of exertion.

What five? Here, monks, a monk is endowed with faith; he places faith in the enlightenment of the Tathāgata thus: ‘The Blessed One is an arahant, perfectly enlightened, accomplished in true knowledge and conduct, fortunate, knower of the world, unsurpassed leader of persons to be tamed, teacher of devas and humans, the Buddha, the Blessed One. “He dwells with energy aroused for the abandoning of unwholesome states and the acquisition of wholesome states; he is steadfast, firm in effort, not remiss in developing wholesome states. “He possesses mindfulness and alertness, being mindful, possessing great alertness, one who remembers and recollects what was done and said long ago. “He is content with any kind of robe, almsfood, lodging, and medicinal requisites for the sick. “He dwells having set up his mind on the higher mind, having attained a measureless concentration of mind, having attained a measureless deliverance of mind. “These, monks, are the five factors of exertion.”
“Bhikkhus, there are these five factors of striving.
What are the five?
In this case, monks, a bhikkhu is endowed with faith; he has faith in the enlightenment of the Tathāgata:

"The Blessed One is indeed an arahant, perfectly enlightened, perfect in knowledge and conduct, sublime, knower of the worlds, unsurpassed leader of persons to be tamed, teacher of gods and humans, the Buddha, the Blessed One.
He is free from illness and free from affliction.
He possesses a digestive fire that is well-balanced—neither too cold nor too hot, but moderate and capable of sustaining exertion;
he is not fraudulent and not deceitful;
he reveals himself as he truly is to the Teacher or to wise companions in the holy life.

“He dwells with energy aroused for the abandoning of unwholesome states and for the attainment of wholesome states; he is steadfast, firm in effort, and does not relinquish the burden regarding wholesome states.
He is wise, endowed with the wisdom that discerns arising and passing away—noble, penetrative, and leading to the complete destruction of suffering.
These, monks, are the five factors of striving.”
Third.
Aṅguttara Nikāya 5.54.
Chapter 6: On the Hindrances (Nīvaraṇavagga).
The Discourse on the Wrong Times (Samayasutta): “Bhikkhus,
there are these five wrong times for striving.”
What are the five?
Here, monks, a monk is aged and overcome by old age.
This, monks, is the first unfavorable time for striving.
Furthermore, monks, a monk is afflicted by illness, overcome by sickness.
This, monks, is the second unfavorable time for striving.
Furthermore, monks, there is famine—scarcity of food and alms are hard to obtain; it is not easy to subsist by gleaning or by gathering what is left.
This, monks, is the third unfavorable time for striving.
Furthermore, monks, there may be fear from disturbances in the wilderness, and the people of the countryside, mounted on chariots, roam about.
This, monks, is the fourth unfavorable time for striving.
Furthermore, monks, the Sangha is split.
When the Sangha is split, monks, there is mutual abuse, mutual reviling, mutual exclusion, and mutual rejection.
Therein, those who have no faith do not become faithful, and some of those who are already faithful undergo a change of heart.
"This, monks, is the fifth unfavorable time for striving.
These, monks, are the five unfavorable times for striving.
There are, monks, these five favorable times for striving."
What are the five?
Here, monks, a monk is young, a youth, black-haired, endowed with the blessing of youth, in the prime of life.
This, monks, is the first occasion for striving.

Furthermore, monks, a monk is free from illness and free from affliction; he possesses a digestive system that is well-balanced, being neither too cold nor too hot, but moderate and capable of enduring exertion.
This, monks, is the second occasion for exertion.
Furthermore, monks, there is an abundance of food, a good harvest, and alms are easily obtained; it is easy to subsist by gathering and collecting gleanings.
This, monks, is the third occasion for striving.
Furthermore, monks, there is a time when people dwell together in harmony, in mutual joy, without dispute, like milk and water mixed, looking upon one another with eyes of affection.
This, monks, is the fourth occasion for striving.
Furthermore, monks, the Saṅgha dwells at ease—united, in harmony, without dispute, and with a single recitation.
When the Saṅgha is united, monks, there is no mutual reviling, no mutual abuse, no mutual disparagement, and no mutual rejection.
Therein, those without confidence gain confidence, and for those already confident, there is further growth.
“This, monks, is the fifth occasion for striving.
These, monks, are the five occasions for striving. Thus was the fourth [discourse].

Aṅguttara Nikāya 5.55 6. Nīvaraṇavagga Mātāputtasutta (The Mother and Son) “Bhikkhus, there are these five hindrances. What five? The hindrance of sensual desire, the hindrance of ill will, the hindrance of sloth and torpor, the hindrance of restlessness and remorse, and the hindrance of doubt. These, bhikkhus, are the five hindrances. Just as a mother would protect her only son with her life, even so, bhikkhus, one who has developed the mind should protect the mind with regard to these five hindrances. Suppose, bhikkhus, a man were to carry about a friend’s infant son on his hip. He would think: ‘I must protect this child from fire, from water, from a stick, from a sword, and from any other danger. Even so, bhikkhus, one who has developed the mind should protect the mind with regard to these five hindrances.”
(AN 5.55, PTS AN iii 67) On one occasion the Blessed One was dwelling at Sāvatthī in Jeta’s Grove, Anāthapiṇḍika’s Park.
Now on that occasion both mother and son in Sāvatthī had entered upon the rains residence.
The bhikkhu and the bhikkhunī were desirous of seeing one another frequently. The mother, too,
was desirous of seeing her son frequently.
The son, too, was constantly desirous of seeing his mother.
From their frequent meetings there arose intimacy;
when there was intimacy, there was trust.
When there was trust, an opportunity arose.
With their minds having fallen away, they engaged in sexual intercourse without having renounced the training and without disclosing their weakness.

Then a number of bhikkhus approached the Blessed One; having approached and paid homage to the Blessed One, they sat down to one side. Sitting to one side, those bhikkhus said this to the Blessed One:
“Here, Bhante, in Sāvatthī, both a mother and son entered the rains residence—one as a bhikkhu and the other as a bhikkhunī.
They were desirous of seeing one another frequently; the mother was desirous of seeing her son frequently, and the son was also desirous of seeing his mother frequently.
From their frequent meetings, intimacy arose; when there is intimacy, trust arises; when there is trust, [confusion arises].”
They fell away; with their minds fallen away, they failed to renounce the training and, without disclosing their weakness, engaged in sexual intercourse.
“Bhikkhus, what does that foolish man think? Does he not think:
‘A mother does not feel lust for her son, nor does a son feel lust for his mother’?”
“Monks, I do not perceive even a single other form that is so alluring, so desirable, so intoxicating,
so binding, so deluding, and so obstructive to the attainment of the unsurpassed security from bondage as this, monks: the form of a woman.”
“Bhikkhus, beings are infatuated with, greedy for, attached to, infatuated by, and clinging to the form of a woman.
Following the power of the form of a woman, they sorrow for a long time.
Bhikkhus, I do not see even a single sound, a single scent, a single taste, or a single touch [that leads to such suffering].”
I consider this touch of a woman, monks, to be so alluring, so desirable, so intoxicating,
so binding, so infatuating, and so an obstacle to the attainment of the unsurpassed security from bondage.
Monks, beings are enamored of, greedy for, tied to, infatuated with, and obsessed by the touch of a woman.
They grieve for a long time, driven by their attachment to the touch of women.
Monks, a woman— whether walking, standing, sitting, lying down, laughing, speaking, singing, weeping, being embraced, or even dead— remains obsessing the mind of a man.
For if anyone, monks, speaking rightly were to say:
‘Māra’s universal snare,’ it is of women alone that one could rightly say:
‘Māra’s universal snare.’
One may converse even with one who has a sword in hand,
one may converse even with a piśāca,
and one may even step upon a venomous snake.
One bitten by whom does not survive;
yet one should certainly not converse alone with a single woman.
They bind one who is heedless with a glance and a smile,
and even with ill-clad garments.
And by speaking gently;
this person is not one who gives comfort,
but is considered to be merely provoked.
These five strands of sensual pleasure are seen in the form of a woman:
forms, sounds, tastes, and scents.
And delightful tactile objects—
for those who are swept away by the flood of sensual desire and do not fully understand sense pleasures—
Time, destiny, and various states of existence are placed before one in this cycle of saṃsāra;
yet those who have fully understood sensual pleasures—
They wander about free from fear;
they indeed have reached the further shore in this world,
those who have attained the destruction of the taints.
The Fifth. Aṅguttara Nikāya 5.56 6.
The Chapter on Hindrances (Nīvaraṇavagga)
Upajjhāyasutta (AN 5.56, PTS AN iii 69):
Then a certain bhikkhu approached his own preceptor; having approached, he said this to his own preceptor:
“Venerable sir, at present my body has become as if drugged; the directions are no longer clear to me; the teachings do not manifest to me;
sloth and torpor persist, overwhelming my mind; I am practicing the holy life without joy;
and I have doubt regarding the teachings.”
Then that bhikkhu, taking his co-resident bhikkhu with him, approached the Blessed One;
having approached and paid homage to the Blessed One, he sat down to one side.
Sitting there, that bhikkhu said this to the Blessed One:
“Venerable sir, this bhikkhu says:
‘At present, venerable sir, my body has become as if drugged; the directions are not clear to me; the teachings do not manifest to me;
sloth and torpor persist, overwhelming my mind; and I am dissatisfied.’”
“I live the holy life, yet I have doubt regarding the teachings.
“It is indeed so, bhikkhu, for one who does not guard the doors of the sense faculties, who is immoderate in eating, who is not devoted to wakefulness,
and who lacks insight into wholesome states, [regarding] the factors conducive to enlightenment during the first and last watches of the night.”
For one who dwells without being devoted to the cultivation of the teachings, the body becomes sluggish, the directions do not become clear,
the teachings do not manifest to him, sloth and torpor persist in overwhelming his mind, he leads the holy life without enthusiasm, and doubt arises regarding the teachings.
Therefore, bhikkhu, you should train yourself thus:
"I will be one who guards the doors of the sense faculties, moderate in eating, devoted to wakefulness,
possessing insight into wholesome states, and during the first and last watches of the night, devoted to the development of the qualities conducive to enlightenment."
“I shall dwell devotedly [to this].
“In this way, bhikkhu, you should train yourself.
Then that bhikkhu, having been exhorted by the Blessed One with this instruction, rose from his seat, paid homage to the Blessed One, circumambulated him keeping him to his right, and departed.
Then, dwelling alone, withdrawn, diligent, ardent, and resolute, that bhikkhu, in no long time,

having realized for himself with direct knowledge in this very life that supreme goal of the holy life, for the sake of which clansmen rightly go forth from the home life into homelessness, entered upon and abided in it.
“Birth is exhausted, the holy life has been lived, what was to be done has been done, there is no more of this state of being”—thus he directly knew.
That bhikkhu became one of the arahants.
Then, having attained arahantship, that bhikkhu approached his own preceptor; having approached, he said this to his preceptor:
“Venerable sir, at present my body is not yet grown weary, the directions are clear to me, the teachings are manifest to me,
sloth and torpor do not persist in taking possession of my mind, I dwell delighting in the holy life,
and I have no doubt regarding the teachings.”
Then that bhikkhu, taking his co-resident bhikkhu with him, approached the Blessed One;
having approached and paid homage to the Blessed One, he sat down to one side. Sitting to one side, that bhikkhu said this to the Blessed One:
“Venerable sir, this bhikkhu says:
‘At present, venerable sir, my body is not yet refreshed; the directions are clear to me; the teachings are manifest to me;
sloth and torpor do not persist, taking possession of my mind; and I am delighted with the holy life.’”
“I live, and I have no doubt regarding the teachings.
“It is indeed so, bhikkhu, for one who guards the doors of the sense faculties, who is moderate in eating, who is devoted to wakefulness,
and who possesses insight into wholesome states, throughout the first and last watches of the night, regarding the factors conducive to enlightenment.”
For one who dwells devoted to the practice of developing the qualities (dhammas), the body does not become heavy,
the quarters become clear to him, the teachings manifest to him, sloth and torpor do not persist by taking hold of his mind,
he lives delighting in the holy life, and no doubt arises in him regarding the teachings.
Therefore, monks, you should train yourselves thus:
"We shall guard the doors of our sense faculties; we shall be moderate in eating; we shall be devoted to wakefulness;

we shall be practitioners of insight regarding wholesome states; and during the first and last watches of the night, we shall be devoted to the development of the qualities conducive to enlightenment."
‘We shall dwell devotedly [to this]’—
in this way, monks, you should train yourselves.
The sixth.
Aṅguttara Nikāya 5.57 6.
The Chapter on Hindrances (Nīvaraṇavagga) The Discourse on the Bases to be Frequently Reflected Upon (Abhiṇhapaccavekkhitabbaṭhānasutta)
“Bhikkhus, there are these five things that should be frequently reflected upon by a woman or a man, whether a householder or one gone forth. What are the five? [The text continues with the list.]”
‘I am subject to aging; I have not transcended aging’—this should be frequently reflected upon by a woman or a man, by one who is a householder or one who has gone forth.
‘I am subject to illness; I have not transcended illness’—this should be frequently reflected upon by a woman or a man, by one who is a householder or one who has gone forth.
‘I am subject to death; I have not transcended death’—this should be frequently reflected upon by a woman or a man, by one who is a householder or one who has gone forth.
‘I shall be separated and parted from all that is dear and beloved,’ this should be frequently reflected upon by a woman or a man, by one who is a householder or one who has gone forth.
‘I am the owner of my actions, the heir of my actions, born of my actions, related to my actions, and have my actions as my refuge.
Whatever action I shall do—whether good or evil—’
‘I shall be an heir to that,’ should be frequently reflected upon by a woman or a man, by one who is a householder or one who has gone forth.
And for what purpose, monks, should ‘I am subject to aging; I have not transcended aging’ be frequently reflected upon by a woman or a man, by one who is a householder or one who has gone forth?
“Monks, there exists among beings a pride of youth in their youth, intoxicated by which they engage in misconduct of body, misconduct of speech, and misconduct of mind.
For one who frequently reflects upon that state, whatever pride of youth there was in their youth is either entirely abandoned or becomes diminished.”
“Monks, it is for this purpose that a woman or a man, whether a householder or one gone forth, should frequently reflect: ‘I am subject to aging; I have not transcended aging.
And for what purpose, monks, should a woman or a man, whether a householder or one gone forth, frequently reflect: ‘I am subject to illness; I have not transcended illness’?”
“Monks, there exists among beings a pride of health regarding health, intoxicated by which they engage in misconduct of body, misconduct of speech, and misconduct of mind.
For one who frequently reflects upon that state, whatever pride of health there was regarding health is either completely abandoned or at least diminished.”

“Monks, it is for this purpose that ‘I am subject to illness; I am not exempt from illness’ should be frequently reflected upon, whether by a woman or a man, by one who is a householder or one who has gone forth.

And for what purpose, monks, should ‘I am subject to death; I am not exempt from death’ be frequently reflected upon, whether by a woman or a man, by one who is a householder or one who has gone forth?”
“Bhikkhus, there exists among beings a intoxication with life, by which intoxication they become intoxicated and engage in misconduct of body, misconduct of speech, and misconduct of mind.
For one who frequently reflects upon that state, whatever intoxication with life there may be is either completely abandoned or at least diminished.”
“Monks, it is for this purpose that ‘I am subject to death; I have not transcended death’ should be frequently reflected upon by a woman or a man, by a householder or one gone forth.
And for what purpose, monks, should ‘I am separated and parted from all that is dear and beloved’ be frequently reflected upon by a woman or a man, by a householder or one gone forth?”

“Monks, there exists in beings a desire and lust for those things that are dear and pleasing, by which lust they are inflamed and engage in misconduct by body, misconduct by speech, and misconduct by mind.
When one frequently reflects upon that state, whatever desire and lust there is for those things that are dear and pleasing is either completely abandoned or at least diminished.”

“Monks, it is for this purpose that a woman or a man, whether a householder or one gone forth, should frequently reflect: ‘I am subject to separation and dissociation from all that is dear and beloved.

And for what purpose, monks, should one reflect: ‘I am the owner of my actions, the heir to my actions, born of my actions, related to my actions, and have my actions as my refuge; whatever action I shall do—’”
"Whether it be wholesome or unwholesome, I shall be the heir to that"—should this be frequently reflected upon by a woman or a man, by one who is a householder or one who has gone forth?
There is, monks, misconduct of body, misconduct of speech, and misconduct of mind among beings.
For one who frequently reflects upon that state, such misconduct is either abandoned entirely or becomes diminished.

“Monks, it is for this purpose that a woman or a man, whether a householder or one who has gone forth, should frequently reflect: ‘I am the owner of my actions, the heir of my actions; action is my matrix, action is my kin, action is my refuge. Whatever action I shall perform—whether good or evil—that I shall become the heir to.’”
“Monks, that noble disciple reflects thus:

‘I am not the only one subject to old age and not exempt from old age; for as far as the coming and going, the passing away and rebirth of beings extends, all beings are subject to old age and none are exempt from old age.
As he frequently reviews this state, the path is born.”
Thus he pursues, develops, and cultivates that path.
As he pursues, develops, and cultivates that path, his fetters are completely abandoned and his underlying tendencies are brought to an end. He reflects:

"It is not only I who am subject to illness and have not transcended illness; rather, as far as there is coming and going, passing away and rebirth for beings, all beings are subject to illness and have not transcended illness."
As he frequently reflects upon that state, the path arises within him.
He cultivates, develops, and repeatedly practices that path.
As he cultivates, develops, and repeatedly practices that path, his fetters are completely abandoned and his underlying tendencies are brought to an end.

‘It is not only I alone who am subject to death and have not transcended death; rather, as far as the coming and going, the passing away and rebirth of beings extends, all beings are subject to death and have not transcended death.
As he frequently reflects on this state, the path is born within him.
He pursues, develops, and cultivates that path.
As he pursues, develops, and cultivates that path, the fetters are entirely abandoned and the underlying tendencies are eradicated. He reflects:

"It is not only for me alone that there is separation and parting from all that is dear and pleasing; rather, for all beings—however far their coming and going, their passing away and reappearing—there is separation and parting from all that is dear and pleasing.
As he frequently contemplates this state, the path is born.
Thus he pursues, develops, and cultivates that path.
As he pursues, develops, and cultivates that path, his fetters are completely abandoned and his underlying tendencies are brought to an end.

"It is not only I who am the owner of my actions, the heir of my actions, born of my actions, related to my actions, and have my actions as my refuge; whatever action I shall do—whether good or evil—I will be its heir."
Then, as far as the coming and going, the passing away and rebirth of beings extends, all beings are owners of their actions,
heirs of their actions, born of their actions, related by their actions, and have their actions as their refuge; whatever action they shall perform—
whether good or evil— they will be the heirs of that.
As he frequently reflects upon that state, the path arises within him.
He cultivates, develops, and makes much of that path.
As he cultivates, develops, and makes much of that path, his fetters are completely abandoned and his underlying tendencies are brought to an end.
Subject to disease, subject to aging,
and likewise subject to death;
as are the phenomena, so are sentient beings.
Ordinary people feel revulsion for it.
If I were to feel revulsion for that,
I would likewise feel revulsion toward all phenomena.
This is not fitting for me who dwells thus; dwelling in this way, I—
Having understood the Dhamma that is free from acquisitions,
[one should abandon] those intoxications regarding health, youth, and life.
I have overcome all intoxications,
seeing renunciation as security;
thus, enthusiasm arose within me.
For one who beholds Nibbāna,
I am no longer capable of indulging in sensual pleasures.
"I shall not turn back;
I am devoted to the holy life. Thus ends the seventh [sutta].

Aṅguttara Nikāya 5.58 6. The Chapter on Hindrances (Nīvaraṇavagga) The Discourse on the Licchavi Youth (Licchavikumārakasutta) “Monks, there are these five hindrances. What five? The hindrance of sensual desire, the hindrance of ill will, the hindrance of sloth and torpor, the hindrance of restlessness and remorse, and the hindrance of doubt. These, monks, are the five hindrances. Just as a young, tender infant lying on its back might have a small piece of flesh stuck in its mouth, so too, monks, these five hindrances are like a small piece of flesh in the mouth of a young, tender infant. For what reason? Because they are a source of suffering for one who dwells with them. Suppose, monks, a man were to take a sharp sword and plunge it into the heart of a young, tender infant lying on its back. That would be painful for that infant.

Yet, monks, the pain caused by that man plunging a sharp sword into the heart of that young, tender infant lying on its back is not even a fraction, a small part, a mere comparison, a mere likeness, a mere shadow, of the suffering caused by these five hindrances for one who dwells with them. Suppose, monks, a man were to seize a young, tender infant by the head or by the feet and dash it against a rough stone wall. That would be painful for that infant. Yet, monks, the pain caused by that man seizing a young, tender infant by the head or by the feet and dashing it against a rough stone wall is not even a fraction, a small part, a mere comparison, a mere likeness, a mere shadow, of the suffering caused by these five hindrances for one who dwells with them. Suppose, monks, a man were to wrap a young, tender infant in a red-hot iron sheet heated and glowing, or in a black-hot iron sheet heated and glowing, or in both a red-hot and a black-hot iron sheet heated and glowing. That would be painful for that infant. Yet, monks, the pain caused by that man wrapping a young, tender infant in a red-hot iron sheet heated and glowing, or in a black-hot iron sheet heated and glowing, or in both a red-hot and a black-hot iron sheet heated and glowing, is not even a fraction, a small part, a mere comparison, a mere likeness, a mere shadow, of the suffering caused by these five hindrances for one who dwells with them. Suppose, monks, a man were to take a young, tender infant and, having anointed its body with sesame oil, were to rub it with a rough brush made of horsehair. That would be painful for that infant. Yet, monks, the pain caused by that man taking a young, tender infant and, having anointed its body with sesame oil, rubbing it with a rough brush made of horsehair, is not even a fraction, a small part, a mere comparison, a mere likeness, a mere shadow, of the suffering caused by these five hindrances for one who dwells with them. Suppose, monks, a man were to take a young, tender infant and, having anointed its body with sesame oil, were to place it in a hot iron tub heated and glowing, or in a hot iron pit heated and glowing, or in both a hot iron tub and a hot iron pit heated and glowing. That would be painful for that infant. Yet, monks, the pain caused by that man taking a young, tender infant and, having anointed its body with sesame oil, placing it in a hot iron tub heated and glowing, or in a hot iron pit heated and glowing, or in both a hot iron tub and a hot iron pit heated and glowing, is not even a fraction, a small part, a mere comparison, a mere likeness, a mere shadow, of the suffering caused by these five hindrances for one who dwells with them. Therefore, monks, you should train yourselves thus: ‘We shall abandon the unarisen hindrance of sensual desire, and we shall make the arisen hindrance of sensual desire abandon; we shall abandon the unarisen hindrance of ill will, and we shall make the arisen hindrance of ill will abandon; we shall abandon the unarisen hindrance of sloth and torpor, and we shall make the arisen hindrance of sloth and torpor abandon; we shall abandon the unarisen hindrance of restlessness and remorse, and we shall make the arisen hindrance of restlessness and remorse abandon; we shall abandon the unarisen hindrance of doubt, and we shall make the arisen hindrance of doubt abandon. Thus, monks, should you train yourselves.”
On one occasion the Blessed One was dwelling at Vesālī in the Great Wood, in the Hall with the Peaked Roof.
Then, in the morning, the Blessed One dressed, took his bowl and robe, and entered Vesālī for alms.
Having walked for alms in Vesālī and returned from his almsround after the meal, he entered the Great Wood and sat down at the foot of a certain tree for his midday rest.
Now at that time, a number of Licchavi youths, taking up their strung bows and surrounded by a pack of dogs,
were walking and wandering about in the Great Wood when they saw the Blessed One sitting at the foot of a certain tree.
Having seen this, they laid aside their strung bows, sent the pack of dogs to one side,
and approached the Blessed One. Having approached and paid homage to the Blessed One, they stood waiting upon him in silence with palms joined in reverence.
Now at that time, while the Licchavi Mahānāma was walking for exercise in the Great Wood, he saw those Licchavi youths sitting in silence with palms joined, attending upon the Blessed One.
Having seen them, he approached the Blessed One; having approached and paid homage to the Blessed One, he sat down to one side.
As he was sitting there, the Licchavi Mahānāma uttered this inspired exclamation:
“The Vajjis will endure, the Vajjis will endure!
“But why, Mahānāma, do you say:
‘The Vajjis will endure, the Vajjis will endure’?”
“Venerable sir, these Licchavi youths are fierce, harsh, and violent.
Even when those family gifts—whether sugarcane, jujube fruits, cakes, sweetmeats, or confections—are being sent from one family to another, they snatch them up and eat them repeatedly;
they even throw clods of earth at women of good families and girls of good families.”
“Now they sit in silence, with palms joined, attending upon the Blessed One. “Mahānāma,
for whichever clansman these five qualities are found—
whether he be an anointed Khattiya king, or a provincial official, or a village headman— ”
Whether it be for the commander of an army, or for a village headman, or for a guild leader,
or for those who exercise independent authority over families— only growth is to be expected, not decline. What are the five?

In this case, Mahānāma, a clansman honors, reveres, respects, and venerates his mother and father with wealth acquired through industry and energy, gathered by the strength of his own arms, earned through sweat, righteous, and righteously obtained.
His parents, being thus honored, revered, respected, and venerated, favor him with a virtuous mind, saying:
“Live long! May you enjoy a long life!”
“Mahānāma, for a clansman who is compassionate toward his mother and father, only growth is to be expected, not decline. Furthermore, Mahānāma, with wealth acquired through industry and energy,
gathered by the strength of his arms, earned through sweat, righteous, and righteously obtained, a clansman honors his wife, children, slaves, laborers, and servants.”
He honors, respects, reveres, and venerates them.
Being thus honored, respected, revered, and venerated, his children, wife, slaves, laborers, and servants regard him with a virtuous mind and feel compassion for him, saying:
“May you live long; may you enjoy a full span of life!”
“Mahānāma, for a clansman who is compassionate toward his wives, children, slaves, servants, and laborers, growth alone is to be expected, not decline. Furthermore, Mahānāma,
with wealth acquired through exertion and energy, gathered by the strength of his own arms,
earned through sweat, righteous, and righteously obtained, a clansman honors those engaged in the management of fields, business, and commerce.”
He honors, respects, reveres, and venerates him.
Because he is thus honored, respected, revered, and venerated, those who deal with him in matters of agriculture, business, and commerce feel compassion for him with a virtuous mind, saying:
"May you live long; may you enjoy a full span of life."
“Mahānāma, for a clansman who is compassionate toward his fields, his laborers, and his neighbors, only growth is to be expected,
not decline. Furthermore, Mahānāma, with wealth acquired through initiative and energy, gathered by the strength of his arms,
born of sweat, righteous, and righteously gained, he honors those deities who accept offerings.”
One honors, respects, reveres, and worships him.
Those deities who receive offerings, being thus honored, respected, revered, and worshipped, favor him with a virtuous mind, thinking:
"May you live long; may you enjoy a full span of life!"
“Mahānāma, for a clansman who is favored by the deities, only growth is to be expected, not decline.

Furthermore, Mahānāma, with wealth acquired through initiative and energy, gathered by the strength of his arms, earned by sweat, righteous, and righteously obtained, a clansman honors, respects, reveres, and venerates recluses and brahmins.
When he has thus honored, respected, revered, and venerated them, those recluses and brahmins favor him with a virtuous mind, thinking:”
"Live long! May you enjoy a long life!
For a clansman who is thus shown compassion by recluses and brahmins, Mahānāma, only growth is to be expected, not decline.
For whichever clansman, Mahānāma, these five qualities are present—
Whether it be for a head-anointed kṣatriya king, or for a provincial chieftain,
or for a commander of an army, or for a village headman, or for a guild leader,
or for those who exercise individual authority over families— only growth is to be expected, not decline.
Performing his duties toward mother and father,
always providing for his wife and children,
and for the welfare of his household members;
And those who depend upon him—
for the sake of both,
he is generous and virtuous.
To one's kinsmen who have passed away,
to those living in this present life,
and to recluses and brahmins—
And the wise person,
living by righteous means in the household life, becomes a source of joy for the deities.
Having thus performed what is wholesome,
one becomes worthy of honor and praise;
even here in this world, they praise him.
“Having passed away, one rejoices in heaven.
Thus ends the eighth [sutta]. Aṅguttara Nikāya 5.59

6. Nīvaraṇavagga Paṭhamavuḍḍhapabbajitasutta (AN 5.59, PTS AN iii 78) “Monks, there are these five hindrances. What five? The hindrance of sensual desire, the hindrance of ill will, the hindrance of sloth and torpor, the hindrance of restlessness and remorse, and the hindrance of doubt. These, monks, are the five hindrances. When this was said, a certain monk addressed the Blessed One: “Venerable sir, what is the cause, what is the reason, why some beings here do not attain final Nibbāna in this very life? “Here, monk, some being is possessed by the hindrance of sensual desire; he does not understand as it really is: ‘The hindrance of sensual desire exists in me,’ nor does he understand: ‘This is the origin of the hindrance of sensual desire,’ nor does he understand: ‘This is the cessation of the hindrance of sensual desire,’ nor does he understand: ‘This is the way leading to the cessation of the hindrance of sensual desire. He is not intent upon renunciation, does not incline toward renunciation, does not lean toward renunciation. He is possessed by the hindrance of ill will... the hindrance of sloth and torpor... the hindrance of restlessness and remorse... and the hindrance of doubt; he does not understand as it really is: ‘The hindrance of doubt exists in me,’ nor does he understand: ‘This is the origin of the hindrance of doubt,’ nor does he understand: ‘This is the cessation of the hindrance of doubt,’ nor does he understand: ‘This is the way leading to the cessation of the hindrance of doubt. He is not intent upon renunciation, does not incline toward renunciation, does not lean toward renunciation. This, monk, is the cause, this is the reason, why some beings here do not attain final Nibbāna in this very life. “But, venerable sir, what is the cause, what is the reason, why some beings here attain final Nibbāna in this very life? “Here, monk, some being is not possessed by the hindrance of sensual desire; he understands as it really is: ‘The hindrance of sensual desire does not exist in me,’ and he understands: ‘This is the origin of the hindrance of sensual desire,’ and he understands: ‘This is the cessation of the hindrance of sensual desire,’ and he understands: ‘This is the way leading to the cessation of the hindrance of sensual desire. He is intent upon renunciation, inclines toward renunciation, leans toward renunciation. He is not possessed by the hindrance of ill will... the hindrance of sloth and torpor... the hindrance of restlessness and remorse... and the hindrance of doubt; he understands as it really is: ‘The hindrance of doubt does not exist in me,’ and he understands: ‘This is the origin of the hindrance of doubt,’ and he understands: ‘This is the cessation of the hindrance of doubt,’ and he understands: ‘This is the way leading to the cessation of the hindrance of doubt. He is intent upon renunciation, inclines toward renunciation, leans toward renunciation. This, monk, is the cause, this is the reason, why some beings here attain final Nibbāna in this very life. Then that monk addressed the Blessed One: “Venerable sir, how many kinds of persons who have gone forth in old age are found existing in the world? “There are, monk, these five kinds of persons who have gone forth in old age who are found existing in the world. What five?

Here, monk, one person who has gone forth in old age is full of longing for the household life, full of longing for his children, full of longing for his wife, full of longing for his relatives, full of longing for his wealth, and full of longing for his circle of friends. This, monk, is the first kind of person who has gone forth in old age who is found existing in the world. Again, monk, another person who has gone forth in old age is full of longing for the household life, full of longing for his children, full of longing for his wife, full of longing for his relatives, full of longing for his wealth, and full of longing for his circle of friends; yet he dwells with a mind obsessed by ill will, with a mind full of enmity. This, monk, is the second kind of person who has gone forth in old age who is found existing in the world. Again, monk, another person who has gone forth in old age is full of longing for the household life... and full of longing for his circle of friends; yet he dwells with a mind obsessed by sloth and torpor, with a mind shrouded in darkness. This, monk, is the third kind of person who has gone forth in old age who is found existing in the world. Again, monk, another person who has gone forth in old age is full of longing for the household life... and full of longing for his circle of friends; yet he dwells with a mind obsessed by restlessness and remorse, with a mind that is unquiet. This, monk, is the fourth kind of person who has gone forth in old age who is found existing in the world. Again, monk, another person who has gone forth in old age is full of longing for the household life... and full of longing for his circle of friends; yet he dwells with a mind obsessed by doubt, with a mind wavering. This, monk, is the fifth kind of person who has gone forth in old age who is found existing in the world. These, monk, are the five kinds of persons who have gone forth in old age who are found existing in the world. But, monk, there are these five kinds of persons who have gone forth in old age who are found existing in the world who are arahants, whose taints are destroyed, who have lived the holy life, done what was to be done, laid down the burden, reached their own goal, utterly destroyed the fetters of existence, and are completely liberated through final knowledge. What five? Here, monk, one person who has gone forth in old age is not full of longing for the household life, not full of longing for his children, not full of longing for his wife, not full of longing for his relatives, not full of longing for his wealth, and not full of longing for his circle of friends. This, monk, is the first kind of person who has gone forth in old age who is found existing in the world who is an arahant, whose taints are destroyed... and is completely liberated through final knowledge. Again, monk, another person who has gone forth in old age is not full of longing for the household life... and not full of longing for his circle of friends; yet he dwells with a mind free from ill will, with a mind full of loving-kindness. This, monk, is the second kind of person who has gone forth in old age who is found existing in the world who is an arahant, whose taints are destroyed... and is completely liberated through final knowledge. Again, monk, another person who has gone forth in old age is not full of longing for the household life... and not full of longing for his circle of friends; yet he dwells with a mind free from sloth and torpor, with a mind luminous. This, monk, is the third kind of person who has gone forth in old age who is found existing in the world who is an arahant, whose taints are destroyed... and is completely liberated through final knowledge. Again, monk, another person who has gone forth in old age is not full of longing for the household life... and not full of longing for his circle of friends; yet he dwells with a mind free from restlessness and remorse, with a mind quieted. This, monk, is the fourth kind of person who has gone forth in old age who is found existing in the world who is an arahant, whose taints are destroyed... and is completely liberated through final knowledge. Again, monk, another person who has gone forth in old age is not full of longing for the household life... and not full of longing for his circle of friends; yet he dwells with a mind free from doubt, with a mind that is unwavering. This, monk, is the fifth kind of person who has gone forth in old age who is found existing in the world who is an arahant, whose taints are destroyed... and is completely liberated through final knowledge. These, monk, are the five kinds of persons who have gone forth in old age who are found existing in the world who are arahants, whose taints are destroyed, who have lived the holy life, done what was to be done, laid down the burden, reached their own goal, utterly destroyed the fetters of existence, and are completely liberated through final knowledge.”
“Bhikkhus, one who has gone forth in old age and possesses five qualities is rare.
Which five?

Bhikkhus, one who has gone forth in old age is rare if he is skillful; rare if he is accomplished in deportment; rare if he is learned; rare if he is an expounder of the Dhamma; rare if he is an upholder of the Vinaya.”
"Monks, one endowed with these five qualities is rare among those who have gone forth in old age.
(The Ninth) Aṅguttara Nikāya 5.60
6. Nīvaraṇavagga The Second Discourse on Those Who Went Forth in Old Age (AN 5.60, PTS AN iii 78)
“Bhikkhus, one who has gone forth in old age and possesses five qualities is rare.
Which five?

Bhikkhus, one who has gone forth in old age is rare who is easy to speak to; rare is one who grasps well what is taught; rare is one who grasps in the proper order; rare is one who is a preacher of the Dhamma; rare is one who is an upholder of the Vinaya.”
“Bhikkhus, one who possesses these five qualities is rare among those who have gone forth in old age.
Tenth. The First Chapter on Hindrances.
Its summary verse:
Obstruction, heap, factors,
occasion, and the mother-and-son [simile].
Upajjhā, Ṭhānā, Licchavi,
Kumāra, and two others.
— Aṅguttara Nikāya 5.61

7. Saññāvagga First Discourse on Perception (Paṭhamasaññāsutta) “Bhikkhus, there are these six classes of perception. What six? The perception of forms, the perception of sounds, the perception of odors, the perception of tastes, the perception of tangibles, and the perception of mental phenomena. These, bhikkhus, are the six classes of perception.”
“Bhikkhus, these five perceptions, when developed and cultivated, are of great fruit and great benefit; they have the Deathless as their ground and the Deathless as their consummation.
What five?
The perception of foulness, the perception of death, the perception of danger, the perception of the repulsiveness of food, and the perception of non-delight in the entire world.”
“Monks, these five perceptions, when developed and cultivated, are of great fruit and great benefit; they have the Deathless as their destination and the Deathless as their consummation.
Thus was the first [discourse]. Aṅguttara Nikāya 5.62
7. Saññāvagga The Second Discourse on Perception (Dutiyasaññāsutta) (AN 5.62, PTS AN iii 79)
“Bhikkhus, these five perceptions, when developed and cultivated, are of great fruit and great benefit; they have the deathless as their ground and the deathless as their consummation.
What five?
The perception of impermanence, the perception of non-self, the perception of death, the perception of the repulsiveness of food, and the perception of non-delight in the entire world.”
“Monks, these five perceptions, when developed and cultivated, are of great fruit and great benefit; they have the Deathless as their goal and the Deathless as their consummation.
This is the second [discourse]. Aṅguttara Nikāya 5.63.

7. Saññāvagga First Discourse on Growth (Paṭhamavaḍḍhisutta) “Bhikkhus, there are these five bases for growth. What five? Growth in faith, growth in virtuous behavior, growth in learning, growth in generosity, and growth in wisdom. These, bhikkhus, are the five bases for growth.”
“Bhikkhus, when growing by five kinds of growth, a noble disciple grows by the noble growth; he becomes one who takes up the essence and takes up what is excellent for his body.
By which five?
He grows in faith, he grows in virtue, he grows in learning, he grows in generosity, and he grows in wisdom.”
“Monks, by these five kinds of growth, a noble disciple who is growing grows by noble growth; he becomes one who takes hold of the essence and takes hold of what is excellent regarding the body.
“He who grows in faith and in virtue, In wisdom, generosity, and learning—both;”
Thus such a wise and noble person takes up for himself only that which is substantial in this very world.
Third.
Aṅguttara Nikāya 5.64 7.

Saññāvagga Dutiyavaḍḍhisutta (The Second Discourse on Growth) “Bhikkhus, there are these five bases for growth. What five? Growth in faith, growth in virtue, growth in learning, growth in generosity, and growth in wisdom. These, bhikkhus, are the five bases for growth.”

“Bhikkhus, when a noble disciple grows by five kinds of growth, she grows by noble growth; she becomes one who takes up the essence and takes up what is excellent regarding the body. By which five? [The Sutta continues with the fivefold growth.]”
She grows in faith, she grows in virtue, she grows in learning, she grows in generosity, and she grows in wisdom.
It is by these five kinds of growth, monks, that a noble disciple who is growing grows in noble growth; she becomes one who takes hold of the essence and takes hold of what is excellent for her body.
She who grows in faith and in virtue...
“Through wisdom, generosity, and learning— both together—
that kind of virtuous female lay follower takes hold of what is essential for herself right here.”
The Fourth.
Aṅguttara Nikāya 5.65 7. Saññāvagga (The Chapter on Perceptions)
Sākacchasutta: “Bhikkhus,
possessing five qualities, a bhikkhu is fit for discussion with his fellow celibate companions.”
By which five?
Here, monks, a monk is himself accomplished in virtue and is able to answer questions that arise concerning the accomplishment of virtue;
he is himself accomplished in concentration and is able to answer questions that arise concerning the accomplishment of concentration.
He himself is endowed with wisdom and is able to answer questions that arise regarding the perfection of wisdom;
he himself is endowed with liberation and is able to answer questions that arise regarding the perfection of liberation;
he himself is endowed with the knowledge and vision of liberation and is able to answer questions that arise regarding the perfection of the knowledge and vision of liberation.
“Bhikkhus, a bhikkhu endowed with these five qualities is fit for conversation with his fellow celibates.
The fifth. *Aṅguttara Nikāya* 5.66

7. Saññāvagga Sājīvasutta (AN 5.66, PTS AN iii 81) “Bhikkhus, there are these five kinds of livelihoods that are not right and do not lead to the goal. What five? There is the case where a certain person, for the sake of his own belly’s fill, for the sake of his own comfort, out of desire for gain, honor, and renown, speaks in praise of what is contrary to the Dhamma as being in accordance with the Dhamma, and speaks in dispraise of what is in accordance with the Dhamma as being contrary to the Dhamma. This is the first kind of livelihood that is not right and does not lead to the goal. Furthermore, there is the case where a certain person, for the sake of his own belly’s fill, for the sake of his own comfort, out of desire for gain, honor, and renown, speaks in praise of what is contrary to the Vinaya as being in accordance with the Vinaya, and speaks in dispraise of what is in accordance with the Vinaya as being contrary to the Vinaya. This is the second kind of livelihood that is not right and does not lead to the goal. Furthermore, there is the case where a certain person, for the sake of his own belly’s fill, for the sake of his own comfort, out of desire for gain, honor, and renown, speaks in praise of what has not been taught by the Tathāgata as having been taught by him, and speaks in dispraise of what has been taught by the Tathāgata as not having been taught by him. This is the third kind of livelihood that is not right and does not lead to the goal. Furthermore, there is the case where a certain person, for the sake of his own belly’s fill, for the sake of his own comfort, out of desire for gain, honor, and renown, speaks in praise of what was not spoken by the Blessed One as having been spoken by him, and speaks in dispraise of what was spoken by the Blessed One as not having been spoken by him. This is the fourth kind of livelihood that is not right and does not lead to the goal. Furthermore, there is the case where a certain person, for the sake of his own belly’s fill, for the sake of his own comfort, out of desire for gain, honor, and renown, speaks in praise of what was not practiced by the Blessed One as having been practiced by him, and speaks in dispraise of what was practiced by the Blessed One as not having been practiced by him. This is the fifth kind of livelihood that is not right and does not lead to the goal. These, bhikkhus, are the five kinds of livelihoods that are not right and do not lead to the goal. There are, however, these five kinds of livelihoods that are right and lead to the goal. What five? There is the case where a certain person, for the sake of his own belly’s fill, for the sake of his own comfort, out of desire for gain, honor, and renown, speaks in dispraise of what is contrary to the Dhamma as being contrary to the Dhamma, and speaks in praise of what is in accordance with the Dhamma as being in accordance with the Dhamma. This is the first kind of livelihood that is right and leads to the goal. Furthermore, there is the case where a certain person, for the sake of his own belly’s fill, for the sake of his own comfort, out of desire for gain, honor, and renown, speaks in dispraise of what is contrary to the Vinaya as being contrary to the Vinaya, and speaks in praise of what is in accordance with the Vinaya as being in accordance with the Vinaya. This is the second kind of livelihood that is right and leads to the goal. Furthermore, there is the case where a certain person, for the sake of his own belly’s fill, for the sake of his own comfort, out of desire for gain, honor, and renown, speaks in dispraise of what has not been taught by the Tathāgata as not having been taught by him, and speaks in praise of what has been taught by the Tathāgata as having been taught by him. This is the third kind of livelihood that is right and leads to the goal. Furthermore, there is the case where a certain person, for the sake of his own belly’s fill, for the sake of his own comfort, out of desire for gain, honor, and renown, speaks in dispraise of what was not spoken by the Blessed One as not having been spoken by him, and speaks in praise of what was spoken by the Blessed One as having been spoken by him. This is the fourth kind of livelihood that is right and leads to the goal. Furthermore, there is the case where a certain person, for the sake of his own belly’s fill, for the sake of his own comfort, out of desire for gain, honor, and renown, speaks in dispraise of what was not practiced by the Blessed One as not having been practiced by him, and speaks in praise of what was practiced by the Blessed One as having been practiced by him. This is the fifth kind of livelihood that is right and leads to the goal. These, bhikkhus, are the five kinds of livelihoods that are right and lead to the goal.”
“Bhikkhus, a bhikkhu endowed with five qualities is fit to live together with his fellow practitioners in the holy life.
With which five?
Here, bhikkhus, a bhikkhu is himself accomplished in virtue, and he is able to answer questions posed regarding the accomplishment in virtue.
He himself is accomplished in concentration and is able to answer questions posed regarding the accomplishment of concentration;
he himself is accomplished in wisdom and is able to answer questions posed regarding the accomplishment of wisdom;
he himself is accomplished in liberation and is able to answer questions posed regarding the accomplishment of liberation.
“He himself is accomplished in the knowledge and vision of liberation, and he is able to answer questions posed during a discussion on the accomplishment of the knowledge and vision of liberation.
Possessing these five qualities, monks, a bhikkhu is fit to live together with his fellow celibates.
The sixth.
Aṅguttara Nikāya 5.67 7.
Saññāvagga First Discourse on the Bases of Spiritual Power (Paṭhama-iddhipāda-sutta)
“Bhikkhus, whatever bhikkhu or bhikkhunī develops five qualities and cultivates them frequently, one of two fruits may be expected for them:
final knowledge in this very life, or, if there is a residue remaining, the state of non-returning.”
Which five?

Here, monks, a monk develops the basis for psychic power endowed with concentration due to desire and volitional formations of striving; [he develops] the basis for psychic power endowed with concentration due to energy … [and so on] … [he develops] the basis for psychic power endowed with concentration due to mind … [he develops] the basis for psychic power endowed with concentration due to investigation and volitional formations of striving.

He develops the basis for psychic power endowed with concentration of mind and volitional formations of striving; he develops the basis for psychic power endowed with concentration of investigation and volitional formations of striving—
exertion being the fifth.
“Bhikkhus, whatever bhikkhu or bhikkhunī develops these five qualities and cultivates these five qualities, one of two fruits may be expected for him:
final knowledge in this very life, or, if there is a residue remaining, the state of non-returning.
The seventh.

Aṅguttara Nikāya 5.68 7. Saññāvagga Dutiyaiddhipādasutta (The Second Discourse on the Bases for Spiritual Power) "Bhikkhus, there are these four bases for spiritual power. What four? The basis for spiritual power consisting of concentration due to desire and volitional formations of striving; the basis for spiritual power consisting of concentration due to energy and volitional formations of striving; the basis for spiritual power consisting of concentration due to mind and volitional formations of striving; and the basis for spiritual power consisting of concentration due to investigation and volitional formations of striving. These, bhikkhus, are the four bases for spiritual power."
“Bhikkhus, before my enlightenment,
while I was still an unenlightened bodhisatta, I developed five things and cultivated five things.
What five?

I developed the basis for psychic power endowed with concentration through desire and volitional formations of striving; [I developed] the basis for psychic power endowed with concentration through energy … [I developed] the basis for psychic power endowed with concentration through mind … [I developed] the basis for psychic power endowed with concentration through investigation and volitional formations of striving.
I developed the basis for psychic power endowed with the concentration of investigation and volitional formations of striving;
this was the fifth, namely, exertion itself.

Monks, through the development and cultivation of these five things, including exertion as the fifth, I directed my mind toward whatever state was to be realized through direct knowledge, for the sake of realizing it through direct knowledge.
In each and every case, wherever there was a suitable basis, I attained the capacity for realization.

If I so desired: "May I exercise mastery with the body as far as the Brahma-world—even to the point of experiencing the various kinds of psychic power"—in each and every case, wherever there was a suitable basis, I attained the capacity for realization.

"So if I wished... [as before] ... 'Having realized for myself with direct knowledge in this very life the taintless liberation of mind and liberation by wisdom through the destruction of the taints, may I dwell having attained it,' then I would attain the capability of being a witness in each and every case, in whatever sphere there might be.
The eighth.

Aṅguttara Nikāya 5.69 7. Saññāvagga Nibbidāsutta (The Discourse on Disenchantment) “Bhikkhus, there are these five kinds of persons found existing in the world. What five? The person who is intent on sensual pleasures; the person who is intent on form; the person who is intent on the formless;

the person who is intent on cessation; and the person who is intent on neither-perception-nor-non-perception. And how, bhikkhus, is one a person intent on sensual pleasures? Here, bhikkhus, a certain person has not abandoned lust for sensual pleasures, has not abandoned hatred for sensual pleasures, has not abandoned delusion regarding sensual pleasures. This is called a person intent on sensual pleasures. And how, bhikkhus, is one a person intent on form? Here, bhikkhus, a certain person has not abandoned lust for forms, has not abandoned hatred for forms, has not abandoned delusion regarding forms. This is called a person intent on form. And how, bhikkhus, is one a person intent on the formless? Here, bhikkhus, a certain person has not abandoned lust for the formless, has not abandoned hatred for the formless, has not abandoned delusion regarding the formless. This is called a person intent on the formless. And how, bhikkhus, is one a person intent on cessation? Here, bhikkhus, a certain person has abandoned lust for sensual pleasures, has abandoned hatred for sensual pleasures, has abandoned delusion regarding sensual pleasures; he has abandoned lust for forms, has abandoned hatred for forms, has abandoned delusion regarding forms; he has abandoned lust for the formless, has abandoned hatred for the formless, has abandoned delusion regarding the formless. This is called a person intent on cessation. And how, bhikkhus, is one a person intent on neither-perception-nor-non-perception? Here, bhikkhus, a certain person has not abandoned lust for the base of neither-perception-nor-non-perception, has not abandoned hatred for the base of neither-perception-nor-non-perception, has not abandoned delusion regarding the base of neither-perception-nor-non-perception. This is called a person intent on neither-perception-nor-non-perception. These, bhikkhus, are the five kinds of persons found existing in the world.”

“Bhikkhus, these five things, when developed and cultivated, lead to utter disenchantment, to dispassion, to cessation, to peace, to direct knowledge, to enlightenment, and to Nibbāna. What five? [The rest of the passage follows].”
“Here, monks, a monk dwells contemplating the unattractiveness of the body, perceiving the repulsiveness of food, perceiving non-delight in the entire world,
contemplating impermanence in all conditioned phenomena, and the perception of death is well-established within him.
These five things, monks, when developed and cultivated, lead to utter disenchantment, to dispassion, to cessation, to peace, to direct knowledge, to enlightenment, and to Nibbāna.”
The Ninth. Aṅguttara Nikāya 5.70 7.
Saññāvagga (The Chapter on Perceptions)
Āsavakkhayasutta (AN 5.70, PTS AN iii 83): “Bhikkhus,
these five things, when developed and cultivated, lead to the destruction of the taints.”
What are the five? Here, monks,
a monk dwells contemplating the foulness of the body, perceiving the repulsiveness of food, perceiving non-delight in the entire world,
contemplating impermanence in all conditioned phenomena, and the perception of death is well-established within him.
“Monks, these five qualities, when developed and cultivated, lead to the destruction of the taints.
Tenth. The Second Chapter on Perception.
Its summary verse:
Two perceptions, two increases,
discussion, and livelihood.
The bases of spiritual power are said to be two:
disenchantment and the destruction of the taints.
(Aṅguttara Nikāya 5.71)
8. Yodhājīva Chapter First Discourse on the Fruit of Liberation of Mind (Paṭhamacetovimuttiphalasutta) (AN 5.71, PTS AN iii 84)

“Bhikkhus, these five things, when developed and cultivated, have liberation of mind as their fruit and liberation of mind as their benefit; they have liberation by wisdom as their fruit and liberation by wisdom as their benefit.
What are the five?
Here, bhikkhus, a bhikkhu dwells contemplating the unattractiveness of the body, perceiving the repulsiveness of food, [perceiving the dispassion in all the world]...”
Perceiving non-delight, contemplating impermanence in all conditioned phenomena, and having the perception of death well-established within oneself.

These five things, monks, when developed and cultivated, have liberation of mind as their fruit and liberation of mind as their benefit; they have liberation by wisdom as their fruit and liberation by wisdom as their benefit.
When, monks, a monk is both liberated in mind and liberated by wisdom—

“Monks, this bhikkhu is called one who has ‘removed the crossbar,’ one who has ‘filled in the moat,’ one who has ‘pulled out the pillar,’ one who is ‘without a bolt,’ and one who is ‘a noble one with banner lowered, burden laid down, and unyoked.
And how, monks, is a bhikkhu one who has removed the crossbar?
Here, monks, a bhikkhu’s ignorance has been abandoned, cut off at the root, made like a palm stump, obliterated so that it is no more subject to future arising.”
In this way, monks, a monk has the crossbar lifted.
And how, monks, does a monk have the moat filled in?

Here, monks, a monk’s cycle of birth and wandering-on in existence leading to renewed becoming has been abandoned; it is cut off at the root, made like a palm stump, obliterated, and is no longer subject to future arising.
"In this way, monks, a monk has filled the moat.
And how, monks, does a monk pull out the pillar?
Here, monks, a monk’s craving has been abandoned, cut off at the root, made like a palm stump, obliterated so that it is no more subject to future arising."
"In this way, monks, a monk has pulled out the pillar.
And how, monks, is a monk one who has no bolt?
Here, monks, a monk has abandoned the five lower fetters; they have been cut off at the root, made like a palm stump, obliterated so that they are no more subject to future arising."
In this way, monks, a monk is one who has no bolt.
And how, monks, is a monk noble, with his banner lowered, his burden laid down, and unyoked?
Here, monks, a monk’s conceit of “I am” has been abandoned, cut off at the root, made like a palm stump, obliterated so that it is no more subject to future arising.
“In this way, monks, a monk is noble, with his banner lowered, his burden laid down, and unyoked.
Thus was the first [discourse]. Aṅguttara Nikāya 5.72
8. The Chapter on Warriors (Yodhājīva-vagga) The Second Discourse on the Fruit of Liberation of Mind (Dutiyacetovimuttiphalasutta) (AN 5.72, PTS AN iii 85)

“Bhikkhus, these five things, when developed and cultivated, have liberation of mind as their fruit and liberation of mind as their benefit; they have liberation by wisdom as their fruit and liberation by wisdom as their benefit.
What are the five?
The perception of impermanence, the perception of suffering in what is impermanent, the perception of non-self in what is suffering, the perception of abandoning, and the perception of dispassion.”

“Monks, these five things, when developed and cultivated, have liberation of mind as their fruit and liberation of mind as their benefit; they have liberation by wisdom as their fruit and liberation by wisdom as their benefit.

When, monks, a monk is liberated in mind and liberated by wisdom, he is called a monk who has ‘lifted the crossbar,’ who has ‘filled in the moat,’ who has ‘pulled out the pillar,’ who is ‘without bolts,’ and who is ‘a noble one with banner lowered, burden dropped, and unyoked.’”
“And how, bhikkhus, is a bhikkhu one who has removed the crossbar?
Here, bhikkhus, a bhikkhu has abandoned ignorance, cut it off at the root, made it like a palm stump, obliterated it so that it is no more subject to future arising.
It is in this way, bhikkhus, that a bhikkhu is one who has removed the crossbar.”
And how, monks, is a monk one who has filled in the moat?

Here, monks, a monk’s cycle of births leading to renewed existence has been abandoned; it is cut off at the root, made like a palm stump, rendered non-existent, and is subject to non-arising in the future.
In this way, monks, a monk is one who has filled in the moat.
And how, monks, is a monk one who has pulled out the pillar?
Here, monks, a monk’s craving has been abandoned, cut off at the root, made like a palm stump, obliterated so that it is no more subject to future arising.
It is in this way, monks, that a monk is one who has pulled out the pillar.
And how, monks, is a monk one who has no bolt?
Here, monks, a monk has abandoned the five lower fetters; they have been cut off at the root, made like a palm stump, obliterated so that they are no more subject to future arising.
It is in this way, monks, that a monk is one who has no bolt.
“And how, bhikkhus, is a bhikkhu a noble one whose banner is lowered, whose burden is laid down, who is unfettered?
Here, bhikkhus, a bhikkhu has abandoned the conceit ‘I am,’ cut it off at the root, made it like a palm stump, obliterated it so that it is no more subject to future arising.
It is in this way, bhikkhus, that a bhikkhu is a noble one whose banner is lowered, whose burden is laid down, who is unfettered.”
The Second.
Aṅguttara Nikāya 5.73 8.
The Chapter on Warriors (Yodhājīva-vagga)
Paṭhamadhammavihārīsutta (AN 5.73).
Then a certain bhikkhu approached the Blessed One; having approached and paid homage to the Blessed One, he sat down to one side. As he was sitting there, that bhikkhu said this to the Blessed One:
“Venerable sir, it is said, ‘one who dwells in the Dhamma, one who dwells in the Dhamma.
In what way, venerable sir, is a bhikkhu one who dwells in the Dhamma?
“In this case, bhikkhu, a bhikkhu masters the Dhamma...”

The discourses (sutta), mixed prose and verse (geyya), expositions (veyyākaraṇa), verses (gāthā), inspired utterances (udāna), "thus-it-was-said" (itivuttaka), birth stories (jātaka), marvelous qualities (abbhutadhamma), and analytical teachings (vedalla).
He spends his days with that study of the Dhamma; he neglects seclusion and does not apply himself to internal tranquility of mind.
This, bhikkhu, is called a bhikkhu who is "one devoted to study, not one who dwells in the Dhamma."
Furthermore, monk, a monk teaches the Dhamma in detail to others exactly as he has heard it and mastered it.
He spends his day with that exposition of the Dhamma; he neglects seclusion and does not devote himself to internal tranquility of mind.
This, monk, is called a monk who is "full of expositions," not one who dwells in the Dhamma.
Furthermore, bhikkhu, a bhikkhu recites the Dhamma in detail exactly as he has heard it and mastered it.
He spends the day with that recitation, neglects seclusion, and does not devote himself to internal tranquility of mind.
This, bhikkhu, is called a bhikkhu who is devoted to recitation, not one who dwells in the Dhamma.
Furthermore, bhikkhu, a bhikkhu mentally reflects upon, examines, and contemplates with his mind the Dhamma as he has heard it and mastered it.
He spends the day with those reflections on the Dhamma; he neglects seclusion and does not apply himself to internal tranquility of mind.
This, bhikkhu, is called a bhikkhu who is full of discursive thought, not one who dwells in the Dhamma.

In this case, bhikkhu, a bhikkhu masters the Dhamma—the discourses, mixed prose and verse, expositions, verses, inspired utterances, "Thus-it-was-said" passages, birth stories, accounts of marvelous phenomena, and questions-and-answers.
He does not spend his days merely with that mastery of the Dhamma; nor does he neglect seclusion, but devotes himself to internal tranquility of mind.
"In this way, bhikkhu, a bhikkhu is one who dwells in the Dhamma.

Thus, bhikkhu, I have taught that which abounds in learning, I have taught that which abounds in exposition, I have taught that which abounds in recitation, I have taught that which abounds in reflection, and I have taught the one who dwells in the Dhamma.
Whatever, bhikkhu, ought to be done by a Teacher seeking the welfare of his disciples out of compassion, taking compassion upon them—that has been done by me for you."
“Bhikkhu, these are the roots of trees; these are empty huts. Meditate, bhikkhu; do not be negligent, lest you later come to regret it. This is our instruction to you.
Thus was the third [discourse]. Aṅguttara Nikāya 5.74
8. Yodhājīva Chapter:
The Second Discourse on Dwellers in the Dhamma (AN 5.74, PTS AN iii 88)
Then a certain bhikkhu approached the Blessed One; having approached and paid homage to the Blessed One, he sat down to one side. As he was sitting there, that bhikkhu said this to the Blessed One:
“Venerable sir, it is said, ‘one who dwells in the Dhamma, one who dwells in the Dhamma.
In what way, venerable sir, is a bhikkhu one who dwells in the Dhamma?”
“Here, bhikkhu, a bhikkhu masters the Dhamma—
the discourses, mixed prose and verse, expositions, verses, inspired utterances, ‘Thus-it-was-said’ passages, birth stories, marvelous qualities, and questions-and-answers—
but he does not further understand their meaning with wisdom.”
“Monk, this is called a monk who is rich in learning but does not dwell in the Dhamma.
Furthermore, monk, a monk teaches the Dhamma in detail to others exactly as he has heard it and exactly as he has learned it, yet he does not understand its meaning through higher wisdom.
Monk, this is called a monk who is rich in exposition but does not dwell in the Dhamma.”
Furthermore, bhikkhu, a bhikkhu recites in detail the Dhamma as he has heard it and as he has mastered it, yet he does not understand its meaning further through wisdom.
This, bhikkhu, is called a bhikkhu who is devoted to recitation, but not one who dwells in the Dhamma.

Furthermore, bhikkhu, a bhikkhu reflects upon and examines with his mind the Dhamma as he has heard it and as he has mastered it, and he contemplates it with his intellect, yet he does not understand its meaning further through wisdom.
“Monk, this is called a monk who is full of discursive thought, not one who dwells in the Dhamma.
Here, monk, a monk masters the Dhamma:

the discourses (sutta), mixed prose and verse (geyya), expositions (veyyākaraṇa), verses (gāthā), inspired utterances (udāna), ‘Thus it was said’ (itivuttaka), birth stories (jātaka), marvelous qualities (abbhutadhamma), and analytical treatises (vedalla).”
Furthermore, he understands the meaning through wisdom.
In this way, bhikkhu, a bhikkhu dwells in the Dhamma.

Thus, bhikkhu, I have taught that which abounds in learning, I have taught that which abounds in exposition, I have taught that which abounds in recitation, I have taught that which abounds in reflection, and I have taught the one who dwells in the Dhamma.
“Bhikkhu, whatever should be done for disciples by a teacher who seeks their welfare, out of compassion, having taken compassion upon himself—that has been done by me for you.
Here, bhikkhu, are the roots of trees; here are empty huts. Meditate, bhikkhu; do not be negligent, lest you later come to regret it. This is my instruction to you.
This is the fourth [discourse].

Aṅguttara Nikāya 5.75 8. Yodhājīvavagga Paṭhamayodhājīvasutta (The First Discourse on Warriors) “Bhikkhus, there are these four kinds of warriors. What four? There is the warrior who, when his army is drawn up in battle array against the enemy, turns back and flees.

There is the warrior who, when his army is drawn up in battle array against the enemy, does not turn back, but he is wounded by arrows and spears. There is the warrior who, when his army is drawn up in battle array against the enemy, does not turn back, nor is he wounded by arrows and spears; rather, he seizes the enemy’s banner and standard. There is the warrior who, when his army is drawn up in battle array against the enemy, does not turn back, nor is he wounded by arrows and spears, nor does he seize the enemy’s banner and standard; rather, he slays the enemy, puts him to flight, and establishes himself as the victor. These, bhikkhus, are the four kinds of warriors. So too, bhikkhus, there are these four kinds of persons similar to warriors. What four? There is the person who, when the Dhamma is being taught, turns back and flees. There is the person who, when the Dhamma is being taught, does not turn back, but he is wounded by the arrows and spears of the teachings. There is the person who, when the Dhamma is being taught, does not turn back, nor is he wounded by the arrows and spears of the teachings; rather, he grasps the meaning of the teachings. There is the person who, when the Dhamma is being taught, does not turn back, nor is he wounded by the arrows and spears of the teachings, nor does he merely grasp the meaning of the teachings; rather, he penetrates the Dhamma with wisdom, he attains liberation through non-clinging, and he stands as the victor. These, bhikkhus, are the four kinds of persons similar to warriors.”
“Bhikkhus, there are these five types of warriors found existing in the world. Which five? [The text continues with the description of each type.]”
“Here, monks, a certain warrior, upon seeing a cloud of dust alone, falters, desponds, does not steady himself, and is unable to enter the battle.
Such, monks, is one kind of warrior found here in the world.
This, monks, is the first warrior existing and to be found in the world.”
Furthermore, monks, here a certain warrior can withstand a cloud of dust;
yet, upon seeing only the top of the banner, he falters, desponds, does not steady himself, and is unable to enter the battle.
Such, monks, is one kind of warrior.
This, monks, is the second type of warrior found existing in the world.
Furthermore, monks, here a certain warrior withstands the cloud of dust and withstands the top of the banner;
yet, upon hearing the shouting alone, he falters, desponds, does not steady himself, and is unable to enter the battle.
"Monks, such is one kind of warrior found here in the world.
This, monks, is the third warrior found existing in the world.
Furthermore, monks, there is another kind of warrior here who withstands the cloud of dust, withstands the top of the banner, and withstands the tumult."
Moreover, he is struck and wounded in the clash.
Such, monks, is one kind of warrior found here in the world.
This, monks, is the fourth warrior found existing in the world.

Furthermore, monks, here a certain warrior is able to withstand a cloud of dust, he is able to withstand the tops of banners, he is able to withstand the shouting, and he is able to withstand the clash of weapons.
Having won that battle, victorious in battle, he presides over the very front of that battlefield.
Such, monks, is one kind of warrior found here.
“Monks, this is the fifth type of warrior found existing in the world.
These, monks, are the five types of warriors found existing in the world.
In the same way, monks, there are these five persons resembling warriors found existing among the monks.”
What are the five?
Here, monks, having seen a cloud of dust, a monk sinks down, desponds, does not steady himself, and is unable to maintain the holy life.
Having revealed his weakness in the training, he renounces the training and reverts to the lower life.
What is its "dust-cloud"?
Here, monks, a monk hears:
"In such-and-such a village or town, there is a woman or a girl who is beautiful, handsome, pleasing, and endowed with the highest excellence of complexion."
Having heard that, he sinks down, desponds, does not steady himself, and is unable to maintain the holy life.
Having revealed his weakness in training and renounced the training, he returns to the lower life.
This is his "dust-storm."
"Just as that warrior, bhikkhus, upon seeing a cloud of dust alone, becomes despondent, sinks down, does not steady himself, and is unable to enter the battle;
even so, bhikkhus, do I speak of this person.
Such a person, bhikkhus, exists here in the world."
This, monks, is the first person resembling a warrior found existing among the bhikkhus.
Furthermore, monks, there is a bhikkhu who can withstand a cloud of dust;
yet, upon seeing only the tip of the banner, he falters, he desponds, he does not steady himself, and he is unable to maintain the holy life.
Having revealed his weakness in the training, he renounces the training and returns to the lower life.
What is his "summit of the banner"?
Here, monks, a monk does not indeed hear:
‘In such-and-such a village or town there is a woman or a girl who is beautiful, attractive, pleasing, and endowed with the highest excellence of complexion’;
or else, he personally sees a woman or a girl who is beautiful, attractive, pleasing, and endowed with the highest excellence of complexion.
Having seen her, he becomes despondent and dejected; he does not steady himself and is unable to maintain the holy life.
Having revealed his weakness in the training, he renounces the training and returns to the lower life.
This is his "summit of the banner.
Just as that warrior, monks, withstands the cloud of dust;
Moreover, monks, upon seeing the very tip of the banner, he falters, he desponds; he does not steady himself, and he is unable to enter the battle.
Monks, I say that this person is just like that.
Such a person, monks, exists here in the world.
This, monks, is the second person resembling a warrior found existing among the bhikkhus.
