Furthermore, monks, there is a bhikkhu who can withstand a cloud of dust and can withstand the top of an enemy’s banner;
yet, upon merely hearing the tumultuous shouting, he falters, desponds, does not steady himself, and is unable to maintain the holy life.
Having revealed weakness in the training, having renounced the training, he returns to the lower life.
What is his "shooing away"?
Here, monks, a woman approaches a monk who has gone to the forest, or to the foot of a tree, or to an empty hut, and she mocks him, addresses him, laughs at him, and ridicules him.
Thus, when being teased, addressed, laughed at, or ridiculed by women, he becomes dejected and dispirited; he does not steady himself and is unable to maintain the holy life.
Revealing his weakness in training, he renounces the training and returns to the lower life.
This is the "shouting out" regarding him.
"Just as that warrior, monks, withstands the cloud of dust and withstands the tip of the banner,
yet upon hearing the tumult alone, he falters, desponds, does not steady himself, and is unable to enter the battle—
such, monks, do I say this person is."
"Monks, such a person as this also exists here.
This, monks, is the third warrior-like person found existing among the monks.
Furthermore, monks, a monk withstands the cloud of dust, withstands the crest of the banner, and withstands the tumult."
Moreover, one is struck and harmed in a conflict.
What, monks, is that conflict?
Here, monks, a woman approaches a monk who has gone to the forest, or to the foot of a tree, or to an empty hut; she sits down beside him, lies down next to him, and throws herself upon him.
Thus, while being sat upon, reclined upon, or overwhelmed by a woman, he engages in sexual intercourse without having renounced the training and without disclosing his weakness.
This is his case regarding the clash.

Just as that warrior, monks, withstands the cloud of dust, withstands the tip of the banner, and withstands the shouting, yet in the actual clash he is struck and wounded; so too is this the case for him.
“Monks, I say that this person is just like that. Monks, there is such a person as this here among you.
This, monks, is the fourth warrior-like person existing and found among the monks.”
Furthermore, monks, a monk endures the cloud of dust, endures the top of the banner, endures the shouting, and endures the clash;
having completely conquered that battle, victorious in battle, he dwells at the very head of that battlefield.
What is his victory in battle?
In this case, monks, when a monk has gone to the forest, to the foot of a tree, or to an empty hut, a woman approaches him, sits down beside him, lies down next to him, or sprawls over him.
When he is being sat upon, laid down with, or sprawled over by the woman, he disentangles himself, frees himself, and departs wherever he wishes.
He frequents secluded lodgings: the forest, the foot of a tree, a mountain, a glen, a hillside cave, a charnel ground, a jungle thicket, an open space, or a heap of straw.
Thus, having gone to the forest, or to the foot of a tree, or to an empty hut, he sits down, folding his legs crosswise, setting his body erect, and establishing mindfulness before him.
Having abandoned covetousness for the world, he dwells with a mind free from covetousness; he purifies his mind of covetousness.
Having abandoned ill will and hatred, he dwells with a mind free from ill will, compassionate toward all living beings; he purifies his mind of ill will and hatred.
Having abandoned sloth and torpor, he dwells free from sloth and torpor, percipient of light, mindful and clearly comprehending; he purifies his mind of sloth and torpor.
Having abandoned restlessness and remorse, he dwells unagitated, with a mind calmed within; he purifies his mind of restlessness and remorse.
Having abandoned doubt, he dwells having crossed over doubt, free from uncertainty regarding wholesome phenomena; he purifies his mind of doubt.
Thus, having abandoned these five hindrances—defilements of the mind that weaken wisdom—he, secluded from sensual pleasures... [as before] ...
enters and dwells in the fourth jhāna.

When his mind is thus concentrated, purified, bright, unblemished, rid of imperfection, malleable, wieldy, steady, and attained to imperturbability, he directs it toward the knowledge of the destruction of the taints.
He understands as it really is: "This is suffering"; he understands as it really is: "This is the origin of suffering";
he understands as it really is: "This is the cessation of suffering"; he understands as it really is: "This is the way leading to the cessation of suffering."
One understands as it really is: "These are the taints"; one understands as it really is: "This is the origin of the taints"; one understands as it really is:
"This is the cessation of the taints"; one understands as it really is: "This is the practice leading to the cessation of the taints."
One understands it as it truly is.
For one who knows and sees thus, the mind is liberated from the influx of sensual desire, the mind is liberated from the influx of existence, and the mind is liberated from the influx of ignorance.
When it is liberated, there arises the knowledge: "It is liberated."
‘Birth is destroyed, the holy life has been lived, what had to be done has been done, there is no more of this state of being’—he understands this.
This is his victory in battle.
Just as that warrior, monks, withstands the cloud of dust, withstands the tip of the banner, and withstands the tumult.
He withstands the onslaught; having completely conquered that battle, he, as a victor in battle, presides over that very head of the battlefield.
Monks, I say this person is just like that.
Such a person, monks, exists here in the world.
“This, monks, is the fifth person resembling a warrior found existing among the monks.
These, monks, are the five persons resembling warriors found existing among the monks.
Thus [ends] the fifth.
Aṅguttara Nikāya 5.76 8.
Yodhājīvavagga Dutiyayodhājīvasutta (The Second Discourse on Warriors)
“Bhikkhus, there are these five types of warriors found existing in the world.
Which five?”
In this case, monks, a certain warrior takes up his sword and shield, fastens on his bow and quiver, and enters a drawn-out battle.
He exerts himself and strives in that battle,
yet while he is exerting himself and striving, his enemies kill him and finish him off.
"Monks, such is one kind of warrior found here in the world.
This, monks, is the first warrior existing and to be found in the world.
Furthermore, monks, there is another kind of warrior who, taking up sword and shield and buckling on his bow and quiver, enters a drawn-up battle array."
Thus he exerts himself and strives in that battle.
While he is exerting himself and striving, his enemies wound him;
they carry him off, and having carried him off, they lead him away to his kinsmen.
Thus, being led away by his kinsmen, he dies along the way before reaching them.
Such, monks, is one kind of warrior who exists here.
This, monks, is the second type of warrior found existing in the world.
Furthermore, monks, here a certain warrior takes up sword and shield, fastens on his bow and quiver, and enters a drawn-up battle array.
He exerts himself and strives in that battle,
but while he is exerting himself and striving, his enemies wound him, and they carry him off.
Having removed him, they lead him away to his relatives.
His relatives attend to him and care for him.
While being attended to and cared for by his relatives, he passes away from that very illness.
"Monks, such is one kind of warrior found here in the world.
This, monks, is the third warrior existing and found in the world.
Furthermore, monks, here another kind of warrior takes up sword and shield, fastens on his bow and quiver, and enters the thick of battle."
Thus he exerts himself and strives in that battle.
While he is exerting himself and striving, his enemies wound him;
they carry him off, and having carried him off, they lead him away to his kinsmen.
His kinsmen attend upon him and nurse him.
Being attended to and nursed by his kinsmen, he recovers from that illness.
Such, monks, is one kind of warrior.
This, monks, is the fourth warrior found existing in the world.
Furthermore, monks, here a certain warrior, taking up sword and shield and buckling on his bow and quiver, enters a drawn-up battle array.
Having won that battle, he emerges victorious and occupies the very front of the battlefield.
"Monks, such is one kind of warrior found here in the world.
This, monks, is the fifth warrior existing and found in the world.
These, monks, are the five warriors existing and found in the world."
"In the same way, monks, there are these five types of persons resembling warriors found existing among the monks.
What are the five?
Here, monks, a monk dwells in dependence upon a certain village or town."
Thus, having dressed in the morning and taken his bowl and robe, he enters that very village or town for alms with body unguarded,
speech unguarded, mind unguarded, mindfulness unestablished,
and the sense faculties unrestrained.
Thus, he sees there a woman poorly dressed or poorly clad.
Having seen that woman poorly dressed or poorly clad, lust invades his mind.
With a mind invaded by lust, he engages in sexual intercourse without having renounced the training and without disclosing his weakness.
"Just as if, monks, that warrior, having taken up sword and shield and having fastened on his bow and quiver, were to enter a drawn-up battle array;
and while he was striving and exerting himself in that battle, others were to kill him and finish him off—I say, monks, that this person is just like that. Such a one, too..."
“Monks, there is here a certain person.
This, monks, is the first person resembling a warrior found existing among the monks.
Furthermore, monks, a monk dwells in dependence upon a certain village or town.”
Thus, having dressed in the morning and taken his bowl and robe, he enters that very village or town for alms with body unguarded,
speech unguarded, mind unguarded, mindfulness unestablished,
and the sense faculties unrestrained.
Thus, there he sees a woman poorly dressed or poorly clad.
Having seen that woman poorly dressed or poorly clad, lust invades his mind.
With a mind invaded by lust, he is consumed by bodily heat and consumed by mental heat.
It occurs to him:
“Suppose I were to go to the monastery and inform the monks:
‘Friends, I am overwhelmed by lust, I am obsessed by lust; I am unable to maintain the holy life.’”
‘Having declared my weakness in the training, I shall renounce the training and return to the lower life.
While going to the monastery, before even reaching it, he declares his weakness in the training on the way, renounces the training, and returns to the lower life.
Just as that warrior, monks, having taken up sword and shield and girded himself with bow and quiver, [enters] the arrayed battle...
He enters the battle; he exerts himself and strives in that battle, but while he is exerting himself and striving, his enemies wound him, and they carry him off;
having carried him off, they lead him to his kinsmen.
While being led by his kinsmen, he dies on the way before reaching them. Monks, I say this person is just like that.
I say: such a person, monks, exists here in this world.
This, monks, is the second person resembling a warrior found existing among the bhikkhus.
Furthermore, monks, a bhikkhu dwells in dependence upon a certain village or town.
Thus, having dressed in the morning and taken his bowl and robe, he enters that very village or town for alms with body unguarded,
speech unguarded, mind unguarded, mindfulness unestablished,
and the sense faculties unrestrained.
There he sees a woman poorly dressed or poorly clad.
Having seen that woman poorly dressed or poorly clad, lust invades his mind.
With his mind invaded by lust, he is consumed by bodily fever and consumed by mental fever.
It occurs to him:
“What if I were to go to the monastery and inform the bhikkhus:
‘Friends, I am obsessed by lust, overcome by lust; I am unable to maintain the holy life.’”
‘Having confessed my weakness in the training, I shall renounce the training and return to the lower life.
He goes to the monastery and tells the monks:
‘Friends, I am overwhelmed by lust, I am oppressed by lust; I am unable to maintain the holy life.’
‘Having revealed my weakness in the training, and having renounced the training, I shall return to the lower life.
Then his fellow celibates exhort and instruct him:
‘Friend, sensual pleasures have been called “of little gratification” by the Blessed One; they are full of suffering, full of despair, and the danger therein is greater.’
The Blessed One has said that sensual pleasures are like a skeleton—full of suffering, full of despair, and the danger herein is even greater.
The Blessed One has said that sensual pleasures are like a lump of flesh—full of suffering, full of despair, and the danger herein is even greater.
The Blessed One has said that sensual pleasures are like a grass torch—full of suffering, full of despair, and the danger herein is even greater.
The Blessed One has said that sensual pleasures are like embers: they bring much suffering and much despair; the danger therein is even greater.
The Blessed One has said that sensual pleasures are like a dream: they bring much suffering and much despair; the danger therein is even greater.
The Blessed One has said that sensual pleasures are like borrowed goods: they bring much suffering and much despair; the danger therein is even greater.
The Blessed One has said that sensual pleasures are like the fruit of a tree—full of suffering, full of despair; herein the danger is greater.
The Blessed One has said that sensual pleasures are like a butcher’s block—full of suffering, full of despair; herein the danger is greater.
The Blessed One has said that sensual pleasures are like a spear and a stake—full of suffering, full of despair; herein the danger is greater.
“Sensual pleasures have been compared by the Blessed One to the likeness of a snake’s venom; they bring much suffering and much despair, and the danger therein is even greater.
May the Venerable One take delight in the holy life;
let the Venerable One not, having manifested weakness in the training, renounce the training and return to the lower life.”
Being thus exhorted and thus instructed by his fellow celibates, he says:

“Friends, although it has been said by the Blessed One that sensual pleasures provide little gratification, much suffering, and much despair, and that the danger therein is greater—nevertheless, I am unable to maintain the holy life.
Having declared my weakness in the training, I shall renounce the training and return to the lower life.”
Thus, having revealed his weakness in the training and renounced the training, he returns to the lower life.
Just as that warrior, monks, having taken up sword and shield and girded himself with bow and quiver, enters a drawn-up battle array;
and while he exerts himself and strives in that battle, as he is exerting himself and striving—
Others scrape away at him, and they remove him; having removed him, they lead him to his kinsmen, and his kinsmen attend upon him and care for him.
While being attended to and cared for by his kinsmen, he passes away from that very affliction.
"I say, monks, that this person is just like that. Such, monks, is one kind of person found here."
This, monks, is the third person resembling a warrior who exists among the monks.
Furthermore, monks, a monk dwells in dependence upon a certain village or town.
Having dressed in the morning and taken his bowl and robe, he enters that very village or town for alms.
He enters with body unguarded, speech unguarded, mind unguarded, with mindfulness unestablished,
and with the sense faculties unrestrained.
There he sees women poorly dressed or poorly clad.
Seeing that woman poorly dressed or poorly clad, lust invades his mind.
With his mind invaded by lust, he is consumed by body and consumed by mind.
It occurs to him:
‘What if I were to go to the monastery and inform the bhikkhus:
“Friends, I am obsessed by lust, overcome by lust; I am unable to maintain the holy life.
Having declared my weakness in the training, I shall renounce the training and return to the lower life”?’
So, having gone to the monastery, he informs the bhikkhus:
“Friends, I am overwhelmed by lust, I am overcome by lust; I am unable to maintain the holy life.
Having declared my weakness in the training, I shall renounce the training and return to the lower life.”
His fellow celibates advise and instruct him:
“Friend, sensual pleasures have been described by the Blessed One as providing little gratification, but much suffering and much despair; the danger in them is greater.
Sensual pleasures have been compared by the Blessed One to a skeleton; they provide little gratification, but much suffering and much despair; the danger in them is greater.”

The Blessed One has said that sensual pleasures are like a lump of meat... he has said they are like a torch of grass... he has said they are like a pit of glowing coals... he has said they are like a dream... he has said they are like borrowed goods...
he has said they are like the fruit of a tree... he has said they are like a butcher’s block and knife.
… “Sensual pleasures have been compared by the Blessed One to a spear and a stake… sensual pleasures have been compared by the Blessed One to the head of a snake—full of suffering, full of despair;
the danger here is even greater.
May the venerable one take delight in the holy life.”
‘Let not the venerable one, having revealed weakness in his training and renounced the training, return to the lower life.
Being thus exhorted and instructed by his fellow celibates, he says:
‘I shall strive, friends; I shall exert myself, friends; I shall take delight, friends.’”
"Friend, it is not that I shall reveal my weakness in the training, renounce the training, and return to the lower life.
Bhikkhus, just as that warrior, having taken up sword and shield and girded with his bow and quiver,
enters a drawn-up battle array, exerts himself and strives in that battle— him, as he exerts himself and strives...
Others lick him, and they carry him away; having carried him away, they bring him to his relatives, and his relatives attend to him and nurse him.
Being attended to and nursed by his relatives, he recovers from that illness.
Monks, I say that this person is just like that.
“Monks, such a person as this also exists here.
This, monks, is the fourth person resembling a warrior found existing among the monks.
Furthermore, monks, a monk dwells in dependence upon a certain village or town.”
Thus, having dressed in the morning and taken his bowl and robe,
he enters that very village or town for alms with body guarded, speech guarded, mind guarded, with mindfulness established,
and sense faculties restrained.
Thus, having seen a form with the eye, he does not grasp at its signs or its secondary characteristics.
Since, if he were to dwell with the faculty of the eye unrestrained, covetousness, dejection, and evil unwholesome states might flow in upon him, he practices for its restraint;
he guards the faculty of the eye; he attains mastery over the faculty of the eye.
Having heard a sound with the ear...
having smelled an odor with the nose...
having tasted a flavor with the tongue...
Having touched a tangible object with the body...
having cognized a mental phenomenon with the mind, one does not grasp at its signs nor grasp at its secondary characteristics.
For if one dwells with this faculty of the mind unrestrained, covetousness and dejection—evil, unwholesome states—[might arise].

If states of covetousness and unwholesome intentions were to flow in regarding these things, he practices for their restraint; he guards the faculty of the mind and achieves mastery over the faculty of the mind.
Having returned from his almsround after his meal, he resorts to a secluded lodging:
a forest, the foot of a tree, a mountain, a glen, a hillside cave, a charnel ground, a jungle thicket, an open space, or a heap of straw.
Thus, having gone to the forest, or to the foot of a tree, or to an empty hut, he sits down, folding his legs crosswise, setting his body erect, and establishing mindfulness before him.
Having abandoned covetousness for the world... [and so on] ...having abandoned these five hindrances, which are defilements of the mind that weaken wisdom, secluded from sensual pleasures...
[and so on] ...he enters and dwells in the fourth jhāna.

When his mind is thus concentrated, purified, cleansed, stainless, free from defilements, supple, wieldy, steady, and attained to imperturbability, he directs his mind toward the knowledge of the destruction of the taints (*āsava*).
He understands, as it really is: "This is suffering" ... [and so on] ...
he understands: "There is no further state of being."
"Just as that warrior, monks, having taken up his sword and shield and equipped himself with bow and quiver,
enters the arrayed battle; and having won that battle, victorious in combat, he stands at the very head of the battlefield—
even so, monks, do I describe this person."
“Such a person, monks, is found here in this world.
This, monks, is the fifth person comparable to a warrior found existing among the monks.
These, monks, are the five persons comparable to warriors found existing among the monks.”
The Sixth. Aṅguttara Nikāya 5.77 8.
The Chapter on Warriors (Yodhājīva-vagga)
The First Discourse on Future Dangers (AN 5.77): “Bhikkhus,
for a forest-dwelling bhikkhu who perceives these five future dangers, it is sufficient [to dwell in the forest].”
To dwell heedful, ardent, and resolute for the attainment of the unattained, for the reaching of the unreached,
for the realization of the unrealized—
what are these five?
In this case, monks, a forest-dwelling bhikkhu reflects thus:
"At present, I am dwelling alone in the forest.
While I am dwelling alone in the forest..."
‘A snake might bite me, or a scorpion might sting me, or a centipede might bite me;
because of that, my death would come about, and that would be an obstacle for me.
Come now, I shall arouse energy for the attainment of the unattained, for the reaching of the unreached, for the realization of the unrealized.’”
"Monks, seeing this first future danger, it is sufficient for a forest-dwelling bhikkhu to dwell heedful,
ardent, and resolute, for the attainment of the unattained, for the reaching of the unreached,
for the realization of the unrealized."
Furthermore, monks, a forest-dwelling bhikkhu reflects thus:
‘At present I am dwelling alone in the forest.
While I am dwelling alone in the forest, [I might encounter danger].’
‘I might stumble and fall into a pit, or the food I have eaten might cause illness, or my bile might be disturbed, or my phlegm might be disturbed, or my piercing winds might be disturbed;
because of that, my death would come about, and that would be an obstacle for me.
Come now, I shall arouse energy for the attainment of the unattained, for the reaching of the unreached, for the realization of the unrealized.’”
"Monks, seeing this second future danger, it is sufficient for a forest-dwelling bhikkhu to dwell heedful,
ardent, and resolute, for the attainment of the unattained, for the reaching of the unreached,
for the realization of the unrealized."
Furthermore, monks, a forest-dwelling bhikkhu reflects thus:
"At present, I am dwelling alone in the forest.
While dwelling alone in the forest..."
‘I might encounter wild beasts—either a lion, a tiger, a leopard, a bear, or a hyena—and they might take my life;
because of that, I would die, and that would be an obstacle for me.
Come now, I shall arouse energy for the attainment of the unattained, for the reaching of the unreached, for the realization of the unrealized.’”
"Monks, seeing this third future danger, it is sufficient for a forest-dwelling bhikkhu to dwell heedful,
ardent, and resolute, for the attainment of the unattained, for the reaching of the unreached,
and for the realization of the unrealized."
Furthermore, monks, a forest-dwelling bhikkhu reflects thus:
‘At present, I am dwelling alone in the forest.
While I am dwelling alone in the forest, [I might encounter danger].’
‘I might encounter young men, whether they have performed their duties or not, who might deprive me of life;
because of that, my death would come about, and that would be an obstacle for me.
Come now, I shall arouse energy for the attainment of the unattained, for the achievement of the unachieved, for the realization of the unrealized.’”
This, monks, is the fourth future danger; considering it, it is sufficient for a forest-dwelling bhikkhu to dwell heedful,
ardent, and resolute, for the attainment of the unattained, for the reaching of the unreached,
and for the realization of the unrealized.
Furthermore, monks, a forest-dwelling bhikkhu reflects thus:
‘At present I am living alone in the forest.
Now there are wild non-human beings in the forest who might take my life.’
‘If I were to die because of that, it would be an obstacle for me;
come now, I shall arouse energy for the attainment of the unattained, for the realization of the unrealized, for the actualization of the unactualized.
This, monks, is the fifth future danger that a forest-dwelling bhikkhu should consider.
"To dwell heedful, ardent, and resolute for the attainment of the unattained, for the reaching of the unreached,
for the realization of the unrealized— monks,
it is indeed sufficient for a forest-dwelling monk, considering these five future perils, [to live thus]."
“By one who is diligent, ardent, and resolute, it is possible to dwell for the attainment of the unattained, the reaching of the unreached,
and the realization of the unrealized.
This is the seventh.
Aṅguttara Nikāya 5.78 8.
Yodhājīva-vagga Dutiya-anāgata-bhaya-sutta (The Second Discourse on Future Perils)
“Bhikkhus, when a bhikkhu perceives these five future perils, it is sufficient for him to dwell diligent,
ardent, and resolute, for the attainment of the unattained, for the reaching of the unreached, for the realization of the unrealized.
What are the five?
Here, monks, a monk reflects thus:
"I am now young, a youth with black hair, endowed with the blessing of youth, in the prime of life."
There comes a time when this body is touched by old age.
For one who is aged and overcome by old age, it is not easy to attend to the teaching of the Buddhas, nor is it easy to resort to remote lodgings in forest thickets and wilderness retreats.
Before that state—which is undesirable, unwelcome, and disagreeable—comes upon me, [I must practice now].

‘Come now, let me arouse energy for the attainment of the unattained, for the reaching of the unreached, for the realization of the unrealized, so that—endowed with this Dhamma—I may dwell at ease even when old.

This, monks, is the first future danger; seeing it, it is enough for a monk to dwell heedful, ardent, and resolute for the attainment of the unattained, for the reaching of the unreached, for the realization of the unrealized.
Furthermore, monks, a bhikkhu reflects thus:
‘At present I am free from illness and affliction, endowed with a healthy digestion that is neither too cold nor too hot, but moderate and fit for striving.
Yet there will come a time when this body is struck by disease.’
"When one is afflicted and overcome by illness, it is not easy to attend to the teaching of the Buddhas, nor is it easy to resort to remote lodgings in forest and jungle retreats.
Before that undesirable, unwelcome, and disagreeable condition comes upon me,

let me rather exert energy in advance for the attainment of the unattained, for the reaching of the unreached, for the realization of the unrealized— so that, endowed with such a state, I may dwell in comfort even while ill."
"Monks, seeing this second future danger, it is enough for a monk to dwell heedful,
ardent, and resolute, for the attainment of the unattained, for the reaching of the unreached, for the realization of the unrealized.
Furthermore, monks, a monk reflects thus:"
‘At present, indeed, there is good food, an abundance of crops, and alms are easily obtained; it is easy to subsist by gleaning and gathering.
But there will come a time when there is famine, a scarcity of crops, and alms are difficult to obtain; it will not be easy to subsist by gleaning and gathering.
During a famine, people migrate to where there is plenty.’
In that case, there is dwelling in company, dwelling in bustle.
When there is dwelling in company and dwelling in bustle, it is not easy to attend to the teaching of the Buddhas, nor is it easy to resort to remote lodgings in forest groves and wilderness areas.
Before that doctrine—which is undesirable, unlovely, and disagreeable—comes upon me;

‘Come now, let me arouse energy for the attainment of the unattained, for the achievement of the unachieved, for the realization of the unrealized, so that endowed with this quality I may dwell at ease even in a time of famine.
Monks, seeing this third future peril, it is sufficient for a monk to dwell heedful, ardent,
and resolute for the attainment of the unattained, for the achievement of the unachieved, for the realization of the unrealized.
Furthermore, monks, a monk reflects thus:
‘At present, people live together in harmony, in mutual affection, without dispute, like milk and water mixed, looking upon one another with eyes of love.
But there will come a time when there is danger and turmoil in the wilderness, and the people of the countryside, mounted on their chariots, will flee in all directions.’
When there is fear, people flock toward places of safety.
There, one dwells in company and in a crowded place.
When one dwells in company and in a crowded place, it is not easy to attend to the teaching of the Buddhas, nor is it easy to resort to remote lodgings in forests and jungle-thickets.
‘In the past, that Dhamma came upon me—undesirable, unlovely, and disagreeable.

Come now, let me exert effort beforehand for the attainment of the unattained, for the reaching of the unreached, for the realization of the unrealized, so that, endowed with that Dhamma, I may dwell in comfort even in the face of danger.
This, monks, is the fourth future peril which a monk, seeing it clearly, ought to regard as sufficient reason to be diligent.
To dwell ardent and resolute for the attainment of the unattained, for the realization of the unrealized, and for the direct experience of the as-yet-unexperienced.
Furthermore, monks, a monk reflects thus:
"At present, the Saṅgha is harmonious, living in mutual joy, without dispute, with a single recitation, and dwelling in comfort."
There comes a time when the Saṅgha is split.
When the Saṅgha is split, it is not easy to attend to the teaching of the Buddhas, nor is it easy to resort to remote lodgings in forest groves and wilderness areas.

“Bhikkhus, there are these five future dangers that have not yet arisen but will arise in the future.
You should be awake to them.”
And having awakened, one should strive for their abandonment.
What are the five?
There will be, monks, in a future time, monks who have not developed the body, have not developed virtue, have not developed the mind, and have not developed wisdom.
Being untrained in body, untrained in virtue, untrained in mind, and untrained in wisdom, they will ordain others;
yet they will not be able to discipline them in higher virtue, higher mind, and higher wisdom.
Those too will become untrained in body, untrained in virtue, untrained in mind, and untrained in wisdom.
Being themselves undeveloped in body, undeveloped in virtue, undeveloped in mind, and undeveloped in wisdom, they will ordain others.
They too will not be able to train them in higher virtue, higher mind, and higher wisdom;
they too will be undeveloped in body, undeveloped in virtue, undeveloped in mind, and undeveloped in wisdom.
"Thus, monks, through corruption of the Dhamma comes corruption of the Vinaya;
through corruption of the Vinaya comes corruption of the Dhamma.
This, monks, is the first future peril that has not yet arisen but will arise in the future."
This you must awaken to; and having awakened to it, you must strive for its abandonment.
Furthermore, monks, in the future there will be monks who have not developed the body, have not developed virtue, have not developed the mind, and have not developed wisdom.
Being themselves undeveloped in body, undeveloped in virtue, undeveloped in mind, and undeveloped in wisdom, they will grant dependence to others;
yet they will not be able to train them in higher virtue, higher mind, and higher wisdom.
They too will become undeveloped in body, undeveloped in virtue, undeveloped in mind, and undeveloped in wisdom.
Being themselves undeveloped in body, undeveloped in virtue, undeveloped in mind, and undeveloped in wisdom, they will grant dependence to others;
yet they will not be able to train them in higher virtue, higher mind, and higher wisdom.
They too will become undeveloped in body, undeveloped in virtue, undeveloped in mind, and undeveloped in wisdom.
Thus, monks, through corruption of the Dhamma comes corruption of the Vinaya;
through corruption of the Vinaya comes corruption of the Dhamma.
This, monks, is the second future peril that has not yet arisen but will arise in the future.
That you must awaken to; and having awakened, you must strive for its abandonment.
Furthermore, monks, in the future there will be monks who have not developed the body, have not developed virtue, have not developed the mind, and have not developed wisdom.
Being undeveloped in body, undeveloped in virtue, undeveloped in mind, and undeveloped in wisdom, they will speak on the Abhidhamma and the Vedalla discourses while falling into dark states;
thus they will not awaken. In this way, monks, from corruption of the Dhamma comes corruption of the Vinaya;
from corruption of the Vinaya comes corruption of the Dhamma.
This, monks, is the third future danger that has not yet arisen but will arise in the future.
You must be awake to it;
having become awake to it, you must strive for its abandonment.
Furthermore, monks, in the future there will be monks who have not developed the body, have not developed virtue, have not developed the mind, and have not developed wisdom.
Being thus undeveloped in body, virtue, mind, and wisdom, when those discourses spoken by the Tathāgata—
which are profound, profound in meaning, transcendent, and connected with emptiness— are being recited, they will not wish to listen.
They will not lend an ear, they will not apply their minds toward understanding,
nor will they consider those teachings as something to be learned and mastered.
As for those discourses that are merely poetic compositions, works of verse, with elegant phrasing and refined expression— external texts spoken by disciples—
When those teachings are being recited, they will listen with eager intent, lend an ear, apply their minds to understanding,
and consider those teachings as something to be mastered and learned by heart.
Thus, monks, from corruption of the Dhamma comes corruption of the Vinaya.
Corruption of the discipline is corruption of the Dhamma.
This, monks, is the fourth future danger that has not yet arisen but will arise in the future.
You must wake up to it.
And having awakened to this, one should strive for its abandonment.
Furthermore, monks, in a future time there will be monks who have not developed the body, have not developed virtue, have not developed the mind, and have not developed wisdom.
Being thus undeveloped in body, virtue, mind, and wisdom, those elder monks will become luxurious.
They will become lax, leaders in falling away, having abandoned the burden of solitude;
they will not arouse energy for the attainment of the unattained, for the reaching of the unreached, for the realization of the unrealized.
Subsequent generations, seeing them, will follow their example.

She too will become one who is luxurious, lax, a leader in falling away, having abandoned the burden of seclusion, and she will not arouse energy for the attainment of the unattained, for the reaching of the unreached, for the realization of the unrealized.
Thus, monks, from corruption of the Dhamma comes corruption of the Vinaya;

The Ninth. Aṅguttara Nikāya 5.80 8.
The Chapter on Warriors (Yodhājīva-vagga)
The Fourth Discourse on Future Dangers (Catuttha-anāgata-bhaya-sutta): “Monks,
there are these five future dangers that have not yet arisen but will arise in the future.”
These you must awaken to;
having awakened to them, you must strive for their abandonment.
Which five?
“Bhikkhus, in the future there will be bhikkhus who desire fine robes.
Desiring fine robes, they will abandon the practice of wearing rag-robes; they will abandon remote lodgings in forests and jungle-thickets;
having flocked to villages, towns, and royal capitals, they will make their homes there, and for the sake of robes they will engage in various kinds of improper and unseemly modes of livelihood.”
“Monks, this is the first future danger that has not yet arisen but will arise in the future.
You must be awake to it;
having become awake to it, you must strive for its abandonment.”
Furthermore, monks, in the future there will be monks who desire fine almsfood.
Desiring fine almsfood, they will neglect the practice of living on alms; they will neglect remote lodgings in forests and jungle-thickets.

Having descended to villages, towns, and royal capitals, they will make their dwelling while seeking the finest flavors with the tip of their tongue, and for the sake of almsfood, they will engage in various kinds of improper and unsuitable searches.
“Monks, this is the second future peril that has not yet arisen but will arise in the future.
You must be awake to it;
having become awake, you must strive for its abandonment.”
Furthermore, monks, in the future there will be monks who desire fine lodgings.
Desiring fine lodgings, they will neglect dwelling at the foot of trees; they will neglect remote lodgings in forests and jungle-thickets.

Having descended to villages, towns, and royal capitals, they will make their dwellings there, and for the sake of lodgings, they will engage in various kinds of improper and unseemly search for alms.
“Monks, this is the third future danger that has not yet arisen but will arise in the future.
You must be awake to it;
having become awake to it, you must strive for its abandonment.”
Furthermore, monks, in the future there will be monks who dwell in association with bhikkhunīs, sikkhamānās, and samaṇuddesas.
When there is such association with bhikkhunīs, sikkhamānās, and samaṇuddesas, monks, this may be expected:
either they will lead the holy life without enthusiasm, or they will fall into some defiled offense, or they will abandon the training and return to the lower life.
“Monks, this is the fourth future peril that has not yet arisen but will arise in the future.
You must be awakened to it;
and having been awakened, you must strive for its abandonment.”
Furthermore, monks, in the future there will be monks who dwell in close association with monastery attendants and novices.
When there is such association with monastery attendants and novices, monks, this is to be expected:
they will dwell devoted to various kinds of hoarding and enjoyment; they will even make manifest signs upon the earth and upon the tips of green grass.
Monks, this is the fifth future peril that has not yet arisen but will arise in the future.
You must be awake to it;
having become awake, you must strive for its abandonment.
“Monks, these five future dangers, which have not yet arisen but will arise in the future,
must be recognized by you; and having recognized them,
you must strive for their abandonment.”

Aṅguttara Nikāya 5.81, Chapter 9: The Chapter on Elders (Theravagga).
The Discourse on the Attractive (Rajanīyasutta): “Bhikkhus,
possessing five qualities, an elder bhikkhu is displeasing and disagreeable to his fellow practitioners of the holy life, and he is neither respected nor esteemed by them.
Which five?

He lusts after what is lust-inducing, hates what is hate-inducing, is deluded by what is delusion-inducing, becomes agitated by what is agitation-inducing, and is intoxicated by what is intoxication-inducing.
Possessing these five qualities, monks, an elder bhikkhu is disliked and displeasing to his fellow celibate practitioners, and he is neither respected nor esteemed.
“Bhikkhus, possessing five qualities, an elder bhikkhu is dear and agreeable to his fellow celibates, and is respected and esteemed by them.

What are the five? He is not lustful toward what is lust-inducing; he is not hateful toward what is hate-inducing; he is not deluded by what is delusion-inducing; he is not agitated by what is agitation-inducing; he is not intoxicated by what is intoxication-inducing. Possessing these five qualities, an elder bhikkhu is dear and agreeable to his fellow celibates, and is respected and esteemed by them.”
“Bhikkhus, a senior bhikkhu endowed with these five qualities is dear and agreeable to his fellow celibates, and is respected and esteemed by them.
Thus was the first [discourse]. Aṅguttara Nikāya 5.82

9. Theravagga Vītarāgasutta (AN 5.82, PTS AN iii 111) “Monks, there are these four kinds of persons found existing in the world. What four? The person who is free from lust; the person who is free from hatred; the person who is free from delusion; and the person who is completely liberated. These, monks, are the four kinds of persons found existing in the world.”
“Bhikkhus, possessing five qualities, an elder bhikkhu is displeasing and disagreeable to his fellow practitioners, and he is neither respected nor esteemed by them.
What are the five?
He is not free from lust, he is not free from hatred, he is not free from delusion, he is a slanderer, and he is a spiteful person.”

Monks, an elder monk endowed with five qualities is dear and pleasing to his fellow practitioners, and he is respected and esteemed by them.
With which five?
“He is free from lust, free from hatred, free from delusion, and he is without malice and without disparagement.
Possessing these five qualities, monks, an elder bhikkhu is dear and agreeable to his fellow practitioners of the holy life, and he is respected and esteemed by them.
The second [sutta].

Aṅguttara Nikāya 5.84 9. Theravagga (The Chapter on Elders)
Assaddhasutta (AN 5.84):

“Bhikkhus, possessing five qualities, an elder bhikkhu is disliked and displeasing to his fellow celibates, and he is neither respected nor esteemed. What five? He is faithless, unvirtuous, unlearned, lazy, and muddle-minded.”
Which five?
He is faithless, he is shameless, he is unafraid of wrongdoing, he is lazy, and he is unwise.
