“Bhikkhus, possessing five qualities, an elder bhikkhu is dear and agreeable to his companions in the holy life, and he is respected and esteemed by them.
What are the five?
He is endowed with faith, he has a sense of shame, he has moral dread, he is energetic, and he is wise.”
“Monks, a senior monk endowed with these five qualities is dear and pleasing to his fellow practitioners of the holy life, and is respected and esteemed by them. Thus was the fourth [sutta].
Aṅguttara Nikāya 5.85

9. Theravagga Akkhamasutta (AN 5.85) “Monks, there are these four kinds of persons found existing in the world. What four? The person who is intolerant; the person who is patient; the person who is both intolerant and patient; and the person who is neither intolerant nor patient. And how, monks, is one a person who is intolerant? Here, monks, someone is angry when criticized and does not become calm; he is angry when praised and does not become calm; he is angry when given a gift and does not become calm; he is angry when receiving a gift and does not become calm. This, monks, is called a person who is intolerant. And how, monks, is one a person who is patient? Here, monks, someone is not angry when criticized and becomes calm; he is not angry when praised and becomes calm; he is not angry when given a gift and becomes calm; he is not angry when receiving a gift and becomes calm. This, monks, is called a person who is patient. And how, monks, is one a person who is both intolerant and patient? Here, monks, someone is angry when criticized and does not become calm; yet he is not angry when praised and becomes calm; he is angry when given a gift and does not become calm; yet he is not angry when receiving a gift and becomes calm. This, monks, is called a person who is both intolerant and patient. And how, monks, is one a person who is neither intolerant nor patient? Here, monks, someone is neither angry when criticized nor does he become calm; he is neither angry when praised nor does he become calm; he is neither angry when given a gift nor does he become calm; he is neither angry when receiving a gift nor does he become calm. This, monks, is called a person who is neither intolerant nor patient. These, monks, are the four kinds of persons found existing in the world.”
“Bhikkhus, possessing five qualities, an elder bhikkhu is displeasing and disagreeable to his fellow celibates, and he is neither respected nor esteemed by them.
What are the five?
He is intolerant of forms, intolerant of sounds, intolerant of odors, intolerant of tastes, and intolerant of tactile objects.
“Monks, an elder monk endowed with these five qualities is displeasing and disagreeable to his fellow practitioners, and he is neither respected nor esteemed by them.
Monks, an elder monk endowed with five qualities is pleasing and agreeable to his fellow practitioners, and he is respected and esteemed by them. With which five? [The Buddha said:]”
“He is patient with forms, patient with sounds, patient with odors, patient with tastes, and patient with tactile objects.
Possessing these five qualities, monks, an elder bhikkhu is dear and agreeable to his fellow practitioners, and he is respected and esteemed by them.
The fifth.

Aṅguttara Nikāya 5.86 9. Theravagga Paṭisambhidāpatta Sutta: Attaining the Analytical Knowledges “Bhikkhus, there are these five analytical knowledges (*paṭisambhidā*). What five? The analytical knowledge of meaning (*atthapaṭisambhidā*), the analytical knowledge of phenomena (*dhammapaṭisambhidā*), the analytical knowledge of linguistic expression (*niruttipaṭisambhidā*), the analytical knowledge of perspicuity (*paṭibhānapaṭisambhidā*), and the analytical knowledge of the knowledge of liberation (*vimuttiñāṇadassanapaṭisambhidā*). These, bhikkhus, are the five analytical knowledges.

“Bhikkhus, one who possesses these five analytical knowledges is called a ‘master of the Dhamma,’ one who has attained the analytical knowledges, one who has reached the goal, a great sage, a supreme person, one who has accomplished his task, one who has laid down the burden, one who has reached the ultimate end, one who has completely severed the fetters of existence, one who has attained the supreme security from bondage, a Buddha. And how, bhikkhus, is one a master of the Dhamma? Here, bhikkhus, a bhikkhu teaches the Dhamma as he has heard it, as he has learned it, without altering it, without distorting it, without contradicting the Teacher’s instruction, so that it is beneficial and conducive to the goal for those who practice accordingly. It is in this way, bhikkhus, that one is a master of the Dhamma. And how, bhikkhus, is one one who has attained the analytical knowledges? Here, bhikkhus, a bhikkhu understands as it really is: ‘This is suffering’; he understands as it really is: ‘This is the origin of suffering’; he understands as it really is: ‘This is the cessation of suffering’; he understands as it really is: ‘This is the way leading to the cessation of suffering. It is in this way, bhikkhus, that one is one who has attained the analytical knowledges. And how, bhikkhus, is one one who has reached the goal? Here, bhikkhus, a bhikkhu has abandoned lust, hatred, and delusion, and has uprooted them at the root, made them like a palm stump, obliterated them so that they are no longer subject to future arising. It is in this way, bhikkhus, that one is one who has reached the goal. And how, bhikkhus, is one a great sage? Here, bhikkhus, a bhikkhu is one who knows himself as he really is, who knows others as they really are, who knows the world as it really is, who knows the Dhamma as it really is, and who knows the right time as it really is. It is in this way, bhikkhus, that one is a great sage. And how, bhikkhus, is one a supreme person? Here, bhikkhus, a bhikkhu is unsurpassed in virtue, unsurpassed in concentration, unsurpassed in wisdom, unsurpassed in liberation, and unsurpassed in the knowledge and vision of liberation. It is in this way, bhikkhus, that one is a supreme person. And how, bhikkhus, is one one who has accomplished his task? Here, bhikkhus, a bhikkhu has done what was to be done, has laid aside the burden, has attained his own goal, has utterly destroyed the fetters of existence, and is liberated through final knowledge. It is in this way, bhikkhus, that one is one who has accomplished his task. And how, bhikkhus, is one one who has laid down the burden? Here, bhikkhus, a bhikkhu has laid down the burden of greed, the burden of hatred, the burden of delusion, and the burden of all defilements. It is in this way, bhikkhus, that one is one who has laid down the burden. And how, bhikkhus, is one one who has reached the ultimate end? Here, bhikkhus, a bhikkhu has reached the ultimate end of birth, the ultimate end of old age, the ultimate end of death, the ultimate end of sorrow, lamentation, pain, grief, and despair. It is in this way, bhikkhus, that one is one who has reached the ultimate end. And how, bhikkhus, is one one who has completely severed the fetters of existence? Here, bhikkhus, a bhikkhu has severed the fetter of greed, the fetter of hatred, the fetter of delusion, and the fetter of all defilements. It is in this way, bhikkhus, that one is one who has completely severed the fetters of existence. And how, bhikkhus, is one one who has attained the supreme security from bondage? Here, bhikkhus, a bhikkhu has attained the supreme security from bondage regarding greed, the supreme security from bondage regarding hatred, the supreme security from bondage regarding delusion, and the supreme security from bondage regarding all defilements. It is in this way, bhikkhus, that one is one who has attained the supreme security from bondage. And how, bhikkhus, is one a Buddha? Here, bhikkhus, a bhikkhu has awakened to the Dhamma by himself, has awakened to the Dhamma without another, has awakened to the Dhamma independently. It is in this way, bhikkhus, that one is a Buddha. Thus spoke the Blessed One. Having said this, the Sublime One rose from his seat and entered his dwelling. Then, not long after the Blessed One had departed, a certain bhikkhu approached the Venerable Ānanda and said to him: “Friend Ānanda, the Blessed One has spoken in brief of the five analytical knowledges, and having said this, he rose from his seat and entered his dwelling. What, friend, is the detailed exposition of the Blessed One’s brief statement? The Venerable Ānanda replied: “Friend, listen and pay close attention; I will tell you.”—“Yes, friend,” that bhikkhu replied. The Venerable Ānanda said this: “Here, friend, a bhikkhu teaches the Dhamma as he has heard it, as he has learned it... [as above] ...It is in this way, friend, that one is a master of the Dhamma. And how, friend, is one one who has attained the analytical knowledges?... [as above] ...It is in this way, friend, that one is one who has attained the analytical knowledges. And how, friend, is one one who has reached the goal?... [as above] ...It is in this way, friend, that one is one who has reached the goal. And how, friend, is one a great sage?... [as above] ...It is in this way, friend, that one is a great sage. And how, friend, is one a supreme person?... [as above] ...It is in this way, friend, that one is a supreme person. And how, friend, is one one who has accomplished his task?... [as above] ...It is in this way, friend, that one is one who has accomplished his task. And how, friend, is one one who has laid down the burden?... [as above] ...It is in this way, friend, that one is one who has laid down the burden. And how, friend, is one one who has reached the ultimate end?... [as above] ...It is in this way, friend, that one is one who has reached the ultimate end. And how, friend, is one one who has completely severed the fetters of existence?... [as above] ...It is in this way, friend, that one is one who has completely severed the fetters of existence. And how, friend, is one one who has attained the supreme security from bondage?... [as above] ...It is in this way, friend, that one is one who has attained the supreme security from bondage. And how, friend, is one a Buddha? Here, friend, a bhikkhu has awakened to the Dhamma by himself, has awakened to the Dhamma without another, has awakened to the Dhamma independently. It is in this way, friend, that one is a Buddha. When the Venerable Ānanda had finished speaking, that bhikkhu said to him: “Magnificent, friend! Magnificent, friend! Just as if one were to set upright what was overturned, to reveal what was hidden, to show the way to one who was lost, or to carry a lamp into the darkness so that those with eyes might see forms, even so has the Dhamma been made clear by the Venerable Ānanda in many ways. I go for refuge to the Blessed One, to the Dhamma, and to the Saṅgha of bhikkhus. May the Venerable Ānanda accept me as a lay follower who has gone for refuge from this day forth for as long as life lasts.”
“Bhikkhus, possessing five qualities, an elder bhikkhu is dear and agreeable to his fellow celibates, and is respected and esteemed by them. What are the five? [The Buddha said:]”

"He has attained the analytical knowledge of meaning, he has attained the analytical knowledge of phenomena, he has attained the analytical knowledge of linguistic expression, and he has attained the analytical knowledge of eloquence;

furthermore, regarding those various duties for his fellow celibates, whether high or low, he is skillful therein, diligent, endowed with the investigation of appropriate means, and capable of acting and capable of organizing.
Possessing these five qualities, monks, an elder bhikkhu is dear and agreeable to his fellow celibates, and is respected and esteemed by them."
The Sixth.
Aṅguttara Nikāya 5.87 9. Theravagga
Sīlavantasutta:

“Bhikkhus, endowed with five qualities, an elder bhikkhu is dear and agreeable to his fellow celibates, and is respected and esteemed by them. What five? [The text continues with the list of qualities.]”
Which five? He is virtuous;
he dwells restrained by the Pātimokkha. He is perfect in conduct and resort, seeing danger in even the slightest faults, and having undertaken them, he trains himself in the rules of training.
He is learned, a retainer of what he has heard, and a storehouse of what he has heard—those teachings that are excellent in the beginning, excellent in the middle, and excellent in the end.
They proclaim the holy life, which is meaningful and well-phrased, entirely complete and pure.
Such teachings are well-learned by him, retained, mastered through speech, examined by the mind, and thoroughly penetrated by view.
He is a good speaker, one with a fine delivery, endowed with polite speech that is articulate, flawless, and expressive of the meaning.
“He is one who obtains at will, without difficulty, and without trouble, the four jhānas that belong to the higher mind and provide a pleasant dwelling in this very life.

And with the destruction of the taints, he dwells having realized for himself with direct knowledge, in this very life, the taintless liberation of mind and liberation by wisdom, having entered upon it.
It is, monks, when a senior monk possesses these five qualities that he is dear and agreeable to his fellow celibates, and is respected and esteemed.”
Seventh. Aṅguttara Nikāya 5.88 9.
Theravagga (The Chapter on Elders)
Therasutta (AN 5.88, PTS AN iii 114): “Bhikkhus,

endowed with five qualities, an elder bhikkhu is practicing for the harm of many people, for the unhappiness of many people, for the ruin, harm, and suffering of many people, including gods and humans.”
Which five?
He is an elder, of long-standing seniority, and long-ordained;
he is well-known and renowned among both householders and those who have gone forth, and has a large retinue of followers.
He obtains robes, almsfood, lodgings, and medicinal requisites for the sick;

he is learned, a retainer of what he has heard, and a storehouse of learning—those teachings that are excellent in the beginning, excellent in the middle, and excellent in the end, which proclaim in both spirit and letter the holy life that is entirely complete and pure. Such are his [teachings].
The teachings are well-learned by him, retained, mastered through speech, examined by the mind, yet not penetrated by his view.
He holds wrong views and has a perverted perspective; having led many people away from the true Dhamma, he establishes them in what is not the true Dhamma.
Even an elder monk—long-venerated and long-ordained—falls into following his example, for that elder is well-known.
A monk who is famous, surrounded by a great multitude of both householders and those gone forth, others follow in his footsteps;
an elder monk who gains robes, almsfood, lodgings, and medicinal requisites for the sick, others follow in his footsteps;
an elder monk who is learned, a bearer of the teachings, and one who has accumulated what he has heard—others follow in his footsteps.
They fall into conformity with his views.

Endowed with these five qualities, monks, an elder bhikkhu acts for the harm of many people, for the unhappiness of many people, for the ruin, harm, and suffering of many people, including gods and humans.

Endowed with five other qualities, monks, an elder bhikkhu acts for the welfare of many people, for the happiness of many people, for the benefit, welfare, and happiness of many people, including gods and humans.
By which five?
He is an elder, of long-standing seniority, long-ordained;
he is well-known and famous, with a large retinue of both householders and those who have gone forth.
He gains robes, almsfood, lodgings, and medicinal requisites for the sick;

he is learned, a retainer of what he has heard, and a storehouse of learning—those teachings that are beautiful in the beginning, beautiful in the middle, and beautiful in the end, in spirit and in letter, which proclaim the holy life that is entirely complete and pure; such [teachings] belong to him.
The teachings have been heard much by him, remembered, mastered by word, examined by the mind, and well-penetrated by view.
He possesses right view and is one whose vision is undistorted; having raised many people out of what is not the true Dhamma, he establishes them in the true Dhamma.
An elder monk, known for his long-standing seniority and long-ordained status—people follow in the footsteps of his view, for he is a renowned elder.
A monk who is famous, surrounded by a large retinue of both householders and those gone forth, others follow in accordance with his views;
an elder monk who is a recipient of robes, almsfood, lodgings, and medicinal requisites for the sick, others follow in accordance with his views;
an elder monk who is learned, a bearer of the teachings, and a storehouse of what has been heard, others follow in accordance with his views...
They follow in accordance with his view.

Endowed with these five qualities, monks, an elder bhikkhu practices for the welfare of many people, for the happiness of many people, for the benefit, welfare, and happiness of many people, including gods and humans.
Thus it was said. The eighth.
Aṅguttara Nikāya 5.89 9. Theravagga Paṭhamasekhasutta (The First Discourse on the Trainee) "Bhikkhus, there are these five qualities of one who is a trainee.

What five? Here, a bhikkhu is virtuous; he dwells restrained by the Pātimokkha, possessed of good conduct and resort, seeing danger in the slightest fault; having undertaken the training rules, he trains in them. He has learned much, remembers what he has learned, and accumulates what he has learned. These teachings, which are good in the beginning, good in the middle, and good in the end, with the right meaning and phrasing, which proclaim the perfectly complete and pure spiritual life—such teachings as these he has learned much of, retained in mind, recited verbally, investigated with the mind, and penetrated well through view. He is one who gains at will, without trouble or difficulty, the four jhānas that constitute the higher mind and are pleasant dwellings in this very life. He possesses the wisdom of a trainee, which is noble and penetrative, leading to the complete destruction of suffering. These, bhikkhus, are the five qualities of one who is a trainee."
“Bhikkhus, these five things lead to the decline of a bhikkhu in training. Which five? [Text continues]”
Delight in work, delight in talk, delight in sleep, delight in company, and not reviewing the mind as it is liberated— these, monks,
are the five things that lead to the decline of a monk in training. There are, monks,
these five things that lead to the non-decline of a monk in training.
Which five?
Delight in work, delight in talk, delight in sleep, delight in company, and not reviewing one’s mind as it is liberated.
These, monks, are the five qualities that lead to the non-decline of a bhikkhu who is a trainee.”
The Ninth. Aṅguttara Nikāya 5.90 9.
Theravagga (The Chapter on Elders)
The Second Discourse on the Trainee (Dutiyasekhasutta):
“Bhikkhus, there are these five qualities that lead to the decline of a bhikkhu who is a trainee.”
What are the five?
Here, monks, a bhikkhu who is a trainee has many duties and much to do; he is competent in his various tasks.
He neglects seclusion and does not devote himself to internal tranquility of mind.
“Monks, this is the first quality that leads to the decline of a bhikkhu in training.
Furthermore, monks, a bhikkhu in training spends the day on trifling tasks;
he neglects seclusion and does not apply himself to internal tranquility of mind.”
This, monks, is the second quality that leads to the decline of a bhikkhu in training.
Furthermore, monks, a bhikkhu in training dwells in association with householders and renunciants, through improper intimacy with householders;
he neglects seclusion and does not devote himself to internal tranquility of mind.
This, monks, is the third quality that leads to the decline of a bhikkhu in training.
Furthermore, monks, a bhikkhu in training enters the village at an improper time and returns too late in the day;
he neglects seclusion and does not devote himself to internal tranquility of mind.
This, monks, is the fourth quality that leads to the decline of a bhikkhu in training.
Furthermore, monks, a bhikkhu in training does not enjoy a discourse that is conducive to effacement and the opening of the mind, such as:
a discourse on fewness of desires, contentment, solitude, non-association, the arousal of energy, and virtue.
Discourse on concentration, discourse on wisdom, discourse on liberation, and discourse on the knowledge and vision of liberation—
one does not obtain such discourse at will, nor without difficulty, nor without trouble;
one neglects seclusion and does not apply oneself to internal tranquility of mind.
“Monks, this is the fifth quality that leads to the decline of a bhikkhu in training.
Monks, these five qualities lead to the decline of a bhikkhu in training.
Monks, there are these five qualities that lead to the non-decline of a bhikkhu in training.”
Which five?
Here, monks, a bhikkhu in training is not overburdened with duties nor occupied with many tasks, being competent in what needs to be done;
he does not neglect seclusion and devotes himself to internal tranquility of mind.
This, monks, is the first quality that leads to the non-decline of a bhikkhu in training.
Furthermore, monks, a bhikkhu in training does not spend his day on trifling tasks;
he does not neglect seclusion, but devotes himself to internal tranquility of mind.
This, monks, is the second quality that leads to the non-decline of a monk in training.
Furthermore, monks, a monk in training dwells unassociated with householders and renunciants, avoiding improper association with householders;
he does not neglect seclusion and devotes himself to internal tranquility of mind.
This, monks, is the third quality that leads to the non-decline of a bhikkhu in training.
Furthermore, monks, a bhikkhu in training does not enter the village too early, nor does he return from it too late;
he does not neglect seclusion, and he devotes himself to internal tranquility of mind.
This, monks, is the fourth quality that leads to the non-decline of a bhikkhu in training.
Furthermore, monks, a bhikkhu in training engages in that discourse which is conducive to effacement and the opening of the mind, namely:
discourse on fewness of desires, discourse on contentment, discourse on seclusion, discourse on non-association, discourse on the arousal of energy, and discourse on virtue.

He is one who gains at will, without difficulty or trouble, such talk as discourse on concentration, discourse on wisdom, discourse on liberation, and discourse on the knowledge and vision of liberation;
he does not neglect seclusion and devotes himself to internal tranquility of mind.
“Monks, this is the fifth quality that leads to the non-decline of a bhikkhu in training.
Monks, these five qualities lead to the non-decline of a bhikkhu in training.
The tenth.
The fourth chapter, the Chapter on Elders (Theravagga).
Its summary verse (uddāna) is:
"The one subject to passion, the one free from passion..."
The deceivers and those who endure faith;
the analytical knowledges and virtue—
these are the Elder and the two types of trainees.
Aṅguttara Nikāya 5.91 10.

Kakudha-vagga First Discourse on Accomplishment (Paṭhama-sampadā-sutta) “Bhikkhus, there are these five accomplishments. What five? Accomplishment in faith, accomplishment in virtue, accomplishment in learning, accomplishment in generosity, and accomplishment in wisdom. These, bhikkhus, are the five accomplishments.”
“Bhikkhus, there are these five accomplishments.
Which five?
“Bhikkhus, there are these five accomplishments: accomplishment in faith, accomplishment in virtue, accomplishment in learning, accomplishment in generosity, and accomplishment in wisdom.
These, bhikkhus, are the five accomplishments. Thus was the first [discourse].

Aṅguttara Nikāya 5.92 10. Kakudha-vagga Second Discourse on Accomplishment (Dutiyasampadāsutta) "Bhikkhus, there are these five accomplishments. What five? Accomplishment in faith, accomplishment in virtuous behavior, accomplishment in learning, accomplishment in generosity, and accomplishment in wisdom. And what, bhikkhus, is accomplishment in faith? Here, a noble disciple possesses faith; he places faith in the Tathāgata’s enlightenment thus: ‘The Blessed One is an arahant, perfectly enlightened, accomplished in true knowledge and conduct, fortunate, knower of the world, unsurpassed leader of persons to be tamed, teacher of devas and humans, the Buddha, the Blessed One. This is called accomplishment in faith. And what, bhikkhus, is accomplishment in virtuous behavior? Here, a noble disciple is possessed of virtuous behavior that is restrained by the Pātimokkha, which is flawless, unbroken, unspotted, unsullied, liberating, praised by the wise, not misapprehended, and conducive to concentration. This is called accomplishment in virtuous behavior. And what, bhikkhus, is accomplishment in learning? Here, a noble disciple has learned much, remembers what he has learned, and consolidates what he has learned. Those teachings that are good in the beginning, good in the middle, and good in the end, with the right meaning and phrasing, which proclaim the perfectly complete and pure spiritual life—such teachings as these he has learned much of, retained in mind, recited verbally, mentally investigated, and penetrated well by view. This is called accomplishment in learning. And what, bhikkhus, is accomplishment in generosity? Here, a noble disciple dwells at home with a heart devoid of the stain of stinginess, freely generous, open-handed, delighting in relinquishing, one devoted to charity, responsive to requests, delighting in the distribution of gifts. This is called accomplishment in generosity. And what, bhikkhus, is accomplishment in wisdom? Here, a noble disciple is wise; he possesses the wisdom that discerns arising and passing away, which is noble and penetrative, leading to the complete destruction of suffering. This is called accomplishment in wisdom. These, bhikkhus, are the five accomplishments."
“Bhikkhus, there are these five accomplishments.
What five?
“Perfection of virtue, perfection of concentration, perfection of wisdom, perfection of liberation, and perfection of the knowledge and vision of liberation—
these, monks, are the five perfections.
The second [sutta].
Aṅguttara Nikāya 5.93 10.

Kakudhavagga Byākaraṇasutta (The Discourse on the Declaration) “Monks, there are these five kinds of declarations. What five? ‘I know this,’ monks, is one kind of declaration; ‘I see this’ is another kind of declaration; ‘It will be so for me’ is another kind of declaration; ‘It will not be so for me’ is another kind of declaration; and ‘There is no other way’ is another kind of declaration. These, monks, are the five kinds of declarations.”
“Bhikkhus, there are these five declarations of final knowledge.
Which five?
One declares another [state] due to being instructed or due to delusion;
one declares another due to evil desires and being overcome by longing;
one declares another due to insanity or mental derangement.
One declares final knowledge through overweening pride;
one declares final knowledge correctly.
These, monks, are the five ways of declaring final knowledge.”
Third.
Aṅguttara Nikāya 5.94 10. Kakudha-vagga
The Discourse on Comfortable Abiding (Phāsuvihārasutta): “Bhikkhus,
there are these five comfortable abidings.”
Which five?

Here, monks, a monk, quite secluded from sensual pleasures, secluded from unwholesome states, enters and dwells in the first jhāna, which is accompanied by applied and sustained thought, with rapture and pleasure born of seclusion;
with the stilling of applied and sustained thought... [as before] ...he enters and dwells in the second jhāna... the third jhāna... and the fourth jhāna.

With the destruction of the taints, he dwells having realized for himself with direct knowledge, in this very life, the taintless liberation of mind and liberation by wisdom, and having entered upon it.
These, monks, are the five dwellings in comfort. Thus ends the fourth [discourse].

Aṅguttara Nikāya 5.95 10. Kakudha-vagga Akuppa-sutta (The Unshakable) “Bhikkhus, there are these five kinds of persons found existing in the world. What five? The person who is unshakable; the person who is bound by one fetter; the person who is bound by two fetters; the person who is bound by three fetters; and the person who is bound by four fetters. And how, bhikkhus, is a person ‘unshakable’? Here, a bhikkhu is an arahant with taints destroyed, one who has lived the holy life, done what was to be done, laid down the burden, reached his own goal, utterly destroyed the fetters of existence, and is liberated through final knowledge. This, bhikkhus, is called a person who is unshakable. And how, bhikkhus, is a person ‘bound by one fetter’? Here, a bhikkhu is a stream-enterer, no longer subject to rebirth in the lower worlds, fixed in destiny, with enlightenment as his destination. He is bound by only one fetter: the fetter of greed for sensual pleasures. This, bhikkhus, is called a person who is bound by one fetter. And how, bhikkhus, is a person ‘bound by two fetters’? Here, a bhikkhu is a once-returner who, having returned to this world only once more, will make an end of suffering. He is bound by two fetters: the fetter of greed for sensual pleasures and the fetter of ill will. This, bhikkhus, is called a person who is bound by two fetters. And how, bhikkhus, is a person ‘bound by three fetters’? Here, a bhikkhu is a non-returner who, having completely destroyed the five lower fetters, will reappear spontaneously [in the Pure Abodes] and will there attain final Nibbāna without ever returning from that world. He is bound by three fetters: the fetter of conceit, the fetter of restlessness, and the fetter of ignorance. This, bhikkhus, is called a person who is bound by three fetters. And how, bhikkhus, is a person ‘bound by four fetters’? Here, a bhikkhu is a candidate for the fruit of stream-entry. He is bound by four fetters: the fetter of doubt, the fetter of adherence to rules and observances, the fetter of sensual lust, and the fetter of ill will. This, bhikkhus, is called a person who is bound by four fetters. These, bhikkhus, are the five kinds of persons found existing in the world.”
“Bhikkhus, endowed with five qualities, a bhikkhu will before long penetrate the unshakable. With which five? [The Buddha said:]”

“Here, bhikkhus, a bhikkhu has attained the analytical knowledge of meaning, the analytical knowledge of phenomena, the analytical knowledge of language, and the analytical knowledge of eloquence; he reviews his mind as it is liberated.
Possessing these five qualities, bhikkhus, a bhikkhu will before long penetrate the unshakable.”
The Fifth.
Aṅguttara Nikāya 5.96 10. Kakudha-vagga
Sutadharasutta:

“Bhikkhus, endowed with five qualities, a bhikkhu who cultivates mindfulness of breathing will, before long, penetrate the unshakable. What five? [He is] one who remembers, one who masters what he has heard, one who is mindful, one who is wise, and one who is content.”
By which five?
Here, monks, a monk has few concerns, few duties, is easy to support, and is easily contented with the requisites of life;
he eats little and is devoted to not being gluttonous.
He is free from sloth, devoted to wakefulness;

he is learned, a retainer of what he has heard, and a storehouse of learning—those teachings that are excellent in the beginning, excellent in the middle, and excellent in the end, both in meaning and in phrasing, which proclaim the holy life in its entirety, perfectly complete and pure; such [teachings] are his.
The teachings are well-learned by him, retained, mastered through speech, examined by the mind, and well-penetrated by view.
He reviews his mind according to how it has been liberated.
Possessing these five qualities, monks, a bhikkhu who cultivates mindfulness of breathing will, before long, penetrate the unshakable.”
The Sixth.
Aṅguttara Nikāya 5.97 10. Kakudhavagga
The Discourse on the Story (Kathāsutta): “Bhikkhus,
endowed with five qualities, a bhikkhu who develops mindfulness of breathing will, before long, penetrate the unshakable.
By which five?
Here, monks, a monk has few concerns, few duties, is easy to support, and is easily contented with the requisites of life;
he eats little and is devoted to moderation in food.
He is free from sloth and is devoted to wakefulness;

he is one who gains at will, without difficulty, and without trouble, such talk as is conducive to effacement and the opening of the heart, namely: talk on fewness of desires … [and so on] … talk on the knowledge and vision of liberation.
He reviews the mind as it is liberated.
Possessing these five qualities, monks, a bhikkhu who develops mindfulness of breathing penetrates the unshakable state before long.
Thus ends the seventh [discourse].
Aṅguttara Nikāya 5.98 10.

Kakudhavagga Āraññakasutta (The Forest-Dweller) “Bhikkhus, there are these five qualities of a forest-dwelling bhikkhu that lead to his welfare and happiness for a long time. What five? Here, a forest-dwelling bhikkhu is content with any kind of robe, any kind of almsfood, any kind of lodging, and any kind of medicinal requisites for the sick. He dwells contemplating impermanence in all conditioned phenomena, he dwells detached from sensual pleasures, and he dwells having fully understood the nature of suffering. These, bhikkhus, are the five qualities of a forest-dwelling bhikkhu that lead to his welfare and happiness for a long time.”
“Bhikkhus, possessing five qualities, a bhikkhu who cultivates mindfulness of breathing will, before long, penetrate the unshakable. What are the five? [Text continues]”
In this case, monks, a bhikkhu has few concerns, few duties, is easy to support, and is easily contented with the requisites of life;
he eats little, is devoted to moderation in food;
he is free from sloth and is devoted to wakefulness.
“He is a forest-dweller who uses remote lodgings;
he reviews his mind as it is liberated.
Possessing these five qualities, monks, a bhikkhu who cultivates mindfulness of breathing will before long penetrate the unshakable.”
The Eighth. Aṅguttara Nikāya 5.99 10.
Kakudha-vagga (The Chapter on Kakudha)
The Lion Sutta (AN 5.99): “Bhikkhus,
in the evening time, the lion, the king of beasts, emerges from his lair;”
Having emerged from his lair, he stretches;
having stretched, he surveys the four directions all around;
having surveyed the four directions all around, he roars three times the lion’s roar.
Having roared his lion’s roar three times, he sets out for his range.
If he strikes the elephant, he strikes him respectfully, not disrespectfully;
if he strikes the buffalo, he strikes him respectfully, not disrespectfully.
Even if he strikes a cow, he strikes it with care and not without care;
even if he strikes a lamp, he strikes it with care and not without care;
and even if he strikes small creatures, down to rabbits and cats, he strikes them with care and not without care.
And for what reason?
"Lest my path of training be lost.
"Lion," monks, is a designation for the Tathāgata, the Arahant, the Perfectly Enlightened One.
When, monks, the Tathāgata teaches the Dhamma to an assembly, this constitutes his lion’s roar.
Whether the Tathāgata teaches the Dhamma to the monks, monks, he teaches it with due respect, not without respect;
whether the Tathāgata teaches the Dhamma to the nuns, monks, he teaches it with due respect, not without respect.
Bhikkhus, even when the Tathāgata teaches the Dhamma to lay followers, he teaches it with due respect, not without respect;
even when the Tathāgata teaches the Dhamma to female lay followers, he teaches it with due respect, not without respect;
even when the Tathāgata teaches the Dhamma to worldlings—even down to those who carry food for hire—he teaches it with due respect, not without respect.
And why is that? Because, monks, the Tathāgata reveres the Dhamma and honors the Dhamma.
The ninth [sutta].

Aṅguttara Nikāya 5.100 10. Kakudhavagga Kakudha Thera Sutta Thus have I heard. On one occasion the Venerable Kakudha was dwelling at Sāvatthī in Jeta’s Grove, Anāthapiṇḍika’s Park. There the Venerable Kakudha addressed the bhikkhus: “Friends, bhikkhus! “Friend,” those bhikkhus replied to the Venerable Kakudha. The Venerable Kakudha said this: “Friends, when a bhikkhu is possessed of five qualities, he is capable of achieving the destruction of the taints in this very life. What five? Here, friends, a bhikkhu is virtuous; he dwells restrained by the Pātimokkha, possessed of good conduct and resort, seeing danger in minute faults. Having undertaken the training rules, he trains in them. He has learned much, remembers what he has learned, and accumulates what he has learned.

Those teachings that are good in the beginning, good in the middle, and good in the end, with the right meaning and phrasing, which proclaim the perfectly complete and pure spiritual life—such teachings he has learned much of, retained in mind, recited verbally, mentally examined, and penetrated well by view. He gains at will, without trouble or difficulty, the four jhānas that constitute the higher mind and are pleasant dwellings in this very life. With the destruction of the taints, he realizes for himself with direct knowledge, in this very life, the taintless liberation of mind, liberation by wisdom, and having entered upon it, dwells therein. Friends, when a bhikkhu is possessed of these five qualities, he is capable of achieving the destruction of the taints in this very life. When the Venerable Kakudha had spoken thus, the Venerable Ānanda said to him: “It is wonderful, friend, it is marvelous, friend! How well this has been stated by the Venerable Kakudha! If a bhikkhu is possessed of these five qualities, he is capable of achieving the destruction of the taints in this very life. What five? Here, friend, a bhikkhu is virtuous... [as above] ...he dwells therein. It is wonderful, friend, it is marvelous, friend! How well this has been stated by the Venerable Kakudha! When the Venerable Ānanda had spoken thus, the Venerable Kakudha said to him: “It is wonderful, friend, it is marvelous, friend! How well this has been stated by the Venerable Ānanda! If a bhikkhu is possessed of these five qualities, he is capable of achieving the destruction of the taints in this very life. What five? Here, friend, a bhikkhu is virtuous... [as above] ...he dwells therein. It is wonderful, friend, it is marvelous, friend! How well this has been stated by the Venerable Kakudha! Then the Venerable Ānanda and the Venerable Kakudha rose from their seats and paid homage to the Blessed One. Then the Venerable Ānanda sat down to one side and said to the Blessed One: “Venerable sir, it is wonderful, it is marvelous how well this was stated by the Venerable Kakudha! If a bhikkhu is possessed of these five qualities, he is capable of achieving the destruction of the taints in this very life. What five? Here, venerable sir, a bhikkhu is virtuous... [as above] ...he dwells therein. It is wonderful, venerable sir, it is marvelous how well this was stated by the Venerable Kakudha! “It is wonderful, Ānanda, it is marvelous how well this was stated by the bhikkhu Kakudha! Ānanda, if a bhikkhu is possessed of these five qualities, he is capable of achieving the destruction of the taints in this very life. What five? Here, Ānanda, a bhikkhu is virtuous... [as above] ...he dwells therein. Ānanda, if a bhikkhu is possessed of these five qualities, he is capable of achieving the destruction of the taints in this very life. This is what the Blessed One said. Elated, the Venerable Ānanda delighted in the Blessed One’s words. Thus have I heard. On one occasion the Venerable Kakudha was dwelling at Sāvatthī in Jeta’s Grove, Anāthapiṇḍika’s Park. There the Venerable Kakudha addressed the bhikkhus: “Friends, bhikkhus! “Friend,” those bhikkhus replied to the Venerable Kakudha. The Venerable Kakudha said this: “Friends, when a bhikkhu is possessed of five qualities, he is incapable of achieving the destruction of the taints in this very life. What five? Here, friends, a bhikkhu is not virtuous; he does not dwell restrained by the Pātimokkha, he is not possessed of good conduct and resort, he does not see danger in minute faults. Having undertaken the training rules, he does not train in them. He has not learned much... [as above] ...he does not penetrate well by view. He does not gain at will, without trouble or difficulty, the four jhānas that constitute the higher mind and are pleasant dwellings in this very life. With the destruction of the taints, he does not realize for himself with direct knowledge, in this very life, the taintless liberation of mind, liberation by wisdom, and having entered upon it, he does not dwell therein. Friends, when a bhikkhu is possessed of these five qualities, he is incapable of achieving the destruction of the taints in this very life. (AN 5.100, PTS AN iii 122) Thus have I heard:
at one time the Blessed One was dwelling at Kosambī in Ghosita’s Park.
Now at that time, Koliyaputta named Kakudha, who had been the attendant of the Venerable Mahāmoggallāna, had recently passed away and was reborn in a certain mind-made body.
His acquisition of a personal form was such that it was like two or three Magadhan village-fields in size.
By means of that acquisition of a personal form, he harmed neither himself nor others.
Then the young deva Kakudha approached the Venerable Mahāmoggallāna;
having approached, he paid homage to the Venerable Mahāmoggallāna and stood to one side. Standing to one side, the young deva Kakudha said this to the Venerable Mahāmoggallāna:
“Venerable sir, such a desire arose in Devadatta:
‘I shall lead the Saṅgha of bhikkhus.
And with the arising of that thought, venerable sir, Devadatta fell away from that psychic power.”
This is what the young deva Kakudha said.
Having said this, he paid homage to the Venerable Mahāmoggallāna, kept him on his right, and vanished right there.
Then the Venerable Mahāmoggallāna approached the Blessed One; having approached, he [approached] the Blessed One...
Having paid homage, he sat down to one side. As he was sitting there, the Venerable Mahāmoggallāna said this to the Blessed One:
"Bhante, my attendant named Kakudha, the son of a Koliyan, has recently passed away and has been reborn in a certain mind-made body.
His acquisition of a physical form is such that it is like two or three Magadhan village-fields."
Thus, with that acquisition of a new body, he harms neither himself nor others.
Then, venerable sir, the young deva Kakudha approached me; having approached and paid homage to me, he stood to one side. Standing to one side, venerable sir, the young deva Kakudha said this to me:
“Venerable sir, such a desire arose in Devadatta:”
“I shall lead the Saṅgha of bhikkhus.
With the mere arising of that thought, venerable sir, Devadatta fell away from that psychic power.
This is what the young deva Kakudha said, venerable sir.
“Having said this, he paid homage to me, circumambulated me keeping me to his right, and vanished right there.
“But, Moggallāna, did you encompass Kakudha the deva-son’s mind with your own mind and know:
‘Whatever Kakudha the deva-son says, all that is exactly so and not otherwise’?”
“Venerable sir, having encompassed his mind with my own mind, I have known the young deva Kakudha thus:
‘Whatever the young deva Kakudha speaks, all that is exactly so and not otherwise.
“Moggallāna, you must guard those words.”
“Guard your speech regarding this, Moggallāna!
Now that foolish man will reveal himself by his own words.
There are, Moggallāna, these five teachers found existing in the world.”
What are the five?
Here, Moggallāna, a certain teacher, being of impure virtue, claims: “I am of pure virtue; my virtue is pure, bright, and undefiled.
Yet his disciples know him thus:
‘This venerable teacher, though being of impure virtue, claims: “I am pure in virtue,” and “My virtue is pure, bright, and undefiled.
Now, if we were to report this to householders, it would not be pleasing to him. And how could we address him with that which is displeasing to him?’
"Furthermore, he is honored with robes, almsfood, lodgings, and medicinal requisites for the sick;
whatever he does will be known through that alone.
Moggallāna, it is in this way that disciples protect such a teacher by means of his virtue.
Moreover, such a teacher expects protection from his disciples by way of virtue.
Furthermore, Moggallāna, here some teacher, being one whose livelihood is impure, claims: "I am pure in livelihood; my livelihood is pure, bright, and undefiled.
His disciples know him thus:
‘This venerable teacher, while being one whose livelihood is impure, claims: “I am one whose livelihood is pure”; he declares, “My livelihood is pure, bright, and undefiled.
Now, if we were to report this to householders, it would not be pleasing to him. How could we address him with that which is displeasing to him?’
‘But he is honored with robes, almsfood, lodgings, and medicinal requisites for the sick;
whatever he does, by that alone will he be known.
It is in this way, Moggallāna, that disciples protect such a teacher regarding his livelihood.
Moreover, such a teacher expects protection for his livelihood from his disciples.

Furthermore, Moggallāna, here some teacher, while being one whose teaching of the Dhamma is impure, claims: "I am one whose teaching of the Dhamma is pure; my teaching of the Dhamma is pure, radiant, and undefiled.
His disciples know him thus:
‘This venerable teacher, while his teaching of the Dhamma is actually impure, claims: “I am one whose teaching of the Dhamma is pure,” and “My teaching of the Dhamma is pure, radiant, and undefiled.
Now, if we were to report this to householders, it would not be pleasing to him. And how could we address him with what is displeasing to him?’
“Moreover, he is honored with robes, almsfood, lodgings, and medicinal requisites for the sick;
whatever he shall do, by that alone will he be known.
It is in this way, Moggallāna, that disciples protect such a teacher from the teaching of the Dhamma.
Furthermore, such a teacher expects protection from his disciples for his teaching of the Dhamma.
Moreover, Moggallāna, here a certain teacher, while his own exposition is impure, claims: "I am one whose exposition is pure; my exposition is pure, bright, and undefiled.
His disciples know him thus:
“This teacher, while his own explanations are impure, claims: ‘I am one whose explanations are pure; my explanations are pure, bright, and undefiled.
Now, if we were to report this to householders, it would not be pleasing to him.
Since it is displeasing to him, how could we address him with such [words]?”
"But he is supported by robes, almsfood, lodgings, and medicinal requisites for the sick;
whatever he does will be known through that alone.
It is in this way, Moggallāna, that disciples protect such a teacher from having to give an account.
Furthermore, such a teacher expects protection from his disciples by way of explanation.
Moreover, Moggallāna, here some teacher, while possessing impure knowledge and vision, claims: “I possess pure knowledge and vision; my knowledge and vision is pure, bright, and undefiled.
His disciples know him thus:
‘This venerable teacher, while his knowledge and vision are actually impure, claims: “I am one whose knowledge and vision are pure; my knowledge and vision are pure, cleansed, and undefiled.
Now, if we were to report this to householders, it would not be pleasing to him. And how could we address him with what is displeasing to him?’
"Furthermore, he is honored with robes, almsfood, lodgings, and medicinal requisites for the sick;
whatever he shall do, by that alone will he be known.
It is in this way, Moggallāna, that disciples protect such a teacher from [the scrutiny of] knowledge and vision.
Furthermore, such a teacher expects protection from his disciples in terms of knowledge and vision.
These, Moggallāna, are the five kinds of teachers found existing in the world.
But as for me, Moggallāna, being pure in virtue, I claim: ‘I am pure in virtue. I declare: ‘My virtue is pure, cleansed, and undefiled.’
My disciples do not protect me in regard to my virtue, nor do I expect protection from my disciples in regard to my virtue.
Being one whose livelihood is pure, I claim, ‘My livelihood is pure; my livelihood is purified, stainless, and undefiled.
My disciples do not protect me in regard to my livelihood, nor do I expect protection from my disciples in regard to my livelihood.
Being one whose teaching of the Dhamma is pure, I claim: "I am one whose teaching of the Dhamma is pure; my teaching of the Dhamma is pure, radiant, and undefiled.
My disciples do not protect me regarding the teaching of the Dhamma, nor do I expect protection from my disciples regarding the teaching of the Dhamma.
Being one whose exposition is pure, I claim: "I am one whose exposition is pure; my exposition is pure, radiant, and undefiled."
My disciples do not protect me from being questioned, nor do I expect protection from being questioned by my disciples.
Being one whose knowledge and vision are purified, I claim: ‘My knowledge and vision are purified; my knowledge and vision are bright and undefiled.
My disciples do not protect me from [the scrutiny of] knowledge and vision, nor do I expect protection from [the scrutiny of] knowledge and vision by my disciples.”
Tenth. The fifth chapter, Kakudha.
Its summary verse:
Two accomplishments, the exposition, ease, the unshakable as fifth;
learning, discussion, and the forest-dweller.
Sīha, Kakudha, and Dasaka.
The second fiftieth chapter is completed.
Aṅguttara Nikāya 5.101.

11. Phāsuvihāravagga Sārajjasutta (AN 5.101) "Bhikkhus, there are these five grounds for timidity. What five? One is timid regarding gain; one is timid regarding loss; one is timid regarding fame; one is timid regarding disrepute; one is timid regarding honor. These, bhikkhus, are the five grounds for timidity."
“Bhikkhus, there are these five qualities that produce confidence in one who is in training.
What five?
Here, bhikkhus, a bhikkhu is endowed with faith, he is virtuous, he is learned, he is energetic, and he is wise.”
“Bhikkhus, that timidity which exists in one who lacks faith does not exist in one who has faith;
therefore, this Dhamma produces self-confidence in those still in training.
Bhikkhus, that timidity which exists in one who is immoral does not exist in one who is virtuous.”
Therefore, this Dhamma produces fearlessness in one who is still in training.
That which is a cause for fear in one of little learning, bhikkhus, is not a cause for fear in one of great learning.
Therefore, this Dhamma produces fearlessness in one who is still in training.
“Bhikkhus, that timidity which exists in one who is lazy does not exist in one who has aroused energy;
therefore, this Dhamma produces self-confidence in those still in training.
Bhikkhus, that timidity which exists in one who is lacking in wisdom does not exist in one who possesses wisdom.”
Therefore, this Dhamma produces the intrepidity of one in training.
These, monks, are the five qualities that produce the intrepidity of one in training. Thus was the first [discourse].

Aṅguttara Nikāya 5.102 11. Phāsuvihāravagga Ussaṅkitasutta (The Discourse on Suspicion) "Bhikkhus, there are these five kinds of persons found existing in the world. What five? The person who is suspicious; the person who is prone to suspicion; the person who is given to suspicion; the person who delights in suspicion; and the person who makes others suspicious. And how, bhikkhus, is one a person who is suspicious?

Here, bhikkhus, a bhikkhu is suspicious regarding the Teacher, suspicious regarding the Dhamma, suspicious regarding the Saṅgha, suspicious regarding the training, and suspicious regarding his fellow monks. It is in this way that one is a person who is suspicious. And how, bhikkhus, is one a person who is prone to suspicion? Here, bhikkhus, a bhikkhu is prone to suspicion regarding the Teacher, prone to suspicion regarding the Dhamma, prone to suspicion regarding the Saṅgha, prone to suspicion regarding the training, and prone to suspicion regarding his fellow monks. It is in this way that one is a person who is prone to suspicion. And how, bhikkhus, is one a person who is given to suspicion? Here, bhikkhus, a bhikkhu is given to suspicion regarding the Teacher, given to suspicion regarding the Dhamma, given to suspicion regarding the Saṅgha, given to suspicion regarding the training, and given to suspicion regarding his fellow monks. It is in this way that one is a person who is given to suspicion. And how, bhikkhus, is one a person who delights in suspicion? Here, bhikkhus, a bhikkhu delights in suspicion regarding the Teacher, delights in suspicion regarding the Dhamma, delights in suspicion regarding the Saṅgha, delights in suspicion regarding the training, and delights in suspicion regarding his fellow monks. It is in this way that one is a person who delights in suspicion. And how, bhikkhus, is one a person who makes others suspicious? Here, bhikkhus, a bhikkhu makes others suspicious regarding the Teacher, makes others suspicious regarding the Dhamma, makes others suspicious regarding the Saṅgha, makes others suspicious regarding the training, and makes others suspicious regarding his fellow monks. It is in this way that one is a person who makes others suspicious. These, bhikkhus, are the five kinds of persons found existing in the world."
“Bhikkhus, possessing five qualities, a bhikkhu is suspected and distrusted as a wicked bhikkhu, even if he is of unshakable nature. Which five? [The text continues with the list of qualities.]”

"Here, monks, a monk frequents the company of courtesans, or he frequents the company of widows, or he frequents the company of unmarried girls, or he frequents the company of eunuchs, or he frequents the company of bhikkhunīs.
Possessing these five qualities, monks, a monk is suspected and mistrusted as a 'bad monk,' even if he is one whose nature is unshakable.
This is the second [sutta].

Aṅguttara Nikāya 5.103 11. Phāsuvihāravagga Mahācorasutta – The Great Robber “Monks, there are these five kinds of great robbers. What five? Here, monks, a certain great robber is one who has stolen much gold and silver; this is the first kind of great robber. Furthermore, monks, a certain great robber is one who has stolen much wealth belonging to others; this is the second kind of great robber. Furthermore, monks, a certain great robber is one who has stolen much grain; this is the third kind of great robber.

Furthermore, monks, a certain great robber is one who has stolen many women; this is the fourth kind of great robber. Furthermore, monks, a certain great robber is one who has stolen many villages and market towns; this is the fifth kind of great robber. These, monks, are the five kinds of great robbers. Monks, there are these five kinds of great thieves. What five? Here, monks, a certain great thief is one who has stolen much gold and silver; this is the first kind of great thief. Furthermore, monks, a certain great thief is one who has stolen much wealth belonging to others; this is the second kind of great thief. Furthermore, monks, a certain great thief is one who has stolen much grain; this is the third kind of great thief. Furthermore, monks, a certain great thief is one who has stolen many women; this is the fourth kind of great thief. Furthermore, monks, a certain great thief is one who has stolen many villages and market towns; this is the fifth kind of great thief. These, monks, are the five kinds of great thieves. Just as, monks, those five kinds of great robbers are to be found in the world, so too, monks, these five kinds of great thieves are to be found in the Saṅgha. What five? Here, monks, a certain bhikkhu is one who has stolen much gold and silver; this is the first kind of great thief in the Saṅgha. Furthermore, monks, a certain bhikkhu is one who has stolen much wealth belonging to others; this is the second kind of great thief in the Saṅgha. Furthermore, monks, a certain bhikkhu is one who has stolen much grain; this is the third kind of great thief in the Saṅgha. Furthermore, monks, a certain bhikkhu is one who has stolen many women; this is the fourth kind of great thief in the Saṅgha. Furthermore, monks, a certain bhikkhu is one who has stolen many villages and market towns; this is the fifth kind of great thief in the Saṅgha. These, monks, are the five kinds of great thieves in the Saṅgha. Just as, monks, those five kinds of great robbers are to be found in the world, so too, monks, these five kinds of great thieves are to be found in the Saṅgha. Therefore, monks, you should train yourselves thus: ‘We will not steal even so much as a blade of grass or a stick from the Saṅgha. Thus, monks, should you train yourselves.”

“Bhikkhus, possessing five factors, a great thief breaks into houses, carries off plunder, commits robbery in lonely places, and lies in ambush on the road. What are the five? [The text continues with the list of factors.]”
“Here, monks, a great thief relies on uneven terrain, relies on thickets, relies on powerful people, is generous with his wealth, and travels alone.
And how, monks, does a great thief rely on uneven terrain?
Here, monks, a great thief relies on a river difficult to cross or on mountainous ruggedness.”
"Thus, monks, a great thief relies on uneven terrain.
And how, monks, does a great thief rely on thickets?
Here, monks, a great thief relies on a thicket of grass, or a thicket of trees, or a marsh, or a dense forest grove."
In this way, monks, a great thief relies on a thicket.
And how, monks, does a great thief rely on the powerful?
Here, monks, a great thief relies on a king or on royal ministers.
It occurs to him:
"If anyone says anything to me, these kings or royal ministers will explain the meaning to me in its full detail.
And if anyone says something to him, those kings or royal ministers explain the meaning to him in its full detail.
In this way, monks, a great thief relies on the powerful.
And how, monks, is a great thief one who squanders his wealth?
Here, monks, a great thief is wealthy, possessing great riches and great possessions.
It occurs to him:
"If anyone says anything to me, I will welcome them with wealth.
If anyone says anything to him, he welcomes them with wealth from that point on.
In this way, monks, a great thief is one who gives away his wealth.
And how, monks, is a great thief a solitary wanderer?
Here, monks, a great thief commits robberies all alone.
And why is that? “Lest my secret counsel should leak out to others.
In this way, monks, a great thief travels alone.
“Monks, possessed of these five factors, a great thief breaks into houses, plunders wealth, commits robbery, and lies in ambush on the road.

In the same way, monks, a wicked monk who possesses five qualities maintains himself wounded and ruined; he is blameworthy and subject to reproach by the wise, and he generates much demerit. What are the five? [The text continues with the specific qualities.]”
"Here, monks, a wicked monk relies on the uneven, relies on the dense thickets, relies on the powerful, is a consumer of wealth, and wanders alone.
And how, monks, does a wicked monk rely on the uneven?
Here, monks, a wicked monk is endowed with uneven bodily action, he is endowed with uneven verbal action, and he is endowed with uneven mental action."
In this way, monks, a wicked monk relies on what is uneven.
And how, monks, does a wicked monk rely on what is dense?
Here, monks, a wicked monk holds wrong view and is possessed of a view that clings to extremes.
In this way, monks, a wicked monk relies on a thicket.
And how, monks, does a wicked monk rely on the powerful?
Here, monks, a wicked monk relies on a king or on a king’s high ministers.
It occurs to him:
"If anyone says anything to me, these kings or royal ministers will explain the meaning to me in its proper context.
And if anyone says something to him, those kings or royal ministers explain the meaning to him in its proper context.
In this way, monks, an evil monk relies on the powerful.
And how, monks, does an evil monk give away his wealth?
Here, monks, an evil monk is a recipient of robes, almsfood, lodgings, and medicinal requisites for the sick.
It occurs to him:
"If anyone says anything to me, I will welcome them with a gift from this wealth.
If anyone says anything to him, he welcomes them with a gift from that wealth.
In this way, monks, a wicked monk is one who gives away his wealth.
And how, monks, is a wicked monk a solitary wanderer?
Here, monks, a wicked monk dwells all alone in remote border regions.
Thus, by visiting families there, he gains gain.
In this way, monks, a wicked monk is one who wanders alone.
Endowed with these five qualities, monks, a wicked monk maintains himself wounded and injured; he is blameworthy and subject to reproach by the wise, and he produces much demerit.”
The Third [Sutta].
Aṅguttara Nikāya 5.104.
Chapter 11: On Dwelling in Comfort (Phāsuvihāravagga).
The Discourse on the Delicate Ascetic (Samaṇasukhumālasutta):
“Bhikkhus, possessing five qualities, a bhikkhu is a delicate ascetic among ascetics.”
By which five?
Here, monks, a monk for the most part uses robes that have been requested, and only seldom those not requested;
he for the most part consumes almsfood that has been requested, and only seldom that not requested; he for the most part uses lodgings that have been requested...
He makes use of medicinal requisites for the support of the sick—such as medicines and provisions—mostly when they are requested, and only rarely when unrequested.
Furthermore, with regard to those fellow celibates with whom he dwells, they mostly approach him with agreeable bodily conduct and only rarely with disagreeable;
they mostly approach him with agreeable verbal conduct and only rarely...
They treat one mostly with agreeable mental actions and only rarely with disagreeable ones;
they offer only agreeable gifts and only rarely disagreeable ones.
Furthermore, as for those feelings arising from bile, phlegm, or wind:

Whether arising from the humors, from a combination of humors, from changes in the seasons, from irregularities in lifestyle, from external injury, or from the ripening of kamma—such ailments do not arise in him to any great extent.
He is free from illness; he obtains at will, without difficulty, and without hardship, the four jhānas that are states of mental mastery and provide a pleasant dwelling in this very life.

With the destruction of the taints, he dwells having realized for himself with direct knowledge, in this very life, the taintless liberation of mind and liberation by wisdom, and having entered upon it.
Possessing these five qualities, monks, a monk is a delicate ascetic among ascetics.
For if anyone, monks, speaking rightly were to say: "A delicate ascetic among ascetics," it is of me, monks, that one would rightly say: "A delicate ascetic among ascetics."
For I, monks, for the most part use robes only when they have been requested, seldom when they have not been requested;

I use almsfood for the most part only when it has been requested, seldom when it has not been requested; I use lodgings for the most part only when they have been requested, seldom when they have not been requested;
I use medicinal requisites for the sick for the most part only when they have been requested, seldom when they have not been requested.
Furthermore, those monks with whom I dwell mostly treat me with agreeable bodily action and only rarely with disagreeable bodily action;
they mostly treat me with agreeable verbal action and only rarely with disagreeable verbal action;
they mostly treat me with agreeable mental action and only rarely with disagreeable mental action.
They offer only what is agreeable and very little that is disagreeable.
Furthermore, as for those feelings—whether arising from bile, phlegm, or wind; or from a combination of these;
or born of seasonal changes, or from an irregular lifestyle, or from physical trauma, or as the result of kamma—
Or rather—those [ailments] do not arise in me very often. I am free from illness.
Furthermore, I am one who gains at will, without difficulty, and without hardship, the four jhānas that are higher mental states and provide a pleasant dwelling in this very life;
and, through the destruction of the taints... having realized it for myself, I dwell having attained it.

“Monks, if one were speaking rightly, saying: ‘Among ascetics, he is the most delicate of ascetics,’ it is of me alone, monks, that one would rightly say: ‘Among ascetics, he is the most delicate of ascetics.
This was the fourth.
(Aṅguttara Nikāya 5.105)
11. The Chapter on Comfortable Living:
The Discourse on Comfortable Living (Phāsuvihārasutta) (AN 5.105, PTS AN iii 132)
“Monks, there are these five conditions for living at ease.
What are the five?
Here, monks, a monk maintains bodily action imbued with loving-kindness toward his fellow practitioners, both openly and...”
And loving verbal action, and loving mental action, are established toward his fellow practitioners both openly and in private.
Regarding those virtues that are unbroken, untorn, unblemished, unmottled, liberating,
praised by the wise, unadhered-to, and conducive to concentration— he dwells having attained a commonality of virtue with others through such virtues.
“Whether in public or in private,
he dwells in conformity with his fellow celibates regarding that noble view which leads out, leading its practitioner to the complete destruction of suffering.
These, monks, are the five conditions for living at ease.”
The Fifth. Aṅguttara Nikāya 5.106.
Chapter 11: On Dwelling at Ease.
The Ānanda Sutta (AN 5.106).
On one occasion the Blessed One was dwelling at Kosambī in Ghosita’s Park.

Then the Venerable Ānanda approached the Blessed One; having approached and paid homage to the Blessed One, he sat down to one side. Sitting to one side, the Venerable Ānanda said this to the Blessed One:
"To what extent, Bhante, might a bhikkhu dwelling in the Saṅgha live in comfort?
"Ānanda, when a bhikkhu is himself accomplished in virtue, yet does not urge others toward higher virtue;..."
"To this extent, Ānanda, a bhikkhu dwelling in the Saṅgha might dwell at ease.
"But, Bhante, could there be another way in which a bhikkhu dwelling in the Saṅgha might dwell at ease?
"There could be, Ānanda."
"Ānanda, when a bhikkhu is himself accomplished in virtue, yet does not urge others toward higher virtue;
when he is self-reflective, yet does not reflect on others—
even to this extent, Ānanda, a bhikkhu dwelling in the Saṅgha would live in comfort."
“But, Bhante, might there be another way by which a bhikkhu dwelling in the Saṅgha could dwell in comfort?
“There might be, Ānanda.
When, Ānanda, a bhikkhu is himself accomplished in virtue, yet does not urge others toward higher virtue;”
“He is one who observes himself, not one who observes others;
he is unrenowned, yet he does not tremble because of that lack of renown.
To this extent, Ānanda, a bhikkhu dwelling in the Saṅgha might dwell in comfort.”
“But, Bhante, might there be another way by which a bhikkhu dwelling in the Saṅgha would dwell in comfort?
“There might be, Ānanda.
When, Ānanda, a bhikkhu is himself accomplished in virtue, but does not urge others toward higher virtue;”
He is equanimous toward himself but not toward others;
he is unrenowned, yet he does not tremble because of that lack of renown;
and he is one who obtains at will, without difficulty, and without trouble, the four jhānas that belong to the higher mind and provide a pleasant dwelling in this very life.
"To this extent, Ānanda, a bhikkhu dwelling in the Saṅgha might dwell at ease.
"But, Bhante, might there be another way in which a bhikkhu dwelling in the Saṅgha might dwell at ease?
"There might be, Ānanda."
But when, Ānanda, a bhikkhu is himself accomplished in virtue, yet does not urge others toward higher virtue;
when he is self-reflective, yet does not reflect on others;
and when he is not renowned, yet is not distressed by that lack of renown; then...
He gains at will, without difficulty, and without toil, the four jhānas that belong to the higher mind and provide a pleasant dwelling in this very life;

and through the destruction of the taints, he dwells having realized for himself with direct knowledge, in this very life, the taintless liberation of mind and liberation by wisdom, and having entered upon it.
To this extent, Ānanda, a bhikkhu dwelling in the Saṅgha may dwell in comfort.
"And from this state of ease, Ānanda, I say there is no other state of ease that is more excellent or more sublime.
The sixth. *Aṅguttara Nikāya* 5.107.

11. Phāsuvihāravagga Sīlasutta (AN 5.107, PTS AN iii 134) “Bhikkhus, possessing four qualities, a bhikkhu dwells at ease. What four? Here, a bhikkhu is possessed of virtue; he is possessed of concentration; he is possessed of wisdom; and he is possessed of liberation. Possessing these four qualities, a bhikkhu dwells at ease.”
“Bhikkhus, possessing five qualities, a bhikkhu is worthy of gifts, worthy of hospitality, worthy of offerings, worthy of reverential salutation, an unsurpassed field of merit for the world.
What are the five?
Here, bhikkhus, a bhikkhu is accomplished in virtue, accomplished in concentration, accomplished in wisdom, accomplished in liberation, and accomplished in the knowledge and vision of liberation.”
“Bhikkhus, a bhikkhu endowed with these five qualities is worthy of gifts, worthy of hospitality, worthy of offerings, worthy of reverential salutation, an unsurpassed field of merit for the world.
The seventh.

11. Phāsuvihāravagga Asekhasutta (AN 5.108, PTS AN iii 134) “Bhikkhus, there are these four kinds of persons found existing in the world. What four? The person who is beyond training (*asekha*), the person in training (*sekha*), the ordinary person (*puthujjana*) who has entered the stream (*sotāpanna*), and the ordinary person who has not yet entered the stream. And how, bhikkhus, is one a person beyond training? Here, bhikkhus, a bhikkhu is an arahant with taints destroyed, one who has lived the holy life, done what was to be done, laid down the burden, reached the true goal, destroyed the fetters of existence, and is liberated through final knowledge. This, bhikkhus, is called a person beyond training. And how, bhikkhus, is one a person in training? Here, bhikkhus, a bhikkhu is a learner, one who has entered the path, possessing the seven factors of enlightenment, still subject to rebirth, still subject to future existence. This, bhikkhus, is called a person in training. And how, bhikkhus, is one an ordinary person who has entered the stream? Here, bhikkhus, a noble disciple is possessed of unwavering confidence in the Buddha: ‘Thus indeed is the Blessed One: worthy, perfectly enlightened, accomplished in true knowledge and conduct, fortunate, knower of the worlds, unsurpassed leader of persons to be tamed, teacher of devas and humans, the Buddha, the Blessed One. He is possessed of unwavering confidence in the Dhamma: ‘Well-proclaimed by the Blessed One is the Dhamma, visible here and now, timeless, inviting inspection, leading onward, to be realized by the wise, each for themselves. He is possessed of unwavering confidence in the Saṅgha: ‘Well-directed is the Saṅgha of the Blessed One’s disciples, practicing the good way, practicing the straight way, practicing the true way, practicing the proper way; that is, the four pairs of persons, the eight types of individuals. This Saṅgha of the Blessed One’s disciples is worthy of gifts, worthy of hospitality, worthy of offerings, worthy of reverential salutation, the unsurpassed field of merit for the world. This, bhikkhus, is called an ordinary person who has entered the stream. And how, bhikkhus, is one an ordinary person who has not yet entered the stream? Here, bhikkhus, a person is not possessed of unwavering confidence in the Buddha... nor in the Dhamma... nor in the Saṅgha. This, bhikkhus, is called an ordinary person who has not yet entered the stream. These, bhikkhus, are the four kinds of persons found existing in the world.”
“Bhikkhus, possessing five qualities, a bhikkhu is worthy of gifts, worthy of hospitality, worthy of offerings, worthy of reverential salutation, an unsurpassed field of merit for the world.
What are the five?
Here, bhikkhus, a bhikkhu possesses the aggregate of virtue of one beyond training; he possesses the aggregate of concentration of one beyond training...”
He is endowed with the aggregate of wisdom of one beyond training; he is endowed with the aggregate of liberation of one beyond training;
he is endowed with the aggregate of the knowledge and vision of liberation of one beyond training.
Endowed with these five qualities, monks, a bhikkhu is worthy of gifts … [as before] … an unsurpassed field of merit for the world.”
The Eighth. Aṅguttara Nikāya 5.109 11.
Phāsuvihāravagga (The Chapter on Living at Ease)
The Discourse on the Four Quarters (Cātuddisasutta):
“Bhikkhus, endowed with five qualities, a bhikkhu is one who belongs to the four quarters.”
By which five?

Here, monks, a monk is virtuous; he dwells restrained by the Pātimokkha, possessed of proper conduct and resort, seeing danger in even the slightest faults, and having undertaken them, he trains himself in the rules of training.
He is learned, a retainer of what he has heard, a storehouse of what he has heard—those teachings that are good in the beginning, good in the middle, and good in the end.
They proclaim the holy life in its entirety, perfect and pure, with its meaning and its phrasing.
Such teachings as these are well-learned by him, retained, mastered verbally, examined by the mind, and thoroughly penetrated by view.
He is content with any kind of robes, almsfood, lodgings, and medicinal requisites for the sick.
“He is one who obtains at will, without difficulty, and without trouble, the four jhānas that constitute higher mental states and provide a pleasant dwelling in this very life;

and through the destruction of the taints, he dwells having realized for himself with direct knowledge, in this very life, the taintless liberation of mind and liberation by wisdom, having entered upon it.
It is by possessing these five qualities, monks, that a monk is ‘one who faces in all four directions.’”
The Ninth. Aṅguttara Nikāya 5.110 11.

he is learned... [as before] ...his view is well-penetrated.
He dwells with energy aroused, steadfast, firm in his exertion, not casting off the burden regarding wholesome states;
he is one who gains at will, without difficulty, and without trouble, the four jhānas that belong to the higher mind and provide a pleasant dwelling in this very life;

and through the destruction of the taints, he dwells having realized for himself with direct knowledge, in this very life, the taintless liberation of mind and liberation by wisdom, having entered upon it.

12. Andhakavinda Chapter:
The Discourse on Family Dependents (Kulūpaka Sutta) (AN 5.111, PTS AN iii 136)
“Bhikkhus, a bhikkhu who visits families and possesses five qualities is displeasing and disagreeable to those families, and he is neither respected nor esteemed.
What are the five?
He is one who trusts without being intimate; he makes requests without being granted authority; he attends upon them with abandon; he whispers into their ears; and he is one who asks too much.
“Monks, a monk who visits families and possesses these five qualities is disliked and displeasing to those families, and he is neither respected nor esteemed.

Monks, a monk who visits families and possesses five qualities is dear and pleasing to those families, and he is respected and esteemed. What are the five? [The Buddha then enumerates the five qualities.]”

He does not place undue trust in those with whom he is not well-acquainted; he does not make improper requests; he does not attend upon people with misplaced intimacy; he does not whisper into their ears; and he is not one who makes excessive demands.
Endowed with these five qualities, monks, a monk who visits families becomes dear, agreeable, respected, and esteemed among them. Thus it was said. First.

Aṅguttara Nikāya 5.112 12. Andhakavindavagga Pacchāsamaṇasutta (The Discourse on the Attendant Monk) At one time the Blessed One was dwelling at Andhakavinda. There the Blessed One addressed the bhikkhus: “Bhikkhus! “Venerable sir,” those bhikkhus replied to the Blessed One. The Blessed One said this: “Bhikkhus, when a bhikkhu has a companion monk who possesses five qualities, it is enough for him to live with that companion monk; he should not abandon him. What five? Here, bhikkhus, a bhikkhu’s companion monk is virtuous, restrained by the restraint of the Pātimokkha, perfect in conduct and resort, and seeing fear in even the slightest transgression; he trains himself, having undertaken the training rules. He is one who, when asked, can explain the meaning of what has been stated in brief by the Tathāgata in detail. He is one who, when asked, can explain the meaning of what has been stated in detail by the Tathāgata in brief. He is one who, when asked, can explain the meaning of what has been stated in brief and in detail by the Tathāgata in both ways. He is one who, when asked, can explain the Dhamma in accordance with the Dhamma. When a bhikkhu has a companion monk who possesses these five qualities, it is enough for him to live with that companion monk; he should not abandon him.”
“Monks, one endowed with five qualities should not be accepted as a junior attendant.
With which five?

He walks either too far ahead or too close; he does not take up what has fallen within his reach; he does not stop one who is speaking on a subject bordering on an offense; he interrupts the speech of one who is talking; he is of poor wisdom, dull, and muddled.
Monks, one who possesses these five qualities should not be taken as a junior attendant.
Monks, one who possesses five qualities should be taken as a junior attendant.

“Which five? He does not go too far away, nor too close; he takes what is placed in his bowl; he restrains one who speaks near to an offense; he does not interrupt the conversation of one who is speaking; and he is wise, not dull-witted, and not deaf-mute.
Possessing these five qualities, monks, a junior attendant should be accepted.”

Sammāsamādhisutta: “Bhikkhus,
