12. Andhakavinda Chapter:
The Discourse at Andhakavinda (AN 5.114, PTS AN iii 138)
On one occasion the Blessed One was dwelling among the Magadhans at Andhakavinda.

Then the Venerable Ānanda approached the Blessed One; having approached and paid homage to the Blessed One, he sat down to one side. As the Venerable Ānanda was sitting to one side, the Blessed One said this to him:
"Ānanda, those bhikkhus who are new, recently gone forth, and have only lately come to this Dhamma and Discipline—those bhikkhus, Ānanda, you should encourage, settle, and establish in five things."
In which five?

“Come, friends, be virtuous; dwell restrained by the Pātimokkha, possessed of proper conduct and resort, seeing danger in even the slightest faults, and train yourselves by undertaking the rules of training”—thus is restraint according to the Pātimokkha.
They should be encouraged, settled, and established [in this]:

"Come, friends, dwell with the doors of the sense faculties guarded, with mindfulness as your protector, with watchful mindfulness, with your minds well-restrained, endowed with a mind protected by mindfulness.
Thus should they be encouraged, settled, and established in the restraint of the sense faculties.
"Come, friends, be moderate in speech; set limits to your talk"—thus should they be encouraged, settled, and established in moderation of speech.
"Come, friends, be forest-dwellers; resort to remote lodgings in forests and jungle-thickets"—thus should they be encouraged, settled, and established in the seclusion of the body.
“Come, friends, be possessed of right view and endowed with right vision.
In this way, Ānanda, those monks who are new, recently gone forth, and have newly arrived at this Dhamma and Discipline should be encouraged, settled, and established in these five things.
(The fourth.)
Aṅguttara Nikāya 5.115 12. Andhakavindavagga Maccharinīsutta — The Discourse on the Miserly Woman At Sāvatthī.

“Bhikkhus, there are these five kinds of miserliness. What five? Miserliness regarding dwellings, miserliness regarding families, miserliness regarding gains, miserliness regarding praise, and miserliness regarding the Dhamma. These, bhikkhus, are the five kinds of miserliness. When a woman is miserly in these five ways, with the breakup of the body, after death, she is reborn in a state of misery, in a bad destination, in the nether world, in hell. But when a woman is not miserly in these five ways, with the breakup of the body, after death, she is reborn in a good destination, in a heavenly world.”
“Bhikkhus, possessing five qualities, a bhikkhunī is deposited in hell as if carried there. What are the five? [The Sutta continues with the list.]”
She is stingy regarding dwellings, stingy regarding families, stingy regarding gains, stingy regarding praise, and stingy regarding the Dhamma.
Possessing these five qualities, monks, a bhikkhunī is placed in hell as if carried there.
Possessing five qualities, monks, a bhikkhunī is placed in heaven as if carried there.
“By which five?
She is not miserly regarding her dwelling, she is not miserly regarding families, she is not miserly regarding gains, she is not miserly regarding praise, and she is not miserly regarding the Dhamma.
Possessing these five qualities, bhikkhus, a bhikkhunī is placed in heaven as if carried there.”
The Fifth. Aṅguttara Nikāya 5.116 12.
The Chapter at Andhakavinda
The Discourse on Description (Vaṇṇanāsutta):
“Bhikkhus, possessed of five qualities, a bhikkhunī is deposited in hell as if carried there. [End of AN 5.116]” (PTS AN iii 139)
Which five?
Without investigating and without scrutinizing, one speaks in praise of one who deserves blame;
without investigating and without scrutinizing, one speaks in blame of one who deserves praise.
Without investigating and without scrutinizing, one conceives confidence in a matter that inspires lack of confidence;
without investigating and without scrutinizing, one conceives lack of confidence in a matter that inspires confidence;
and one squanders what has been given out of faith.
“Monks, a bhikkhunī endowed with these five qualities is placed in hell as if carried there.
Monks, a bhikkhunī endowed with five qualities is placed in heaven as if carried there. With which five? [The Buddha said:]”
Having investigated and scrutinized, one speaks dispraise of one who deserves dispraise;
having investigated and scrutinized, one speaks praise of one who deserves praise;
and having investigated and scrutinized, one expresses lack of confidence regarding a matter that merits a lack of confidence.
Having investigated and scrutinized, she manifests confidence in a matter that inspires confidence;
she does not squander what has been given out of faith.
Endowed with these five qualities, monks, a bhikkhunī is deposited in heaven as if carried there.”
The Sixth.

The Discourse on Wrong Speech (Micchāvācāsutta):

The Discourse on the Sick (Gilānasutta).
On one occasion the Blessed One was dwelling at Vesālī in the Great Wood, in the Hall with the Peaked Roof.
Then, in the evening, the Blessed One emerged from seclusion and went to the sick ward.
There he saw a certain bhikkhu who was weak and ill;
having seen him, he sat down on the prepared seat.
Having sat down, the Blessed One addressed the bhikkhus:
“Bhikkhus, when five things do not abandon a bhikkhu who is weak and ill, it can be expected of him:

‘Before long, with the destruction of the taints, he will realize for himself with direct knowledge, in this very life, the taintless liberation of mind and liberation by wisdom, and having entered upon it, he will dwell therein.’”
What are the five? Here, monks,
a monk dwells contemplating the foulness of the body, perceiving the repulsiveness of food, perceiving non-delight in the entire world,
contemplating impermanence in all conditioned phenomena, and the perception of death is well-established within him.

“Bhikkhus, whatever bhikkhu is weak and ill, these five qualities do not leave him; it can be expected of him that, before long, through the destruction of the taints, he will realize for himself with direct knowledge, in this very life, the taintless liberation of mind and liberation by wisdom, and having entered upon it, will dwell therein.
Thus was the first [discourse].

The Discourse on Being Established in Mindfulness “Monks, when one is established in mindfulness, these five benefits are to be expected. What five? One dwells with a mind that is guarded; one does not become remorseful; one dies without regret; at the breaking up of the body, after death, one is reborn in a good destination, a heavenly world; and even here and now, one experiences happiness. When one is established in mindfulness, these five benefits are to be expected.”
“Bhikkhus, whatever bhikkhu or bhikkhunī develops five qualities and cultivates them frequently, one of two fruits may be expected for them:
final knowledge in this very life, or, if there is a residue remaining, the state of a non-returner.”
What are the five?
Here, monks, a bhikkhu’s mindfulness is well-established precisely within himself regarding the wisdom that leads to the arising and passing away of phenomena;
he dwells contemplating the foulness of the body, perceiving the repulsiveness of food, and perceiving non-delight in the entire world.
"Contemplating impermanence in all conditioned phenomena.
For whatever bhikkhu or bhikkhunī, monks, develops these five qualities and cultivates these five qualities, one of two fruits may be expected for them:
final knowledge in this very life, or, if there is a residue remaining, the state of a non-returner."
The Second.

Gilānavagga (The Chapter on the Sick)
The Discourse on the First Attendant (AN 5.123).
“Bhikkhus, a patient who possesses five qualities is difficult to attend upon. What five? [The text continues with the list of those qualities.]”
Which five? He does what is unwholesome;
he does not know moderation in what is wholesome; he does not take his medicine;
he does not disclose his illness as it truly is to the attendant who wishes for his welfare, saying, "I am getting worse," when he is getting worse; or, "I am improving," when he is improving.
Or, thinking "he is walking back" when he is walking back, or "he is standing" when he is standing,
such a person is by nature unable to endure arisen bodily feelings that are painful, sharp, harsh, bitter, disagreeable, unpleasant,
and life-threatening. Monks, a patient endowed with these five qualities is difficult to attend to.
“Monks, a patient endowed with five qualities is easy to attend to.
With which five?
He does what is beneficial; he knows the proper measure regarding what is beneficial; he takes his medicine; and he is desirous of his own welfare.”
He accurately describes the illness of the attendant to the sick, saying, "When he moves forward, he moves forward;
when he moves backward, he moves backward; when he stands, he stands.
He is one who is capable of enduring arisen bodily feelings that are painful, racking, sharp, piercing, bitter, disagreeable, unpleasant, and life-threatening.
“Bhikkhus, a patient endowed with these five qualities is easy to attend to.
The third [sutta].

13. Gilānavagga The Second Discourse on Attendants (Dutiya-upaṭṭhāka-sutta) “Monks, there are these five qualities of an attendant that are conducive to inspiration. What five? “Bhikkhus, a nurse endowed with five qualities is not fit to attend to the sick.

He is not capable of providing medicine;”
He does not know what is suitable and what is unsuitable; he offers what is unsuitable and withdraws what is suitable.
He attends to the sick for the sake of material gain, not with a mind of loving-kindness.
He feels disgust at having to remove excrement, urine, vomit, or spittle.
He is not capable of instructing, exhorting, inspiring, and gladdening the sick from time to time with a talk on the Dhamma.
Monks, one who attends to the sick endowed with these five qualities is not fit to attend to the sick.
Monks, one who attends to the sick endowed with five qualities is fit to attend to the sick.
Which five?
He is capable of providing medicine;
he knows what is suitable and what is unsuitable; he discards what is unsuitable and offers what is suitable.
He attends to the sick with a mind of loving-kindness, not for the sake of material gain;
he is not disgusted by removing excrement, urine, vomit, or spittle;
and he is capable from time to time of instructing, exhorting, inspiring, and gladdening the sick person with a talk on the Dhamma.
“Bhikkhus, a nurse endowed with these five qualities is competent to attend to the sick.
The fourth.

“Bhikkhus, there are these five things that shorten life. What are the five? One acts in a way that is unwholesome;

Gilānavagga Dutiya-anāyussasutta (The Second Discourse on Not Living Long)
“Bhikkhus, there are these five things that shorten life.
Which five?”
One acts in a way that is unwholesome; one does not know moderation regarding what is wholesome; one eats food that is undigested; one is immoral; and one has evil friends.
These, monks, are the five things that lead to a short life.
There are, monks, these five things that lead to a long life.
Which five?
One acts in a way that is beneficial; one knows the proper measure regarding what is beneficial; one eats food that is well-digested; one is virtuous; and one has good friends.
These, monks, are the five things that lead to longevity.”

Aṅguttara Nikāya 5.128 13. Gilānavagga Samaṇasukhasutta: The Happiness of a Recluse “Monks, there are these five kinds of happiness for a recluse that are not shared with householders. What five? Here, monks, a noble disciple possesses confirmed confidence in the Buddha thus: ‘The Blessed One is an arahant, perfectly enlightened, accomplished in true knowledge and conduct, fortunate, knower of the world, unsurpassed trainer of persons to be tamed, teacher of devas and humans, the Buddha, the Blessed One. This, monks, is the first kind of happiness for a recluse that is not shared with householders. Furthermore, monks, a noble disciple possesses confirmed confidence in the Dhamma thus: ‘The Dhamma is well-expounded by the Blessed One, directly visible, immediate, inviting one to come and see, applicable, to be personally experienced by the wise. This, monks, is the second kind of happiness for a recluse that is not shared with householders. Furthermore, monks, a noble disciple possesses confirmed confidence in the Saṅgha thus: ‘The Saṅgha of the Blessed One’s disciples is practicing the good way, practicing the straight way, practicing the true way, practicing the proper way; that is, the four pairs of persons, the eight types of individuals—this Saṅgha of the Blessed One’s disciples is worthy of gifts, worthy of hospitality, worthy of offerings, worthy of reverential salutation, the unsurpassed field of merit for the world. This, monks, is the third kind of happiness for a recluse that is not shared with householders. Furthermore, monks, a noble disciple possesses the virtues dear to the noble ones—unbroken, untorn, unblemished, unmottled, freeing, praised by the wise, ungrasped, leading to concentration. This, monks, is the fourth kind of happiness for a recluse that is not shared with householders. Furthermore, monks, a noble disciple has abandoned the five lower fetters. This, monks, is the fifth kind of happiness for a recluse that is not shared with householders. These, monks, are the five kinds of happiness for a recluse that are not shared with householders.”
“Monks, there are these five sufferings of a recluse.
What are the five?
In this case, monks, a bhikkhu is not content with any kind of robe,
he is not content with any kind of almsfood, he is not content with any kind of lodging,
and he is not content with any kind of medicinal requisites for the sick; and he leads the holy life without delighting in it.
These, monks, are the five kinds of suffering for ascetics.
There are, monks, these five kinds of happiness for ascetics. Which five?
In this case, monks, a bhikkhu is content with any kind of robe,
content with any kind of almsfood, content with any kind of lodging, and content with any kind of medicinal requisites for the sick;
and he lives devoted to the holy life.
“Monks, these indeed are the five pleasures of the ascetic.
The eighth.

13. Gilānavagga Parikuppa Sutta (The Discourse on Being Agitated) At Sāvatthī. “Monks, when a monk is agitated, he does not understand as it really is: ‘This is suffering. He does not understand as it really is: ‘This is the origin of suffering. He does not understand as it really is: ‘This is the cessation of suffering. He does not understand as it really is: ‘This is the way leading to the cessation of suffering. “Being thus ignorant, he does not develop the path; because he does not develop the path, he does not attain the fruit of the path. “But when a monk is not agitated, he understands as it really is: ‘This is suffering. He understands as it really is: ‘This is the origin of suffering. He understands as it really is: ‘This is the cessation of suffering. He understands as it really is: ‘This is the way leading to the cessation of suffering. “Being thus knowledgeable, he develops the path; because he develops the path, he attains the fruit of the path. Thus spoke the Blessed One. Having said this, the Fortunate One, the Teacher, further said this: “When one is agitated, the mind is not concentrated; The mind of one who is agitated does not know the Dhamma. One who does not know the Dhamma does not see the Truth; Not seeing the Truth, one does not cross over the flood. “But when one is not agitated, the mind is concentrated; The mind of one who is not agitated knows the Dhamma. One who knows the Dhamma sees the Truth; Seeing the Truth, one crosses over the flood.”
“Bhikkhus, there are these five who are destined for the states of deprivation, bound for hell, incurable, and beyond remedy.

Which five? One who has deprived his mother of life; one who has deprived his father of life; one who has deprived an arahant of life; one who, with a mind of hatred, has drawn blood from a Tathāgata; and one who has caused a schism in the Saṅgha.”
“Monks, these five are destined for the states of deprivation, bound for hell, incurable, and beyond remedy.
Thus was the ninth [discourse]. Aṅguttara Nikāya 5.130.
13. Gilānavagga Byasanasutta (AN 5.130, PTS AN iii 147) “Monks, there are these five perils. What five?
The peril of fire, the peril of water, the peril of kings, the peril of thieves, and the peril of non-human beings. These, monks, are the five perils.”
“Monks, there are these five calamities.
What are the five?
The calamity of relatives, the calamity of wealth, the calamity of disease, the calamity of moral failure, and the calamity of wrong view.”

“Bhikkhus, beings do not, on account of the loss of relatives, the loss of wealth, or the loss of health, at the breaking up of the body after death, reappear in a state of deprivation, in an unhappy destination, in perdition, even in hell.

But on account of the loss of virtue or the loss of right view, bhikkhus, beings—at the breaking up of the body after death—reappear in a state of deprivation, in an unhappy destination, in perdition, even in hell.
These, bhikkhus, are the five kinds of loss.”
“Monks, there are these five accomplishments. What five?
Accomplishment in kinsmen, accomplishment in wealth, accomplishment in health, accomplishment in virtue, and accomplishment in view.”

“Monks, beings do not, because of success in relatives, or because of success in wealth, or because of success in health, arise in a happy destination, in a heavenly world, after the breakup of the body, after death.
Rather, monks, it is because of success in virtue or because of success in view that beings arise in a happy destination, in a heavenly world, after the breakup of the body, after death.
These, monks, are the five successes.”
The tenth.

The First Discourse on Turning the Wheel (AN 5.131): “Bhikkhus,
endowed with five factors, a wheel-turning monarch turns the wheel by means of the Dhamma alone.”
That wheel becomes irreversible by any human adversary, any enemy, or any living being.
By what five qualities?
Here, monks, a wheel-turning monarch knows the right purpose, knows the right principle, knows the proper measure, knows the right time, and knows the assembly.
“Monks, when a wheel-turning monarch is endowed with these five qualities, he turns the wheel by means of the Dhamma alone;
that wheel cannot be turned back by any human adversary or enemy.
In the same way, monks, when a Tathāgata, an Arahant, a perfectly enlightened Buddha is endowed with five qualities, he turns the unsurpassed Wheel of the Dhamma by means of the Dhamma alone.”
That wheel is irreversible by any ascetic, brahmin, deva, Māra, Brahmā, or anyone in the world.
By what five qualities?
Here, monks, the Tathāgata, the Arahant, the Perfectly Enlightened One, knows the goal, knows the Dhamma, knows moderation, knows the right time, and knows the assembly.
“Bhikkhus, endowed with these five qualities, the Tathāgata, the Arahant, the Perfectly Enlightened One, sets in motion by means of the Dhamma alone the unsurpassed Wheel of the Dhamma;
that Wheel of the Dhamma cannot be turned back by any ascetic or brahmin, or by any deva, Māra, Brahmā, or anyone in the world.
Thus was the first [discourse].

Aṅguttara Nikāya 5.132 14. Rājavagga The Second Discourse on Following the Wheel “Monks, there are these five qualities that a wheel-turning monarch possesses by which he turns the wheel. What five? Here, monks, a wheel-turning monarch is virtuous, possessed of virtue; he is a king who has undertaken the training, trained in the training rules, and is restrained by the restraint of the training rules.

He does not take life, he abstains from taking life; with the rod laid aside and the sword, he dwells modest, compassionate, and merciful toward all living beings. He does not take what is not given, he abstains from taking what is not given; he takes only what is given, expects only what is given, and dwells with a mind free from theft. He does not engage in sexual misconduct, he abstains from sexual misconduct; he does not have sexual relations with women who are protected by their mother, father, mother and father, brother, sister, or relatives, nor with those who are married or under protection, nor even with those who have a garland upon their head. He does not speak falsehood, he abstains from false speech; he speaks truth, adheres to truth, is trustworthy and reliable, and does not deceive anyone in the world. He does not drink intoxicants, he abstains from intoxicants; he is not intoxicated, not negligent, but mindful and clearly comprehending. Monks, when a wheel-turning monarch possesses these five qualities, he turns the wheel. Just so, monks, there are these five qualities that a Tathāgata, an Arhat, a Perfectly Enlightened One possesses by which he turns the unsurpassed wheel of the Dhamma. What five? Here, monks, a Tathāgata, an Arhat, a Perfectly Enlightened One is virtuous, possessed of virtue; he is a king who has undertaken the training, trained in the training rules, and is restrained by the restraint of the training rules. He does not take life, he abstains from taking life; with the rod laid aside and the sword, he dwells modest, compassionate, and merciful toward all living beings. He does not take what is not given, he abstains from taking what is not given; he takes only what is given, expects only what is given, and dwells with a mind free from theft. He does not engage in sexual misconduct, he abstains from sexual misconduct; he does not have sexual relations with women who are protected by their mother, father, mother and father, brother, sister, or relatives, nor with those who are married or under protection, nor even with those who have a garland upon their head. He does not speak falsehood, he abstains from false speech; he speaks truth, adheres to truth, is trustworthy and reliable, and does not deceive anyone in the world. He drinks no intoxicants, he abstains from intoxicants; he is not intoxicated, not negligent, but mindful and clearly comprehending. Monks, when a Tathāgata, an Arhat, a Perfectly Enlightened One possesses these five qualities, he turns the unsurpassed wheel of the Dhamma.”

“Bhikkhus, endowed with five qualities, the eldest son of a wheel-turning monarch continues to turn the wheel set in motion by his father solely through Dhamma; that wheel becomes irreversible by any human adversary or enemy. What five? Here, bhikkhus, the eldest son of a wheel-turning monarch is virtuous, guarded in conduct, restrained by the restraint of the Pātimokkha, accomplished in good conduct and proper behavior, seeing fear even in the slightest fault; he trains himself, having undertaken the training rules. He is one who honors, respects, reveres, and venerates mother and father. He is one who honors, respects, reveres, and venerates ascetics and brahmins. He is one who honors, respects, reveres, and venerates the elders in his family who are aged, advanced in years, and come to the last stage of life. He is one who possesses wealth acquired by energetic striving, amassed by the strength of his arms, earned by the sweat of his brow, righteous wealth righteously gained; and when he has such wealth, he enjoys it himself and shares it with others. Endowed with these five qualities, bhikkhus, the eldest son of a wheel-turning monarch continues to turn the wheel set in motion by his father solely through Dhamma; that wheel becomes irreversible by any human adversary or enemy.”
Which five?
Here, monks, the eldest son of a wheel-turning monarch is one who knows the goal, knows the Dhamma, knows moderation, knows the right time, and knows the assembly.
Endowed with these five factors, monks, the eldest son of a wheel-turning monarch lawfully continues the wheel set in motion by his father.
That wheel cannot be turned back by any human adversary, nor by any living being.
In the same way, monks, endowed with five qualities, Sāriputta correctly sets in motion the unsurpassed Wheel of Dhamma set in motion by the Tathāgata;
that wheel cannot be turned back by any ascetic, or brahmin, or deva, or Māra, or Brahmā, or by anyone in the world.
"By which five?
Here, monks, Sāriputta knows the meaning, knows the Dhamma, knows the proper measure, knows the right time, and knows the assembly.
Endowed with these five qualities, monks, Sāriputta correctly continues to turn the unsurpassed wheel of Dhamma set in motion by the Tathāgata."
That wheel is irreversible by any ascetic or brahmin, by any deva, Māra, Brahmā, or anyone else in the world. Thus ends the second [sutta].
Aṅguttara Nikāya 5.133.

14. Rājavagga: Dhammarājāsutta (AN 5.133, PTS AN iii 149) “Monks, there are these four kinds of kings. What four? The dhamma-king, the adharmic king, the king who has conquered one quarter, and the king who has conquered all four quarters. These, monks, are the four kinds of kings. Of these four kinds of kings, monks, the dhamma-king is the foremost, the best, the most excellent, the most sublime, and the most supreme. Just as, monks, among the various kinds of trees, the sāla tree is the foremost, the best, the most excellent, the most sublime, and the most supreme; even so, monks, of these four kinds of kings, the dhamma-king is the foremost, the best, the most excellent, the most sublime, and the most supreme. And how, monks, is one a dhamma-king? Here, monks, a king is himself virtuous, he encourages others in virtue, he is himself established in the practice of dharma, he encourages others in the practice of dharma, he is himself established in the practice of truth, he encourages others in the practice of truth, he is himself established in the practice of gentleness, he encourages others in the practice of gentleness, he is himself established in the practice of self-restraint, he encourages others in the practice of self-restraint, he is himself established in the practice of non-violence, he encourages others in the practice of non-violence, he is himself established in the practice of patience, he encourages others in the practice of patience, he is himself established in the practice of non-opposition, he encourages others in the practice of non-opposition, he is himself established in the practice of non-harming, he encourages others in the practice of non-harming, he is himself established in the practice of non-injury, he encourages others in the practice of non-injury. It is in this way, monks, that one is a dhamma-king.”
“Bhikkhus, even that wheel-turning monarch, righteous and a king of Dhamma, does not turn the wheel without a king.
When this was said, a certain bhikkhu asked the Blessed One:
“But who, Bhante, is the king of the righteous wheel-turning monarch, the king of Dhamma?”
“Dhamma, bhikkhus,” the Blessed One said. “In this case, bhikkhu,
a wheel-turning monarch who is righteous, a king of Dhamma, relying solely on Dhamma, honoring Dhamma, revering Dhamma,
venerating Dhamma, having Dhamma as his banner, Dhamma as his standard, and Dhamma as his authority— ”
He provides righteous protection, defense, and security for his household. Furthermore, bhikkhus,
a wheel-turning monarch who is righteous, a king of righteousness, relying solely on Dhamma—
honoring Dhamma, revering Dhamma, and venerating Dhamma— has Dhamma as his banner, Dhamma as his standard, and Dhamma as his authority.
He provides righteous protection, defense, and security for his kṣatriya vassals...
[and so on] ...for his army, for brahmins and householders, for those in towns and the countryside, for ascetics and brahmins, and for beasts and birds.
That wheel-turning monarch, bhikkhu, being righteous and a king of righteousness, relies solely upon the Dhamma—upon the Dhamma.
Honoring the Dhamma, revering the Dhamma, and paying homage to the Dhamma— having the Dhamma as his banner, the Dhamma as his standard,
and the Dhamma as his authority— he established righteous protection, defense, and security for his own household; having established righteous protection, defense, and security for his household,
he likewise established it among the kshatriya vassals, the army, the brahmins and householders, and the people of the towns and countryside.
Among recluses and brahmins, and among beasts and birds, he turns the wheel by means of the Dhamma alone;
that wheel cannot be turned back by any human adversary or living being.
Even so, bhikkhu, the Tathāgata, the Arahant, the Perfectly Enlightened One, the righteous one, the King of Dhamma, [turns] the Dhamma alone...

Relying on the Dhamma, honoring the Dhamma, revering the Dhamma, making the Dhamma his banner, making the Dhamma his standard, and being governed by the Dhamma, he provides for the monks righteous protection, defense, and security, saying:
"Such bodily action should be practiced; such bodily action should not be practiced."
Such verbal action should be cultivated; such verbal action should not be cultivated.
Such mental action should be cultivated; such mental action should not be cultivated.
Such livelihood should be cultivated; such livelihood should not be cultivated.
‘A village or town of such a kind should be frequented; a village or town of such a kind should not be frequented.

Furthermore, monks, the Tathāgata, the Arahant, the Perfectly Enlightened One, the righteous one, the King of Dhamma, relying on the Dhamma alone—honoring the Dhamma, revering the Dhamma, venerating the Dhamma, having the Dhamma as his banner—[proceeds].”
Having the Dhamma as his banner and the Dhamma as his authority, he provides righteous protection, defense, and security for the bhikkhunīs...
[and so on] ...for the male lay followers... [and so on] ...for the female lay followers:
"Such bodily action should be practiced; such bodily action should not be practiced."
Such verbal action should be cultivated; such verbal action should not be cultivated.
Such mental action should be cultivated; such mental action should not be cultivated.
Such livelihood should be cultivated; such livelihood should not be cultivated.
‘Such a village or town should be frequented; such a village or town should not be frequented.

Now, that Tathāgata, the Worthy One, the Perfectly Enlightened One, the righteous King of Dhamma, relying on the Dhamma alone—honoring the Dhamma, revering the Dhamma, venerating the Dhamma, having the Dhamma as his banner—[proceeds].
Having established righteous protection, defense, and security for the monks,
having established righteous protection, defense, and security for the nuns, having established righteous protection, defense, and security for the laymen,
and having established righteous protection, defense, and security for the laywomen, [he governed] by the Dhamma alone— Dhamma-bannered, with the Dhamma as his supreme authority.
He sets in motion the unsurpassed Wheel of Dhamma;
that wheel is irreversible by any ascetic, or brahmin, or deva, or Māra, or Brahmā, or by anyone in the world.
This is the third [sutta].

Aṅguttara Nikāya 5.134 14. Rājavagga Yassandisaṁ Sutta (The Discourse on Whose Kindness) “Bhikkhus, there are these five kinds of persons found existing in the world. What five? The one who is kind to himself but not to others; the one who is kind to others but not to himself; the one who is kind neither to himself nor to others;

the one who is kind neither to himself nor to others but is a source of suffering for both; and the one who is kind to both himself and to others. And how, bhikkhus, is a person kind to himself but not to others? Here, bhikkhus, someone maintains himself by means of wrong view, wrong intention, wrong speech, wrong action, wrong livelihood, wrong effort, wrong mindfulness, and wrong concentration. This, bhikkhus, is called a person who is kind to himself but not to others. And how, bhikkhus, is a person kind to others but not to himself? Here, bhikkhus, someone maintains others by means of right view, right intention, right speech, right action, right livelihood, right effort, right mindfulness, and right concentration, but does not maintain himself in that way. This, bhikkhus, is called a person who is kind to others but not to himself. And how, bhikkhus, is a person kind neither to himself nor to others? Here, bhikkhus, someone maintains neither himself nor others by means of wrong view, wrong intention, wrong speech, wrong action, wrong livelihood, wrong effort, wrong mindfulness, and wrong concentration. This, bhikkhus, is called a person who is kind neither to himself nor to others. And how, bhikkhus, is a person kind neither to himself nor to others but is a source of suffering for both? Here, bhikkhus, someone maintains himself by means of wrong view... [as above] ...and wrong concentration, and he maintains others by means of wrong view... [as above] ...and wrong concentration. This, bhikkhus, is called a person who is kind neither to himself nor to others but is a source of suffering for both. And how, bhikkhus, is a person kind to both himself and to others? Here, bhikkhus, someone maintains himself by means of right view, right intention, right speech, right action, right livelihood, right effort, right mindfulness, and right concentration, and he maintains others by means of right view, right intention, right speech, right action, right livelihood, right effort, right mindfulness, and right concentration. This, bhikkhus, is called a person who is kind to both himself and to others. These, bhikkhus, are the five kinds of persons found existing in the world.”
“Bhikkhus, possessed of five qualities, an anointed khattiya king dwells wherever he may dwell, dwelling only within his own realm. Which five? [The rest of the sūtra follows].”

In this case, monks, a head-anointed kṣatriya king is well-born on both sides, from his mother’s side and from his father’s side, of pure descent for seven generations back through his paternal lineage, unblemished and irreproachable by birth;
he is wealthy, possessing great riches and vast enjoyments, with his treasuries and granaries full;
and he is powerful, endowed with a fourfold army that is obedient and responsive to his commands.
Furthermore, he has a counselor who is wise, competent, intelligent, and capable of considering matters pertaining to the past, future, and present.
These four qualities bring his fame to maturity.
Endowed with this fifth quality—fame—in whichever direction he dwells, he dwells only within his own domain.
And why is that? Because it is so for those who have conquered, monks.
In the same way, monks, a monk endowed with five qualities, in whatever direction he dwells, dwells with a mind liberated.
By which five?

Here, monks, a monk is virtuous; he dwells restrained by the Pātimokkha, possessed of proper conduct and resort, seeing danger in even the slightest faults, and having undertaken them, he trains in the rules of training—like a consecrated Khattiya king, endowed with noble birth.
He is learned, a retainer of what he has heard, and a storehouse of what he has heard; those teachings that are good in the beginning,
good in the middle, and good in the end, with the right meaning and phrasing, which proclaim the perfectly complete and pure holy life—
such teachings as these are well-learned by him, mastered by word, examined by mind, and well-penetrated by view.
Just as a head-anointed kṣatriya king who is wealthy, of great riches, and of great possessions, with his treasuries and storehouses full;
he dwells with energy aroused for the abandoning of unwholesome states and the attainment of wholesome states, steadfast, firm in effort, not casting off the burden regarding wholesome states—
just as a head-anointed kṣatriya king is endowed with power.
He is wise, endowed with the wisdom that discerns arising and passing away— noble, penetrative, and leading to the complete destruction of suffering—
just as a consecrated kshatriya king is endowed with a skilled counselor.
These four qualities bring his liberation to full maturity.
Thus, endowed with this fifth quality of liberation, in whatever direction he dwells, he dwells with a liberated mind.
For what reason?
Because it is thus, monks, for those whose minds are liberated.”
The Fourth.
Aṅguttara Nikāya 5.135 14.
Rājavagga (The Chapter on Kings)
The Discourse on the First Aspiration (Paṭhamapatthanāsutta): "Bhikkhus,
endowed with five factors, the eldest son of a consecrated Khattiya king aspires for the kingdom."
By which five?
Here, monks, the eldest son of a consecrated Khattiya king is well-born on both sides,
from his mother and from his father, of pure descent, unblemished and irreproachable by birth as far back as the seventh generation of ancestors.
He is handsome, beautiful, pleasing, endowed with the highest excellence of complexion;
he is dear and agreeable to his mother and father;
he is dear and agreeable to the people of the towns and the countryside.
He is trained and proficient in those skills required of anointed Kṣatriya kings—whether in elephant-riding, horsemanship, charioteering, archery, or swordsmanship.
He thinks to himself:
“I am well-born on both sides, from mother and father, of pure descent, unblemished and irreproachable by birth as far back as the seventh generation of ancestors.”
Why should I not aspire for kingship?
For I am handsome, beautiful, pleasing, and endowed with the highest excellence of complexion.
Why should I not aspire for kingship?
"I am dear and pleasing to my mother and father;
why should I not aspire for the kingdom?
I am dear and pleasing to the people of the towns and the countryside."
"Why should I not aspire for kingship?
For I am trained and proficient in those very skills of the anointed Khattiya kings—whether in elephants, horses, chariots, archery, or swordsmanship.
Why should I not aspire for kingship?"
“Monks, when the eldest son of a consecrated Khattiya king possesses these five qualities, he aspires for the kingship.
In the same way, monks, when a bhikkhu possesses five qualities, he aspires for the destruction of the taints. What are the five? [The text continues with the specific qualities.]”
In this case, monks, a bhikkhu is endowed with faith; he has faith in the enlightenment of the Tathāgata:

"Thus indeed is that Blessed One: an arahant, perfectly enlightened, perfect in knowledge and conduct, sublime, knower of the worlds, unsurpassed leader of persons to be tamed, teacher of gods and humans, the Buddha, the Blessed One.
He is free from illness and affliction, possessing a digestive system that is well-balanced—neither too cold nor too hot, but moderate and capable of bearing the strain of striving.
He is not fraudulent and not deceitful; he reveals himself as he really is to the Teacher or to wise companions in the holy life.

He dwells with energy aroused for the abandoning of unwholesome states and for the acquisition of wholesome states; he is steadfast, firm in his exertion, and does not lay down the burden regarding wholesome states.
He is wise, endowed with the wisdom that discerns arising and passing away—noble, penetrative, and leading to the complete destruction of suffering.
It occurs to him:
"I am endowed with faith; I have faith in the enlightenment of the Tathāgata:
'Thus indeed is that Blessed One—worthy, perfectly enlightened... the Teacher of gods and humans, the Buddha, the Blessed One.'"
Why should I not aspire to the destruction of the taints?
I am free from illness and affliction, endowed with a digestive system that is well-balanced—neither too cold nor too hot, but moderate and capable of enduring exertion.
Why should I not aspire to the destruction of the taints?
I am indeed free from deceit and guile, revealing myself as I truly am to the Teacher or to wise companions in the holy life.
Why should I not aspire for the destruction of the taints?

I dwell with energy aroused for the abandoning of unwholesome states and for the acquisition of wholesome states; I am steadfast, firm in my exertion, and do not lay down the burden regarding wholesome states.
"Why should I not aspire to the destruction of the taints?
For I am wise, endowed with the wisdom that discerns arising and passing away, which is noble, penetrative, and leads to the complete destruction of suffering.
Why should I not aspire to the destruction of the taints?"
“Bhikkhus, a bhikkhu endowed with these five qualities aspires for the destruction of the taints.
The fifth. *Aṅguttara Nikāya* 5.136.

14. Rājavagga The Second Discourse on Aspiration (Dutiyapatthanāsutta) “Monks, there are these four noble aspirations. What four? ‘May I be rich, with great wealth and property! This is the first noble aspiration. ‘May I be well-born, born into a high family! This is the second noble aspiration. ‘May I be handsome, beautiful, and pleasing to look upon! This is the third noble aspiration. ‘May I be long-lived, living for a hundred years! This is the fourth noble aspiration. These, monks, are the four noble aspirations. But, monks, there is one noble aspiration that surpasses these four noble aspirations. What is that one noble aspiration? It is this: ‘May I live with a mind free from enmity, free from ill will, free from affliction, compassionate, and kind toward all living beings. This, monks, is the one noble aspiration that surpasses those four noble aspirations.”
“Bhikkhus, when the eldest son of a head-anointed khattiya king possesses five qualities, he aspires for the vice-regency.
What are the five?
Here, bhikkhus, the eldest son of a head-anointed khattiya king is well-born on both sides.”
He is of pure descent on both his mother’s and father’s side, unblemished and irreproachable in regard to birth for seven generations back;
he is handsome, pleasing, attractive, endowed with the highest excellence of complexion;
he is dear and beloved by his parents.
He is dear and pleasing to the army;
he is wise, learned, and intelligent, capable of reflecting upon matters past, future, and present.
It occurs to him thus:
‘I am well-born on both sides, from mother and father, of pure descent, with unblemished lineage back through seven generations, unassailable and beyond reproach regarding my birth.
Why should I not aspire to the position of viceroy?
I am handsome, pleasing, attractive, endowed with the highest excellence of complexion.’
Why should I not aspire for the position of viceroy?
For I am dear and pleasing to my mother and father;
why should I not aspire for the position of viceroy?
I am dear and pleasing to the army.
Why should I not aspire to the position of viceroy?
I am wise, competent, and intelligent, capable of deliberating upon matters of the past, future, and present.
"Why should I not aspire for the vice-regency?
Monks, it is when he possesses these five qualities that the eldest son of a consecrated Khattiya king aspires for the vice-regency.
In the same way, monks, when a bhikkhu possesses five qualities, he aspires for the destruction of the taints.
By which five?
Here, monks, a monk is virtuous ... [as above] ... he trains himself in the rules of training he has undertaken;
he is learned ... [as above] ... he has well penetrated the view.
His mind is well-established in the four foundations of mindfulness;
he dwells with energy aroused for the abandoning of unwholesome states and for the acquisition of wholesome states, steadfast, firm in effort, not relinquishing the burden regarding wholesome states;
he is wise, endowed with the wisdom that discerns arising and passing away, which is noble, penetrative, and leads to the complete destruction of suffering.
It occurs to him:

"I am indeed virtuous; I dwell restrained by the restraint of the Pātimokkha, perfected in conduct and resort, seeing danger in even the slightest faults, and having undertaken them, I train myself in the rules of training.
Why should I not aspire to the destruction of the taints?"
I am one who has heard much, who retains what he has heard, and who has accumulated what he has heard; those teachings that are good in the beginning, good in the middle, and good in the end,
which proclaim the holy life in its meaning and its phrasing,
entirely complete and pure— such teachings have been heard much by me, retained, mastered verbally, and examined with the mind.
View has been well-penetrated.
Why should I not aspire for the destruction of the taints?
For my mind is well-established in the four foundations of mindfulness.
Why should I not aspire to the destruction of the taints?

For I dwell with energy aroused for the abandoning of unwholesome states and the acquisition of wholesome states; I am steadfast, firm in effort, and have not laid down the burden regarding wholesome states.
Why should I not aspire to the destruction of the taints?
“I am wise; I am endowed with the wisdom that discerns arising and passing away—noble, penetrative, and leading rightly to the destruction of suffering.
Why should I not aspire to the destruction of the taints?
“Monks, it is by being endowed with these five qualities that a monk aspires to the destruction of the taints.”
The Sixth. Aṅguttara Nikāya 5.137 14.
Rājavagga (The Chapter on Kings)
Appaṁsupatisutta: “Bhikkhus,
these five sleep little by night and keep much awake.”
Which five?
A woman, monks, who desires a man sleeps little by night and stays awake much.
A man, monks, who desires a woman sleeps little by night and stays awake much.
“Bhikkhus, a thief who intends to steal sleeps little by night and keeps much wakefulness.
A king occupied with royal duties sleeps little by night and keeps much wakefulness.
A bhikkhu who intends to achieve disengagement sleeps little by night and keeps much wakefulness.”
“Monks, these five sleep little at night and stay awake much.
The seventh.
Aṅguttara Nikāya 5.138

14. Rājavagga: Bhattādakasutta (AN 5.138, PTS AN iii 156) “Monks, there are these four kinds of persons found existing in the world. What four? The person who eats his food like a glutton; the person who eats his food with mindfulness; the person who eats his food with reflection; and the person who eats his food as one who has conquered hunger. And how, monks, is one a person who eats his food like a glutton? Here, monks, someone eats his food for the sake of amusement, for the sake of intoxication, for the sake of smartening, for the sake of beautification, and not for the sake of sustaining the body, for the sake of ending discomfort, and for assisting the practice of the holy life; thinking, ‘Thus, my old feelings will be stilled and no new feelings will arise, and I shall be healthy, blameless, and dwell at ease. This, monks, is called a person who eats his food like a glutton. And how, monks, is one a person who eats his food with mindfulness? Here, monks, someone eats his food reflecting on its origin and its passing away, and he does not contemplate the gratification, the danger, and the escape in regard to it. This, monks, is called a person who eats his food with mindfulness. And how, monks, is one a person who eats his food with reflection? Here, monks, someone eats his food reflecting on its origin and its passing away, and he contemplates the gratification, the danger, and the escape in regard to it. This, monks, is called a person who eats his food with reflection. And how, monks, is one a person who eats his food as one who has conquered hunger? Here, monks, someone eats his food simply for the purpose of sustaining this body, for keeping it going, for ending discomfort, and for assisting the practice of the holy life; thinking, ‘Thus, I shall terminate the old feeling and not give rise to a new feeling, and I shall be healthy, blameless, and dwell at ease. This, monks, is called a person who eats his food as one who has conquered hunger. These, monks, are the four kinds of persons found existing in the world.”
“Bhikkhus, possessing five factors, a king’s elephant is a consumer of food, occupies space, excretes dung, receives its ration of fodder, and is reckoned simply as ‘a king’s elephant.
What are the five?
Here, bhikkhus, a king’s elephant is intolerant of forms, intolerant of sounds, intolerant of odors, intolerant of tastes, and intolerant of tactile objects.”
“Monks, possessed of these five factors, a king’s elephant is a consumer of food, an occupier of space, a digger of dung, and a drawer of lots; it is reckoned simply as ‘a king’s elephant.
In the same way, monks, possessed of five qualities, a monk is a consumer of food, an occupier of space, a defiler of beds and chairs, and a drawer of lots; he is reckoned simply as ‘a monk.
What are the five? ”
“Here, monks, a bhikkhu is intolerant of forms, intolerant of sounds, intolerant of odors, intolerant of tastes, and intolerant of tactile objects.

Possessing these five qualities, monks, a bhikkhu is a consumer of food, one who occupies space, a defiler of beds and seats, and a voter; he is reckoned only as a bhikkhu. Thus was the eighth [discourse].

Aṅguttara Nikāya 5.139 14. Rājavagga Akṣamasutta (The Discourse on Intolerance) “Monks, there are these five qualities of a king that lead to his non-decline. What five? Here, monks, a king is patient; he does not strike one who strikes him, nor insult one who insults him. This is the first quality of a king that leads to his non-decline. Furthermore, monks, a king is generous; he gives freely and opens his hands to all.

He is pure-handed, delighting in charity and distribution. This is the second quality of a king that leads to his non-decline. Furthermore, monks, a king is righteous; he acts with justice and not unjustly. He treats all beings with impartiality and without partiality. This is the third quality of a king that leads to his non-decline. Furthermore, monks, a king is wise; he possesses wisdom regarding rise and fall that is noble, penetrative, and leads to the complete destruction of suffering. This is the fourth quality of a king that leads to his non-decline. Furthermore, monks, a king has a retinue that is disciplined, well-trained, experienced, and skilled in both the arts and the duties. This is the fifth quality of a king that leads to his non-decline. These, monks, are the five qualities of a king that lead to his non-decline. Just as, monks, these five qualities of a king lead to his non-decline, so too, monks, there are these five qualities of a bhikkhu that lead to his non-decline. What five? Here, monks, a bhikkhu is patient; he does not strike one who strikes him, nor insult one who insults him. This is the first quality of a bhikkhu that leads to his non-decline. Furthermore, monks, a bhikkhu is generous; he gives freely and opens his hands to all. He is pure-handed, delighting in charity and distribution. This is the second quality of a bhikkhu that leads to his non-decline. Furthermore, monks, a bhikkhu is righteous; he acts with justice and not unjustly. He treats all beings with impartiality and without partiality. This is the third quality of a bhikkhu that leads to his non-decline. Furthermore, monks, a bhikkhu is wise; he possesses wisdom regarding rise and fall that is noble, penetrative, and leads to the complete destruction of suffering. This is the fourth quality of a bhikkhu that leads to his non-decline. Furthermore, monks, a bhikkhu has a retinue that is disciplined, well-trained, experienced, and skilled in both the arts and the duties. This is the fifth quality of a bhikkhu that leads to his non-decline. These, monks, are the five qualities of a bhikkhu that lead to his non-decline.”

“Bhikkhus, possessing five factors, a king’s elephant is not worthy of a king, not a royal possession, and does not even count as a limb of the king. What are these five? [The text continues with the list of factors.]”
"Here, monks, a king’s elephant is intolerant of forms, intolerant of sounds, intolerant of odors, intolerant of tastes, and intolerant of tactile objects.
And how, monks, is a king’s elephant intolerant of forms?
Here, monks, when a king’s elephant has entered the fray and sees a troop of elephants, or sees a troop of horses, or a troop of chariots..."
Or seeing a chariot-division, or seeing an infantry-division, he sinks down, he desponds; he does not steady himself and is unable to enter the battle.
In this way, monks, a king’s elephant is unenduring of forms.
And how, monks, is a king’s elephant unenduring of sounds?
In this case, monks, when a king’s elephant has entered the battle, upon hearing the sound of elephants,
or the sound of horses, or the sound of chariots, or the sound of infantry, or the resounding noise of kettledrums,
tabors, conchs, and drums, it becomes despondent and dispirited; it does not steady itself and is unable to enter the fray.
In this way, monks, the king’s elephant is intolerant of sounds.
And how, monks, is the king’s elephant intolerant of smells?
Here, monks, when the king’s elephant has entered the battle, there are those royal elephants of noble breed who are experienced in combat.
Having smelled the smell of urine and excrement, he sinks down, he desponds; he does not steady himself and is unable to enter the battle.
In this way, monks, a king’s elephant is intolerant of smells.
And how, monks, is a king’s elephant intolerant of tastes?
In this case, monks, when a king’s elephant has entered battle, if it is deprived of one supply of grass and water,
or deprived of two, three, four, or five supplies of grass and water, it becomes despondent and dispirited;
it does not steady itself and is unable to engage in the battle.
In this way, monks, a king’s elephant is intolerant of tastes.
And how, monks, is a king’s elephant intolerant of tactile objects?
Here, monks, when a king’s elephant has entered battle, it is pierced by one arrow or two or three arrows from the force of a reed-shaft.
Or, pierced by four or five swift arrows, he sinks down, falters, does not steady himself,
and is unable to enter the battle.
In this way, monks, a king’s elephant is unenduring of tactile sensations.
“Monks, possessed of these five factors, a king’s elephant is not worthy of a king, not a royal possession, and does not even count as a limb of the king.

In the same way, monks, a monk possessed of five factors is not worthy of offerings, not worthy of hospitality, not worthy of gifts, not worthy of reverential salutation, and is not an unsurpassed field of merit for the world. What are the five? [The text continues with the list of five factors.]”
"Here, monks, a bhikkhu is intolerant of forms, intolerant of sounds, intolerant of odors, intolerant of tastes, and intolerant of tactile objects.
And how, monks, is a bhikkhu intolerant of forms?
Here, monks, having seen a form with the eye, a bhikkhu becomes infatuated with a form that provokes passion; he is unable to concentrate his mind."
In this way, monks, a monk is intolerant of forms.
And how, monks, is a monk intolerant of sounds?
Here, monks, having heard a sound with the ear, a monk becomes infatuated with a sound that incites passion; he is unable to concentrate his mind.
In this way, monks, a monk is intolerant of sounds.
And how, monks, is a monk intolerant of odors?
Here, monks, having smelled an odor with the nose, a monk becomes infatuated with an odor that provokes passion; he is unable to concentrate his mind.
In this way, monks, a monk is intolerant of odors.
And how, monks, is a monk intolerant of tastes?
Here, monks, having tasted a taste with the tongue, a monk becomes infatuated with a taste that causes passion; he is unable to concentrate his mind.
In this way, monks, a monk is intolerant of tastes.
And how, monks, is a monk intolerant of tangibles?
Here, monks, having touched a tangible with the body, a monk becomes infatuated with a tantalizing tangible and is unable to concentrate his mind.
"In this way, monks, a monk is intolerant of tactile sensations.

Endowed with these five qualities, monks, a monk is not worthy of offerings, not worthy of hospitality, not worthy of gifts, not worthy of reverential salutation, and is not an unsurpassed field of merit for the world.
"Endowed with five factors, monks, a king’s elephant is worthy of the king, is a royal possession, and is indeed reckoned as a limb of the king."
Which five?
Here, monks, a king’s elephant is patient with forms, patient with sounds, patient with odors, patient with tastes, and patient with tactile objects.
And how, monks, is a king’s elephant patient with forms?

In this case, monks, when a king’s elephant has entered the battle, upon seeing a body of infantry, a body of cavalry, a body of chariots, or a body of foot soldiers, it does not falter, it does not despair; it steadies itself and is able to engage in the battle.
In this way, monks, a king’s elephant is patient with forms.
And how, monks, is a king’s elephant patient with sounds? Here, monks,
when a king’s elephant has entered the fray of battle, it hears the sound of elephants,
or the sound of horses, or the sound of chariots, or the sound of infantry, or the clamor of drums, kettledrums, conchs, and cymbals.
Having heard it, he does not become despondent, nor does he become discouraged; he steadies himself and is able to enter the battle.
In this way, monks, a king’s elephant is patient with sounds.
And how, monks, is a king’s elephant patient with odors?

In this case, monks, when a king’s elephant has entered the fray of battle, it does not sink or despond upon smelling the scent of the urine and dung of those noble royal elephants who are experienced in combat; it steadies itself and is able to enter the battle.
In this way, monks, a king’s elephant is tolerant of odors.
And how, monks, is a king’s elephant patient with tastes? Here, monks,
when a king’s elephant has entered battle, even if it is deprived of one ration of grass and water,
or deprived of two, three, four, or five rations of grass and water, it does not become despondent, nor does it lose heart.
He steadies himself and is able to enter the battle.
In this way, monks, a king’s elephant is patient with tastes.
And how, monks, is a king’s elephant patient with tactile sensations?
In this case, monks, when a king’s elephant has entered battle, even if it is pierced by one arrow-shot, or by two, three, four,
or five arrow-shots, it does not falter, it does not despair; it steadies itself and is able to engage in the battle.
"Thus, monks, a king’s elephant is patient with tactile sensations.
Endowed with these five factors, monks, a king’s elephant is worthy of a king, a royal possession, and is truly reckoned as a limb of the king.

In the same way, monks, a bhikkhu endowed with five qualities is worthy of offerings, worthy of hospitality, worthy of gifts, worthy of reverential salutation, and is an unsurpassed field of merit for the world."
Which five?
Here, monks, a monk is patient with forms, patient with sounds, patient with odors, patient with tastes, and patient with tactile objects.
And how, monks, is a monk patient with forms?
"Here, monks, having seen a form with the eye, a monk is not infatuated by a form that causes passion; he is able to concentrate his mind.
In this way, monks, a monk is patient toward forms.
And how, monks, is a monk patient toward sounds?"
"Here, bhikkhus, having heard a sound with the ear, a bhikkhu is not infatuated by a sound that might cause passion; he is able to concentrate his mind.
In this way, bhikkhus, a bhikkhu is patient with sounds.
And how, bhikkhus, is a bhikkhu patient with odors?"
"Here, monks, having smelled an odor with the nose, a monk does not become infatuated with an odor that causes passion; he is able to concentrate his mind.
In this way, monks, a monk is patient with odors.
And how, monks, is a monk patient with tastes?"
"Here, monks, having tasted a flavor with the tongue, a monk does not become infatuated with a flavor that causes passion; he is able to concentrate his mind.
In this way, monks, a monk is patient with flavors.
And how, monks, is a monk patient with tangibles?"
“Here, bhikkhus, having touched a tangible object with the body, a bhikkhu does not become infatuated with a tangible object that causes passion; he is able to concentrate his mind.
In this way, bhikkhus, a bhikkhu is patient with tangible objects.
Possessing these five qualities, bhikkhus, a bhikkhu is worthy of gifts, worthy of hospitality, worthy of offerings, worthy of reverential salutation, an unsurpassed field of merit for the world.”

Rājavagga (The Chapter on Kings)
Sotasutta (AN 5.140, PTS AN iii 161):

“Bhikkhus, possessed of five factors, a king’s elephant is worthy of a king, an asset to a king, and is reckoned as a very limb of the king. What five? [The text continues with the description of these five qualities.]”
Which five?
Here, monks, a king’s elephant is a listener, a striker, a protector, a patient, and a goer.
And how, monks, is a king’s elephant a listener?
In this case, monks, when the elephant tamer gives a command to the king’s elephant—
whether it be something previously performed or not previously performed—
the elephant attends to it with firmness, attends to it with the mind, applies his whole heart to it, and listens with an attentive ear.
"In this way, monks, a king’s elephant is a listener.
And how, monks, is a king’s elephant a slayer?
Here, monks, when a king’s elephant has entered the fray, it slays elephants and elephant-riders, it slays horses and horse-riders, it slays chariots and chariot-warriors, and it slays infantry."
In this way, monks, a king’s elephant is a slayer.
And how, monks, is a king’s elephant a protector?
Here, monks, when a king’s elephant has entered the fray, it protects its forequarters and it protects its hindquarters.

He protects his body; he protects his forefeet, he protects his hindfeet, he protects his head, he protects his ears, he protects his tusks, he protects his trunk, he protects his tail, and he protects the rider.
In this way, monks, a king’s elephant is well-protected.
And how, monks, is a king’s elephant patient?

Here, monks, when the king’s elephant has entered the battle, it is patient with blows from spears, blows from swords, blows from javelins, blows from axes, and with the sounds of the clamor and din of drums, kettledrums, conchs, and cymbals.
It is in this way, monks, that a king’s elephant is patient.
And how, monks, does a king’s elephant go? Here, monks, the king’s elephant goes to whatever direction the elephant trainer sends him—
whether it be a place he has gone before or one he has not gone before.
He goes quickly.
In this way, monks, a king’s elephant is one who goes.
Possessed of these five factors, monks, a king’s elephant is worthy of a king, an asset to a king, and is reckoned as a very limb of the king.

"In the same way, monks, a monk endowed with five qualities is worthy of gifts, worthy of hospitality, worthy of offerings, worthy of reverential salutation, and is an unsurpassed field of merit for the world.
With which five?
Here, monks, a monk is a listener, a slayer, a protector, a patient one, and a goer."
And how, bhikkhus, is a bhikkhu a listener?

Here, bhikkhus, when the Dhamma and Vinaya proclaimed by the Tathāgata is being taught, a bhikkhu listens to the Dhamma with attentive ears, applying his whole mind, attending to it with mindfulness, and taking it to heart.
It is in this way, bhikkhus, that a bhikkhu is a listener.
And how, monks, is a monk a slayer?
Here, monks, a monk does not tolerate a thought of sensual desire that has arisen;

he abandons it, dispels it, destroys it, brings it to an end, and makes it non-existent. He does not tolerate a thought of ill will that has arisen... [and so on] ...a thought of cruelty that has arisen.
...pe... whatever evil, unwholesome states arise, he does not tolerate them; he abandons them, dispels them, destroys them, eliminates them, and brings them to non-existence.
In this way, monks, a monk is a destroyer.
And how, monks, is a monk a protector?
Here, monks, a bhikkhu, having seen a form with the eye, does not grasp at its signs nor grasp at its secondary characteristics.
Since, if he were to dwell with this faculty unrestrained, covetousness, dejection, and evil unwholesome states might flow in upon him, he practices for its restraint;
he guards the eye-faculty; he attains mastery over the eye-faculty.
Having heard a sound with the ear...
having smelled an odor with the nose...
having tasted a flavor with the tongue...
Having touched a tangible object with the body...
having cognized a mental phenomenon with the mind, one does not grasp at its signs nor grasp at its secondary characteristics.
If one dwells with this faculty of the mind unrestrained, covetousness and dejection—evil, unwholesome states—might arise.
If states of covetousness or unwholesome mental qualities were to flow into him, he practices for their restraint; he guards the faculty of mind; he attains restraint over the faculty of mind.
In this way, monks, a monk is one who guards.
And how, monks, is a monk patient?
In this case, monks, a monk is patient with cold, heat, hunger, thirst, and the touch of gadflies, mosquitoes, wind, sun, and creeping things;
he is one who is accustomed to enduring arisen bodily feelings that are painful,
racking, sharp, piercing, bitter, disagreeable, unpleasant, and life-threatening.
In this way, monks, a monk is one who endures.
And how, monks, is a monk one who goes?
Here, monks, a monk has not previously gone to that direction throughout this long course of time, namely, the stilling of all formations.
The relinquishing of all acquisitions, the destruction of craving, dispassion, cessation, Nibbāna—he goes swiftly to that.
In this way, monks, a monk is one who goes.
Endowed with these five qualities, monks, a monk is worthy of gifts, worthy of hospitality, worthy of offerings, worthy of reverential salutation, an unsurpassed field of merit for the world.”

The Discourse on Disparagement (Avajānātisutta): “Bhikkhus,
these five persons are found existing in the world.”
Which five? He despises after giving; he despises through living together; he is a ready listener; he is fickle; he is dull and deluded.
And how, monks, does a person despise after giving?
In this case, monks, a person gives to another person robes, almsfood, lodgings, and medicinal requisites for the sick.
It occurs to him:
“I am giving.”
‘This one accepts it.
Having given to him, he treats him with contempt.
It is in this way, monks, that a person treats with contempt after having given.
And how, monks, does a person despise another through living together?
Here, monks, a person lives together with another for two or three years;
it is by that living together that he comes to despise him.
"In this way, monks, a person despises by means of living together.
And how, monks, is a person one who is open-mouthed for receiving [criticism]?
Here, monks, when someone’s praise or blame is being spoken, that person quickly becomes convinced of it."
In this way, monks, a person is one whose mouth is open for receiving.
And how, monks, is a person fickle?
Here, monks, a certain person has limited faith, limited devotion, limited affection, and limited confidence.
In this way, monks, a person is fickle.
And how, monks, is a person dull and deluded?

Here, monks, a certain person does not know wholesome and unwholesome states; he does not know blameworthy and blameless states; he does not know inferior and superior states; he does not know dark and bright states that contrast with one another.
"In this way, monks, a person is dull and deluded.
These, monks, are the five kinds of persons found existing in the world. Thus was the first [discourse].

Tikaṇḍakīvagga Ārabhati-sutta (The Discourse on Undertaking) “Monks, there are these three kinds of persons found existing in the world. What three? The person who undertakes what is harmful and does not abandon it; the person who undertakes what is harmful and abandons it; and the person who neither undertakes what is harmful nor abandons it. These, monks, are the three kinds of persons found existing in the world.”
“Bhikkhus, these five persons are found existing in the world. Which five? [The text continues with the description of each.]”
In this case, monks, a certain person exerts himself and yet feels remorse,
and he does not understand, as it really is, that liberation of mind and liberation by wisdom wherein those arisen evil unwholesome states cease without remainder.
But in this case, monks, a certain person exerts himself and does not feel remorse.
And he does not understand, as it really is, that liberation of mind and liberation by wisdom wherein those arisen evil unwholesome states cease without remainder.
Furthermore, monks, here a certain person does not undertake [an action], yet he feels remorse;
and he does not understand, as it really is, that liberation of mind and liberation by wisdom wherein those arisen evil unwholesome states cease without remainder.
"Furthermore, monks, here a certain person does not initiate [unwholesome actions] and does not feel remorse;
yet he does not understand, as it really is, that liberation of mind and liberation by wisdom wherein those arisen evil unwholesome states cease without remainder.
Furthermore, monks, here a certain person does not initiate [unwholesome actions] and does not feel remorse..."
And he understands, as it really is, that liberation of mind and liberation by wisdom wherein those arisen evil unwholesome states cease without remainder.
In this regard, monks, as for the person who both exerts himself and becomes remorseful,
yet does not understand, as it really is, that liberation of mind and liberation by wisdom wherein those arisen evil unwholesome states cease without remainder—
He should be addressed thus:

“The taints born of agitation are present in the venerable one, and the taints born of remorse increase. It would be well if the venerable one, having abandoned the taints born of agitation and dispelled the taints born of remorse, were to develop the mind and wisdom.
In this way, the venerable one will become equal to that fifth person.”
In this regard, monks, that person who commits an offense but does not feel remorse,
and who does not understand as it really is that liberation of mind and liberation by wisdom wherein those arisen evil unwholesome states cease without remainder—
of him it should be said:

‘The taints born of exertion are present in the venerable one, but the taints born of remorse do not increase. It would be well if the venerable one, having abandoned the taints born of exertion, were to develop the mind and wisdom;
in this way, the venerable one will become equal to that fifth person.
In this regard, monks, as for the person who does not exert himself and becomes remorseful:
And if he does not understand as it really is that liberation of mind and liberation by wisdom wherein those arisen evil unwholesome states cease without remainder, he should be told this:

"In the venerable one, the taints born of exertion do not exist, but the taints born of remorse increase. It would be well if the venerable one, having dispelled the taints born of remorse, were to develop the mind and wisdom."
"In this way, venerable sir, you will become equal to that fifth person.
In this regard, monks, as for that person who does not initiate [evil] and does not feel remorse,
yet does not understand, as it really is, that liberation of mind and liberation by wisdom wherein those arisen evil unwholesome states cease without remainder—
He should be told this:
“The taints born of exertion do not exist in the venerable one, and the taints born of remorse do not increase. It would be well indeed if the venerable one were to develop both the mind and wisdom;
in this way, the venerable one will become equal to that fifth type of person.”
“Thus, monks, these four persons, when exhorted and instructed in this way by this fifth person, gradually reach the destruction of the taints.
The second.

15. Tikaṇḍakī-vagga: The Discourse to Sārandada (Sārandadasutta) At one time, the Blessed One was dwelling at Rājagaha in the Bamboo Grove, the Squirrels’ Sanctuary. Then the Licchavi Sārandada approached the Blessed One; having approached, he paid homage to the Blessed One and sat down to one side. As he was sitting there, the Licchavi Sārandada said to the Blessed One: “Venerable sir, what is the cause, what is the reason, why some beings here, with the breakup of the body, after death, are reborn in a state of misery, a bad destination, a lower realm, or in hell? “Sārandada, it is because they have destroyed life, taken what was not given, committed sexual misconduct, spoken falsehood, and indulged in liquor, wine, and intoxicants that cause heedlessness, that some beings here, with the breakup of the body, after death, are reborn in a state of misery, a bad destination, a lower realm, or in hell. “What is the cause, venerable sir, what is the reason, why some beings here, with the breakup of the body, after death, are reborn in a good destination, a heavenly world? “Sārandada, it is because they have abstained from destroying life, abstained from taking what was not given, abstained from sexual misconduct, abstained from false speech, and abstained from liquor, wine, and intoxicants that cause heedlessness, that some beings here, with the breakup of the body, after death, are reborn in a good destination, a heavenly world. When this was said, the Licchavi Sārandada said to the Blessed One: “Magnificent, venerable sir! Magnificent, venerable sir! Just as one might set upright what had been overturned, or reveal what was hidden, or show the way to one who was lost, or bring an oil lamp into the darkness so that those with eyes might see forms, even so has the Dhamma been made clear by the Blessed One in many ways. I go for refuge to the Blessed One, to the Dhamma, and to the Saṅgha of bhikkhus. May the Blessed One accept me as a lay follower who has gone for refuge from this day forth for as long as life shall last. Thus have I heard. On one occasion the Blessed One was dwelling at Vesālī in the Great Wood in the Gabled Hall.
Then, in the morning, the Blessed One dressed, took his bowl and robe, and entered Vesālī for alms.
Now at that time, about five hundred Licchavis were seated together and assembled at the Sārandada Shrine when this discussion arose among them:
“The appearance of five treasures is rare in the world. Which five?
The appearance of the elephant-treasure is rare in the world; the appearance of the horse-treasure is rare in the world.”
The appearance of the jewel-treasure is rare in the world; the appearance of the woman-treasure is rare in the world;
the appearance of the householder-treasure is rare in the world.
The appearance of these five treasures is rare in the world.”
Then those Licchavis stationed a man on the road, saying:
"When you, good man, see the Blessed One approaching, then inform us.
That man saw the Blessed One coming from afar.
Having seen him, he approached those Licchavis; having approached them, he said this to the Licchavis:
"Venerable sirs, here comes the Blessed One, the Worthy One, the Perfectly Self-Awakened One.
Now is the time for you to do as you deem fit."
Then those Licchavis approached the Blessed One; having approached and paid homage to the Blessed One, they stood to one side. Standing to one side, those Licchavis said this to the Blessed One:
"It would be well, Bhante, if the Blessed One would approach the Sārandada Shrine out of compassion.
The Blessed One consented by remaining silent.
Then the Blessed One approached the Sārandada Shrine; having approached, he sat down on the prepared seat. Having sat down, the Blessed One said this to those Licchavis:
"Licchavis, for what discussion are you gathered here now, and what was the conversation of yours that remained unfinished?
"Venerable sir, while we were sitting together in assembly, this conversation arose among us: [text continues]"
“The appearance of five treasures is rare in the world. Which five?
The appearance of the elephant-treasure is rare in the world; the appearance of the horse-treasure is rare in the world.”
"The appearance of the jewel-treasure is rare in the world; the appearance of the woman-treasure is rare in the world;
the appearance of the householder-treasure is rare in the world.
The appearance of these five treasures is rare in the world."
“Indeed, friends Licchavis, this discussion arose among you who are intent on sensual pleasures, concerning nothing but sensual pleasures.
Friends Licchavis, the appearance of five treasures in the world is rare. Which five?
The manifestation of a Tathāgata, an Arahant, a Perfectly Enlightened One, is rare in the world;
a person who teaches the Dhamma and Vinaya proclaimed by a Tathāgata is rare in the world;
a person who understands the Dhamma and Vinaya taught and proclaimed by a Tathāgata is rare in the world.
"A person who understands the Dhamma and Vinaya proclaimed by the Tathāgata and taught, one who practices in accordance with the Dhamma, is rare in the world;
a person who is grateful and appreciative is rare in the world.
Indeed, Licchavis, the appearance of these five jewels is rare in the world."

On one occasion the Blessed One was dwelling at Sāketa in the Tikaṇḍakī Grove.
There the Blessed One addressed the bhikkhus: "Bhikkhus.
"Venerable sir," those bhikkhus replied to the Blessed One.
The Blessed One said this:
“It is good, monks, that a monk should dwell from time to time perceiving the repulsive in the non-repulsive.
It is good, monks, that a monk should dwell from time to time perceiving the non-repulsive in the repulsive.”
"It is good, monks, for a bhikkhu from time to time to dwell perceiving the repulsive in both the repulsive and the non-repulsive.
It is good, monks, for a bhikkhu from time to time to dwell perceiving the non-repulsive in both the repulsive and the non-repulsive.
