And for what purpose, monks, should a monk dwell perceiving the unrepulsive in the repulsive?
“May no aversion arise in me toward things that provoke aversion”—
it is for this purpose, monks, that a monk should dwell perceiving the unrepulsive in the repulsive.
And for what purpose, monks, should a monk dwell perceiving the repulsive in both the non-repulsive and the repulsive?
“May no lust arise in me toward things that provoke lust;
may no hatred arise in me toward things that provoke hatred”—for this purpose, monks, should a monk dwell perceiving the repulsive in both the non-repulsive and the repulsive.
And for what purpose, monks, should a monk dwell perceiving the non-repulsive in both the repulsive and the non-repulsive?
“May no hatred arise in me toward things that provoke hatred;
may no lust arise in me toward things that provoke lust”—for this purpose, monks, should a monk dwell perceiving the non-repulsive in both the repulsive and the non-repulsive.
And for what purpose, monks, should a monk, avoiding both the repulsive and the non-repulsive, dwell in equanimity? [It is] so that:
"Mindful and clearly comprehending, may no lust whatsoever arise in me anywhere toward things that provoke lust;
may no hatred whatsoever arise in me anywhere toward things that provoke hatred; may no delusion whatsoever arise in me anywhere..."
‘Something has arisen among delusive phenomena:
delusion has arisen’—it is for this purpose, monks, that a monk, having avoided both the repulsive and the non-repulsive, should dwell equanimous, mindful, and clearly comprehending.
This is the fourth [discourse].

Aṅguttara Nikāya 5.145 15. Tikaṇḍakīvagga Niraya Sutta (The Hell) “Monks, there are these five kinds of persons found existing in the world. What five? The person who goes to hell; the person who goes to heaven; the person who goes to the animal realm; the person who stands still; and the person who transcends. And how, monks, is one a person who goes to hell? Here, monks, someone is possessed of bad conduct of body, speech, and mind. Having undertaken the training precepts, he does not train in them. He is one who destroys life, takes what is not given, and engages in sexual misconduct; he speaks falsehood, speaks divisively, speaks harshly, and indulges in idle chatter; he is full of covetousness, possesses a mind of ill will, and holds wrong view. With the breakup of the body, after death, he is reborn in a state of misery, in a bad destination, in the nether world, in hell. This, monks, is called a person who goes to hell. And how, monks, is one a person who goes to heaven? Here, monks, someone is possessed of good conduct of body, speech, and mind. Having undertaken the training precepts, he trains in them. He refrains from destroying life, taking what is not given, and engaging in sexual misconduct; he refrains from false speech, divisive speech, harsh speech, and idle chatter; he is free from covetousness, possesses a mind of good will, and holds right view. With the breakup of the body, after death, he is reborn in a good destination, in a heavenly world. This, monks, is called a person who goes to heaven. And how, monks, is one a person who goes to the animal realm? Here, monks, someone is possessed of bad conduct of body, speech, and mind... [as above] ...he holds wrong view. With the breakup of the body, after death, he is reborn in the animal realm. This, monks, is called a person who goes to the animal realm. And how, monks, is one a person who stands still? Here, monks, someone is possessed of good conduct of body, speech, and mind... [as above] ...he holds right view. With the breakup of the body, after death, he is reborn among human beings. This, monks, is called a person who stands still. And how, monks, is one a person who transcends? Here, monks, someone is possessed of good conduct of body, speech, and mind... [as above] ...he holds right view. He attains to the destruction of the taints in this very life, realizing for himself with direct knowledge, attaining the liberation of mind and liberation by wisdom that are taintless, and abiding therein. This, monks, is called a person who transcends. These, monks, are the five kinds of persons found existing in the world.”
“Bhikkhus, one endowed with five qualities is deposited in hell as if carried there. With which five? [The Sutta continues:]”
"He is one who destroys life, takes what is not given, engages in sexual misconduct, speaks falsehood, and indulges in liquor, wine, and intoxicants, which are the basis for negligence.
Possessing these five qualities, monks, one is placed in hell as if carried there.
Possessing five qualities, monks, one is placed in heaven as if carried there."

“By which five? He abstains from the destruction of life; he abstains from taking what is not given; he abstains from sexual misconduct; he abstains from false speech; he abstains from fermented liquor, spirits, and intoxicants that are the basis for negligence.
Endowed with these five qualities, monks, one is placed in heaven as if carried there.”
The Fifth.
Aṅguttara Nikāya 5.146 15. Tikaṇḍakī-vagga
Mittasutta (AN 5.146, PTS AN iii 171):
“Bhikkhus, a bhikkhu who possesses five qualities should not be associated with as a friend.
Which five?
He causes work to be done; he initiates legal disputes; he is antagonistic toward the leading monks;
he dwells devoted to long journeys and unsettled wandering; and he is not capable from time to time of [giving] a discourse on the Dhamma.
To instruct, to encourage, to inspire, and to gladden.
Monks, a monk endowed with these five qualities should not be cultivated as a friend.
Monks, a monk endowed with five qualities should be cultivated as a friend.
Which five?
He does not cause work to be done; he does not initiate legal disputes; he is not antagonistic toward senior monks;
he does not dwell intent upon long journeys or unsettled wandering; and he is capable from time to time—
To instruct, to exhort, to inspire, and to gladden with a discourse on the Dhamma.
Possessing these five qualities, monks, a monk who is a friend should be cultivated.
The sixth.
Aṅguttara Nikāya 5.147 15. Tikaṇḍakīvagga Asappurisadānasutta: The Discourse on the Gift of an Unvirtuous Person "Bhikkhus, there are these five kinds of gifts of an unvirtuous person.

What five? The gift given by one who is not himself giving; the gift given by one who has not given before; the gift given by one who does not expect a reward; the gift given by one who does not believe in the result of giving; and the gift given by one who gives with a mind devoid of faith. These, bhikkhus, are the five kinds of gifts of an unvirtuous person. There are, bhikkhus, these five kinds of gifts of a virtuous person. What five? The gift given by one who is himself giving; the gift given by one who has given before; the gift given by one who expects a reward; the gift given by one who believes in the result of giving; and the gift given by one who gives with a mind full of faith. These, bhikkhus, are the five kinds of gifts of a virtuous person."
“Bhikkhus, there are these five gifts of an untrue person. What are the five? [The text continues with the list.]”
One gives without respect; one gives without honoring; one gives without using one’s own hand; one gives what has been cast away;
one gives while holding the view that there is no rebirth. These, monks, are the five gifts of an untrue person.
There are, monks, these five gifts of a true person.
“What are the five? One gives respectfully; one gives with a sense of appreciation; one gives with one’s own hand; one gives what has not been discarded;
one gives with the view that there will be a future result. These, monks, are the five gifts of a true person.”
Seventh.
Aṅguttara Nikāya 5.148 15. Tikaṇḍakīvagga
Sappurisadānasutta: “Bhikkhus,
there are these five gifts of a true person.”

What are the five? One gives a gift with faith; one gives a gift respectfully; one gives a gift at the proper time; one gives a gift with a mind of assistance; one gives a gift without harming oneself or others.
Monks, having given a gift with faith, wherever the result of that gift ripens, [one will experience its fruit].
He becomes wealthy, possessing great riches and vast enjoyments; he is handsome, beautiful, pleasing, and endowed with the highest excellence of complexion.
Furthermore, monks, having given a gift with due care, wherever the result of that gift is produced, he becomes wealthy, possessing great riches and vast enjoyments.
Even those who are his sons, daughters, slaves, servants, or laborers listen to him, lend an ear, and apply their minds to understand.
Furthermore, monks, by giving a gift at the proper time, wherever the result of that gift ripens, he becomes wealthy, possessing great riches and vast enjoyments;
and when the right time arrives, his resources become abundant.
Moreover, monks, when one gives a gift with a mind full of assistance, wherever the result of that gift ripens, one becomes wealthy, possessing great riches and great wealth;
and one’s mind inclines toward enjoying the five excellent strands of sensual pleasure.
Furthermore, monks, when one gives a gift without harming oneself or others, wherever the result of that gift ripens, one becomes wealthy, possessing great riches and great wealth.
And no harm comes to his wealth from any quarter—neither from fire, nor from water, nor from kings, nor from thieves, nor from those who are disliked, nor from heirs.
These, monks, are the five gifts of a true person.
The eighth.

Aṅguttara Nikāya 5.149 15. Tikaṇḍakīvagga First Discourse on Liberation in This Very Life “Bhikkhus, there are these five kinds of persons found existing in the world. What five? The person liberated in this very life (*diṭṭhadhamma-abhisamaya-vimutto*), the person liberated by faith (*saddhā-vimutto*), the person liberated by Dhamma (*dhamma-vimutto*), the person liberated by both ways (*ubhatobhāga-vimutto*), and the person who is a body-witness (*kāyasakkhī*).

And what, bhikkhus, is the person liberated in this very life? Here, bhikkhus, a bhikkhu possesses the view that is noble and penetrative, leading to the complete destruction of suffering. He understands as it really is: ‘This is suffering’; he understands as it really is: ‘This is the origin of suffering’; he understands as it really is: ‘This is the cessation of suffering’; he understands as it really is: ‘This is the way leading to the cessation of suffering. Through the destruction of the taints, he realizes for himself with direct knowledge, in this very life, the taintless liberation of mind and liberation by wisdom, and having attained it, dwells therein. This, bhikkhus, is called the person liberated in this very life. And what, bhikkhus, is the person liberated by faith? Here, bhikkhus, a bhikkhu possesses the view that is noble and penetrative, leading to the complete destruction of suffering. He understands as it really is: ‘This is suffering’... ‘This is the way leading to the cessation of suffering. With the destruction of the five lower fetters, he becomes one of spontaneous birth, attaining final nibbāna there without ever returning from that world. This, bhikkhus, is called the person liberated by faith. And what, bhikkhus, is the person liberated by Dhamma? Here, bhikkhus, a bhikkhu possesses the view that is noble and penetrative, leading to the complete destruction of suffering. He understands as it really is: ‘This is suffering’... ‘This is the way leading to the cessation of suffering. With the destruction of the three fetters and the weakening of lust, hatred, and delusion, he becomes a once-returner, who, after returning to this world only one more time, makes an end of suffering. This, bhikkhus, is called the person liberated by Dhamma. And what, bhikkhus, is the person liberated by both ways? Here, bhikkhus, a bhikkhu possesses the view that is noble and penetrative, leading to the complete destruction of suffering. He understands as it really is: ‘This is suffering’... ‘This is the way leading to the cessation of suffering. With the destruction of the five lower fetters, he becomes one of spontaneous birth, attaining final nibbāna there without ever returning from that world. This, bhikkhus, is called the person liberated by both ways. And what, bhikkhus, is the person who is a body-witness? Here, bhikkhus, a bhikkhu possesses the view that is noble and penetrative, leading to the complete destruction of suffering. He understands as it really is: ‘This is suffering’... ‘This is the way leading to the cessation of suffering. With the destruction of the five lower fetters, he becomes one of spontaneous birth, attaining final nibbāna there without ever returning from that world. However, he does not attain the peaceful liberation of mind, which is beyond formations, in this very life. This, bhikkhus, is called the person who is a body-witness. These, bhikkhus, are the five kinds of persons found existing in the world.”
“Bhikkhus, these five qualities lead to the decline of a bhikkhu who is temporarily liberated. What five? [The text continues with the list of five qualities.]”
Delight in work, delight in talk, delight in sleep, delight in company, and not reviewing the mind as it is liberated— these, monks,
are the five things that lead to the decline of a monk who is temporarily liberated. These, monks,
are the five things that lead to the non-decline of a monk who is temporarily liberated.
Which five?
Delight in work, delight in talk, delight in sleep, delight in company, and not reviewing the mind as it is liberated.
These, monks, are the five qualities that lead to the non-decline of a monk who is liberated by occasion.”
The Ninth.
Aṅguttara Nikāya 5.150 15. Tikaṇḍakīvagga
The Discourse on Liberation at Another Time (AN 5.150):
“Bhikkhus, there are these five qualities that lead to the decline of a bhikkhu who is liberated at another time.”
Which five?
Delight in work, delight in talk, delight in sleep, lack of restraint over the sense faculties, and lack of moderation in eating.
These, monks, are the five qualities that lead to the decline of a monk who is temporarily liberated.
“Bhikkhus, these five qualities lead to the non-decline of a bhikkhu who is liberated by occasion.
What five?
Not delighting in action, not delighting in talk, not delighting in sleep, guarding the doors of the sense faculties, and moderation in eating.”
“Monks, these five qualities lead to the non-decline of a monk who is liberated by occasion.
The tenth.
The fifth chapter, the Tikaṇḍakī-vagga.
Its summary verse:
Having given [the gift], he despises; he commences;
Sārandada, the triad of stumps, and with hell.
A friend [is distinguished] by an untrue man and a true man;
another two are liberated by occasion.
The third fiftieth chapter is completed.

Aṅguttara Nikāya 5.151 16. Saddhammavagga Paṭhamasammattaniyāmasutta (The First Discourse on Entering the Certainty of Rightness) “Monks, there are these five factors that lead to the decline of a lay follower who has entered the certainty of rightness. What five? Here, monks, a lay follower who has entered the certainty of rightness is devoted to the company of those who follow other sects; he frequents them, converses with them, and engages in discussions with them. He is devoted to the company of those who follow other sects’ teachers; he frequents them, converses with them, and engages in discussions with them. He is devoted to the company of those who follow other sects’ disciples; he frequents them, converses with them, and engages in discussions with them. He is devoted to the company of those who follow other sects’ novices; he frequents them, converses with them, and engages in discussions with them. He is devoted to the company of those who follow other sects’ female novices; he frequents them, converses with them, and engages in discussions with them. These, monks, are the five factors that lead to the decline of a lay follower who has entered the certainty of rightness. Monks, there are these five factors that lead to the non-decline of a lay follower who has entered the certainty of rightness. What five? Here, monks, a lay follower who has entered the certainty of rightness is not devoted to the company of those who follow other sects; he does not frequent them, converse with them, or engage in discussions with them. He is not devoted to the company of those who follow other sects’ teachers; he does not frequent them, converse with them, or engage in discussions with them. He is not devoted to the company of those who follow other sects’ disciples; he does not frequent them, converse with them, or engage in discussions with them. He is not devoted to the company of those who follow other sects’ novices; he does not frequent them, converse with them, or engage in discussions with them. He is not devoted to the company of those who follow other sects’ female novices; he does not frequent them, converse with them, or engage in discussions with them. These, monks, are the five factors that lead to the non-decline of a lay follower who has entered the certainty of rightness.”
“Bhikkhus, possessing five qualities, even while hearing the true Dhamma, one is incapable of entering upon the fixed course of rightness in wholesome states.
What are the five? [Text follows]”

How does one treat with contempt? One treats the speaker with contempt, treats oneself with contempt, listens to the Dhamma with a distracted mind, listens with a non-unified mind, and attends to it improperly.
Possessing these five qualities, monks, even while listening to the true Dhamma, one is incapable of entering upon the fixed course of rightness in wholesome states.
Possessing five qualities, monks, while listening to the true Dhamma, one is capable of entering upon the fixed course of rightness in wholesome states.

“By which five? He does not despise the discourse; he does not despise the speaker; he does not despise himself; he listens to the Dhamma with an undistracted mind; and with a one-pointed mind, he attends to it wisely.
Possessing these five qualities, monks, one who listens to the true Dhamma is capable of entering upon the fixed course of rightness regarding wholesome states.”
First.
Aṅguttara Nikāya 5.152 16.
Saddhammavagga (The Chapter on the True Dhamma)
The Discourse on the Second Certainty of Rightness (AN 5.152). “Bhikkhus,
endowed with five qualities, even while hearing the true Dhamma, one is incapable of entering upon the certainty of rightness regarding wholesome states.
Which five?

He treats the Dhamma with contempt, he treats the teacher with contempt, he treats himself with contempt, he is dull-witted, stupid, and mute-like, and he imagines he has attained what has not been attained.
Possessing these five qualities, monks, even while hearing the true Dhamma, one is incapable of entering upon the fixed course of rightness in wholesome states.

“Monks, one who hears the true Dhamma while endowed with five qualities is capable of entering upon the fixed course of rightness regarding wholesome states. With which five? He does not despise the discourse;

he does not despise the speaker; he does not despise himself; he is wise, unconfused, and not dull-witted; and he does not claim to have known what he has not known. Endowed with these five qualities, one hearing the true Dhamma is capable of entering upon the fixed course of rightness regarding wholesome states.”
“Bhikkhus, one who possesses these five qualities, while hearing the true Dhamma, is capable of entering upon the fixed course of rightness in wholesome states.
The second.
Aṅguttara Nikāya 5.153

16. Saddhammavagga The Third Discourse on Certainty in Rightness (Sammattaniyāmasutta) “Monks, there are these five factors that lead to the decline of a monk who has entered upon the way to certainty in rightness. What five? Here, monks, a monk who has entered upon the way to certainty in rightness dwells without reverence and deference toward the Teacher; he dwells without reverence and deference toward the Dharma; he dwells without reverence and deference toward the Saṅgha; he dwells without reverence and deference toward the training; and he dwells with a mind full of enmity toward his fellow monks. These, monks, are the five factors that lead to the decline of a monk who has entered upon the way to certainty in rightness. There are, however, monks, these five factors that lead to the non-decline of a monk who has entered upon the way to certainty in rightness. What five? Here, monks, a monk who has entered upon the way to certainty in rightness dwells with reverence and deference toward the Teacher; he dwells with reverence and deference toward the Dharma; he dwells with reverence and deference toward the Saṅgha; he dwells with reverence and deference toward the training; and he dwells with a mind free from enmity toward his fellow monks. These, monks, are the five factors that lead to the non-decline of a monk who has entered upon the way to certainty in rightness.”
“Bhikkhus, possessing five qualities, even while listening to the true Dhamma, one is incapable of entering upon the fixed course of rightness in wholesome states.

What are the five? One listens to the Dhamma with contempt, being obsessed by contempt; one listens to the Dhamma with a mind intent on finding fault, seeking for flaws; one harbors resentment and malice toward the teacher of the Dhamma; one is dull-witted, stupid, and mute-like; and one imagines that one has understood what one has not understood. Possessing these five qualities, even while listening to the true Dhamma, one is incapable of entering upon the fixed course of rightness in wholesome states.”
“Monks, one who possesses these five qualities, even while hearing the true Dhamma, is incapable of entering upon the fixed course of rightness in wholesome states.
Monks, one who possesses five qualities, while hearing the true Dhamma, is capable of entering upon the fixed course of rightness in wholesome states.
Which five?”
One listens to the Dhamma without being defiled, not being obsessed by defilement; one listens to the Dhamma with a mind free from criticism, not seeking faults;
one has a heart that is not resentful toward the teacher of the Dhamma and is free from stubbornness; one is wise, not dull-witted, nor deaf and dumb;
and one does not claim to have understood what has not been understood.
“Bhikkhus, one who possesses these five qualities, while hearing the true Dhamma, is capable of entering upon the fixed course of rightness in wholesome states.
Thus was the third [discourse]. Aṅguttara Nikāya 5.154

16. Saddhammavagga First Discourse on the Confusion of the True Dhamma (Saddhammasammosasutta) “Bhikkhus, there will come a time when the true Dhamma will become confused. When the true Dhamma has become confused, beings who have not yet reached the fullness of their development will not reach it; those who have already reached it will fall away from it. And how, bhikkhus, does the true Dhamma become confused? Here, bhikkhus, the bhikkhus do not recite the Suttas in the proper sequence, nor do they explain them in detail as they were heard and learned. As a result, the meaning of the Suttas becomes obscured. They do not recite the Gāthās in the proper sequence, nor do they explain them in detail as they were heard and learned. As a result, the meaning of the Gāthās becomes obscured. They do not recite the Dhammapariyāyas in the proper sequence, nor do they explain them in detail as they were heard and learned. As a result, the meaning of the Dhammapariyāyas becomes obscured. They do not recite the Vedallas in the proper sequence, nor do they explain them in detail as they were heard and learned. As a result, the meaning of the Vedallas becomes obscured. They do not recite the Abbhutadhammas in the proper sequence, nor do they explain them in detail as they were heard and learned. As a result, the meaning of the Abbhutadhammas becomes obscured. They do not recite the Jātakas in the proper sequence, nor do they explain them in detail as they were heard and learned. As a result, the meaning of the Jātakas becomes obscured. They do not recite the Abbhutas in the proper sequence, nor do they explain them in detail as they were heard and learned. As a result, the meaning of the Abbhutas becomes obscured. They do not recite the Paṭisambhidāmagga in the proper sequence, nor do they explain it in detail as it was heard and learned. As a result, the meaning of the Paṭisambhidāmagga becomes obscured. They do not recite the Niddesa in the proper sequence, nor do they explain it in detail as it was heard and learned. As a result, the meaning of the Niddesa becomes obscured. They do not recite the Paṭṭhāna in the proper sequence, nor do they explain it in detail as it was heard and learned. As a result, the meaning of the Paṭṭhāna becomes obscured. It is in this way, bhikkhus, that the true Dhamma becomes confused. And when the true Dhamma has become confused, beings who have not yet reached the fullness of their development will not reach it; those who have already reached it will fall away from it.”
“Monks, there are these five things that lead to the confusion and disappearance of the true Dhamma.
What are the five?
Here, monks, monks do not listen to the Dhamma respectfully; they do not master the Dhamma respectfully.”
They do not respectfully retain the Dhamma; they do not respectfully examine the meaning of the teachings they have retained;
and having neither understood the meaning nor understood the teachings, they do not practice in accordance with the Dhamma.
These, monks, are the five things that lead to the confusion and disappearance of the true Dhamma.
"Monks, there are these five things that lead to the stability, the non-confusion, and the non-disappearance of the true Dhamma.
What are the five?
Here, monks, monks listen to the Dhamma respectfully; they master the Dhamma respectfully."
“They respectfully retain the Dhamma; they respectfully examine the meaning of the teachings they have retained;
and having understood both the meaning and the teaching, they practice in accordance with the Dhamma.
These, monks, are the five qualities that lead to the stability, non-confusion, and non-disappearance of the true Dhamma.”
The Fourth.
Aṅguttara Nikāya 5.155 16.
Saddhammavagga (The Chapter on the True Dhamma)
The Second Discourse on the Confusion and Disappearance of the True Dhamma (AN 5.155): “Bhikkhus,
there are these five things that lead to the confusion and disappearance of the true Dhamma.”
Which five? Here, monks, monks do not master the Dhamma—
the discourses, mixed prose and verse, expositions, verses, inspired utterances, "thus-it-was-said" passages, birth stories, accounts of marvelous phenomena, and analytical expositions.
This, monks, is the first factor that leads to the confusion and disappearance of the true Dhamma.
Furthermore, monks, monks do not teach the Dhamma in detail to others as they have heard it and as they have mastered it.
This, monks, is the second factor that leads to the confusion and disappearance of the true Dhamma.
Furthermore, monks, monks do not teach the Dhamma in detail to others as they have heard it and as they have mastered it.
This, monks, is the third factor that leads to the confusion and disappearance of the true Dhamma.
Furthermore, monks, monks do not recite the Dhamma in detail as they have heard it and as they have mastered it.
This, monks, is the fourth factor that leads to the confusion and disappearance of the true Dhamma.
Furthermore, monks, monks do not reflect upon, investigate, or examine with the mind the Dhamma as it has been heard and mastered.
This, monks, is the fifth factor that leads to the confusion and disappearance of the true Dhamma.
“Monks, these five things lead to the confusion and disappearance of the true Dhamma.
Monks, these five things lead to the stability, non-confusion, and non-disappearance of the true Dhamma.
What are the five?”
"Here, monks, monks master the Dhamma:

the discourses (sutta), mixed prose and verse (geyya), expositions (veyyākaraṇa), verses (gāthā), inspired utterances (udāna), 'Thus-it-was-said' (itivuttaka), birth stories (jātaka), marvelous qualities (abbhutadhamma), and analytical expositions (vedalla).
This, monks, is the first quality that leads to the endurance, non-confusion, and non-disappearance of the true Dhamma."
Furthermore, monks, monks teach the Dhamma in detail to others exactly as they have heard it and exactly as they have mastered it.
This, monks, is the second quality that leads to the endurance, non-confusion, and non-disappearance of the true Dhamma.
Furthermore, monks, monks cause others to recite the Dhamma in detail exactly as they have heard it and exactly as they have mastered it.
This, monks, is the third quality that leads to the stability, non-confusion, and non-disappearance of the true Dhamma.
Furthermore, monks, the monks recite the Dhamma in detail as they have heard it and as they have mastered it.
This, monks, is the fourth quality that leads to the stability, non-confusion, and non-disappearance of the true Dhamma.
Furthermore, monks, monks mentally reflect upon, examine, and contemplate with their minds the Dhamma as it has been heard and mastered.
This, monks, is the fifth quality that leads to the endurance, non-confusion, and non-disappearance of the true Dhamma.
These, monks, are the five qualities that lead to the endurance, non-confusion, and non-disappearance of the true Dhamma.”
The Fifth. Aṅguttara Nikāya 5.156 16.
Saddhammavagga (The Chapter on the True Dhamma)
The Discourse on the Third Cause for the Confusion and Disappearance of the True Dhamma (AN 5.156): “Bhikkhus,
there are these five things that lead to the confusion and disappearance of the true Dhamma.”
Which five?
Here, monks, monks master a discourse that has been wrongly grasped, with words and phrasing poorly set down.
Monks, when the words and phrasing are poorly set down, the meaning is also wrongly interpreted.
“Monks, this is the first factor that leads to the confusion and disappearance of the true Dhamma.
Furthermore, monks, monks become difficult to speak to; they possess qualities that make them difficult to speak to; they are impatient and do not receive instruction respectfully.
Monks, this is the second factor that leads to the confusion and disappearance of the true Dhamma.”

Furthermore, monks, those monks who are learned, who have mastered the tradition, who are bearers of the Dhamma, bearers of the Vinaya, and bearers of the Matikas, do not carefully teach the discourses to others.
With their passing, the discourses become rootless and without a refuge.
This, monks, is the third factor that leads to the confusion and disappearance of the true Dhamma.
Furthermore, monks, the elder bhikkhus become luxurious and lax; they take the lead in backsliding and abandon the burden of solitude.
They do not arouse energy for the attainment of the unattained, for the reaching of the unreached, or for the realization of the unrealized.
The later generation follows their example.

They too become luxurious and lax, taking the lead in decline and casting aside the burden of seclusion; they do not arouse energy for the attainment of the unattained, for the reaching of the unreached, or for the realization of the unrealized.
This, monks, is the fourth factor that leads to the confusion and disappearance of the true Dhamma.
Furthermore, monks, the Saṅgha is split.
When the Saṅgha is split, monks, there are mutual insults, mutual reviling, mutual censuring, and mutual rejection.
Therein, those who have not yet gained confidence do not gain confidence, and some of those who have gained confidence undergo a change of heart.
“Monks, this is the fifth factor that leads to the confusion and disappearance of the true Dhamma.
These, monks, are the five factors that lead to the confusion and disappearance of the true Dhamma.
Monks, there are these five factors that lead to the stability, non-confusion, and non-disappearance of the true Dhamma.”
What five?
Here, monks, monks master discourses that have been well-learned, with well-arranged words and phrases.
Monks, when the words and phrases are well-arranged, the meaning is also easy to follow.
“Monks, this is the first quality that leads to the persistence, non-confusion, and non-disappearance of the true Dhamma.
Furthermore, monks, the monks are easy to speak to; they possess the qualities that make them easy to speak to; they are patient and receptive to instruction.
Monks, this is the second quality that leads to the persistence, non-confusion, and non-disappearance of the true Dhamma.”

Furthermore, monks, those bhikkhus who are learned, who have mastered the tradition, who are bearers of the Dhamma, bearers of the Vinaya, and bearers of the Matikas, carefully teach the discourses to others;
through their passing away, the discourses do not become rootless, for they still have a refuge.
This, monks, is the third quality that leads to the endurance, non-confusion, and non-disappearance of the true Dhamma.
Furthermore, monks, the elder bhikkhus are not luxurious or indolent; they have laid aside the burden of worldly decline and take the lead in solitude.
They arouse energy for the attainment of the unattained, for the realization of the unrealized, and for the manifestation of the unmanifested.
The later generation follows their example.

They too do not become luxurious or lax; they have laid aside the burden of falling away and take the lead in seclusion. They arouse energy for the attainment of the unattained, for the realization of the unrealized, and for the witnessing of the unwitnessed.
This, monks, is the fourth quality that leads to the endurance, non-confusion, and non-disappearance of the true Dhamma.
Furthermore, monks, the Saṅgha dwells at ease—united, in harmony, without dispute, and with a single recitation.
When the Saṅgha is united, monks, there is no mutual reviling, no mutual abuse, no mutual exclusion, and no mutual rejection.
Therein, those without confidence gain confidence, and for those already confident, there is further increase.
“Monks, this is the fifth quality that leads to the endurance, non-confusion, and non-disappearance of the true Dhamma.
Monks, these five qualities lead to the endurance, non-confusion, and non-disappearance of the true Dhamma.
This is the sixth [sutta].
Aṅguttara Nikāya 5.157 16.
Saddhammavagga Dukkathāsutta (The Discourse on Bad Talk)
“Bhikkhus, there are five kinds of persons for whom discourse is ill-spoken when one person is compared with another. Which five? [The text continues as follows:]”
Monks, a talk on faith is ill-spoken for one who lacks faith;
a talk on virtue is ill-spoken for one who is immoral;
a talk on great learning is ill-spoken for one who has heard little.
A talk on generosity for one who is stingy is a poorly delivered talk;
a talk on wisdom for one who lacks wisdom is a poorly delivered talk.
And why, monks, is a talk on faith for one who lacks faith a poorly delivered talk?
“Bhikkhus, when a talk on faith is being given, one who lacks faith becomes resentful, agitated, hostile, and obstinate; he displays anger, hatred, and resentment.
Why is that? Because, bhikkhus, he does not see that perfection of faith within himself, nor does he obtain the rapture and joy born of that cause.”
Therefore, a talk on faith is ill-timed for one who lacks faith.
And why, monks, is a talk on virtue ill-timed for one who is immoral?
Because when a talk on virtue is being delivered, the immoral person becomes resentful, angry, hostile, and stubborn; he manifests anger, hatred, and resentment.
For what reason?
Because, monks, that person does not perceive within himself that accomplishment in virtue, nor does he find the rapture and joy born of it.
Therefore, for one who is immoral, a discourse on virtue is a poorly delivered discourse.
And why, monks, is talk of great learning improper for one who has heard little?
When talk of great learning is being given, monks, one who has heard little becomes resentful, becomes agitated, becomes malevolent, becomes obstinate, and manifests anger, hatred, and resentment.
For what reason?
For that person, monks, does not perceive in himself that perfection of learning, nor does he find the rapture and gladness arising from it.
Therefore, for one who has heard little, talk of great learning is ill-spoken.
And why, monks, is talk of generosity ill-spoken for a miser?
“Monks, when a talk on generosity is being given, a miser becomes resentful, irritated, hostile, and obstinate; he displays anger, hatred, and resentment.
Why is that? Because, monks, he does not perceive that perfection of generosity within himself, nor does he obtain the rapture and joy arising from it.”
Therefore, talk of generosity is ill-suited for one who is stingy.
And why, monks, is talk of wisdom ill-suited for one who lacks wisdom?
When talk of wisdom is being given, monks, one lacking wisdom becomes resentful, becomes angry, becomes hostile, becomes obstinate, and manifests anger, hatred, and resentment.
For what reason?
Because, monks, he does not perceive that perfection of wisdom within himself, nor does he obtain the rapture and gladness born thereof.
Therefore, for one who is lacking in wisdom, a talk on wisdom is ill-spoken.
“Monks, among these five persons, discourse is ill-spoken when one person is compared with another.
Monks, for five persons, discourse is well-spoken when one person is compared with another. Which five?”
Monks, for one who has faith, a discourse on faith is well-spoken;
for one who is virtuous, a discourse on virtue is well-spoken;
for one who is learned, a discourse on great learning is well-spoken.
For one who possesses generosity, a discourse on generosity is well-spoken;
for one who possesses wisdom, a discourse on wisdom is well-spoken.
And why, monks, is a discourse on faith well-spoken for one who has faith?

“Bhikkhus, when a talk on faith is being given, one who possesses faith does not become resentful, does not become irritated, does not fall into ill will, does not become obstinate, and does not manifest anger, hatred, or resentment. Why is that?
Because, bhikkhus, he perceives that perfection of faith within himself and thereby gains rapture and gladness.”
Therefore, for one endowed with faith, a discourse on faith is a well-spoken discourse.
And why, monks, is a discourse on virtue well-spoken for one who is virtuous?

Because when a discourse on virtue is being delivered, the virtuous person does not become resentful, does not become agitated, does not fall into ill will, does not become stubborn, and does not manifest anger, hatred, or resentment.
For what reason?
Because, monks, he perceives that perfection of virtue within himself and gains joy and gladness on that account.
Therefore, for one who is virtuous, a discourse on virtue is a well-delivered discourse.
And why, monks, is talk of great learning well-spoken for one who is greatly learned?

When talk of great learning is being spoken, monks, the greatly learned person does not become resentful, does not become agitated, does not give way to ill will, does not become obstinate, and does not manifest anger, hatred, or resentment.
For what reason?
For he, monks, perceives that perfection of learning within himself and thereby gains rapture and gladness;
therefore, for one who is well-learned, a discourse on great learning is a good discourse.
And why, monks, is a discourse on generosity a good discourse for one who is generous?

Monks, when a discourse on generosity is being delivered, one who is generous does not become resentful, does not become agitated, does not fall into ill will, does not become obstinate, and does not manifest anger, hatred, or resentment. Why is that?
Because, monks, he perceives that perfection of generosity within himself, and he gains joy and gladness on that account.
Therefore, for one who is generous, talk about generosity is well-spoken.
And why, monks, is talk about wisdom well-spoken for one who possesses wisdom?

Because when talk about wisdom is being delivered, the wise person does not become resentful, does not become agitated, does not fall into ill will, does not become obstinate, and does not manifest anger, hatred, or resentment.
For what reason?
Because, monks, he perceives that perfection of wisdom within himself and thereby gains rapture and gladness.
Therefore, for one possessed of wisdom, a discourse on wisdom is well-spoken.
“Monks, among these five persons, it is easy to speak well when comparing one person with another.
Thus was the seventh [discourse]. Aṅguttara Nikāya 5.158

16. Saddhammavagga Sārajjasutta (AN 5.158, PTS AN iii 183) “Bhikkhus, there are these five kinds of timidity. What five? Timidity regarding gain, timidity regarding loss, timidity regarding fame, timidity regarding disrepute, and timidity regarding praise. These, bhikkhus, are the five kinds of timidity.”
“Bhikkhus, possessing five qualities, a bhikkhu has fallen into timidity.
What are the five?
Here, bhikkhus, a bhikkhu is faithless, immoral, of little learning, lazy, and unwise.”
“Monks, a monk endowed with these five qualities has fallen into timidity.
Monks, a monk endowed with five qualities is confident.
With which five?
“Here, monks, a monk is endowed with faith, he is virtuous, he is learned, he is energetic, and he is wise.
Possessing these five qualities, monks, a monk is confident.
This is the eighth [sutta].

Aṅguttara Nikāya 5.159 16. Saddhammavagga Udāyīsutta Then the Venerable Udāyī approached the Blessed One, paid homage to him, sat down to one side, and said to the Blessed One: “Venerable sir, it would be good if the Blessed One would teach me the Dhamma in brief, so that, having heard the Dhamma from the Blessed One, I might dwell alone, withdrawn, diligent, ardent, and resolute. “Udāyī, there are these five aggregates subject to clinging. What five? The form aggregate subject to clinging, the feeling aggregate subject to clinging, the perception aggregate subject to clinging, the volitional formations aggregate subject to clinging, and the consciousness aggregate subject to clinging. These, Udāyī, are the five aggregates subject to clinging. Whatever ascetics or brahmins do not understand as they really are the gratification, the danger, and the escape in the case of these five aggregates subject to clinging:

these I do not consider to be ascetics among ascetics or brahmins among brahmins, and these venerable ones do not, by realizing it for themselves with direct knowledge, in this very life enter and dwell in the goal of asceticism and the goal of brahminhood. But whatever ascetics or brahmins understand as they really are the gratification, the danger, and the escape in the case of these five aggregates subject to clinging: these I consider to be ascetics among ascetics and brahmins among brahmins, and these venerable ones, by realizing it for themselves with direct knowledge, in this very life enter and dwell in the goal of asceticism and the goal of brahminhood. When this was said, the Venerable Udāyī said to the Blessed One: “Venerable sir, it is wonderful, it is marvelous! How well this has been stated by the Blessed One: ‘Whatever ascetics or brahmins do not understand as they really are the gratification, the danger, and the escape in the case of these five aggregates subject to clinging... [The Venerable Udāyī repeated the entire discourse in full. When this was said, the Venerable Udāyī said to the Blessed One: “Venerable sir, it is wonderful, it is marvelous! How well this has been stated by the Blessed One! This is what the Blessed One said. Elated, the Venerable Udāyī delighted in the Blessed One’s words. Thus have I heard. On one occasion the Blessed One was dwelling at Sāvatthī in Jeta’s Grove, Anāthapiṇḍika’s Park. There the Venerable Udāyī approached the Blessed One, paid homage to him, sat down to one side, and said to the Blessed One: “Venerable sir, it would be good if the Blessed One would teach me the Dhamma in brief, so that, having heard the Dhamma from the Blessed One, I might dwell alone, withdrawn, diligent, ardent, and resolute. “Udāyī, there are these five aggregates subject to clinging. What five? The form aggregate subject to clinging... [as above] ...These, Udāyī, are the five aggregates subject to clinging. Whatever ascetics or brahmins do not understand as they really are the origin and the passing away, the gratification, the danger, and the escape in the case of these five aggregates subject to clinging: these I do not consider to be ascetics among ascetics or brahmins among brahmins, and these venerable ones do not, by realizing it for themselves with direct knowledge, in this very life enter and dwell in the goal of asceticism and the goal of brahminhood. (AN 5.159, PTS AN iii 184) Thus have I heard:
at one time the Blessed One was dwelling at Kosambī in Ghosita’s Park.
Now at that time, the Venerable Udāyī was seated, surrounded by a large assembly of householders, teaching the Dhamma.
The Venerable Ānanda saw the Venerable Udāyī seated, surrounded by a large assembly of householders, teaching the Dhamma.
Having seen him, he approached the Blessed One; having approached and paid homage to the Blessed One, he sat down to one side. Sitting to one side, the Venerable Ānanda said this to the Blessed One:
“Venerable sir, the Venerable Udāyī is surrounded by a large assembly of householders and is teaching the Dhamma.
“It is not easy, Ānanda, to teach the Dhamma to others.
One who teaches the Dhamma to others, Ānanda, should teach the Dhamma to others after establishing five qualities within themselves.”
Which five?
One should teach the Dhamma to others thinking, ‘I will speak in progressive order’;
one should teach the Dhamma to others thinking, ‘I will speak by way of method.’
The Dhamma should be taught to others with the thought: ‘I will speak so as to be sympathetic’;
the Dhamma should be taught to others with the thought: ‘I will not speak for the sake of material gain’;
the Dhamma should be taught to others with the thought: ‘I will speak without harming myself or others.’
“It is not easy, Ānanda, to teach the Dhamma to others.
One who teaches the Dhamma to others, Ānanda, should do so having established these five qualities within themselves.
Thus ends the ninth [discourse].

Aṅguttara Nikāya 5.160 16. Saddhammavagga Duppaṭivinodayasutta: Difficult to Dispel “Monks, there are these five things that are difficult to dispel. What five? Sensual desire is difficult to dispel for one who dwells with a mind obsessed by sensual desire. Ill will is difficult to dispel for one who dwells with a mind obsessed by ill will. Sloth and torpor are difficult to dispel for one who dwells with a mind obsessed by sloth and torpor. Restlessness and remorse are difficult to dispel for one who dwells with a mind obsessed by restlessness and remorse. Doubt is difficult to dispel for one who dwells with a mind obsessed by doubt. These, monks, are the five things that are difficult to dispel.”
“Bhikkhus, these five things that have arisen are difficult to dispel. Which five? (AN 5.160, PTS AN iii 184)”

“Bhikkhus, lust that has arisen is difficult to dispel; hatred that has arisen is difficult to dispel; delusion that has arisen is difficult to dispel; a flash of wit that has arisen is difficult to dispel; a mind intent on departure that has arisen is difficult to dispel.
These, bhikkhus, are the five things that have arisen which are difficult to dispel.
The tenth.
The First Chapter on the True Dhamma.
Its summary verse:
Three types of certainty in rightness.
There are three corruptions of the true Dhamma:
ill-spoken discourse, timidity,
and that which is difficult to remove, O Udāyin.

Aṅguttara Nikāya 5.161 17. Āghātavagga First Discourse on the Removal of Resentment (Paṭhama-āghātapaṭivinaya-sutta) "Bhikkhus, there are these five ways of removing resentment. What five? One does not harbor resentment toward those who have already provoked it; one does not harbor resentment toward those who are currently provoking it; one does not harbor resentment toward those who will provoke it in the future; one does not harbor resentment toward those who have provoked it in the past, present, or future; and one does not harbor resentment toward those who have provoked it in the past, are provoking it now, or will provoke it in the future. These, bhikkhus, are the five ways of removing resentment."
“Bhikkhus, there are these five ways of removing resentment, wherein any resentment that has arisen in a bhikkhu should be entirely removed. What are the five? [The text continues with the list.]”
“Monks, toward whichever person anger might arise, loving-kindness should be cultivated toward that person;
in this way, anger toward that person is to be removed.
Monks, toward whichever person anger might arise, compassion should be cultivated toward that person.”
In this way, resentment toward that person should be removed.
Monks, toward whatever person resentment might arise, equanimity toward that person should be cultivated;
in this way, resentment toward that person should be removed.
“Monks, toward whichever person anger might arise, one should apply non-attention and lack of mindfulness toward that person;
in this way, anger toward that person is to be removed.
Monks, toward whichever person anger might arise, one should resolve upon the fact that [the person] is the owner of their own karma.”
‘This venerable one is the owner of his actions, the heir to his actions, born of his actions, related to his actions, and has his actions as his refuge;
whatever action he performs, whether good or evil, he will be its heir.
In this way, resentment toward that person should be removed.
“Monks, these are the five ways of removing resentment, wherein any resentment that has arisen in a monk should be entirely removed.
First.
Aṅguttara Nikāya 5.162

17. Āghātavagga The Second Discourse on the Removal of Malice (Dutiya-āghātapaṭivinaya-sutta) “Monks, there are these six ways of removing malice. What six? ‘May he not harm me,’ this is the first way of removing malice. ‘He has harmed me; may he not harm others,’ this is the second way of removing malice. ‘He has harmed me and others; may he not harm others,’ this is the third way of removing malice. ‘He has harmed me, he has harmed others, and he will harm those who harm him,’ this is the fourth way of removing malice. ‘He has harmed me, he has harmed others, and he will harm those who harm him; may he be for his own welfare and happiness,’ this is the fifth way of removing malice. ‘He has harmed me, he has harmed others, and he will harm those who harm him; may he be for his own welfare and happiness, and may I too be for my own welfare and happiness,’ this is the sixth way of removing malice. These, monks, are the six ways of removing malice.”
There, the Venerable Sāriputta addressed the bhikkhus:
“Friends, bhikkhus.
“Friend,” those bhikkhus replied to the Venerable Sāriputta.
The Venerable Sāriputta said this:
“Friends, there are these five ways of removing resentment, wherein any resentment that has arisen in a bhikkhu should be entirely removed.
What are the five?”
In this case, friends, a certain person has impure conduct of body but pure conduct of speech;
in such a person as well, friends, resentment should be removed.
Furthermore, friends, a certain person has impure conduct of speech but pure conduct of body.
"Friends, resentment should be dispelled even toward such a person.

Furthermore, friends, there is a certain person here whose bodily conduct is impure and whose verbal conduct is impure, yet who from time to time attains an opening of the mind and clarity of the mind;
friends, resentment should be dispelled even toward such a person."
Furthermore, friends, here a certain person is impure in bodily conduct and impure in verbal conduct, and does not from time to time obtain an opening of the mind or clarity of the mind;
even toward such a person, friends, resentment should be removed.
Furthermore, friends, here a certain person is pure in bodily conduct and pure in verbal conduct, and from time to time obtains an opening of the mind or clarity of the mind.
"Friends, resentment should be removed even toward such a person.
In this regard, friends, how should one remove resentment toward a person whose bodily conduct is impure but whose verbal conduct is pure?

It is just as if, friends, a monk who wears rag-robes, seeing a scrap of cloth on a road, were to pick it up with his left foot, spread it out with his right foot, shake out whatever solid matter there might be, and then take it and depart."
In the same way, friends, when there is a person whose bodily conduct is impure but whose verbal conduct is pure,
that which is his impurity of bodily conduct should not be taken to mind at that time; rather,
that which is his purity of verbal conduct should be taken to mind at that time.
In this way, resentment toward that person should be removed.
In this regard, friends, how should resentment be removed toward a person whose verbal conduct is impure but whose bodily conduct is pure?
It is just as if, friends, there were a lotus pond covered over with water-moss and duckweed.
Then, suppose a man were to come along, scorched by the heat, overcome by the heat, exhausted, thirsty, and parched with thirst.
Having plunged into that lotus pond, he would clear away the water-moss and duckweed with both hands, drink from his cupped palms, and depart.
In the same way, friends, is that person whose verbal conduct is impure but whose bodily conduct is pure.
Whatever impurity of verbal conduct he may have, that should not be brought to mind at that time;
rather, whatever purity of bodily conduct he possesses, that should be brought to mind at that time.
In this way, resentment toward that person should be removed.

In this regard, friends, when a person whose bodily conduct is impure and whose verbal conduct is impure occasionally gains an opening of the mind and clarity of the mind, how should resentment toward that person be removed?
It is just as if there were a small amount of water in a cow’s footprint,
and then a man came along, scorched by the heat, overcome by the heat, exhausted, thirsty, and parched.
It would occur to him:
"This is indeed a mere trifle of water in a cow's footprint.
If I were to drink it with my cupped hands or with a vessel, I would stir it up, I would churn it about, and I would make it undrinkable."
‘What if I were to prostrate myself on all fours, drink the cow’s urine, and then depart?
And so he would prostrate himself on all fours, drink the cow’s urine, and depart.
In the same way, friends, is that person whose bodily conduct is impure and whose verbal conduct is impure.
And from time to time he gains an opening of the mind and clarity of the mind; at that time, whatever impurity of bodily conduct he may have should not be brought to mind,
nor should whatever impurity of verbal conduct he may have be brought to mind.
But whenever he obtains from time to time an opening of the mind, a clarity of the mind, that alone should be attended to by him at that time.
In this way, resentment toward that person should be removed.

In this regard, friends, as for that person whose bodily conduct is impure, whose verbal conduct is impure, and who does not obtain from time to time an opening of the mind or a clarity of the mind—how should resentment toward that person be removed?
"Suppose, friends, a man were afflicted, suffering, and gravely ill, traveling along a long road.
The village ahead of him would be far away, and the village behind him would also be far away.
He would not find suitable food, he would not find suitable medicine, he would not find a proper attendant, and he would not find a guide to the interior of the forest."
Suppose a certain man traveling along a highway were to see him.
He would feel compassion for that man, he would feel sympathy for him, and he would feel pity for him, thinking:
“Oh, that this man might obtain suitable food, obtain suitable medicines, obtain a suitable attendant, and obtain a guide to the village!”
"And why is that? Lest this man meet with calamity and disaster right here.
In the same way, friends, as for that person whose bodily conduct is impure and whose verbal conduct is impure...
And one does not obtain from time to time an opening of the mind or clarity of the mind;
even toward such a person, friends, one should maintain only compassion, only sympathy, and only pity, thinking:

"Oh, that this venerable one might abandon bodily misconduct and cultivate bodily good conduct; that he might abandon verbal misconduct and cultivate verbal good conduct; that he might abandon mental misconduct and cultivate mental good conduct."
And why is that? ‘Lest this venerable one, with the breakup of the body, after death, should be reborn in a state of deprivation, a bad destination, a lower realm, or in hell.
In this way, resentment toward that person should be removed.

In this regard, friends, when there is a person whose bodily conduct is pure and whose verbal conduct is pure, who from time to time gains an opening of the mind and clarity of the mind—how should resentment toward such a person be removed?
Suppose, friends, there were a lotus pond with clear water, sweet water, cool water, white water, with good landing places, delightful, and shaded by various trees.
Then a man might come along, scorched by the heat, overcome by the heat, exhausted, thirsty, and parched.
Having plunged into that lotus pond, bathed, drunk, and emerged, he would sit or lie down right there in the shade of a tree.
In the same way, friends, this person whose bodily conduct is pure and whose verbal conduct is pure,
who from time to time gains an opening of the mind and clarity of the mind— this very purity of his bodily conduct...
At that time, he should also attend to his own purity of verbal conduct;
at that time, he should also attend to whatever opening of the mind and clarity of the mind he occasionally attains.
In this way, resentment toward that person should be removed.
Friend, by approaching a person who is pleasing on all sides, the mind becomes serene.
These, friends, are the five ways of removing resentment, wherein any resentment that has arisen in a bhikkhu should be entirely removed.
The Second.
Aṅguttara Nikāya 5.163 17.
Āghātavagga (The Chapter on Resentment)
In that place, the Venerable Sāriputta addressed the bhikkhus: "Sākacchasutta" (AN 5.163, PTS AN iii 190).

Aṅguttara Nikāya 5.164 17. Āghātavagga Sājīvasutta “Bhikkhus, there are these five ways of livelihood that are unrighteous, impure, and not the way of the Noble Ones. What five? Here, bhikkhus, a certain person seeks almsfood by means of singing, dancing, music, lute-playing, drumming, recitation, palmistry, divination, the interpretation of dreams, omens, and signs; he seeks almsfood by means of such various kinds of low arts, crafts, and practices. This, bhikkhus, is the first way of livelihood that is unrighteous, impure, and not the way of the Noble Ones. Again, bhikkhus, here a certain person seeks almsfood by means of cheating, deceiving, trickery, cajoling, and intimidation; he seeks almsfood by means of such various kinds of low arts, crafts, and practices. This, bhikkhus, is the second way of livelihood that is unrighteous, impure, and not the way of the Noble Ones. Again, bhikkhus, here a certain person seeks almsfood by means of the practice of portents, the practice of charms, the practice of exorcism, the practice of quenching fires, the practice of snake-charming, the practice of spirit-possession, the practice of making things disappear, the practice of making things appear, the practice of making things move, and the practice of making things speak; he seeks almsfood by means of such various kinds of low arts, crafts, and practices. This, bhikkhus, is the third way of livelihood that is unrighteous, impure, and not the way of the Noble Ones. Again, bhikkhus, here a certain person seeks almsfood by means of the practice of astrology, the practice of dream-interpretation, the practice of omen-interpretation, the practice of sign-interpretation, the practice of interpreting the marks on the body, the practice of interpreting the marks on cloth, the practice of interpreting the marks on wood, the practice of interpreting the marks on earth, and the practice of interpreting the marks on water; he seeks almsfood by means of such various kinds of low arts, crafts, and practices. This, bhikkhus, is the fourth way of livelihood that is unrighteous, impure, and not the way of the Noble Ones. Again, bhikkhus, here a certain person seeks almsfood by means of the practice of predicting the future, the practice of predicting the past, the practice of predicting both the future and the past, the practice of predicting the results of actions, the practice of predicting the results of the stars, the practice of predicting the results of the moon, the practice of predicting the results of the sun, and the practice of predicting the results of the conjunctions of the planets; he seeks almsfood by means of such various kinds of low arts, crafts, and practices. This, bhikkhus, is the fifth way of livelihood that is unrighteous, impure, and not the way of the Noble Ones. These, bhikkhus, are the five ways of livelihood that are unrighteous, impure, and not the way of the Noble Ones. There are, however, bhikkhus, these five ways of livelihood that are righteous, pure, and the way of the Noble Ones. What five? Here, bhikkhus, a bhikkhu lives by seeking almsfood from house to house in the village or town, relying on what is obtained, without being selective. This, bhikkhus, is the first way of livelihood that is righteous, pure, and the way of the Noble Ones. Again, bhikkhus, a bhikkhu lives by seeking almsfood from one house after another, relying on what is obtained, without being selective. This, bhikkhus, is the second way of livelihood that is righteous, pure, and the way of the Noble Ones. Again, bhikkhus, a bhikkhu lives by seeking almsfood at a single house, relying on what is obtained, without being selective. This, bhikkhus, is the third way of livelihood that is righteous, pure, and the way of the Noble Ones. Again, bhikkhus, a bhikkhu lives by seeking almsfood from a family that has been designated as such, relying on what is obtained, without being selective. This, bhikkhus, is the fourth way of livelihood that is righteous, pure, and the way of the Noble Ones. Again, bhikkhus, a bhikkhu lives by seeking almsfood from a bowl placed before him, relying on what is obtained, without being selective. This, bhikkhus, is the fifth way of livelihood that is righteous, pure, and the way of the Noble Ones. These, bhikkhus, are the five ways of livelihood that are righteous, pure, and the way of the Noble Ones.”
There, the Venerable Sāriputta addressed the bhikkhus:
“…Friends, a bhikkhu endowed with five qualities is capable of living in harmony with his fellow brahmacārins.”
Which five?
Here, friends, a bhikkhu is himself accomplished in virtue and is able to answer questions that arise concerning the accomplishment of virtue;
he is himself accomplished in concentration and is able to answer questions that arise concerning the accomplishment of concentration.
He himself is endowed with wisdom and is able to answer questions that arise regarding the perfection of wisdom;
he himself is endowed with liberation and is able to answer questions that arise regarding the perfection of liberation;
he himself is endowed with the knowledge and vision of liberation and is able to answer questions that arise regarding the perfection of the knowledge and vision of liberation.
“Friends, a bhikkhu endowed with these five qualities is capable of living in harmony with his fellow celibates.

Āghātavagga Pañhapucchāsutta (AN 5.165, PTS AN iii 191) “Monks, when asked these questions, you should answer them thus: ‘The Tathāgata does not assert that “the world is eternal”; nor does he assert that “the world is not eternal. The Tathāgata does not assert that “the world is finite”; nor does he assert that “the world is infinite. The Tathāgata does not assert that “the soul is the same as the body”; nor does he assert that “the soul is one thing and the body another. The Tathāgata does not assert that “a Tathāgata exists after death”; nor does he assert that “a Tathāgata does not exist after death”; nor does he assert that “a Tathāgata both exists and does not exist after death”; nor does he assert that “a Tathāgata neither exists nor does not exist after death. When this was said, the Venerable Ānanda said to the Blessed One: “But why, Bhante, does the Tathāgata not assert these things? “Ānanda, the speculative view that ‘the world is eternal’ is unwholesome, it has suffering as its outcome, it has despair as its outcome, it leads away from the goal; therefore the Tathāgata does not assert it. The speculative view that ‘the world is not eternal’... [and so on for each of the remaining views]... Therefore the Tathāgata does not assert it. Furthermore, Ānanda, when one asserts ‘the world is eternal,’ one asserts what is not true of oneself, and one denies what is true of oneself. When one asserts ‘the world is not eternal,’ one asserts what is not true of oneself, and one denies what is true of oneself. When one asserts ‘the world is finite’... ‘the world is infinite’... ‘the soul is the same as the body’... ‘the soul is one thing and the body another’... ‘a Tathāgata exists after death’... ‘a Tathāgata does not exist after death’... ‘a Tathāgata both exists and does not exist after death’... ‘a Tathāgata neither exists nor does not exist after death,’ one asserts what is not true of oneself, and one denies what is true of oneself. Why is that? Because, Ānanda, the Tathāgata has abandoned all such speculative views, cut them off at the root, made them like a palm stump, obliterated them so that they are no longer subject to future arising. Therefore, Ānanda, the Tathāgata does not assert any of these things.”
There, the Venerable Sāriputta addressed the bhikkhus: “…Friends, whoever asks another a question does so for one of five reasons, or for one of these [five].
What are the five?
One asks another a question out of dullness and stupidity; one asks another a question because of evil desires and being overcome by longing;”
One asks another a question out of contempt; one asks another a question desiring to know; or else one asks another a question with such a thought as this:
"If, when asked my question, he answers correctly, that is well; but if, when asked my question, he does not answer correctly, then I shall answer him correctly myself."
"Friends, whoever asks another a question does so from one of these five positions or another similar one.
But I, friends, ask another a question with this intention:
'If, when asked my question, he answers correctly, that is well; but if, when asked my question, he does not answer correctly, I shall answer it correctly for him.'"

Then the Blessed One, having emerged from seclusion in the evening time, went to the assembly hall; having arrived, he sat down on the prepared seat. Having sat down, the Blessed One said this to the Venerable Upavāṇa:

17. Āghātavagga Codanāsutta (AN 5.167, PTS AN iii 196) “Monks, there are these five ways of censuring. What five? One censures with what is untrue; one censures with what is true; one censures with what is both untrue and true; one censures with what is neither untrue nor true; and one censures without having first reflected. These, monks, are the five ways of censuring.”
There, the Venerable Sāriputta addressed the bhikkhus:
"Friends, a bhikkhu who wishes to reprove another should first establish five qualities within himself before reproving that person.
What are the five?"
I shall speak at the proper time, not at an improper time;
I shall speak what is true, not what is untrue;
I shall speak gently, not harshly.
"I shall speak what is connected with the goal, not what is disconnected from the goal;
I shall speak with a mind of loving-kindness, not with inner hatred.
Friend, a monk who wishes to reprove another should reprove them after having established these five qualities within himself."
In this case, friends, I see a certain person who, when reproved at an improper time, is not angry at the proper time;
who, when reproved with what is untrue, is not angry with what is true; who, when reproved harshly, is not angry with what is gentle;
who, when reproved with what is unbeneficial, is not angry with what is beneficial; and who, when reproved with a mind full of hatred, is not angry with a mind of loving-kindness.
Friends, for a bhikkhu who has been reproved in an unrighteous manner, non-regret should be established in five ways:
"Venerable sir, you were reproved at an improper time, not at a proper time; this is sufficient for you to be without regret.
You were reproved with what is untrue, not with what is true; this is sufficient for you to be without regret."
‘Venerable sir, you have been reproved harshly, not gently; that is sufficient for you to be free from remorse.
You have been reproved with what is unbeneficial, not with what is beneficial; that is sufficient for you to be free from remorse.
You have been reproved with a mind of ill will, not with a mind of loving-kindness; that is sufficient for you to be free from remorse.’”
Friends, remorse should be induced in a monk who has been reproved contrary to the Dhamma by means of these five ways.
Friends, remorse should be induced in a monk who reproves contrary to the Dhamma by means of five ways:
"Friend, you reproved him at the wrong time, not at the right time; that is sufficient for you to feel remorse."
Friend, you have been reproved by what is untrue, not by what is true; that is sufficient reason for you to feel remorse.
You have been reproved harshly, not gently; that is sufficient reason for you to feel remorse.
You have been reproved with what is unbeneficial, not with what is beneficial; that is sufficient reason for you to feel remorse.
"Friend, you have reproached me with ill will, not with a mind of loving-kindness; it is enough for you to feel remorse.
Friend, in these five ways should remorse be induced in a monk who reproaches another unrighteously. And why is that?
"So that no other bhikkhu might think, 'One should not accuse another with what is untrue.
Furthermore, friends, here I see a certain person who, when accused at the proper time, is not provoked by being accused at an improper time;
who, when accused of what is true, is not provoked by being accused of what is untrue; and who, when accused gently, is not provoked by being accused harshly."
When one is reproved for what is connected with the goal and not for what is unconnected with the goal, and when one is reproved with a mind of loving-kindness and not with a mind of hatred;
for a bhikkhu who has been reproved in accordance with the Dhamma, friends, remorse should be induced in five ways:
‘The Venerable One was reproved at the proper time, not at an improper time; that is sufficient for you to feel remorse.
The Venerable One was reproved with truth, not with falsehood; that is sufficient for you to feel remorse.
The Venerable One was reproved gently, not harshly; that is sufficient for you to feel remorse.’
‘The Venerable One has been reproved for what is connected with the goal, not for what is unconnected with the goal; this is sufficient reason for you to feel remorse.
The Venerable One has been reproved with a mind of loving-kindness, not with inner hatred; this is sufficient reason for you to feel remorse.
Friends, in these five ways, remorse should be instilled in a bhikkhu who has been reproved in accordance with the Dhamma.
Friends, a monk who reproves another should be made free from remorse in five ways:
"Friend, you were reproved at the proper time, not at an improper time; this is sufficient for you to be free from remorse.
Friend, you were reproved based on fact, not on what is not a fact; this is sufficient for you to be free from remorse."
"Friend, you have been reproved by me gently, not harshly; this is sufficient for you to be free from remorse.
You have been reproved by me for what is beneficial, not for what is harmful; this is sufficient for you to be free from remorse.
You have been reproved by me with a mind of loving-kindness, not with inner hatred; this is sufficient for you to be free from remorse."
Friends, non-regret should be established for a monk who reproves by means of these five ways.
For what reason?
So that another monk might also think, "He should be reproved with what is factual."
"Friends, a person who has been criticized should establish himself in two qualities:
truthfulness and imperturbability.

In that place, the Venerable Sāriputta addressed the bhikkhus: "Sīlasutta" (AN 5.168, PTS AN iii 200).
Thus spoke the Venerable Sāriputta, addressing the bhikkhus.
“Friend, for one who is immoral, for one deficient in virtue, right concentration lacks its proximate cause.
When right concentration is absent, for one deficient in right concentration, the knowledge and vision of things as they really are lacks its proximate cause.

When the knowledge and vision of things as they really are is absent, for one deficient in the knowledge and vision of things as they really are, disenchantment and dispassion lack their proximate cause.”
When disenchantment and dispassion are absent, for one deficient in disenchantment and dispassion, the knowledge and vision of liberation lacks its proximate cause.

Just as, friend, a tree deficient in branches and foliage does not reach fulfillment in its bark, nor in its inner bark, nor in its softwood, nor in its heartwood; so too, when disenchantment and dispassion are absent... [the knowledge and vision of liberation lacks its proximate cause].
In the same way, friends, for one who is immoral and deficient in virtue, right concentration lacks its proximate cause.
When right concentration is absent, for one who is deficient in right concentration, the knowledge and vision of things as they really are lacks its proximate cause.
When the knowledge and vision of things as they really are is absent, for one who is deficient in that knowledge and vision, disenchantment and dispassion lack their proximate cause.
When there is no disenchantment and dispassion, for one who has failed in disenchantment and dispassion, the knowledge and vision of liberation lacks its proximate cause.
For a virtuous person, friend, who is accomplished in virtue, right concentration possesses its proximate cause;
when right concentration exists, for one accomplished in right concentration, the knowledge and vision of things as they truly are possesses its proximate cause.

When there is knowledge and vision of things as they really are, for one endowed with knowledge and vision of things as they really are, disenchantment and dispassion become fully supported by that condition.
When there is disenchantment and dispassion, for one endowed with disenchantment and dispassion, the knowledge and vision of liberation becomes fully supported by that condition.
Just as, friends, when a tree is endowed with branches and foliage, its shoots reach full growth, and its bark, inner bark, and heartwood also reach full growth.
In the same way, friends, for one who is virtuous and perfected in virtue, right concentration is supported by its proximate cause.
When there is right concentration, for one perfected in right concentration, the knowledge and vision of things as they truly are is supported by its proximate cause.

When there is the knowledge and vision of things as they truly are, for one perfected in the knowledge and vision of things as they truly are, disenchantment and dispassion are supported by their proximate cause.
“When there is disenchantment and dispassion, for one endowed with disenchantment and dispassion, the knowledge and vision of liberation possesses its proximate cause.
Thus was the eighth. Aṅguttara Nikāya 5.169

17. Āghātavagga Khippanisanti Sutta (The Discourse on Quick Peace) At Sāvatthī. “Monks, there are these five qualities of one who is quick to attain peace. What five? Here, monks, a monk is quick to understand the meaning of what is said; he is quick to retain it in mind; he is able to explain in detail what has been stated in brief; he is able to state in brief what has been explained in detail; and he is capable of teaching the Dhamma with its causes and reasons. These, monks, are the five qualities of one who is quick to attain peace.”
Then the Venerable Ānanda approached the Venerable Sāriputta; having approached, he exchanged greetings with the Venerable Sāriputta.
When they had concluded their polite and friendly conversation, he sat down to one side. Sitting there, the Venerable Ānanda said this to the Venerable Sāriputta:

"To what extent, friend Sāriputta, is a bhikkhu one who is quick-witted regarding wholesome states, one who grasps well what is taught, one who learns much, and one who does not forget what has been learned?"
“The Venerable Ānanda is learned.
Let it occur to the Venerable Ānanda himself.
“In that case, friend Sāriputta, listen and pay close attention; I shall speak.”
“Yes, friend,” the Venerable Sāriputta replied to the Venerable Ānanda.
The Venerable Ānanda said this:
“In this case, friend Sāriputta, a bhikkhu is skilled in the meaning, skilled in the Dhamma, skilled in the phrasing, skilled in the language, and skilled in what precedes and follows.”
"To this extent, friend Sāriputta, a bhikkhu is one of quick intuition regarding wholesome states, one who grasps well, one who learns much, and one who does not forget what has been learned.
"It is wonderful, friend! It is marvelous, friend!
How well this has been spoken by the Venerable Ānanda!"
"And for these five qualities we remember the Venerable Ānanda as being endowed with them:
'The Venerable Ānanda is skilled in the meaning, skilled in the Dhamma, skilled in the phrasing, skilled in language, and skilled in what precedes and what follows.
(The ninth.)
