(AN 5.170, PTS AN iii 202) At one time the Venerable Ānanda was dwelling at Kosambī in Ghosita’s Park.
Then the Venerable Bhaddaji approached the Venerable Ānanda; having approached, he exchanged greetings with the Venerable Ānanda.
Having exchanged greetings and pleasantries, he sat down to one side. As the Venerable Bhaddaji was sitting there, the Venerable Ānanda said this to him:
"Friend Bhaddaji, what is the foremost of sights? What is the foremost of things to hear? What is the foremost of pleasures? What is the foremost of perceptions? What is the foremost of existences?
"Friend, there is Brahmā Abhibhū, the Unconquered, who sees all and wields power. To see that Brahmā—this is the foremost of sights."
"Friends, there are the devas called Ābhassara, who are completely saturated and suffused with happiness.
From time to time they utter this inspired exclamation:
'Oh, what happiness! Oh, what happiness!'"
Whoever hears that sound—this is the foremost of hearings.
There are, friends, the gods called the Subhakinhā.
They, being peaceful, experience the bliss of contentment; this is the foremost of pleasures.
“There are, friends, gods who have reached the base of nothingness; this is the foremost of perceptions.
There are, friends, gods who have reached the base of neither-perception-nor-non-perception; this is the foremost of states of existence.
“Does this agree with what the Venerable Bhaddaji says, as it does for the many people?”
“The Venerable Ānanda is learned.
Let it occur to the Venerable Ānanda himself.
“In that case, friend Bhaddaji, listen and pay close attention; I shall speak.”
“Yes, friend,” the Venerable Bhaddaji replied to the Venerable Ānanda.
The Venerable Ānanda said this:
“Friend, that vision by which the immediate destruction of the taints occurs—this is the foremost of visions.”
That for one who hears, the destruction of the taints occurs immediately thereafter—this is the foremost of hearings.
That for one who is happy, the destruction of the taints occurs immediately thereafter—this is the foremost of happinesses.
That for one who possesses perception, the destruction of the taints occurs immediately thereafter—this is the foremost of perceptions.
“The immediate destruction of the taints for one who has become thus—this is the foremost of states.
Tenth. The second chapter on resentment is finished.
Its summary verse:
Two methods for removing resentment,
discussion, and a question regarding livelihood.
Inquiry, cessation, and exhortation;
virtue, composure, and one who lives auspiciously.
Aṅguttara Nikāya 5.171

18. Upāsakavagga Sārajjasutta (AN 5.171) “Monks, there are these five grounds for self-confidence in a lay follower. What five? ‘I am one who has gone for refuge to the Buddha, and it is not possible that he is not a Buddha, fully awakened; this is the first ground for self-confidence in a lay follower. ‘I am one who has gone for refuge to the Dhamma, and it is not possible that it is not the Dhamma, well-expounded by the Blessed One; this is the second ground for self-confidence in a lay follower. ‘I am one who has gone for refuge to the Saṅgha, and it is not possible that it is not the Saṅgha of the Blessed One’s disciples who have practiced well; this is the third ground for self-confidence in a lay follower. ‘I am one whose conduct is not blameworthy in regard to my deeds of body, speech, and mind; this is the fourth ground for self-confidence in a lay follower. ‘Whatever state of existence there may be, whatever kind of rebirth, wherever I may be born, I shall never be deprived of the sight of the Buddhas, the Blessed Ones; this is the fifth ground for self-confidence in a lay follower. These, monks, are the five grounds for self-confidence in a lay follower.”
Thus have I heard:
at one time the Blessed One was dwelling at Sāvatthī in Jeta’s Grove, Anāthapiṇḍika’s monastery.
There the Blessed One addressed the bhikkhus:
“Monks,” [the Blessed One said]. “Venerable sir,” those monks replied to the Blessed One.
The Blessed One spoke as follows:
“Bhikkhus, possessing five qualities, a lay follower has fallen into timidity.
Which five?

He is a destroyer of life, a taker of what is not given, one who engages in sexual misconduct, a speaker of falsehood, and one who indulges in liquor, wine, and intoxicants, which are the basis for negligence.
“Monks, a lay follower endowed with these five qualities has fallen into timidity.
Monks, a lay follower endowed with five qualities is confident.
With which five?

“He abstains from the destruction of life, he abstains from taking what is not given, he abstains from sexual misconduct, he abstains from false speech, and he abstains from fermented and distilled liquors that cause negligence.
Endowed with these five qualities, monks, a lay follower is confident. Thus was the first [discourse].

Aṅguttara Nikāya 5.172 18. Upāsakavagga Visāradasutta (The Discourse on Confidence) “Monks, there are these five qualities of a lay follower that lead to confidence. What five? Here, monks, a lay follower is endowed with faith; he places faith in the Tathāgata’s enlightenment thus: ‘Indeed, the Blessed One is an arahant, perfectly enlightened, accomplished in true knowledge and conduct, fortunate, knower of the world, unsurpassed leader of persons to be tamed, teacher of devas and humans, the Buddha, the Blessed One. He is endowed with virtue; he dwells restrained by the restraint of the Pātimokkha, possessed of good conduct and resort, seeing danger in even the slightest faults; having undertaken the training rules, he trains in them. He is endowed with learning; he has learned much, retained what he has learned, accumulated what he has learned; those teachings that are good in the beginning, good in the middle, and good in the end, with the right meaning and phrasing, which proclaim the perfectly complete and pure holy life—such teachings as these he has learned much of, retained, recited verbally, mentally examined, and penetrated well through view. He is endowed with generosity; he dwells as a giver, one who opens his hands, who takes delight in relinquishing, one who is generous and liberal with his hand, who delights in the distribution of gifts. He is endowed with wisdom; he possesses the wisdom that discerns arising and passing away, which is noble and penetrative, leading to the complete destruction of suffering. These, monks, are the five qualities of a lay follower that lead to confidence.”
“Bhikkhus, possessing five qualities, a lay follower dwells at home without confidence. Which five? [Text follows].”
“He is a destroyer of life... he is one who indulges in fermented and distilled liquors, which are the basis for negligence.
Possessing these five qualities, monks, a lay follower dwells at home without confidence.
Possessing five qualities, monks, a lay follower dwells at home with confidence.”
“By which five?
He abstains from the destruction of life …pe… he abstains from the use of fermented and distilled liquors and intoxicants, which are the basis for negligence.
It is, monks, by being endowed with these five qualities that a lay follower dwells at home confident and fearless.”
The Second [Discourse]. Aṅguttara Nikāya 5.173 18.
Upāsakavagga (The Chapter on Lay Followers)
Nirayasutta (AN 5.173,
PTS AN iii 204): “Bhikkhus,
endowed with five qualities, a lay follower is deposited in hell as if brought there.
Which five?
He destroys life... [and so on] ...he is one who indulges in fermented liquor, spirits, and intoxicants, which are the basis for negligence.
Endowed with these five qualities, monks, a lay follower is placed in hell as if carried there.
“Bhikkhus, possessing five qualities, a lay follower is deposited in heaven as if brought there.
What are the five?
He abstains from the destruction of life … [and so on] … he abstains from the use of fermented and distilled liquors that cause heedlessness.”
“Bhikkhus, a lay follower endowed with these five qualities is deposited in heaven as if carried there.
The third.
*Aṅguttara Nikāya* 5.174.

18. Upāsakavagga Verasutta (AN 5.174, PTS AN iii 204) “Monks, there are these four kinds of persons found existing in the world. What four? The person who is full of enmity toward himself; the person who is full of enmity toward others; the person who is full of enmity toward both himself and others; and the person who is full of enmity toward neither himself nor others. And how, monks, is a person full of enmity toward himself? Here, monks, a certain person dwells with a mind obsessed by ill will and accompanied by hatred. This is called a person full of enmity toward himself. And how, monks, is a person full of enmity toward others? Here, monks, a certain person dwells with a mind obsessed by ill will and accompanied by hatred. This is called a person full of enmity toward others. And how, monks, is a person full of enmity toward both himself and others? Here, monks, a certain person dwells with a mind obsessed by ill will and accompanied by hatred. This is called a person full of enmity toward both himself and others. And how, monks, is a person full of enmity toward neither himself nor others? Here, monks, a certain person dwells with a mind free from ill will, pure and cleansed of hatred. This is called a person full of enmity toward neither himself nor others. These, monks, are the four kinds of persons found existing in the world.”
Then the householder Anāthapiṇḍika approached the Blessed One;
having approached and paid homage to the Blessed One, he sat down to one side. As the householder Anāthapiṇḍika was sitting to one side, the Blessed One said this to him:
“Householder, without abandoning five fears and enmities, one is called ‘immoral,’ and one is reborn in hell.”
Which five? Taking life, taking what is not given, sexual misconduct, false speech, and the use of fermented and distilled liquors that cause heedlessness—
householder, it is one who has not abandoned these five fears and enmities who is called "immoral" and is reborn in hell.
Householder, having abandoned five fears and enmities, one is called "virtuous" and is reborn in a happy destination.
What are the five?
Killing living beings, taking what is not given, sexual misconduct, false speech, and the use of fermented and distilled liquors that cause heedlessness.
Householder, having abandoned these five fears and enmities, one is called "virtuous" and is reborn in a happy destination.
Householder, one who takes life generates fear and enmity both in this present life and in future lives on account of taking life,
and experiences mental pain and dejection.
One who abstains from taking life does not engender fear or enmity pertaining to the present life,
nor does he engender fear or enmity pertaining to future lives, nor does he experience mental suffering or dejection.
For one who abstains from taking life, that fear and enmity are thus stilled.
“Householder, as for one who takes what is not given… [as before] … Householder,
as for one who engages in sexual misconduct… [as before] … Householder,
as for one who speaks falsehood… [as before] …”

Householder, when one who indulges in fermented liquor, distilled spirits, and intoxicants as a basis for negligence produces fear and enmity both in this present life and in future lives, and experiences mental pain and dejection, one who abstains from fermented liquor, distilled spirits, and intoxicants as a basis for negligence produces neither fear and enmity in this present life... [nor in future lives]... nor does he experience mental pain and dejection.
One produces fear and enmity; one does not produce fear and enmity pertaining to the future life, nor does one experience mental suffering and dejection.
For one who abstains from the use of fermented liquor, spirits, and intoxicants which are the basis for negligence, that fear and enmity are thus stilled.
He who takes life,
speaks falsehood,
and takes what is not given in the world;
He goes to another's wife,
and that man who is devoted to the drinking of fermented and distilled liquors.
Having not abandoned the five enmities,
one is called "immoral";
at the breaking up of the body, the one of poor wisdom—
He is reborn in hell—
he who does not take life and does not speak falsehoods.
In this world, he does not take what is not given,
he does not go to another's wife,
and [he abstains from] the drinking of fermented and distilled liquors.
The person who does not pursue [the five hindrances],
having abandoned the five enmities,
is called "virtuous."
With the breakup of the body,
the wise one is reborn in a happy destination. Thus ends the fourth [sutta].

Aṅguttara Nikāya 5.175 18. Upāsakavagga Caṇḍālasutta “Bhikkhus, there are these five kinds of outcasts. What five? One who is an outcast by birth; one who is an outcast by conduct; one who is an outcast by both birth and conduct; one who is not an outcast by birth but is an outcast by conduct; and one who is not an outcast by birth nor an outcast by conduct. And how, bhikkhus, is one an outcast by birth? Here, someone is born of an outcast mother, or of an outcast father, or of an outcast mother and father. This is how one is an outcast by birth. And how, bhikkhus, is one an outcast by conduct? Here, someone destroys life, takes what is not given, engages in sexual misconduct, speaks falsely, and indulges in fermented liquor and spirits, which are the basis for negligence. This is how one is an outcast by conduct. And how, bhikkhus, is one an outcast by both birth and conduct? Here, someone is born of an outcast mother, or of an outcast father, or of an outcast mother and father, and he also destroys life, takes what is not given, engages in sexual misconduct, speaks falsely, and indulges in fermented liquor and spirits, which are the basis for negligence. This is how one is an outcast by both birth and conduct. And how, bhikkhus, is one not an outcast by birth but is an outcast by conduct? Here, someone is not born of an outcast mother, or of an outcast father, or of an outcast mother and father, yet he destroys life, takes what is not given, engages in sexual misconduct, speaks falsely, and indulges in fermented liquor and spirits, which are the basis for negligence. This is how one is not an outcast by birth but is an outcast by conduct. And how, bhikkhus, is one not an outcast by birth nor an outcast by conduct? Here, someone is not born of an outcast mother, or of an outcast father, or of an outcast mother and father, and he does not destroy life, take what is not given, engage in sexual misconduct, speak falsely, or indulge in fermented liquor and spirits, which are the basis for negligence. This is how one is not an outcast by birth nor an outcast by conduct. These, bhikkhus, are the five kinds of outcasts.”

“Bhikkhus, possessing five qualities, a lay follower is a candāla among lay followers, a stain among lay followers, and a reproach among lay followers. What are the five? [The text continues with the list of these qualities.]”
He is faithless;
he is immoral;
he is a superstitious omens-seeker, relying on auspicious signs rather than on kamma.
And he seeks out those worthy of offerings outside of this [Saṅgha],
and there he performs meritorious deeds first.
Endowed with these five qualities, monks, a lay follower is a Caṇḍāla among lay followers, a stain among lay followers, and one who is despised among lay followers.
“Monks, endowed with five qualities, a lay follower is a jewel among lay followers, a lotus among lay followers, and a white lotus among lay followers.
With which five?
He is possessed of faith;”
He is virtuous;
he does not regard superstitious omens as auspicious, but trusts in kamma rather than omens;
he does not seek out those worthy of offerings outside of this [Sāsana].
And here he performs meritorious deeds first.
Possessing these five qualities, monks, a lay follower is a jewel among lay followers, a lotus among lay followers, and a white lotus among lay followers.
The fifth.
Aṅguttara Nikāya 5.176 18.

Upāsakavagga Pītisutta (The Discourse on Rapture) “Monks, there are these five kinds of rapture. What five? Rapture born of seclusion, rapture born of concentration, rapture born of tranquility, rapture born of happiness, and rapture born of equanimity. These, monks, are the five kinds of rapture.”
Then the householder Anāthapiṇḍika, surrounded by about five hundred lay followers, approached the Blessed One;
having approached and paid homage to the Blessed One, he sat down to one side. To one side...
As the householder Anāthapiṇḍika was seated, the Blessed One said this to him:
“Householder, you have attended upon the Saṅgha of bhikkhus with robes, almsfood, lodgings, and medicinal requisites for the sick.
But, householder, one should not be satisfied with that alone.”
‘We have attended upon the Saṅgha of bhikkhus with robes, almsfood, lodgings, and medicinal requisites for the sick.
Therefore, householder, you should train yourself thus:
‘How can we, from time to time, dwell having attained the rapture of seclusion?’”
“In this way, householder, you should train yourself.
When this was said, the Venerable Sāriputta said to the Blessed One:
“It is wonderful, Bhante! It is marvelous, Bhante!”
“Excellent indeed, Bhante, has this been well-spoken by the Blessed One:
‘Householder, you have attended upon the Saṅgha of bhikkhus with robes, almsfood, lodgings, and medicinal requisites for the sick.
But, householder, one should not be satisfied with that alone.’”
“We attend upon the Saṅgha of bhikkhus with robes, almsfood, lodgings, and medicinal requisites for the sick.
Therefore, householder, you should train yourself thus:
“How can we, from time to time, enter and dwell in the rapture of seclusion?”
"In this way, householder, you should train yourself.
"Venerable sir, when a noble disciple dwells having attained the rapture of seclusion, five things do not exist for him at that time.
Whatever suffering and mental distress associated with sensual pleasures there may be, that too does not exist for him at that time."
At that time, whatever pleasure and joy associated with sensual desires he might have does not exist;
at that time, whatever pain and grief associated with the unwholesome he might have does not exist;
at that time, whatever pleasure and joy associated with the unwholesome he might have does not exist.
“Even that suffering and mental distress associated with the wholesome does not exist for him at that time.
Venerable sir, when a noble disciple dwells having attained the rapture of seclusion, these five states do not exist for him at that time.
“Excellent, excellent, Sāriputta!”
Sāriputta, at whatever time a noble disciple dwells having attained the rapture of seclusion, five things do not exist for him at that time.
Whatever suffering and grief associated with sensual pleasures he might have, that too does not exist for him at that time.
Whatever pleasure and joy associated with sensual pleasures he might have, that too does not exist for him at that time.
At that time, whatever suffering and mental distress associated with the unwholesome he may have, that too does not exist for him at that time.
Whatever pleasure and mental joy associated with the unwholesome he may have, that too does not exist for him at that time.
Whatever suffering and mental distress associated with the wholesome he may have, that too does not exist for him at that time.
“Sāriputta, at whatever time a noble disciple dwells having attained the rapture of seclusion, on that occasion these five states do not exist for him.
(The Sixth) Aṅguttara Nikāya 5.177

18. Upāsakavagga Vaṇijjāsutta (Discourse on Commerce) “Monks, there are these five kinds of commerce that should not be practiced by a lay follower who has gone for refuge. What five? Commerce in weapons, commerce in human beings, commerce in meat, commerce in intoxicants, and commerce in poisons. These, monks, are the five kinds of commerce that should not be practiced by a lay follower who has gone for refuge.”
“Bhikkhus, there are these five trades that a lay follower should not engage in.
Which five?
Trading in weapons, trading in living beings, trading in meat, trading in intoxicants, and trading in poisons.”
“Monks, these five trades should not be practiced by a lay follower.
The seventh.
Aṅguttara Nikāya 5.178.

18. Upāsakavagga Rājāsutta (AN 5.178, PTS AN iii 208) “Monks, there are these four kinds of kings. What four? The wheel-turning monarch, monks; the universal monarch, monks; the regional king, monks; and the bandit-king, monks. These, monks, are the four kinds of kings. Of these four kinds of kings, monks, which one is the best? “It is the wheel-turning monarch, venerable sir. “But why, monks, is the wheel-turning monarch the best among these four kinds of kings? “Because, venerable sir, the wheel-turning monarch is one who has conquered by the Dhamma, who rules by the Dhamma, and who possesses the seven treasures. Therefore, venerable sir, the wheel-turning monarch is the best among these four kinds of kings. “Monks, there are these four kinds of persons. What four? Of these four kinds of persons, monks, which one is the best? “It is the wheel-turning monarch, venerable sir. “But why, monks, is the wheel-turning monarch the best among these four kinds of persons? “Because, venerable sir, the wheel-turning monarch is one who has conquered by the Dhamma, who rules by the Dhamma, and who possesses the seven treasures. Therefore, venerable sir, the wheel-turning monarch is the best among these four kinds of persons. “Monks, there are these four kinds of persons. What four? The person who is like a wheel-turning monarch; the person who is like a universal monarch; the person who is like a regional king; and the person who is like a bandit-king. These, monks, are the four kinds of persons. Of these four kinds of persons, monks, which one is the best? “It is the person who is like a wheel-turning monarch, venerable sir. “But why, monks, is the person who is like a wheel-turning monarch the best among these four kinds of persons? “Because, venerable sir, the person who is like a wheel-turning monarch is one who has conquered by the Dhamma, who rules by the Dhamma, and who possesses the seven treasures. Therefore, venerable sir, the person who is like a wheel-turning monarch is the best among these four kinds of persons. “Monks, there are these four kinds of persons. What four? The person who is like a wheel-turning monarch; the person who is like a universal monarch; the person who is like a regional king; and the person who is like a bandit-king. Of these four kinds of persons, monks, which one is the best? “It is the person who is like a wheel-turning monarch, venerable sir. “But why, monks, is the person who is like a wheel-turning monarch the best among these four kinds of persons? “Because, venerable sir, the person who is like a wheel-turning monarch is one who has conquered by the Dhamma, who rules by the Dhamma, and who possesses the seven treasures. Therefore, venerable sir, the person who is like a wheel-turning monarch is the best among these four kinds of persons. “What, monks, is the treasure of the wheel for the person who is like a wheel-turning monarch? Here, monks, the person who is like a wheel-turning monarch is a noble warrior, consecrated by sprinkling, a conqueror of the earth, having reached its ocean boundaries, established in the Dhamma, ruling by the Dhamma. When he rises on the morning of the full-moon day, having bathed his head and ascended the upper palace chamber, surrounded by his ministers, that great divine wheel-treasure appears before him, thousand-spoked, complete with felloe and hub, made of gold, and perfectly formed. ‘Wherever the lord wishes, let the wheel-turning monarch turn the wheel,’ they say. Then, monks, the wheel-turning monarch rises from his seat, takes a ceremonial cloth, and places it on his right shoulder. He descends from the palace, mounts his state elephant adorned with trappings, and proceeds toward the eastern direction, followed by the fourfold army. There, wherever the wheel-turning monarch turns the wheel, the rival kings in the eastern direction come out to meet him, saying: ‘Come, sire! Welcome, sire! We are yours, sire; we belong to you, sire. May the lord rule over us as our overlord. Thus, monks, the wheel-turning monarch conquers the eastern direction by the Dhamma, without violence, without weapons.

Having conquered the eastern direction by the Dhamma, without violence, without weapons, he establishes security. Then, monks, the wheel-turning monarch proceeds toward the southern direction, followed by the fourfold army... [and so on for the western and northern directions] ...Thus, monks, the wheel-turning monarch conquers the four quarters by the Dhamma, without violence, without weapons. Having conquered the four quarters by the Dhamma, without violence, without weapons, he establishes security. When he has conquered the earth, bounded by the ocean, this great divine wheel-treasure remains in the royal capital, stationed in the air, as a sign of his sovereignty. This, monks, is the treasure of the wheel for the person who is like a wheel-turning monarch. What, monks, is the treasure of the elephant for the person who is like a wheel-turning monarch? Here, monks, the person who is like a wheel-turning monarch has an elephant-treasure, white as a snow-clad mountain, with a head like a choice bull, with sevenfold limbs, a trunk like a choice bull’s, and a tail like a brocade banner. It is well-trained, obedient, and swift, able to go wherever the lord wishes. This, monks, is the treasure of the elephant for the person who is like a wheel-turning monarch. What, monks, is the treasure of the horse for the person who is like a wheel-turning monarch? Here, monks, the person who is like a wheel-turning monarch has a horse-treasure, the color of an antelope, with a head like a choice bull, with sevenfold limbs, a mane like a choice bull’s, and a tail like a brocade banner. It is well-trained, obedient, and swift, able to go wherever the lord wishes. This, monks, is the treasure of the horse for the person who is like a wheel-turning monarch. What, monks, is the treasure of the jewel for the person who is like a wheel-turning monarch? Here, monks, the person who is like a wheel-turning monarch has a jewel-treasure, pure, eight-faceted, well-cut, brilliant, possessing all excellent qualities, and radiant. This, monks, is the treasure of the jewel for the person who is like a wheel-turning monarch. What, monks, is the treasure of the woman for the person who is like a wheel-turning monarch? Here, monks, the person who is like a wheel-turning monarch has a woman-treasure, beautiful, fair to behold, charming, not inferior in complexion, with skin like fine gold, neither too tall nor too short, neither too thin nor too stout, neither too dark nor too pale. She is endowed with the supreme beauty of women. Her eyes do not tire of gazing at her, nor does she tire of being gazed upon. This, monks, is the treasure of the woman for the person who is like a wheel-turning monarch. What, monks, is the treasure of the steward for the person who is like a wheel-turning monarch? Here, monks, the person who is like a wheel-turning monarch has a steward-treasure, wise, intelligent, and astute, capable of managing wealth. Whatever kind of wealth there is—whether gold, silver, gems, pearls, lapis lazuli, shells, crystals, or coral—he knows how to acquire it, how to preserve it, and how to increase it. This, monks, is the treasure of the steward for the person who is like a wheel-turning monarch. What, monks, is the treasure of the counselor for the person who is like a wheel-turning monarch? Here, monks, the person who is like a wheel-turning monarch has a counselor-treasure, wise, intelligent, and astute, capable of discerning what is beneficial and what is harmful. He knows the proper time for the king to go forth, the time to return, the time for peace, the time for war, and the time for the mobilization of the fourfold army. This, monks, is the treasure of the counselor for the person who is like a wheel-turning monarch. These, monks, are the seven treasures of the person who is like a wheel-turning monarch. And what, monks, is the person who is like a universal monarch? Here, monks, a certain person is a noble warrior, consecrated by sprinkling, a conqueror of the earth, having reached its ocean boundaries, established in the Dhamma, ruling by the Dhamma. “What do you think, monks?
Have you ever seen or heard:
‘This person, having abandoned the taking of life, abstains from taking life’?”
“Would kings, having seized him, on account of his abstention from taking life, kill him, imprison him, banish him, or subject him to whatever penalty is appropriate?
“Certainly not, Bhante.
“Good, monks.”
“Monks, I too have neither seen nor heard this:
‘This person, having abandoned the taking of life, abstains from taking life;
yet kings, having seized him on account of that very abstinence from taking life, kill him, imprison him, banish him, or subject him to whatever treatment they see fit.’”
Moreover, they proclaim his evil deed exactly as it was:
"This man has deprived a woman or a man of life.
Then the kings, having seized him, for the sake of taking life, either kill him, bind him, banish him, or deal with him according to the circumstances.
“Have you ever seen or heard of such a thing?
“We have seen it, venerable sir, we have heard of it, and we shall hear of it.
“What do you think, monks?”
“Have you ever seen or heard of this: that kings,
having seized a man for abandoning taking what is not given and for abstaining from taking what is not given,
kill him, imprison him, banish him, or subject him to whatever penalty is appropriate on account of his abstention from taking what is not given?”
“No, venerable sir.
“Good, bhikkhus.
This too, bhikkhus, has neither been seen nor heard by me:”
‘This man, having abandoned taking what is not given, abstains from taking what is not given.
Then the kings, having seized him on account of his abstention from taking what is not given, either execute him, imprison him, banish him, or subject him to various penalties.
Moreover, they proclaim his evil deed exactly as it was.
‘This man has taken from a village or from a forest what was not given, which constitutes theft.
When kings have him seized on account of that taking of what was not given, do they not then kill him, or bind him, or banish him, or deal with him according to the circumstances?
“Have you ever seen or heard of such a thing? he asked.
“Venerable sir, we have seen it, heard it, and shall hear it again.
“What do you think, bhikkhus?
Have you ever seen or heard this:”
“‘This person, having abandoned sexual misconduct, abstains from sexual misconduct.
Would kings, having seized him for that reason of abstaining from sexual misconduct, kill him, imprison him, banish him, or subject him to some other penalty?
“Certainly not, Bhante.”
“Excellent, bhikkhus!
Even by me, bhikkhus, this has neither been seen nor heard:
‘This person, having abandoned sexual misconduct, abstains from sexual misconduct.’”
“Having seized him, kings—on account of his abstention from sexual misconduct—either execute him, imprison him, banish him, or impose some other penalty as the case may require.
Furthermore, they proclaim his evil deed thus:
“This man has committed misconduct with another’s wives and with other young maidens.”
“Having seized him, kings—on account of sexual misconduct—either execute him, imprison him, banish him, or deal with him according to the circumstances.
Have you ever seen or heard of such a thing?
“We have seen it, venerable sir, we have heard of it, and we shall hear of it.”
“What do you think, bhikkhus,
have you ever seen or heard this:
‘This person, having abandoned false speech, abstains from false speech’?”
“Having seized him, kings—on account of his abstention from false speech—either execute him, imprison him, banish him, or deal with him as the circumstances require.
“Certainly not, Bhante.
“Good, monks.”
“Monks, I too have neither seen nor heard this: that a king,
having seized a man for the reason that he has abandoned false speech and abstains from false speech,
would execute him, imprison him, banish him, or subject him to whatever penalty is appropriate.”
Moreover, they report his evil deed exactly as it was:
"This man has ruined the interests of a householder or a householder’s son by means of false speech.
Then the kings, having seized him on account of that false speech, either execute him, imprison him, banish him, or deal with him according to the circumstances.
“Have you ever seen or heard of such a thing?
“We have seen it, venerable sir, we have heard of it, and we shall hear of it.
“What do you think, bhikkhus?”
“Have you ever seen or heard this:
‘This man, having abandoned the occasion for negligence consisting of fermented liquor, spirits, and intoxicants, abstains from fermented liquor, spirits, and intoxicants;

yet kings, having seized him on account of that very abstinence from fermented liquor, spirits, and intoxicants, execute him, imprison him, banish him, or subject him to whatever penalty they see fit’?”

“Good, bhikkhus.

‘This man, having abandoned the occasion for negligence consisting in fermented liquor, spirits, and intoxicants, abstains from fermented liquor, spirits, and intoxicants.

Moreover, they proclaim his evil deed exactly as it was.
‘This man, addicted to fermented liquor, spirits, and intoxicants which are the basis for negligence, has deprived a woman or a man of life;
this man, addicted to fermented liquor, spirits, and intoxicants which are the basis for negligence, has taken from a village or a forest what was not given, constituting theft;

“Suppose this man, addicted to fermented liquor, spirits, and intoxicants which cause negligence, were to ruin the affairs of a householder or a householder’s son by means of false speech.

Then the kings, having seized him, would for the sake of his addiction to fermented liquor, spirits, and intoxicants which cause negligence, either execute him, imprison him, banish him, or deal with him according to the circumstances.
Have you ever seen or heard of such a thing?”
“Venerable sir, we have seen it, we have heard it, and we shall hear it again.

18. Upāsakavagga Gihisutta (AN 5.179, PTS AN iii 211) “Monks, there are these five benefits for a householder who is a lay follower (*upāsaka*). What five? First, he gains wealth not previously acquired. Second, whatever wealth he has acquired does not diminish. Third, he acquires a good reputation. Fourth, he enters the assembly with confidence. Fifth, at the breaking up of the body, after death, he is reborn in a happy destination, in a heavenly world. These, monks, are the five benefits for a householder who is a lay follower.”
Then the householder Anāthapiṇḍika, surrounded by about five hundred lay followers, approached the Blessed One; having approached and paid homage to the Blessed One, he sat down to one side.
Then the Blessed One addressed the Venerable Sāriputta:
“Sāriputta, you should know whatever white-robed householder whose conduct is restrained by the five training rules.”
One who gains at will, without difficulty, and without trouble these four higher mental states that provide a pleasant dwelling in this very life, could, if they so desired, declare of themselves:

“Hell is exhausted for me; the animal realm is exhausted for me; the sphere of afflicted spirits is exhausted for me; the states of deprivation, the bad destinations, and the lower realms are exhausted for me. I am a stream-enterer, no longer subject to rebirth in the lower worlds, fixed in destiny, and assured of full enlightenment.”
In what five training rules is his conduct restrained? Here, Sāriputta,
a noble disciple abstains from the destruction of life, abstains from taking what is not given,
abstains from sexual misconduct, abstains from false speech, and abstains from fermented liquor, spirits, and intoxicants which are the basis for negligence.
In these five training rules, one’s actions are restrained.
Of which four higher mental states, pleasant dwellings in this very life, is he a recipient at will, a recipient without difficulty, a recipient without hardship?
Here, Sāriputta, a noble disciple possesses unwavering confidence in the Buddha: [text continues]

‘Such indeed is the Blessed One: worthy, perfectly enlightened, endowed with clear vision and conduct, sublime, knower of the worlds, unsurpassed leader of persons to be tamed, teacher of gods and humans, the Buddha, the Blessed One.
This is his first abiding in happiness in this very life, pertaining to the higher mind, attained for the purification of the impure mind and for the cleansing of the uncleansed mind.
Furthermore, Sāriputta, a noble disciple possesses verified confidence in the Dhamma:
‘The Dhamma has been well-proclaimed by the Blessed One; it is visible here and now, timeless, inviting one to come and see, leading onward, and to be personally realized by the wise.

This is his second attainment of a blissful abiding in this very life, pertaining to the higher mind, which has been reached for the purification of the unpurified mind and for the cleansing of the uncleansed mind.
Furthermore, Sāriputta, a noble disciple possesses unwavering confidence in the Saṅgha:
‘The Saṅgha of the Blessed One’s disciples is practicing well; the Saṅgha of the Blessed One’s disciples is practicing straightly; the Saṅgha of the Blessed One’s disciples is practicing rightly;
the Saṅgha of the Blessed One’s disciples is practicing appropriately—namely, the four pairs of persons, the eight types of individuals.
This Saṅgha of the Blessed One’s disciples is worthy of offerings, worthy of hospitality, worthy of gifts, worthy of reverential salutation.’
‘an unsurpassed field of merit for the world.
This is the third abiding in higher consciousness that he has attained, which is a pleasant dwelling in this very life for the purification of the impure mind and the cleansing of the unclean mind.

Furthermore, Sāriputta, the noble disciple is endowed with virtues dear to the noble ones—virtues that are untorn, unbroken, unspotted, unmottled, liberating, praised by the wise, unadhered-to, and conducive to concentration.
This is his fourth higher mental abiding, a dwelling in happiness in this very life, attained for the purification of the impure mind and for the cleansing of the uncleansed mind.
He becomes one who obtains these four higher mental abidings at will, without difficulty, and without hardship.
Sāriputta, whatever layperson clothed in white you may know who has their conduct restrained by these five training rules—

And as one who obtains at will, without difficulty, and without toil these four states of sublime mind that provide a pleasant dwelling in this very life, he—should he so desire—could declare of himself:

"Hell is exhausted for me; the animal realm is exhausted; the sphere of hungry ghosts is exhausted; states of deprivation, bad destinations, and the lower worlds are exhausted. I am a stream-enterer, no longer subject to rebirth in the lower worlds, fixed in destiny, and assured of full enlightenment."
Having seen the fear in the hells,
one should avoid evil deeds;
having undertaken the noble Dhamma, one should practice it.
The wise person should avoid it.
One should not harm living beings when there is a way to act with restraint.
One should not speak falsely knowing the truth,
nor should one take what is not given;
being content with one's own wife, one should live.
One should not take pleasure in another's wife;
a person should not drink fermented liquor or spirits that delude the mind.
One should recollect the Perfectly Enlightened One and reflect upon the Dhamma;
one's mind should be free from ill will and intent on welfare.
One should cultivate [the mind] for the sake of the world of the gods.
When the gift to be given has been set forth,
for one who desires merit and seeks to attain it;
A gift given first to the virtuous becomes a vast offering.
I shall indeed speak of those who are virtuous:
Listen to me, Sāriputta:
thus it is among those that are black, white,
red, or yellow.
Whether among dappled cows,
or brindled ones, or those as white as pigeons— among any such as these,
A tamed bull is born:
steadfast, endowed with strength,
and possessing noble speed.
They yoke that very one to the burden,
and do not adorn his appearance;
even so it is among human beings.
In whatever birth it may be—
whether as a khattiya, a brahmin,
a vessa, a sudda, a caṇḍāla, or a pukkusa.
Whosoever among these [beings] is born tamed, virtuous,
established in the Dhamma, and endowed with moral discipline—
A speaker of truth, possessed of moral shame,
who has abandoned birth and death,
perfected in the holy life;
One who has laid down the burden, is detached, has done what was to be done, is free from taints,
and has gone beyond all phenomena—
Extinguished through non-clinging;
in that stainless field,
the offering becomes vast.
Foolish, ignorant,
witless, and unlearned,
they give gifts to those outside [the Sangha].
For they do not wait upon those who are virtuous.
But those who wait upon the virtuous— those wise ones esteemed as steadfast— [attain excellence].
And their faith in the Sugata is rooted and firmly established;
they go to the world of the gods.
Or they may be born here in noble families;
the wise gradually attain Nibbāna.”

The Chapter on Lay Followers (Upāsakavagga)
The Gavesī Sutta (AN 5.180).
On one occasion the Blessed One was wandering on tour among the Kosalans together with a large Saṅgha of bhikkhus.
While traveling along the highway, the Blessed One saw a great sāla grove in a certain place.
Having seen it, he left the road and approached that sāla grove. Having approached and entered deep into that sāla grove, he manifested a smile in a certain place.
Then, this thought occurred to the Venerable Ānanda:
“What, indeed, is the cause, what is the reason for the Blessed One’s manifestation of a smile?
Tathāgatas do not manifest a smile without a reason.
Then the Venerable Ānanda said this to the Blessed One:
“Venerable sir, what is the cause, what is the reason for the Blessed One’s manifestation of a smile?
Tathāgatas do not manifest a smile without a reason.
“Formerly, Ānanda, in this very place there was a city, prosperous, flourishing, populous, and crowded with people.”
Now, Ānanda, the Blessed One Kassapa, the Arahant, the Perfectly Enlightened One, lived depending on that city.
And, Ānanda, the Blessed One Kassapa, the Arahant, the Perfectly Enlightened One, had a lay follower named Gavesī who was imperfect in his observance of the precepts.
By that lay follower Gavesī, about five hundred lay followers were encouraged and exhorted to become likewise imperfect in their observance of the precepts.
Then, Ānanda, it occurred to the lay follower Gavesī:

“I have been of great assistance to these five hundred lay followers; I am their leader and their inspirer. Yet I myself am not one who fulfills the precepts, and these five hundred lay followers are also not ones who fulfill the precepts.
Thus we are equal, with nothing whatsoever remaining superior.”
“Come now, let me go beyond [this].
Then, Ānanda, the lay follower Gavesī approached those five hundred lay followers; having approached them, he said to those five hundred lay followers:
“From this day forward, venerable sirs, consider me one who practices the precepts in their entirety.”
Then, Ānanda, it occurred to those five hundred lay followers:
"The venerable Gavesī has been very helpful to us; he was our leader and our inspirer.
Surely the venerable Gavesī will be one who fulfills the precepts."
"What then, indeed, shall we do?
Then, Ānanda, those five hundred lay followers went to where the lay follower Gavesī was; having approached, they said this to the lay follower Gavesī:
"From this day forward, let Master Gavesī consider these five hundred lay followers as well as being fulfillers of the precepts."
Then, Ānanda, it occurred to the lay follower Gavesī:

“I have indeed been of great assistance to these five hundred lay followers, their leader and their inspirer; I am one who practices the precepts in their entirety, and these five hundred lay followers also practice the precepts in their entirety.
Thus, we are equals; there is nothing by which I am superior.”
"Come now, let me go beyond [this].
Then, Ānanda, the lay follower Gavesī approached those five hundred lay followers; having approached them, he said this to those five hundred lay followers:
"From this day forward, venerable sirs, consider me one who lives the holy life, one who acts with restraint, and who has abstained from sexual intercourse, the common practice of village life."
Then, Ānanda, it occurred to those five hundred lay followers:
“The venerable Gavesī has been very helpful to us; he was our forerunner and our inspirer.
Indeed, the venerable Gavesī will be one who leads the holy life, living apart and abstaining from sexual intercourse, that village practice.”
"How much more so, then, should we?
Then, Ānanda, those five hundred lay followers went to where the lay follower Gavesī was; having approached, they said this to the lay follower Gavesī:
"From this day forward, may Master Gavesī consider these five hundred lay followers as celibate practitioners, living apart, abstaining from sexual intercourse and the ways of village life."
Then, Ānanda, it occurred to the lay follower Gavesī:
“I have indeed been of great help to these five hundred lay followers; I am their leader and their inspirer.
And I myself am one who fulfills the precepts.”
These five hundred lay followers as well are fulfillers of the precepts.
I am one who lives the holy life, living far from it and abstaining from sexual intercourse, the village custom;
these five hundred lay followers as well live the holy life, living far from it and abstaining from sexual intercourse, the village custom.
"This is equal, there is nothing superior to it;
come now, let me provide what is superior.
Then, Ānanda, the lay follower Gavesī approached those five hundred lay followers; having approached, he said this to those five hundred lay followers:
"From this day forward, venerable sirs, consider me one who eats but one meal a day, who abstains at night, and who refrains from eating at improper times.
Then, Ānanda, it occurred to those five hundred lay followers:
"The noble Gavesī has been very helpful to us; he is our leader and our inspirer."
“Indeed, Master Gavesī will be one who eats but one meal a day, refrains from eating at night, and abstains from eating at improper times.
Why then should we not do the same?
Then, Ānanda, those five hundred lay followers went to where the lay follower Gavesī was; having approached, they said this to the lay follower Gavesī:

“From this day forward, may the noble Gavesī consider these five hundred lay followers as those who eat but one meal a day, abstaining from eating at night and refraining from food outside the proper time.
Then, Ānanda, it occurred to the lay follower Gavesī:
“I have indeed been of great benefit to these five hundred lay followers; I am their leader and the one who inspired them.”
I am one who fulfills the precepts;
these five hundred lay followers are also ones who fulfill the precepts.
I am a celibate, living far from sexual intercourse, abstaining from the village practice of sexual union.
These five hundred lay followers are celibate, living apart, abstaining from sexual intercourse and the village practice.
And I am one who eats but one meal a day, refraining at night and abstaining from eating at improper times.
These five hundred lay followers are also those who eat but one meal a day, refraining at night and abstaining from eating at improper times.
"This is equal, there is nothing superior to it;
come now, let me seek what is superior.

Then, Ānanda, the lay follower Gavesī approached the Blessed One Kassapa, the Arahant, the Perfectly Enlightened One; having approached, he said this to the Blessed One Kassapa, the Arahant, the Perfectly Enlightened One:
“Venerable sir, may I receive the going-forth in the presence of the Blessed One; may I receive the full admission.
Ānanda, the lay follower Gavesī received the going-forth in the presence of the Blessed One Kassapa, the Arahant, the Perfectly Enlightened One; he received the full admission.
Not long after his full admission, the bhikkhu Gavesī, dwelling alone, withdrawn, diligent, ardent, and resolute...

Dwelling thus, before long he realized for himself through direct knowledge, in this very life, that unsurpassed consummation of the holy life for the sake of which clansmen rightly go forth from the household life into homelessness; and having entered upon it, he dwelt therein.
He directly knew: "Birth is exhausted, the holy life has been lived, what was to be done has been done, there is no more of this state of being."
And furthermore, Ānanda, the bhikkhu Gavesī became an arahant.
Then, Ānanda, it occurred to those five hundred lay followers:
"Master Gavesī has been very helpful to us; he was our leader and our inspirer."
"Indeed, our noble master, seeking [the higher good], will shave off his hair and beard, don saffron robes, and go forth from the home life into homelessness.
How much more so, then, should we?

Then, Ānanda, those five hundred lay followers approached the Blessed One Kassapa, the Arahant, the Perfectly Enlightened One; having approached, they said this to the Blessed One Kassapa, the Arahant, the Perfectly Enlightened One:
“Venerable sir, may we receive the going-forth in the presence of the Blessed One; may we receive the full ordination.
Ānanda, those five hundred lay followers received the going-forth in the presence of the Blessed One Kassapa, the Arahant, the Perfectly Enlightened One, and they received the full ordination.
Then, Ānanda, it occurred to the bhikkhu Gavesī:
‘I am indeed one who obtains this unsurpassed bliss of liberation at will, without difficulty, and without hardship.
Oh, that these five hundred bhikkhus might also obtain this unsurpassed bliss of liberation at will, without difficulty, and without hardship!
Then, Ānanda, those five hundred bhikkhus, secluded, diligent, ardent, and resolute—

Dwelling there, before long they realized for themselves through direct knowledge, in this very life, that unsurpassed culmination of the holy life, for the sake of which young men of good family rightly go forth from the household life into homelessness; and having attained it, they dwelt therein.
They directly knew: "Birth is exhausted, the holy life has been lived, what was to be done has been done, there is no more of this state of being."
"Thus indeed, Ānanda, those five hundred bhikkhus headed by Gavesī, striving for what was ever higher and more sublime, realized unsurpassed liberation.
Therefore, Ānanda, you should train yourselves thus:
'Striving for what is ever higher and more sublime, we shall realize unsurpassed liberation.'"
"In this way, Ānanda, you should train yourselves.
Tenth. The Third Chapter on Lay Followers.
Its summary verse:
Fearfulness, the fearless one, hell,
enmity, and the outcaste as the fifth.
Trade, kings, and householders who seek [the Dhamma]. —
Aṅguttara Nikāya 5.181

19. Araññavagga Āraññikasutta (AN 5.181, PTS AN iii 219) “Monks, there are these five qualities of one who dwells in the forest. What five? He is one who dwells in the forest, he is one who frequents the forest, he is one who delights in the forest, he is one who is content with what is found in the forest, and he is one who has mastery over the states of mind that arise in the forest. These, monks, are the five qualities of one who dwells in the forest.”
“Bhikkhus, there are these five kinds of forest-dwellers.
What are the five?
One is a forest-dweller out of dullness and stupidity; one is a forest-dweller because of evil desires and being overcome by longing; one is a forest-dweller due to insanity or mental derangement...”
He is a forest-dweller; he is a forest-dweller because it is praised by the Buddhas and the disciples of the Buddhas.
Relying on fewness of desires, relying on contentment, relying on effacement, relying on seclusion, and relying on this very purpose, he is a forest-dweller.
These, monks, are the five forest-dwellers.
Of these five forest-dwellers, monks, it is this forest-dweller who, relying on fewness of wishes, relying on contentment,
relying on effacement, relying on seclusion, and relying on the goal of this very [practice]...
Relying on this, one becomes a forest-dweller; this [latter] is the foremost, the best, the most excellent, the highest, and the most sublime among these five types of forest-dwellers.

Just as, monks, from a cow comes milk, from milk curds, from curds butter, from butter ghee, and from ghee the cream of ghee—wherein the cream of ghee is declared to be the pinnacle; so too is this the case.
In the same way, monks, among these five kinds of forest-dwellers,
he who is a forest-dweller by relying on fewness of desires, on contentment, on effacement, on solitude,
and on this very purpose— this one is the foremost, the best, and the most excellent among these five kinds of forest-dwellers.
"And he is supreme and excellent.
First.
Aṅguttara Nikāya 5.182

19. Araññavagga Cīvarasutta (The Discourse on Robes) “Monks, there are these five benefits in wearing robes given by others. What five? One dwells at ease, thinking: ‘I have no concern for the procurement of robes. One dwells at ease, thinking: ‘I am free from the burden of robes. One dwells at ease, thinking: ‘I am free from the attachment to robes. One dwells at ease, thinking: ‘I can go wherever I wish without being hindered by robes. One dwells at ease, thinking: ‘I am independent of others regarding robes. These, monks, are the five benefits in wearing robes given by others.”
“Bhikkhus, there are these five kinds of refuse-rag wearers.
What are the five?
One is a refuse-rag wearer out of dullness and stupidity... [as before] ...one is a refuse-rag wearer depending on this very purpose.”
"These, monks, are the five types of rag-robe wearers.
Second.
Aṅguttara Nikāya 5.183

19. Araññavagga Rukkhamūlikasutta (AN 5.183, PTS AN iii 219) “Bhikkhus, there are these five benefits for one who dwells at the foot of a tree. What five? (1) It is easy to obtain a robe for one who dwells at the foot of a tree. (2) One who dwells at the foot of a tree has few troubles. (3) One who dwells at the foot of a tree is free from debt. (4) One who dwells at the foot of a tree is not dependent on others. (5) One who dwells at the foot of a tree delights in forest-dwelling. These, bhikkhus, are the five benefits for one who dwells at the foot of a tree.”
“Bhikkhus, there are these five kinds of tree-root dwellers.
Which five?
One is a tree-root dweller out of dullness and delusion; ... [as before] ... one is a tree-root dweller depending solely on this very purpose.”
“Monks, these are the five who dwell at the foot of trees.
The third [discourse]. Aṅguttara Nikāya 5.184
19. Araññavagga Sosānikasutta (Discourse on the Charnel-Ground Dweller) (AN 5.184, PTS AN iii 220)
“Bhikkhus, there are these five kinds of charnel-ground dwellers.
What are the five?
One dwells at the charnel ground out of dullness and stupidity; ... [and so on] ... one dwells at the charnel ground depending solely on the purpose [of meditation].”
“Monks, these are the five who frequent charnel grounds.
The fourth.
Aṅguttara Nikāya 5.185

19. Araññavagga Abbhokāsikasutta (AN 5.185, PTS AN iii 220) “Bhikkhus, there are these five benefits for one who dwells in the open air. What five? One becomes accustomed to cold; one becomes accustomed to heat; one becomes accustomed to contact with gadflies, mosquitoes, wind, sunburn, and creeping reptiles; one’s meditation is not dependent on others; and one gains mastery over the mind. These, bhikkhus, are the five benefits for one who dwells in the open air.”
“Bhikkhus, there are these five who dwell in the open air… [as above] … Fifth.
Aṅguttara Nikāya 5.186

19. The Forest-Dwelling Chapter The Discourse on Those Who Sleep in the Sitting Posture (Nesajjikasutta) “Monks, those who sleep in the sitting posture are rare in the world. Monks, those who subsist on forest roots and fruits are rare in the world. Monks, those who live on almsfood are rare in the world. Monks, those who wear rag-robes are rare in the world. Monks, those who dwell at the foot of a tree are rare in the world. Monks, those who dwell in the open air are rare in the world. Monks, those who dwell in a charnel ground are rare in the world. Monks, those who maintain the practice of sitting in the sitting posture are rare in the world.”
“Bhikkhus, there are these five who are perpetual sitters … [as above] … This is the sixth.
Aṅguttara Nikāya 5.187

19. Araññavagga: Yathāsanthatikasutta (AN 5.187, PTS AN iii 220) “Monks, when a bhikkhu is content with whatever seat is provided, he is said to be one who has laid down his burden, who has lived the holy life, who has done what was to be done, and who has shed the state of being subject to further becoming.”
“Bhikkhus, there are these five who are content with whatever seat is provided… [as above] … This is the seventh.
Aṅguttara Nikāya 5.188

19. Araññavagga Ekāsanikasutta (The Discourse on Those Who Eat Only One Meal a Day) “Monks, there are these five kinds of persons who eat only one meal a day. What five? (1) Here, monks, some person who eats only one meal a day dwells devoted to the development of the basis for spiritual power that consists in concentration due to energy and the faculty of energy. This is the first kind of person who eats only one meal a day. (2) Again, monks, some person who eats only one meal a day dwells devoted to the development of the basis for spiritual power that consists in concentration due to mind and the faculty of mind. This is the second kind of person who eats only one meal a day. (3) Again, monks, some person who eats only one meal a day dwells devoted to the development of the basis for spiritual power that consists in concentration due to investigation and the faculty of investigation. This is the third kind of person who eats only one meal a day. (4) Again, monks, some person who eats only one meal a day dwells devoted to the development of the basis for spiritual power that consists in concentration due to tranquility and the faculty of tranquility. This is the fourth kind of person who eats only one meal a day. (5) Again, monks, some person who eats only one meal a day dwells devoted to the development of the basis for spiritual power that consists in concentration due to discernment and the faculty of discernment. This is the fifth kind of person who eats only one meal a day. These, monks, are the five kinds of persons who eat only one meal a day.”
“Bhikkhus, there are these five who eat at a single sitting… [as above] … The eighth.
Aṅguttara Nikāya 5.189

19. Araññavagga Khalupacchābhattikasutta (AN 5.189, PTS AN iii 220) “Bhikkhus, there are these five benefits for one who eats his meal at the proper time and does not eat after the proper time. What five? (1) He has little work to do. (2) He has little to be concerned about. (3) He has little affliction. (4) His digestion is light. (5) He dwells with a mind that is clear and unclouded. These, bhikkhus, are the five benefits for one who eats his meal at the proper time and does not eat after the proper time.”
“Bhikkhus, there are these five who eat only what is left over from their meal… [as above]… Ninth.
Aṅguttara Nikāya 5.190

19. The Chapter on Forests: The Discourse on the Alms-Bowl Beggar (Araññavagga, Pattapiṇḍikasutta) “Bhikkhus, there are these five benefits for one who is a bowl-beggar. What five? (1) He dwells with few undertakings. (2) He dwells with a light livelihood. (3) He does not cause weariness to families. (4) He is free from the taint of storing up goods. (5) He is one who delights in the forest. These, bhikkhus, are the five benefits for one who is a bowl-beggar.”
“Bhikkhus, there are these five kinds of bowl-almsmen. Which five?
One is a bowl-almsman out of dullness and stupidity; one is a bowl-almsman out of evil desire and being overcome by craving; one is a bowl-almsman out of madness... [text continues] ...”
One becomes an eater from an alms-bowl because of mental distraction; one becomes an eater from an alms-bowl thinking, "This is praised by the Buddhas and the disciples of the Buddhas";

it is out of dependence on fewness of wishes, dependence on contentment, dependence on effacement, dependence on seclusion, and dependence on this very purpose that one becomes an eater from an alms-bowl.
"These, monks, are the five kinds of alms-food eaters. Of these five alms-food eaters, monks, it is the one who,
relying on having few desires, relying on contentment, relying on effacement, relying on seclusion, and relying on this very purpose..."
Relying on this, one becomes an alms-food eater; this one is the foremost, the best, the most excellent, the highest, and the most sublime among these five types of alms-food eaters.

Just as, monks, from a cow comes milk, from milk curds, from curds butter, from butter ghee, and from ghee the cream of ghee—wherein the cream of ghee is declared to be the very pinnacle; so too is this one the foremost among these five types of alms-food eaters.
In the same way, monks, among these five kinds of alms-collectors,
that alms-collector who collects alms by relying on fewness of desires, on contentment, on effacement, on seclusion,
and on aiming at this very goal— he is the foremost and the best among these five kinds of alms-collectors.
“Liberation is supreme and most excellent.
Tenth. The Fourth Chapter on Forests.
Its summary verse:
The forest, the robe, the tree,
the charnel ground, and the open-air dweller.
The practice of never lying down, the practice of using a single seat,
and the practice of not accepting food after the proper time.
(Aṅguttara Nikāya 5.191)

20. Brāhmaṇavagga Soṇasutta (AN 5.191, PTS AN iii 221) At Sāvatthī. Then the brahmin Soṇa approached the Blessed One; having approached, he exchanged greetings with the Blessed One. Having exchanged greetings of courtesy and amiable conversation, he sat down to one side. As he was sitting there, the Blessed One said this to him: “Brahmin, when a noble disciple possesses four things, he is one who has reached the ultimate conclusion, one who has done what was to be done, one who has laid down the burden, one who has attained his own goal, one whose fetters of existence are destroyed, one who is liberated through final knowledge. What four? Here, brahmin, a noble disciple possesses confirmed confidence in the Buddha thus: ‘The Blessed One is an arahant, perfectly enlightened, accomplished in true knowledge and conduct, fortunate, knower of the world, unsurpassed leader of persons to be tamed, teacher of devas and humans, the Buddha, the Blessed One. He possesses confirmed confidence in the Dhamma thus: ‘The Dhamma is well-expounded by the Blessed One, directly visible, immediate, inviting one to come and see, applicable, to be personally experienced by the wise. He possesses confirmed confidence in the Saṅgha thus: ‘The Saṅgha of the Blessed One’s disciples is practicing the good way, practicing the straight way, practicing the true way, practicing the proper way; that is, the four pairs of persons, the eight types of individuals—this Saṅgha of the Blessed One’s disciples is worthy of gifts, worthy of hospitality, worthy of offerings, worthy of reverential salutation, the unsurpassed field of merit for the world. And he possesses the virtues dear to the noble ones—virtues that are untorn, unbroken, unspotted, unsplattered, liberating, praised by the wise, untarnished, leading to concentration. When a noble disciple possesses these four things, brahmin, he is one who has reached the ultimate conclusion, one who has done what was to be done, one who has laid down the burden, one who has attained his own goal, one whose fetters of existence are destroyed, one who is liberated through final knowledge. When this was said, the brahmin Soṇa said to the Blessed One: “Magnificent, Master Gotama! Magnificent, Master Gotama! Just as, Master Gotama, one might set upright what had been overturned, or reveal what was hidden, or show the way to one who was lost, or bring an oil lamp into the darkness so that those with eyes might see forms, even so has Master Gotama explained the Dhamma in various ways.

I go to Master Gotama for refuge, and to the Dhamma, and to the Saṅgha of bhikkhus. May Master Gotama accept me as a lay follower who has gone for refuge from this day forward for as long as life lasts. Then the brahmin Soṇa, having delighted and rejoiced in the Blessed One’s words, rose from his seat, paid homage to the Blessed One, and keeping him on his right, departed. Not long after the brahmin Soṇa had left, the Blessed One addressed the bhikkhus: “Bhikkhus, this brahmin Soṇa is not one who has merely heard much; he is a master of the Three Vedas together with their vocabularies, liturgical formulas, phonology, and etymology, and the histories as the fifth. He is a reciter, one who has mastered the hymns, and is fully versed in natural philosophy and in the marks of a Great Man. Now, bhikkhus, there are these thirty-two marks of a Great Man. Possessing these, a Great Man comes to fulfillment in one of two positions. What thirty-two? (1) His feet are level-set. (2) On the soles of his feet are wheels with a thousand spokes, complete with rims and hubs. (3) He has projecting heels. (4) He has long fingers and toes. (5) His hands and feet are soft and tender. (6) His hands and feet are webbed. (7) He has high-arched feet. (8) His legs are like those of an antelope. (9) Standing without bending, he can touch and rub his knees with either hand. (10) His male organs are enclosed in a sheath. (11) His body is proportioned like a banyan tree. (12) His body is straight and tall. (13) His skin is golden-colored. (14) His skin is smooth, and no dust or dirt adheres to his body. (15) His body hairs grow individually, each one separate. (16) Each hair grows upward, blue-black like a collyrium stick, and curls to the right. (17) His torso is like that of a lion. (18) There is no indentation between his shoulders. (19) He has a well-rounded shoulder. (20) He has a perfect sense of taste. (21) He has jaws like a lion’s. (22) He has forty teeth. (23) His teeth are even. (24) His teeth have no gaps between them. (25) His teeth are very white. (26) His tongue is very long. (27) He has a divine voice, like the call of the karavīka bird. (28) His eyes are deep blue. (29) He has eyelashes like those of a cow. (30) Between his eyebrows, there is a tuft of white hair, soft like cotton-down. (31) His head is shaped like a royal turban. Possessing these thirty-two marks of a Great Man, a Great Man comes to fulfillment in one of two positions. What two? Either he becomes a wheel-turning monarch, righteous, a king of righteousness, conqueror of the four quarters, who has established stability in his realm and possesses the seven treasures. Or, if he goes forth from the household life into homelessness, he becomes an arahant, perfectly enlightened, one who draws back the veil from the world. When this was said, the brahmin Soṇa said to the Blessed One: “Master Gotama, it is said: ‘Marks, marks. What, Master Gotama, are the marks, and what is the fruit of the marks? “Brahmin, the thirty-two marks of a Great Man are the ‘marks,’ and the two positions are the ‘fruit of the marks. “Magnificent, Master Gotama! Magnificent, Master Gotama! Just as, Master Gotama, one might set upright what had been overturned, or reveal what was hidden, or show the way to one who was lost, or bring an oil lamp into the darkness so that those with eyes might see forms, even so has Master Gotama explained the Dhamma in various ways. I go to Master Gotama for refuge, and to the Dhamma, and to the Saṅgha of bhikkhus. May Master Gotama accept me as a lay follower who has gone for refuge from this day forward for as long as life lasts. Then the brahmin Soṇa, having delighted and rejoiced in the Blessed One’s words, rose from his seat, paid homage to the Blessed One, and keeping him on his right, departed. Not long after the brahmin Soṇa had left, the Blessed One addressed the bhikkhus: “Bhikkhus, this brahmin Soṇa is not one who has merely heard much; he is a master of the Three Vedas together with their vocabularies, liturgical formulas, phonology, and etymology, and the histories as the fifth. He is a reciter, one who has mastered the hymns, and is fully versed in natural philosophy and in the marks of a Great Man. Now, bhikkhus, there are these thirty-two marks of a Great Man. Possessing these, a Great Man comes to fulfillment in one of two positions. What thirty-two? (1) His feet are level-set. (2) On the soles of his feet are wheels with a thousand spokes, complete with rims and hubs. (3) He has projecting heels. (4) He has long fingers and toes. (5) His hands and feet are soft and tender. (6) His hands and feet are webbed. (7) He has high-arched feet. (8) His legs are like those of an antelope. (9) Standing without bending, he can touch and rub his knees with either hand. (10) His male organs are enclosed in a sheath. (11) His body is proportioned like a banyan tree. (12) His body is straight and tall. (13) His skin is golden-colored. (14) His skin is smooth, and no dust or dirt adheres to his body. (15) His body hairs grow individually, each one separate. (16) Each hair grows upward, blue-black
“Bhikkhus, there are these five ancient brahmin practices that nowadays are seen among dogs, but not among brahmins.
What are the five?
Formerly, bhikkhus, brahmins would mate only with brahmin women, not with non-brahmin women.”
Nowadays, monks, brahmins mate with both those who are brahmin and those who are not brahmin.
Nowadays, monks, dogs mate only with female dogs, not with non-dogs.
This, monks, is the first ancient brahminical custom that is now seen among dogs, but not among brahmins.
In the past, monks, brahmins would approach their brahmin wives only during their fertile period, not outside of that time.
But nowadays, monks, brahmins approach their brahmin wives both during their fertile period and outside of it.
Nowadays, monks, dogs approach their female dogs only during their fertile period, not outside of it.
"This, monks, is the second ancient brahmin custom that is seen nowadays among dogs, but not among brahmins.
Formerly, monks, brahmins neither bought nor sold a brahmin woman; they entered into a marriage out of mutual affection for the sake of kinship.
Nowadays, monks, brahmins both buy and sell a brahmin woman, and they also enter into a marriage out of mutual affection for the sake of kinship."
At present, monks, dogs neither buy nor sell female dogs; they enter into union with them out of mutual affection for the sake of offspring.
This, monks, is the third ancient brahminical custom that is now seen among dogs, but not among brahmins.
Formerly, indeed, monks, brahmins did not make hoards of wealth, grain, silver, or gold.
“Bhikkhus, at present the brahmins store up wealth, grain, silver, and gold;
whereas at present, bhikkhus, dogs do not store up wealth, grain, silver, or gold.
This, bhikkhus, is the fourth ancient brahmin quality that is seen nowadays among dogs, but not among brahmins.”
“In the past, monks, brahmins used to seek alms for their evening meal in the evening and for their morning meal in the morning.
But now, monks, brahmins eat as much as they desire until their bellies are full, and then they depart taking what remains with them.
Now, monks, it is dogs who seek alms for their evening meal in the evening and for their morning meal in the morning.”
“Monks, this is the fifth ancient brahmin quality that is seen nowadays among dogs, but not among brahmins.
These, monks, are the five ancient brahmin qualities that are seen nowadays among dogs, but not among brahmins.
The first.

Aṅguttara Nikāya 5.192 20. Brāhmaṇavagga Doṇabrāhmaṇasutta Thus have I heard. On one occasion the Blessed One was dwelling at Sāvatthī in Jeta’s Grove, Anāthapiṇḍika’s Park. Then the brahmin Doṇa approached the Blessed One and exchanged greetings with him. When they had concluded their polite conversation and cordial greetings, he sat down to one side and said to the Blessed One: “Master Gotama, I am a brahmin who knows the three Vedas, together with their vocabularies, ritual manuals, phonology, and etymology, and the lore of the fifth Veda, the histories as the fifth; skilled in philology and grammar, I am fully versed in natural philosophy and in the marks of a great man. I have heard this, Master Gotama: ‘The ascetic Gotama does not pay homage to brahmins who are aged, elderly, advanced in years, in their final stage of life. Is it true that Master Gotama says this? “It is so, brahmin, it is so. I do not pay homage to brahmins who are aged, elderly, advanced in years, in their final stage of life. “But why is that, Master Gotama? Are there not brahmins who are aged, elderly, advanced in years, in their final stage of life, who have reached the end of their lifespan? “There are indeed such brahmins, brahmin. But even though they are aged, elderly, advanced in years, in their final stage of life, and have reached the end of their lifespan, they are still bound by craving, fettered by clinging, and thus they are far from this Dhamma and Discipline. “But why is that, Master Gotama? Are there not other brahmins who, having abandoned sensual pleasures, dwell in the forest, practicing meditation? “There are indeed such brahmins, brahmin. But even though they have abandoned sensual pleasures and dwell in the forest, practicing meditation, they are still bound by craving, fettered by clinging, and thus they are far from this Dhamma and Discipline.

“But why is that, Master Gotama? Are there not yet other brahmins who, having abandoned sensual pleasures, dwell in the forest, practicing meditation, and who have attained the first jhāna? “There are indeed such brahmins, brahmin. But even though they have abandoned sensual pleasures, dwell in the forest, practice meditation, and have attained the first jhāna, they are still bound by craving, fettered by clinging, and thus they are far from this Dhamma and Discipline. “But why is that, Master Gotama? Are there not yet other brahmins who, having abandoned sensual pleasures, dwell in the forest, practicing meditation, and who have attained the second jhāna... the third jhāna... the fourth jhāna? “There are indeed such brahmins, brahmin. But even though they have abandoned sensual pleasures, dwell in the forest, practice meditation, and have attained the fourth jhāna, they are still bound by craving, fettered by clinging, and thus they are far from this Dhamma and Discipline. “But why is that, Master Gotama? Are there not yet other brahmins who, having abandoned sensual pleasures, dwell in the forest, practicing meditation, and who have realized the state of non-returning? “There are indeed such brahmins, brahmin. But even though they have abandoned sensual pleasures, dwell in the forest, practice meditation, and have realized the state of non-returning, they are still bound by craving, fettered by clinging, and thus they are far from this Dhamma and Discipline. “But why is that, Master Gotama? Are there not yet other brahmins who, having abandoned sensual pleasures, dwell in the forest, practicing meditation, and who have realized the state of once-returning? “There are indeed such brahmins, brahmin. But even though they have abandoned sensual pleasures, dwell in the forest, practice meditation, and have realized the state of once-returning, they are still bound by craving, fettered by clinging, and thus they are far from this Dhamma and Discipline. “But why is that, Master Gotama? Are there not yet other brahmins who, having abandoned sensual pleasures, dwell in the forest, practicing meditation, and who have realized the state of stream-entry? “There are indeed such brahmins, brahmin. But even though they have abandoned sensual pleasures, dwell in the forest, practice meditation, and have realized the state of stream-entry, they are still bound by craving, fettered by clinging, and thus they are far from this Dhamma and Discipline. “But why is that, Master Gotama? Are there not yet other brahmins who, having abandoned sensual pleasures, dwell in the forest, practicing meditation, and who have realized the state of arahantship? “There are indeed such brahmins, brahmin. But even though they have abandoned sensual pleasures, dwell in the forest, practice meditation, and have realized the state of arahantship, they are still bound by craving, fettered by clinging, and thus they are far from this Dhamma and Discipline. “But why is that, Master Gotama? Are there not yet other brahmins who, having abandoned sensual pleasures, dwell in the forest, practicing meditation, and who have realized the state of non-returning, once-returning, stream-entry, and arahantship? “There are indeed such brahmins, brahmin. But even though they have abandoned sensual pleasures, dwell in the forest, practice meditation, and have realized the states of non-returning, once-returning, stream-entry, and arahantship, they are still bound by craving, fettered by clinging, and thus they are far from this Dhamma and Discipline. “But why is that, Master Gotama? Are there not yet other brahmins who, having abandoned sensual pleasures, dwell in the forest, practicing meditation, and who have realized the state of non-returning, once-returning, stream-entry, and arahantship, and who have also abandoned the underlying tendency to conceit? “There are indeed such brahmins, brahmin. But even though they have abandoned sensual pleasures, dwell in the forest, practice meditation, and have realized the states of non-returning, once-returning, stream-entry, and arahantship, and have also abandoned the underlying tendency to conceit, they are still bound by craving, fettered by clinging, and thus they are far from this Dhamma and Discipline. “But why is that, Master Gotama? Are there not yet other brahmins who, having abandoned sensual pleasures, dwell in the forest, practicing meditation, and who have realized the state of non-returning, once-returning, stream-entry, and arahantship, and have also abandoned the underlying tendency to conceit, and who have also abandoned the underlying tendencies to lust for existence and ignorance? “There are indeed such brahmins, brahmin. But even though they have abandoned sensual pleasures, dwell in the forest, practice meditation, and have realized the states of non-returning, once-returning, stream-entry, and arahantship, and have also abandoned the underlying tendency to conceit, and have also abandoned the underlying tendencies to lust for existence and ignorance, they are still bound by craving, fettered by clinging, and thus they are far from this Dhamma and Discipline. “But why is that, Master Gotama?
