Are there not yet other brahmins who, having abandoned sensual pleasures, dwell in the forest, practicing meditation, and who have realized the state of non-returning, once-returning, stream-entry, and arahantship, and have also abandoned the underlying tendency to conceit, and have also abandoned the underlying tendencies to lust for existence and ignorance, and who have also abandoned all defilements? “There are indeed such brahmins, brahmin. But even though they have abandoned sensual pleasures, dwell in the forest, practice meditation, and have realized the states of non-returning, once-returning, stream-entry, and arahantship, and have also abandoned the underlying tendency to conceit, and have also abandoned the underlying tendencies to lust for existence and ignorance, and have also abandoned all defilements, they are still bound by craving, fettered by clinging, and thus they are far from this Dhamma and Discipline. “But why is that, Master Gotama? Are there not yet other brahmins who, having abandoned sensual pleasures, dwell in the forest, practicing meditation, and who have realized the state of non-returning, once-returning, stream-entry, and arahantship, and have also abandoned the underlying tendency to conceit, and have also abandoned the underlying tendencies to lust for existence and ignorance, and have also abandoned all defilements, and who have also attained final Nibbāna in this very life? “There are indeed such brahmins, brahmin. But even though they have abandoned sensual pleasures, dwell in the forest, practice meditation, and have realized the states of non-returning, once-returning, stream-entry, and arahantship, and have also abandoned the underlying tendency to conceit, and have also abandoned the underlying tendencies to lust for existence and ignorance, and have also abandoned all defilements, and have also attained final Nibbāna in this very life, they are still bound by craving, fettered by clinging,
(AN 5.192, PTS AN iii 223) Then the brahmin Doṇa approached the Blessed One; having approached, he exchanged greetings with the Blessed One.
When they had concluded their polite and courteous conversation, he sat down to one side. Sitting there, the brahmin Doṇa said this to the Blessed One:
“I have heard this, Master Gotama:
‘The ascetic Gotama does not pay homage to brahmins who are aged, elderly, advanced in years, come to the last stage of life, nor does he rise for them or invite them to a seat.
And so it is, Master Gotama.”
“Master Gotama does not pay homage to brahmins who are aged, elderly, advanced in years, come to the last stage of life, nor does he rise up for them or invite them to a seat.
This, Master Gotama, is simply not right.
“Do you, Doṇa, claim to be a brahmin?”
“For, Master Gotama, one who would speak rightly might say:
‘A brahmin is well-born on both sides,
from mother and father, of pure descent, with unblemished lineage back through seven generations, neither reproached nor censured.’”
‘He is a reciter, a bearer of the mantras, one who has mastered the three Vedas along with the glossaries (nighaṇṭu) and liturgical formulas (keṭubha),
the phonology (sakkharappabheda), and the fifth, the histories (itihāsa); he is a master of word-analysis and grammar, and is fully proficient in cosmology and the marks of a Great Man’—
if anyone were to say this of me, Master Gotama, they would be speaking correctly.
For I, Master Gotama, am a brahmin well-born on both sides,
from mother and father, of pure descent, with unblemished lineage back through seven generations, unassailable and irreproachable in respect of birth; I am a reciter and a bearer of the mantras,
one who has mastered the three Vedas together with their vocabularies, liturgical formulas, phonology, and etymologies.
“...one who has the histories as the fifth [Veda], a master of the words and of grammar,
and one who is not deficient in the Lokāyata and the marks of a Great Man. “Doṇa, those ancient seers of the brahmins, the authors of the mantras and the promulgators of the mantras—
those whose ancient mantra-words, sung, proclaimed, and compiled, the brahmins of today sing along with— ”
They repeat what was spoken, they repeat what was recited, they recite along with what was recited, and they teach along with what was taught—
namely, Aṭṭhaka, Vāmaka, Vāmadeva, Vessāmitta, Yamadaggi, Aṅgīrasa, Bhāradvāja, Vāseṭṭha, Kassapa, and Bhagu.
These are the five brahmins whom they point out to him.
“The one equal to a Brahmin, the one equal to a deva, the one who observes the boundary, the one who has broken the boundary, and the fifth, the outcaste Brahmin.
Of these, Doṇa, which one are you?
“Sir Gotama, we do not know five types of Brahmins; rather, we know only ‘Brahmin’ as such.”
“It would be well, venerable Gotama, if you would teach me the Dhamma in such a way that I might recognize these five brahmins.
“In that case, brahmin, listen and attend closely; I shall speak.
“Yes, sir,” Doṇa the brahmin replied to the Blessed One.
The Blessed One said this:
“And how, Doṇa, is a brahmin equal to Brahmā?
Here, Doṇa, a brahmin is well-born on both sides—”
He is of pure descent on both his mother’s and father’s side, with unblemished lineage back through seven generations of ancestors, unaccused and irreproachable in respect of birth.
He practices the celibate life of a youth for forty-eight years while studying the mantras.

Having practiced the celibate life of a youth for forty-eight years and having studied the mantras, he seeks the teacher’s fee from his teacher in accordance with the Dhamma alone, and not contrary to the Dhamma.
And in that regard, Doṇa, what is the Dhamma?

It is neither by farming, nor by trade, nor by cattle-herding, nor by archery, nor by service to the king, nor by any other craft, but solely by the practice of alms-gathering, not despising the alms-bowl.
Having handed over his teacher’s fee to his teacher, having shaved off his hair and beard, and having clothed himself in saffron robes, he goes forth from the home life into homelessness.
Having thus gone forth, he dwells pervading one quarter with a mind imbued with loving-kindness;

likewise the second, likewise the third, likewise the fourth; thus above, below, across, everywhere, and to all as to himself, he dwells pervading the entire world with a mind imbued with loving-kindness—vast, exalted, measureless, free from enmity.
He dwells pervading [the world] with a mind imbued with non-malevolence.
[So too with] compassion...
[and] gladness...
He dwells having pervaded one quarter with a mind imbued with equanimity; likewise the second, likewise the third, likewise the fourth;

thus above, below, across, everywhere, in all respects, he dwells having pervaded the entire world with a mind imbued with equanimity—vast, exalted, immeasurable, free from enmity, and free from ill will.
Thus, having developed these four divine abodes, with the breakup of the body, after death, he is reborn in a good destination, in the Brahma-world.
In this way, Doṇa, a brahmin is equal to a Brahmā.
And how, Doṇa, is a brahmin equal to a deva?
In this case, Doṇa, a brahmin is well-born on both sides,
from his mother’s side and from his father’s side, of pure descent, unblemished and irreproachable by birth as far back as the seventh generation of ancestors.
He practices the celibate life of a youth for forty-eight years while studying the mantras.

Having practiced the celibate life of a youth for forty-eight years and having mastered the sacred hymns, he seeks the teacher’s fee from his teacher only by righteous means, not by unrighteous means.
And what, Doṇa, is the righteous way in this case?

Neither by agriculture, nor by trade, nor by cattle-herding, nor by archery, nor by service to the king, nor by any other craft; but solely by the practice of begging, without despising the alms-bowl.
Having thus handed over his teacher’s inheritance to his teacher, he seeks a wife only in accordance with the Dhamma, not contrary to the Dhamma.
And what, Doṇa, is the Dhamma in this regard?
Neither by purchase nor by sale, but only a Brahmin woman who has been sprinkled with water.
Thus he approaches only a brahmin woman; he does not approach a kṣatriya woman, a vaiśya woman, a śūdra woman, a caṇḍāla woman, a neṣāda woman, a veṇa woman, a rathakāra woman, or a pukkusa woman.
He does not approach a pregnant woman, he does not approach a woman nursing, nor does he approach a woman who has not yet had her period.
And why, Doṇa, does a brahmin not approach a pregnant woman?
If, Doṇa, a brahmin were to approach a pregnant woman, the boy or girl born would be called "born of excessive mating.
Therefore, Doṇa, a brahmin does not approach a pregnant woman.
And why, Doṇa, does a brahmin not approach a woman who is nursing?
If, Doṇa, a brahmin were to approach a woman who is nursing, that boy or girl would be called "oppressed by impurity.
Therefore, Doṇa, a brahmin does not approach a woman who is nursing.
His brahmin wife serves him neither for the sake of sensual pleasure, nor for sport, nor for delight; rather, the brahmin’s wife exists solely for the sake of offspring.
Having fathered an heir, he shaves off his hair and beard, puts on saffron robes, and goes forth from the home life into homelessness.
Having thus gone forth, secluded from sensual pleasures... [as above] ...he enters and dwells in the fourth jhāna.
Thus, having developed these four jhānas, with the breakup of the body, after death, he is reborn in a happy destination, in a heavenly world.
In this way, Doṇa, a brahmin is equal to a deva.
And how, Doṇa, is a brahmin one who has crossed the boundary?
In this case, Doṇa, a brahmin is well-born on both sides,
from his mother’s side and from his father’s side, of pure descent, unblemished and irreproachable as far back as the seventh generation in terms of birth.
He practices the celibate life of a youth for forty-eight years while studying the mantras.

Having practiced the celibate life of a student for forty-eight years and having mastered the mantras, he seeks the teacher’s fee from his teacher only in accordance with the Dhamma, not contrary to the Dhamma.
And what, Doṇa, is the Dhamma in this case?

Neither by farming, nor by trade, nor by cattle-rearing, nor by archery, nor by service to the king, nor by any other craft; but solely by the practice of alms-gathering, without disparaging the alms-bowl.
Thus, having handed over his teacher’s inheritance to his teacher, he seeks a wife only in accordance with the Dhamma, not contrary to the Dhamma.
And what, Doṇa, is the Dhamma in this regard?
Neither by purchase nor by sale, but only a Brahmin woman who has been bathed with water.

Thus he approaches only a brahmin woman; he does not approach a kṣatriya woman, nor a vaiśya woman, nor a śūdra woman, nor a caṇḍāla woman, nor a neṣāda woman, nor a veṇa woman, nor a rathakāra woman, nor a pukkusa woman.
He does not approach a pregnant woman, he does not approach a woman nursing, nor does he approach a woman who has not yet had her period.
And why, Doṇa, does a brahmin not approach a pregnant woman?
If, Doṇa, a brahmin were to approach a pregnant woman, the boy or girl born would be called "born of excessive mating.
Therefore, Doṇa, a brahmin does not approach a pregnant woman.
And why, Doṇa, does a brahmin not approach a woman who is nursing?
If, Doṇa, a brahmin were to approach a woman who is nursing, that boy or girl would be called "oppressed by impurity.
Therefore, Doṇa, a brahmin does not approach a woman who is nursing.
His Brahmin wife serves him neither for the sake of sensual pleasure, nor for sport, nor for delight; rather, the Brahmin’s wife exists solely for the sake of offspring.
Having engaged in sexual intercourse, he dwells at home with his family, desiring the enjoyment of having a son, and does not go forth from the household life into homelessness.
He remains within the boundaries established by the ancient Brahmins and does not transgress them.
“Because he stands within the boundary established by the ancient brahmins and does not transgress it, Doṇa, for that reason a brahmin is called ‘one who has a boundary.
In this way, Doṇa, a brahmin has a boundary.
And how, Doṇa, does a brahmin have a broken boundary?”
In this case, Doṇa, a brahmin is well-born on both sides,
from his mother’s side and from his father’s side, of pure descent, unblemished and irreproachable by birth as far back as the seventh generation of ancestors.
He practices the celibate life of a youth for forty-eight years while studying the mantras.

Having practiced the celibate life of a youth for forty-eight years and having mastered the sacred hymns, he seeks the teacher’s fee from his teacher only by the Dhamma, not by what is contrary to the Dhamma.
And what, Doṇa, is the Dhamma in this regard?
Neither by farming, nor by trade, nor by cattle-herding, nor by archery, nor by service to the king, nor by any other craft; but solely by the practice of begging, without despising the alms-bowl.

Thus, having handed over the teacher’s inheritance to his teacher, he seeks a wife— both by lawful and unlawful means, through purchase and sale— even one who has been touched by water [in marriage] by a brahmin.
He approaches a brahmin woman, he approaches a kṣatriya woman, he approaches a vaiśya woman, he approaches a śūdra woman, he approaches a caṇḍāla woman, he approaches a hunter woman,
he approaches a basket-weaver woman, he approaches a chariot-maker woman, and he approaches a scavenger woman.
He approaches a woman who is pregnant; he approaches one who is nursing; he approaches her during her fertile period;
he approaches her outside her fertile period. That Brahmin wife belongs to the Brahmin for the sake of sensual pleasure, for the sake of sport, for the sake of delight, and for the sake of offspring.
She does not abide by the ancient boundary of the Brahmins, but transgresses it.
“Because a brahmin does not stand upon that which was the boundary of the ancient brahmins, but transgresses it—therefore, Doṇa, a brahmin is called one who has broken the boundary.
It is in this way, Doṇa, that a brahmin is one who has broken the boundary.
And how, Doṇa, is a brahmin a brahmin outcaste?”
In this case, Doṇa, a brahmin is well-born on both sides,
from his mother’s side and from his father’s side, of pure descent, unblemished and irreproachable as to birth back through seven generations of ancestors.
He practices the celibate life of a student for forty-eight years, studying the mantras.
Having practiced the celibate life of a youth for forty-eight years and having mastered the sacred hymns, he seeks the teacher’s fee from his teacher,
both righteously and unrighteously— through agriculture, trade, cattle-rearing, archery, service to the king, or other crafts, or even solely by the practice of begging, not despising the alms-bowl.
Having delivered the teacher’s fee to his teacher, he seeks a wife, both righteously and unrighteously— by purchase or sale, or even a Brahmin girl consecrated with water.
Thus he approaches a Brahmin woman, he approaches a Kṣatriya woman, he approaches a Vaiśya woman, he approaches a Śūdra woman, he approaches a Caṇḍāla woman,
he approaches a Nesāda woman, he approaches a Weaver woman, he approaches a Cartwright woman, he approaches a Pukkusa woman; he approaches a pregnant woman,
he approaches a woman nursing, he approaches a woman in her season, and he approaches a woman not in her season.
His Brahmin wife serves him for the sake of sensual pleasure, for sport, for delight, and for offspring; she is the Brahmin’s wife.
He maintains his livelihood through all kinds of work.
Regarding him, the Brahmins say this:
‘Why, sir, does the venerable brahmin, while claiming [to be such], make his living by all kinds of work?
He replied:
‘Just as, good sir, fire burns both the pure and the impure, yet the fire is not defiled by that;’
"In just this way, sir, even if a brahmin makes his living by all kinds of work, he is not defiled by that.
Because he makes his living by all kinds of work, Doṇa, a brahmin is called a 'brahmin outcaste.
It is in this way, Doṇa, that a brahmin becomes a brahmin outcaste."

Doṇa, those ancient seers of the brahmins, the authors of the hymns, the proclaimers of the hymns—whose ancient verses of the hymns are now sung, proclaimed, and rehearsed by the brahmins today, whom they chant after, recite after, repeat what was spoken, recite what was chanted, and teach what was taught; namely, Aṭṭhaka, ... [and so forth] ... Vāmaka.
Vāmaka, Vāmadeva, Vessāmitta, Yamadaggi, Aṅgīrasa, Bhāradvāja, Vāseṭṭha, Kassapa, and Bhagu—
among these they designate five as brahmins:
one equal to Brahmā, one equal to a deva, one who has reached the boundary, one who has transcended the boundary, and a brahmin-cāṇḍāla as the fifth.
“Of these, Doṇa, which one are you?
“If that were so, Master Gotama, we would not even fulfill the status of a ‘brāhmaṇa-cāṇḍāla.
Excellent, Master Gotama! … May Master Gotama accept me as a lay follower who has gone for refuge from this day forth for as long as life shall last.”
The Second.
Aṅguttara Nikāya 5.193.
Chapter 20: On Brahmins.
The Discourse to Saṅgārava (Saṅgāravasutta).
Then the brahmin Saṅgārava approached the Blessed One; having approached, he exchanged greetings with the Blessed One.
Having exchanged greetings and pleasantries, he sat down to one side. Seated to one side, the brahmin Saṅgārava said this to the Blessed One:
"What, Master Gotama, is the cause, what is the reason, why at times even those hymns that have been recited for a long time do not come to mind, let alone those not so recited?
But what, Master Gotama, is the cause, what is the reason, why at times even those hymns that have not been recited for a long time do come to mind, let alone those that have been recited?"
Brahmin, on whatever occasion one dwells with a mind obsessed by sensual lust, dominated by sensual lust, and does not understand, as it really is,
the escape from arisen sensual lust, on that occasion one does not understand or see, as it really is, one's own welfare;
and on that occasion one does not understand or see, as it really is, the welfare of others.
He does not understand and he does not see; on both occasions at that time, he does not understand and does not see things as they truly are.
Even mantras practiced for a long time do not come to mind, let alone those not so practiced.
Just as, brahmin, a bowl of water mixed with lac, turmeric, indigo, or madder [is no longer clear].
In that case, just as a man with good eyesight, while looking at the reflection of his own face, would not understand or see it as it truly is;

even so, brahmin, when one dwells with a mind obsessed by sensual lust, overwhelmed by sensual lust, and does not understand as it truly is the escape from arisen sensual lust, then even for one's own welfare... [in that state]...
At that time, one does not understand and does not see things as they truly are regarding oneself; nor regarding others; nor regarding both.
Even mantras that have been recited for a long time do not manifest to the mind, let alone those not so recited.
Furthermore, brahmin, on whatever occasion one dwells with a mind obsessed and overwhelmed by ill will,
and does not understand as it really is the escape from arisen ill will, on that occasion one does not understand and does not see one’s own welfare as it really is;
nor one’s welfare for others … nor one’s welfare for both, on that occasion.
One does not understand and does not see things as they truly are; even mantras that have been recited for a long time do not manifest, let alone those not so recited.
It is just as if, brahmin, a bowl of water were heated by fire, boiling, and becoming turbid.
In that case, just as a man with sight, while looking at the reflection of his own face, would not understand or see it as it really is; even so, brahmin,
when one dwells with a mind obsessed by ill will and overwhelmed by ill will,
and does not understand as it really is the escape from arisen ill will, then at that time he is unable to attend to his own welfare.

One does not understand and does not see things as they truly are; regarding the welfare of others... [and so on] ...regarding the welfare of both, at that time one does not understand and does not see things as they truly are.
Even mantras that have been recited for a long time do not come to mind, let alone those not recited.

Furthermore, brahmin, on whatever occasion one dwells with a mind obsessed by sloth and torpor, overwhelmed by sloth and torpor, and does not understand as it really is the escape from arisen sloth and torpor—at that time one does not understand and does not see one’s own welfare as it really is;
nor one’s welfare for others... nor both one’s own welfare and the welfare of others at that time.
At such a time, one does not understand or see things as they truly are; even mantras that have been recited for a long time do not manifest in the mind, let alone those not so recited.
It is just like a bowl of water covered with duckweed and moss, O Brahmin.
In that case, just as a man with sight, while examining the reflection of his own face, would not understand or see it as it truly is; even so, brahmin,
at whatever time one dwells with a mind obsessed by sloth and torpor, overcome by sloth and torpor,
and does not understand as it truly is the escape from arisen sloth and torpor— at that time, even for one's own welfare...
At that time, one does not understand and does not see things as they truly are; one does not understand and does not see things as they truly are for the sake of others...
[and so on] ...nor for the sake of both. Even mantras that have been recited for a long time do not manifest, let alone those not recited.
Furthermore, brahmin, on whatever occasion one dwells with a mind obsessed by restlessness and remorse,
dominated by restlessness and remorse, and does not understand as it really is the escape from arisen restlessness and remorse—
at that time, one neither understands nor sees one’s own welfare as it really is, nor the welfare of others.
...pe... on both occasions at that time he does not understand and does not see things as they truly are;
even mantras he has recited for a long time do not occur to him, let alone those he has not recited.
It is just as if, brahmin, there were a bowl of water stirred by the wind, shaken, disturbed, and rippling with waves.
In that case, a man with sight, while reflecting on the reflection of his own face, would not understand or see it as it really is. Even so, Brahmin,
at whatever time one dwells with a mind obsessed by restlessness and remorse,
overwhelmed by restlessness and remorse, one does not understand as it really is the escape from arisen restlessness and remorse.
He does not understand; at that time he does not understand and does not see the welfare of himself as it really is, nor the welfare of others ... nor both welfares as they really are.
Even mantras he has recited for a long time do not occur to him, let alone those he has not recited.

Furthermore, brahmin, on whatever occasion one dwells with a mind obsessed by doubt, overwhelmed by doubt, and does not understand as it really is the escape from arisen doubt, on that occasion one does not understand and does not see as it really is one’s own welfare; nor one’s welfare for others; nor both one’s welfare and the welfare of others.
On that occasion, one is confused about one’s own welfare... [and so on] ...on that occasion, one is confused about both one’s own welfare and the welfare of others.
At such a time, one does not understand and does not see things as they truly are; even mantras that have been recited for a long time do not manifest, let alone those not so recited.
It is just as if, brahmin, there were a bowl of water that was turbid, stirred up, muddy, and placed in the dark.
In that case, a man with sight, while reflecting on the reflection of his own face, would not understand or see it as it truly is. Even so, brahmin,
when one dwells with a mind obsessed by doubt, overwhelmed by doubt,
and does not understand as it truly is the escape from arisen doubt, then even for his own sake— [he is unable to act].
At that time, one does not understand and does not see things as they truly are regarding one's own welfare; nor regarding the welfare of others...
[and so on] ...nor regarding the welfare of both. Even mantras that have been recited for a long time do not manifest, let alone those not recited.
But at whatever time, brahmin, one dwells with a mind that is neither obsessed by sensual lust nor enslaved by sensual lust,
and one understands as it really is the escape from arisen sensual lust— at that time one understands and sees for oneself one’s own welfare as it really is,
and at that time one understands and sees the welfare of others as it really is.
On both occasions at that time, he understands and sees things as they truly are:
even mantras not recited for a long time come to mind, let alone those that have been recited.
Just as, brahmin, a bowl of water is unmixed with lac, turmeric, indigo, or madder.
In this regard, a man with good eyesight, while examining the reflection of his own face, would understand and see it as it truly is.
Even so, brahmin, at whatever time one does not dwell with a mind obsessed by sensual lust...
[as before] ...Furthermore, brahmin, at whatever time one does not dwell with a mind obsessed by ill will... [as before].

"Just as, brahmin, a bowl of water that has not been heated by fire, is not boiling, and has not become turbulent—therein a person with good eyesight, reflecting on the reflection of his own face, would know and see it as it truly is;
even so, brahmin, at whatever time one does not dwell with a mind obsessed by ill will... [and so forth]."
Furthermore, brahmin, at whatever time one does not dwell with a mind obsessed by sloth and torpor...
just as, brahmin, there might be a bowl of water that is not covered over by algae and moss;
therein a person with good eyesight, reflecting on the reflection of his own face, would know and see it as it truly is.
In the same way, brahmin, at whatever time one does not dwell with a mind obsessed by sloth and torpor … [as before] … Furthermore,
brahmin, at whatever time one does not dwell with a mind obsessed by restlessness and remorse … [as before] … Just as,
brahmin, a bowl of water is not stirred by the wind, is not disturbed, is not agitated, and is not rippled.
In this regard, a man with sight, while reflecting upon the reflection of his own face, would understand and see it as it truly is. Even so, brahmin,
at whatever time one does not dwell with a mind obsessed by restlessness and remorse… [as before] …Furthermore, brahmin, at whatever time one does not dwell with a mind obsessed by doubt.
One who is overcome by doubt does not understand, as it really is, the escape from arisen doubt;
at that time, one understands and sees, as it really is, one's own welfare, and at that time, one understands and sees,
as it really is, the welfare of others, and at that time, one understands and sees, as it really is, the welfare of both.
Even mantras not recited for a long time come to mind, let alone those that have been recited.
Just as if, brahmin, there were a bowl of water that was clear, serene, and undisturbed, placed in the light;
there a man with good eyesight, examining the reflection of his own face, would know and see it as it truly is.
In the same way, brahmin, at whatever time one dwells with a mind that is not obsessed by doubt,
nor overwhelmed by doubt, and understands as it really is the escape from arisen doubt—
at that time one understands and sees as it really is one’s own welfare, the welfare of others, and the welfare of both.
At that time, one understands and sees according to reality; even mantras not recited for a long time come to mind, let alone those that have been recited.
This, brahmin, is the cause, this is the condition, why sometimes even mantras that have been recited for a long time do not come to mind, let alone those that have not been recited.
"But this, brahmin, is the cause, this is the condition, by which even those mantras that have not been recited for a long time come to mind, let alone those that have been recited.
"Excellent, Master Gotama! ... May Master Gotama accept me as a lay follower who has gone for refuge from this day forth for as long as life shall last.
This was the third [discourse].

Aṅguttara Nikāya 5.194 20. Brāhmaṇavagga Kāraṇapālīsutta “Bhikkhus, there are these five kinds of persons found existing in the world. What five? The one who is like a stone pillar; the one who is like a wooden post; the one who is like a hollow reed; the one who is like a water jar; and the one who is like a lotus. And how, bhikkhus, is a person like a stone pillar? Here, someone is well-born on both sides, of pure maternal and paternal descent back through seven generations, unmarred, impeccable, and of untarnished birth. But he does not possess wealth, grain, silver, or gold; he does not have elephants, horses, cattle, or sheep; he does not have servants, laborers, or workers; and he does not have wives, sons, or daughters. He is not learned, possessing little knowledge of the scriptures; he does not observe the training; he does not practice meditation; and he does not attain any superhuman states, a state of peace, or a blissful dwelling here and now that transcends the plane of ordinary beings. This, bhikkhus, is called a person like a stone pillar. And how, bhikkhus, is a person like a wooden post? Here, someone is well-born on both sides... [as above] ...and of untarnished birth. He possesses wealth, grain, silver, and gold; he has elephants, horses, cattle, and sheep; he has servants, laborers, and workers; and he has wives, sons, and daughters. But he is not learned, possessing little knowledge of the scriptures; he does not observe the training; he does not practice meditation; and he does not attain any superhuman states, a state of peace, or a blissful dwelling here and now that transcends the plane of ordinary beings. This, bhikkhus, is called a person like a wooden post. And how, bhikkhus, is a person like a hollow reed? Here, someone is well-born on both sides... [as above] ...and of untarnished birth. He possesses wealth, grain, silver, and gold; he has elephants, horses, cattle, and sheep; he has servants, laborers, and workers; and he has wives, sons, and daughters. He is learned, possessing great knowledge of the scriptures; he observes the training; he practices meditation; yet he does not attain any superhuman states, a state of peace, or a blissful dwelling here and now that transcends the plane of ordinary beings. This, bhikkhus, is called a person like a hollow reed. And how, bhikkhus, is a person like a water jar? Here, someone is well-born on both sides... [as above] ...and of untarnished birth. He possesses wealth, grain, silver, and gold; he has elephants, horses, cattle, and sheep; he has servants, laborers, and workers; and he has wives, sons, and daughters. He is learned, possessing great knowledge of the scriptures; he observes the training; he practices meditation; and he attains superhuman states, a state of peace, and a blissful dwelling here and now that transcends the plane of ordinary beings, yet he does not realize the fruit of stream-entry or the fruit of once-returning. This, bhikkhus, is called a person like a water jar. And how, bhikkhus, is a person like a lotus? Here, someone is well-born on both sides... [as above] ...and of untarnished birth. He possesses wealth, grain, silver, and gold; he has elephants, horses, cattle, and sheep; he has servants, laborers, and workers; and he has wives, sons, and daughters. He is learned, possessing great knowledge of the scriptures; he observes the training; he practices meditation; and he realizes the fruit of stream-entry or the fruit of once-returning. This, bhikkhus, is called a person like a lotus. These, bhikkhus, are the five kinds of persons found existing in the world.”
On one occasion the Blessed One was dwelling at Vesālī in the Great Wood, in the Hall with the Peaked Roof.
Now at that time, the brahmin Kāraṇapālī was overseeing the work of the Licchavis.
The brahmin Kāraṇapālī saw the brahmin Piṅgiyānī coming from afar;
seeing him, he said this to the brahmin Piṅgiyānī:
"Well now, from where does the venerable Piṅgiyānī come so early in the day?"
“I am coming here, sir, from the presence of the ascetic Gotama.
“What does Master Piṅgiyānī think of the ascetic Gotama’s lucidity of wisdom? Do you consider him wise?
“Who am I, sir, that I should know the ascetic Gotama’s lucidity of wisdom?”
“Surely he too must be just like him who would understand the clarity of wisdom of the ascetic Gotama.
“Indeed, Master Piṅgiyānī, you praise the ascetic Gotama with lofty praise.
“And who am I, sir, that I should praise the ascetic Gotama?”
“Praised by those who are themselves praised, that venerable Gotama is the best among gods and humans.
“But what reason, Master Piṅgiyānī, do you see for having such great confidence in the ascetic Gotama?
“It is just as if, sir, a man were fully satisfied with the finest flavors and had no longing for other, inferior flavors;”
In the same way, sir, whenever he hears the Dhamma from that Master Gotama—
whether in discourses, or in songs, or in prose-expositions, or in marvelous qualities—
he does not crave the doctrines of other common recluses and brahmins.
"Just as if, sir, a man overcome by hunger and weakness were to find a lump of honey;
wherever he tastes it, he surely finds a sweet flavor that is refreshing—
in the same way, sir, wherever one hears the Dhamma of that Blessed Gotama— "

Whether it be in terms of the discourses (sutta), whether in terms of the songs (geyya), whether in terms of the prose-expositions (veyyākaraṇa), or whether in terms of the marvelous qualities (abbhutadhamma)—
from each of these he surely gains gladness and gains clarity of mind.
Just as if, sir, a man were to find a small box of sandalwood.
Of yellow sandalwood or red sandalwood.
From whichever part one might smell it—
whether from the root, from the middle, or from the top—
One surely attains a fragrant scent that is most pleasing;
even so, sir, from whatever source one hears the Dhamma of Master Gotama—
whether as discourses, or in verse, or as explanations, or as marvelous qualities— [one finds it ever more delightful].
From that, he attains gladness; he attains joy.
Just as, sir, there might be a man who is afflicted, suffering, and gravely ill, and a skilled physician were to remove his affliction instantly;
In just this way, sir, from whatever source one hears the Dhamma of that Blessed Gotama—
whether in the form of discourses (sutta), songs (geyya), expositions (veyyākaraṇa),
or marvelous qualities (abbhutadhamma)— from each of those sources sorrow, lamentation, pain, grief, and despair pass away.
"Master, it is just as if there were a lotus pond with clear water, sweet water, cool water, white water, and fine landing places, delightful.
Then a man might come, scorched by the heat, overcome by the heat, exhausted, thirsty, and parched.
Having plunged into that lotus pond, having bathed and drunk, he would allay every distress, fatigue, and fever."
"In the same way, sir, whenever one hears the Dhamma of that Blessed Gotama—
whether in discourses (sutta), or in mixed prose and verse (geyya), or in explanations (veyyākaraṇa), or in marvelous qualities (abbhutadhamma)—
from each and every instance, all distress, exhaustion, and feverish agitation are stilled."

When this was said, the brahmin Kāraṇapālī rose from his seat, arranged his upper robe over one shoulder, knelt with his right knee on the ground, and extending his joined palms toward the Blessed One, uttered this inspired exclamation three times:
“Homage to the Blessed One, the Worthy One, the Perfectly Self-Awakened One!
Homage to the Blessed One, the Worthy One, the Perfectly Self-Awakened One!”
"Homage to that Blessed One, the Worthy One, the Perfectly Self-Awakened One!
Excellent, Master Piṅgiyānī, excellent!
Just as, Master Piṅgiyānī, one might set upright what had been overturned, or reveal what was hidden, or show the way to one who was lost..."
Or one might point out the path, or hold up a lamp in the darkness so that those with eyes might see forms;
even so has the Dhamma been proclaimed by the venerable Piṅgiyānī in many ways.
Therefore, Master Piṅgiyānī, I go for refuge to the Blessed One Gotama, and to the Dhamma, and to the Saṅgha of bhikkhus.
“May Master Piṅgiyānī remember me as a lay follower who has gone for refuge from this day forth for as long as life lasts.
The fourth.
Aṅguttara Nikāya 5.195

20. Brāhmaṇavagga Piṅgiyānīsutta At Sāvatthī. “Bhikkhus, when a bhikkhu has abandoned five things and possesses five things, he is capable of attaining the unsurpassed security from bondage, which is Nibbāna. What five things has he abandoned? He has abandoned lust, hatred, delusion, conceit, and doubt. What five things does he possess? He possesses the aggregate of virtue, the aggregate of concentration, the aggregate of wisdom, the aggregate of liberation, and the aggregate of the knowledge and vision of liberation. When a bhikkhu has abandoned these five things and possesses these five things, he is capable of attaining the unsurpassed security from bondage, which is Nibbāna. Then the brahmin lady Piṅgiyānī approached the Blessed One, paid homage to him, sat down to one side, and said to him: “Venerable sir, it would be good if the Blessed One would teach me the Dhamma in brief, so that, having heard the Dhamma from the Blessed One, I might dwell alone, withdrawn, diligent, ardent, and resolute. “Lady, those for whom you seek to live the spiritual life under me must first abandon their own views; only then can they dwell here. But you, lady, have long held and cherished your own views, and you are attached to them. “I do not understand in detail the meaning of the Blessed One’s statement, which he has spoken in brief without expounding the meaning in detail. It would be good if the Blessed One would teach me the Dhamma in such a way that I might understand the meaning in detail. “Lady, those for whom you seek to live the spiritual life under me must first abandon their own views; only then can they dwell here. But you, lady, have long held and cherished your own views, and you are attached to them. A second time and a third time, the brahmin lady Piṅgiyānī made the same request, and received the same reply. Then the brahmin lady Piṅgiyānī rose from her seat, paid homage to the Blessed One, and keeping him on her right, she departed. Not long after she had left, the Blessed One addressed the bhikkhus: “Bhikkhus, this brahmin lady Piṅgiyānī is wise, intelligent, and discerning. If she had stayed, I would have taught her the simile of the raft, by means of which one should use even the teachings to cross over, and not to hold onto them. Yet, bhikkhus, this brahmin lady Piṅgiyānī has understood the meaning of the simile of the raft even as it was being spoken in brief. Then a certain bhikkhu approached the Blessed One, paid homage to him, sat down to one side, and said to him: “Venerable sir, how should the simile of the raft be understood in detail? “Bhikkhu, suppose a man in the middle of a jungle were to see a great expanse of water. Its near shore is dangerous and fearful, while its further shore is safe and free from fear. But there is no ferryboat or bridge for crossing over. Then he would think: ‘This is a great expanse of water... Suppose I collect grass, twigs, branches, and foliage, and bind them together into a raft, and supported by the raft and making an effort with my hands and feet, I cross safely to the far shore. And so he would do. Having crossed over, he would think: ‘This raft has been very helpful to me. Supported by it and making an effort with my hands and feet, I crossed safely to the far shore. Suppose now I were to hoist it on my head or load it on my shoulder, and then go wherever I want. What do you think, bhikkhu? Would that man be doing what should be done with that raft? “No, venerable sir. “What should be done with that raft?

Bhikkhu, when that man in need of safety sees the great expanse of water—its near shore dangerous and fearful, its further shore safe and free from fear—he would take the raft and, dragging it along or pushing it ahead, go wherever he wants. That is how that man would be doing what should be done with that raft. So too, bhikkhu, the simile of the raft has been spoken by me as a metaphor for the purpose of crossing over, not for the purpose of retaining. Understanding the simile of the raft in this way, you should abandon even the teachings, let alone what is unteachable. When this was said, the brahmin lady Piṅgiyānī approached the Blessed One, paid homage to him, stood to one side, and said to him: “Venerable sir, it is wonderful, it is marvelous how well the Blessed One has explained the simile of the raft as a metaphor for the purpose of crossing over, not for the purpose of retaining. Venerable sir, I have understood the meaning of the simile of the raft in detail. Venerable sir, just as a man who had taken a loan to develop his business would, upon the success of that business, repay the principal and interest and live in happiness, so too, venerable sir, I have long held and cherished my own views, and I am attached to them. But now, having heard the Blessed One’s teaching, I have abandoned them. Venerable sir, just as a man who had taken an illness-causing poison would, through the power of a mantra or medicine, neutralize the poison and live in happiness, so too, venerable sir, I have long held and cherished my own views, and I am attached to them. But now, having heard the Blessed One’s teaching, I have abandoned them. Venerable sir, just as a man who had stored up wealth for his sons would, upon handing it over to them, live in happiness, so too, venerable sir, I have long held and cherished my own views, and I am attached to them. But now, having heard the Blessed One’s teaching, I have abandoned them. Venerable sir, just as a man who had been a slave would, upon being freed from slavery, live in happiness, so too, venerable sir, I have long held and cherished my own views, and I am attached to them. But now, having heard the Blessed One’s teaching, I have abandoned them. Venerable sir, just as a man who had been in debt would, upon clearing the debt, live in happiness, so too, venerable sir, I have long held and cherished my own views, and I am attached to them. But now, having heard the Blessed One’s teaching, I have abandoned them. Venerable sir, just as a man who had been a traveler would, upon reaching a safe place, live in happiness, so too, venerable sir, I have long held and cherished my own views, and I am attached to them. But now, having heard the Blessed One’s teaching, I have abandoned them. Venerable sir, just as a man who had been ill would, upon recovering from his illness, live in happiness, so too, venerable sir, I have long held and cherished my own views, and I am attached to them. But now, having heard the Blessed One’s teaching, I have abandoned them. Venerable sir, just as a man who had been in prison would, upon being released from prison, live in happiness, so too, venerable sir, I have long held and cherished my own views, and I am attached to them. But now, having heard the Blessed One’s teaching, I have abandoned them. Venerable sir, just as a man who had been a wayfarer would, upon reaching his own home, live in happiness, so too, venerable sir, I have long held and cherished my own views, and I am attached to them. But now, having heard the Blessed One’s teaching, I have abandoned them. Venerable sir, just as a man who had been a merchant would, upon gaining wealth, live in happiness, so too, venerable sir, I have long held and cherished my own views, and I am attached to them. But now, having heard the Blessed One’s teaching, I have abandoned them. Venerable sir, just as a man who had been a king would, upon gaining a kingdom, live in happiness, so too, venerable sir, I have long held and cherished my own views, and I am attached to them. But now, having heard the Blessed One’s teaching, I have abandoned them. Venerable sir, just as a man who had been a pauper would, upon becoming wealthy, live in happiness, so too, venerable sir, I have long held and cherished my own views, and I am attached to them. But now, having heard the Blessed One’s teaching, I have abandoned them. Venerable sir, just as a man who had been a servant would, upon becoming a master, live in happiness, so too, venerable sir, I have long held and cherished my own views, and I am attached to them. But now, having heard the Blessed One’s teaching, I have abandoned them. Venerable sir, just as a man who had been a beggar would, upon becoming a lord, live in happiness, so too, venerable sir, I have long held and cherished my own views, and I am attached to them. But now,
On one occasion the Blessed One was dwelling at Vesālī in the Great Wood in the Gabled Hall.
Now at that time about five hundred Licchavis were attending upon the Blessed One.
Some of those Licchavis were blue—blue in color, dressed in blue, and adorned with blue ornaments; some of those Licchavis were...
Some Licchavis were yellow—yellow in color, wearing yellow garments, and adorned with yellow ornaments;
some Licchavis were red—red in color, wearing red garments, and adorned with red ornaments; and some Licchavis were white—white in color, wearing white garments, and adorned with white ornaments.
Yet the Blessed One outshone them all in both beauty and glory.
Then the brahmin Piṅgiyānī rose from his seat, arranged his upper robe over one shoulder, and extending his joined palms toward the Blessed One, said this to the Blessed One:
“It occurs to me, Blessed One; it occurs to me, Sugata.
“Let it occur to you, Piṅgiyānī,” the Blessed One said.
Then the brahmin Piṅgiyānī praised the Blessed One to his face with a fitting verse:
"Just as a fragrant red lotus might bloom at dawn,
its fragrance not yet faded;"
“Behold Aṅgīrasa shining forth,
blazing like the sun in the sky.
Then those Licchavis covered the brahmin Piṅgiyānī with five hundred upper robes.
Then the brahmin Piṅgiyānī covered the Blessed One with those five hundred upper robes.
Then the Blessed One said this to those Licchavis:
“Licchavis, the appearance of five treasures is rare in the world.”
Of which five?
The appearance of a Tathāgata, an Arahant, a Perfectly Enlightened One, is rare in the world.
A person who teaches the Dhamma and Vinaya proclaimed by the Tathāgata is rare in the world.
A person who understands the Dhamma and Vinaya taught and proclaimed by the Tathāgata is rare in the world.
A person who understands the Dhamma and Vinaya taught and proclaimed by the Tathāgata and practices in accordance with the Dhamma is rare in the world.
A person who is grateful and appreciative is rare in the world.
“Licchavis, the appearance of these five jewels is indeed rare in the world.
The fifth.
*Aṅguttara Nikāya* 5.196.

20. Brāhmaṇavagga Mahāsupinasutta (The Discourse on the Great Dreams) At one time the Blessed One was dwelling at Sāvatthī in Jeta’s Grove, Anāthapiṇḍika’s Park. Then a certain brahmin approached the Blessed One and, having approached, exchanged greetings with him. When they had concluded their courteous and amiable conversation, he sat down to one side. Sitting there, that brahmin said to the Blessed One: “Master Gotama, last night I saw a great dream. I saw the four great oceans turned into milk; I saw the Himalayas, the king of mountains, turned into cotton wool; I saw the earth, as far as its ocean boundaries, strewn with rice; I saw myself wearing a wreath of lotuses, sitting upon a heap of jewels; I saw myself, having mounted a white bull, walking through the village of the Magadhans; I saw myself, having mounted a white bull, walking through the kingdom of Kāsī; I saw myself, having mounted a white bull, walking through the kingdom of Kosala; I saw myself, having mounted a white bull, walking through the kingdom of Magadha; I saw myself, having mounted a white bull, walking through the four great continents; I saw myself, having mounted a white bull, walking through the world-system of a thousand worlds; I saw myself, having mounted a white bull, walking through the world-system of a second thousand worlds; I saw myself, having mounted a white bull, walking through the world-system of a third thousand worlds; I saw myself, having mounted a white bull, walking through the world-system of a fourth thousand worlds; I saw myself, having mounted a white bull, walking through the world-system of a fifth thousand worlds; I saw myself, having mounted a white bull, walking through the world-system of a sixth thousand worlds; I saw myself, having mounted a white bull, walking through the world-system of a seventh thousand worlds; I saw myself, having mounted a white bull, walking through the world-system of an eighth thousand worlds; I saw myself, having mounted a white bull, walking through the world-system of a ninth thousand worlds; I saw myself, having mounted a white bull, walking through the world-system of a tenth thousand worlds; I saw myself, having mounted a white bull, walking through the world-system of an eleventh thousand worlds; I saw myself, having mounted a white bull, walking through the world-system of a twelfth thousand worlds; I saw myself, having mounted a white bull, walking through the world-system of a thirteenth thousand worlds; I saw myself, having mounted a white bull, walking through the world-system of a fourteenth thousand worlds; I saw myself, having mounted a white bull, walking through the world-system of a fifteenth thousand worlds; I saw myself, having mounted a white bull, walking through the world-system of a sixteenth thousand worlds; I saw myself, having mounted a white bull, walking through the world-system of a seventeenth thousand worlds;

I saw myself, having mounted a white bull, walking through the world-system of an eighteenth thousand worlds; I saw myself, having mounted a white bull, walking through the world-system of a nineteenth thousand worlds; I saw myself, having mounted a white bull, walking through the world-system of a twentieth thousand worlds. “Brahmin, you have seen this great dream because of five reasons. What five? Here, brahmin, last night the Tathāgata, the Arahant, the Perfectly Enlightened One, attained final Nibbāna in Parinibbāna. Because of that, brahmin, you have seen this great dream. Furthermore, brahmin, last night the Tathāgata, the Arahant, the Perfectly Enlightened One, set in motion the Wheel of Dhamma. Because of that, brahmin, you have seen this great dream. Furthermore, brahmin, last night the Tathāgata, the Arahant, the Perfectly Enlightened One, performed the Twin Miracle. Because of that, brahmin, you have seen this great dream. Furthermore, brahmin, last night the Tathāgata, the Arahant, the Perfectly Enlightened One, displayed the great compassion toward the world with its devas, Māras, and Brahmās, among this generation with its ascetics and brahmins, its devas and humans. Because of that, brahmin, you have seen this great dream. Furthermore, brahmin, last night the Tathāgata, the Arahant, the Perfectly Enlightened One, surveyed the world with his Buddha-eye. Because of that, brahmin, you have seen this great dream. These, brahmin, are the five reasons why you have seen this great dream. When this was said, that brahmin said to the Blessed One: “Magnificent, Master Gotama! Magnificent, Master Gotama! Just as, Master Gotama, one might set upright what had been overturned, or reveal what was hidden, or show the way to one who was lost, or bring an oil lamp into the darkness so that those with eyes might see forms, even so has Master Gotama explained the Dhamma in various ways. I go for refuge to Master Gotama, to the Dhamma, and to the Saṅgha of bhikkhus. May Master Gotama accept me as a lay follower who has gone for refuge from this day forth for as long as life lasts. Then that brahmin, having delighted and rejoiced in the words of the Blessed One, rose from his seat, paid homage to the Blessed One, and keeping him on his right, departed. Not long after that brahmin had left, the Blessed One addressed the bhikkhus: “Bhikkhus, last night a certain brahmin approached me and spoke thus... [repeating the entire account] ...and keeping me on his right, he departed. When this was said, a certain bhikkhu asked the Blessed One: “Venerable sir, what is the destiny, what is the future destination, of that brahmin? “Bhikkhu, that brahmin has attained the fruit of stream-entry. Thus spoke the Blessed One. Elated, those bhikkhus delighted in the words of the Blessed One. This is what the Blessed One said. Elated, those bhikkhus delighted in the words of the Blessed One. This is the meaning of what was said by the Blessed One, and so it was heard by me. [End of] Mahāsupinasutta, the twenty-first discourse in the Brāhmaṇavagga of the Pañcaka-nipāta.
