“Bhikkhus, before his enlightenment, while he was still a bodhisatta and not yet fully enlightened, five great dreams appeared to the Tathāgata, the Arahant, the Perfectly Enlightened One.
What are the five?
Bhikkhus, before his enlightenment, while he was still a bodhisatta and not yet fully enlightened, [the Tathāgata...]”
While he was still a bodhisatta, this great earth became his great couch; Himavat, the king of mountains, became his pillow;
his left hand was placed in the eastern ocean, his right hand was placed in the western ocean, and both his feet were placed in the southern ocean.
“Monks, before his enlightenment, while he was still a bodhisatta and not yet fully awakened, this first great dream appeared to the Tathāgata,
the Arahant, the Perfectly Enlightened One. Furthermore, monks, before his enlightenment,
while he was still a bodhisatta and not yet fully awakened, a species of grass called *tiriyā* grew from his navel and stood reaching up to touch the sky.”
"Monks, this was the second great dream that appeared to the Tathāgata, the Arahant, the Perfectly Enlightened One, while he was still a Bodhisatta, prior to his enlightenment,

before he had attained full awakening. Furthermore, monks, while the Tathāgata, the Arahant, the Perfectly Enlightened One was still a Bodhisatta, prior to his enlightenment, before he had attained full awakening,
white worms with black heads crawled up from his feet..."
They covered him down to his knees.

Monks, this was the third great dream that appeared to the Tathāgata, the Arahant, the Perfectly Enlightened One, while he was still a Bodhisatta, prior to his enlightenment, before he had attained full awakening.
Furthermore, monks, to the Tathāgata, the Arahant, the Perfectly Enlightened One, prior to his enlightenment...
While he was still a Bodhisatta who had not yet attained full enlightenment, four birds of different colors came from the four directions,
fell at his feet, and became entirely white. Monks,

this was the fourth great dream that appeared to the Tathāgata, the Arahant, the Perfectly Enlightened One, while he was still a Bodhisatta who had not yet attained full enlightenment, prior to his awakening.

Furthermore, monks, before his enlightenment, while he was still a bodhisatta and not yet fully enlightened, the Tathāgata, the Arahant, the Perfectly Enlightened One, walked back and forth upon a great mountain of filth without being soiled by that filth.
Monks, this was the fifth great dream that appeared to the Tathāgata, the Arahant, the Perfectly Enlightened One, while he was still a bodhisatta and not yet fully enlightened.
Furthermore, monks, when the Tathāgata, the Arahant, the Perfectly Enlightened One— prior to his enlightenment,
while he was still a Bodhisatta not yet fully awakened— this great earth became his great couch, Himavā, the king of mountains, was his pillow,
his left hand rested on the eastern ocean, and his right hand on the western ocean.
The right foot was placed [on the shore], and both feet were placed in the southern ocean;
it was there, monks, that the Tathāgata, the Arahant, the Perfectly Enlightened One, fully awakened to unsurpassed perfect enlightenment.
At the time of that awakening, this first great dream appeared.

Furthermore, monks, when the Tathāgata, the Arahant, the Perfectly Enlightened One— while he was still a Bodhisatta, prior to his full enlightenment and before he had awakened— there arose from his navel a kind of grass called *tiriyā* that reached up to touch the sky;
and after the Tathāgata, the Arahant, the Perfectly Enlightened One had awakened to the Noble Eightfold Path and had made it well-proclaimed among gods and humans,
this second great dream appeared as a premonition of that awakening.
Moreover, monks, while the Tathāgata, the Arahant, the Perfectly Enlightened One was still a Bodhisatta before his enlightenment, prior to becoming fully awakened,
white worms with black heads crawled up from his feet as far as his knees and covered them;
many lay followers clad in white, monks, have gone for refuge to the Tathāgata for as long as life lasts.
For his full enlightenment, this third great dream appeared. Furthermore, monks,
before the Tathāgata’s awakening— while he was still a Bodhisatta, an Arahant, a Perfectly Enlightened One who had not yet awakened—
four birds of different colors came from the four directions, fell at the soles of his feet, and...
They all turned entirely white.

"Monks, these four castes—the Khattiyas, Brāhmaṇas, Vessas, and Suddas—having gone forth from the home life into homelessness in the Dhamma and Vinaya proclaimed by the Tathāgata, realize unsurpassed liberation.
This was the fourth great dream that appeared to him for his full enlightenment."

Furthermore, monks, when the Tathāgata—worthy and perfectly enlightened—was formerly, before his awakening, while still an unawakened Bodhisatta, he walked back and forth upon a great mountain of filth without being defiled by that filth.

Monks, the Tathāgata is a recipient of robes, almsfood, lodgings, and medicinal requisites for the sick; yet the Tathāgata uses them without being tied to them, without being infatuated with them, without being obsessed by them, seeing the danger in them and possessing the wisdom of escape.
This was the fifth great dream that appeared to him for the sake of his full awakening.
“Bhikkhus, before his enlightenment, while he was still a bodhisatta and not yet fully enlightened, these five great dreams appeared to the Tathāgata, the Arahant, the Perfectly Enlightened One.
The sixth. Aṅguttara Nikāya 5.197

20. Brāhmaṇavagga Vassasutta (The Discourse on Rainy Seasons) “Bhikkhus, there are these four rainy seasons. What four? The winter rainy season, the summer rainy season, the short rainy season, and the long rainy season. These, bhikkhus, are the four rainy seasons. Just so, bhikkhus, there are these four ‘rainy seasons’ for a person. What four? The winter rainy season of a person, the summer rainy season of a person, the short rainy season of a person, and the long rainy season of a person. And what, bhikkhus, is the winter rainy season of a person? Here, bhikkhus, someone is reborn in a low family—a family of outcasts, bamboo-workers, hunters, chariot-makers, or flower-scavengers—one that is poor, with little food and drink, scanty possessions and meager wealth, where food and clothing are obtained with difficulty. And he is ugly, unsightly, and ill-favored; he has little strength, is short-lived, and is often afflicted by illness. Such a person, having done evil deeds by body, speech, and mind, at the breaking up of the body, after death, is reborn in a state of misery, a bad destination, in perdition, in hell. This, bhikkhus, is called the winter rainy season of a person. And what, bhikkhus, is the summer rainy season of a person? Here, bhikkhus, someone is reborn in a high family—an aristocratic khattiya family or a wealthy brahmin family or a wealthy householder family—one that is rich, with much food and drink, abundant possessions and great wealth, where food and clothing are obtained without difficulty. And he is handsome, attractive, and well-favored; he has great strength, is long-lived, and is seldom afflicted by illness. Such a person, having done good deeds by body, speech, and mind, at the breaking up of the body, after death, is reborn in a good destination, a heavenly world. This, bhikkhus, is called the summer rainy season of a person. And what, bhikkhus, is the short rainy season of a person? Here, bhikkhus, someone is reborn in a high family—an aristocratic khattiya family or a wealthy brahmin family or a wealthy householder family—one that is rich, with much food and drink, abundant possessions and great wealth, where food and clothing are obtained without difficulty. And he is handsome, attractive, and well-favored; he has great strength, is long-lived, and is seldom afflicted by illness. Such a person, having done good deeds by body, speech, and mind, at the breaking up of the body, after death, is reborn in a good destination, a heavenly world. But there, bhikkhus, his life span is short, his lifespan is brief, and he does not remain there for long. This, bhikkhus, is called the short rainy season of a person. And what, bhikkhus, is the long rainy season of a person? Here, bhikkhus, someone is reborn in a high family—an aristocratic khattiya family or a wealthy brahmin family or a wealthy householder family—one that is rich, with much food and drink, abundant possessions and great wealth, where food and clothing are obtained without difficulty. And he is handsome, attractive, and well-favored; he has great strength, is long-lived, and is seldom afflicted by illness. Such a person, having done good deeds by body, speech, and mind, at the breaking up of the body, after death, is reborn in a good destination, a heavenly world. And there, bhikkhus, his life span is long, his lifespan is extensive, and he remains there for a long time. This, bhikkhus, is called the long rainy season of a person. These, bhikkhus, are the four ‘rainy seasons’ for a person.”
“Bhikkhus, there are these five obstacles to the rains, which those who interpret signs do not know, where the vision of those who interpret signs does not reach.
What are the five?
Bhikkhus, in the upper sky, the fire element becomes agitated.”
Because of that, the clouds that have arisen disperse.
This, monks, is the first obstacle to rain, which those who read omens do not know, where the vision of those who read omens does not reach.
Furthermore, monks, the air element becomes agitated in the upper sky.
Because of that, the clouds that have arisen disperse.
This, monks, is the second obstacle to rain that prognosticators do not know, where the eye of prognosticators does not reach.
Furthermore, monks, Rāhu, the lord of the asuras, receives water with his hand and pours it back into the great ocean.
This, monks, is the third obstacle to rain, which prognosticators do not know, where the vision of prognosticators does not reach.
Furthermore, monks, the rain-bearing deities become negligent.
This, monks, is the fourth obstacle to rain, which prognosticators do not know, where the vision of prognosticators does not reach.
"Furthermore, monks, people become unrighteous.
This, monks, is the fifth obstacle to the rains, which the fortune-tellers do not know, where the eye of the fortune-tellers does not reach.
These, monks, are the five obstacles to the rains, which the fortune-tellers do not know, where the eye of the fortune-tellers does not reach."
The Seventh. Aṅguttara Nikāya 5.198 20.
Brāhmaṇavagga (The Chapter on Brahmins)
Vācāsutta:
“Bhikkhus, speech endowed with five factors is well-spoken, not ill-spoken; it is blameless and beyond reproach to the wise.”
"By which five?
It is spoken at the proper time, it is spoken truthfully, it is spoken gently, it is spoken meaningfully, and it is spoken with a mind of loving-kindness.
Endowed with these five factors, monks, speech is well-spoken, not ill-spoken; it is blameless and beyond reproach to the wise."
The Eighth. Aṅguttara Nikāya 5.199 20.
Brāhmaṇavagga (The Chapter on Brahmins)
Kulasutta (AN 5.199, PTS AN iii 244): “Bhikkhus,
when virtuous renunciants visit a family, people there generate much merit on five grounds.”
Which five?

At whatever time, monks, people see virtuous ones who have gone forth approaching their family and their hearts become serene, at that time, monks, that family has entered upon a practice that leads to heaven.
At whatever time, monks, people rise up in respect when virtuous ones who have gone forth approach their family... [and so on].
They greet them and offer them seats; at that time, monks, that family has entered upon the practice that leads to rebirth in a high-born lineage.
At whatever time, monks, people free from the stain of stinginess [greet] virtuous renunciants who have approached their home...
They offer hospitality; at that time, monks, that family has entered upon a practice that leads to high status.

At whatever time, monks, people share with virtuous renunciants who have approached their home according to their means and their power, at that time, monks, that family has entered upon a practice that leads to great wealth.
He has entered upon the way. Monks,
at whatever time people question, cross-examine, and listen to the Dhamma from virtuous renunciants who have approached their family, that family, monks, is heading toward great wisdom.
At that time, he has entered upon the right practice.
Monks, when virtuous renunciants visit a family, people there generate much merit on these five grounds.
Thus ends the ninth [sutta].
Aṅguttara Nikāya 5.200 20. Brāhmaṇavagga Nissāraṇīyasutta (The Discourse on Escape) "Bhikkhus, there are these five things that lead to escape. What five?

"Bhikkhus, for one who has not abandoned lust, hatred, and delusion regarding forms cognizable by the eye, escape from those forms is not possible. But for one who has abandoned lust, hatred, and delusion regarding forms cognizable by the eye, escape from those forms is possible. "Bhikkhus, for one who has not abandoned lust, hatred, and delusion regarding sounds cognizable by the ear... regarding odors cognizable by the nose... regarding tastes cognizable by the tongue... regarding tactile objects cognizable by the body... regarding mental phenomena cognizable by the mind, escape from those mental phenomena is not possible. But for one who has abandoned lust, hatred, and delusion regarding mental phenomena cognizable by the mind, escape from those mental phenomena is possible. "These, bhikkhus, are the five things that lead to escape."
“Bhikkhus, there are these five elements of escape.
Which five?

In this case, monks, when a bhikkhu directs his attention to sensual pleasures, his mind does not leap forward toward them, does not become confident in them, does not settle upon them, and is not liberated from them.
But when he directs his attention to renunciation, his mind leaps forward toward renunciation, becomes confident in it, settles upon it, and is liberated from it.
His mind is well-gone, well-developed, well-emerged, well-liberated, and well-detached from sensual pleasures.
And whatever taints, vexations, and fevers arise conditioned by sensual pleasures—one is freed from those; one does not experience that feeling.
This is declared to be the escape from sensual pleasures.
Furthermore, monks, when a bhikkhu attends to ill will, his mind does not leap forward toward it, does not become confident in it, does not settle in it, and is not liberated from it.
But when he attends to non-ill will, his mind leaps forward into non-ill will, becomes placid, settles, and is liberated.
That mind of his is well-gone, well-developed, well-emerged, well-liberated, and well-detached from ill will.
And as for those taints, distresses, and fevers that arise conditioned by ill will—he is freed from them; he does not experience that feeling.
This is declared to be the escape from ill will.
Furthermore, monks, when a monk attends to cruelty, his mind does not leap forward toward it, does not become settled, does not find stability, and is not liberated.
But when he attends to non-cruelty, his mind leaps forward toward it, becomes settled, finds stability, and is liberated.
His mind is well-gone, well-developed, well-emerged, well-liberated, and well-detached from affliction;
and as for those taints, vexations, and fevers that arise with affliction as their condition—he is freed from them and does not experience that feeling.
This is declared to be the escape from affliction.
Furthermore, monks, when a bhikkhu attends to material form, his mind does not leap forward toward it, does not gain confidence in it, does not settle upon it, and is not liberated from it.
But when he attends to the formless, his mind leaps forward toward it, gains confidence in it, settles upon it, and is liberated from it.
His mind is well-gone, well-developed, well-emerged, well-liberated, and well-detached from material forms.
And whatever taints, vexations, and fevers arise conditioned by form—from those he is freed; he does not experience that feeling.
This is declared to be the escape from forms.

Furthermore, monks, when a monk attends to personal existence (*sakkāya*), his mind does not leap forward toward it, does not find confidence in it, does not settle upon it, and is not liberated from it.
But when he attends to the cessation of identity, his mind leaps forward into the cessation of identity, becomes serene, settles there, and is liberated.
That mind of his is well-gone, well-developed, well-emerged, well-liberated, and well-detached from identity;
and those taints, vexations, and fevers that arise with identity as their condition—from those he is freed, and he no longer experiences that feeling.
This has been declared as the escape from personal existence (*sakkāya*).
In him, delight in sensual desire does not underlie; delight in ill will does not underlie; delight in cruelty does not underlie; delight in form does not underlie;
and delight in personal existence does not underlie. Because he has no underlying tendency toward delight in sensual desire, and no underlying tendency toward delight in ill will...
“Without underlying tendency toward delight in ill will, without underlying tendency toward delight in form, and without underlying tendency toward delight in identity—

this, monks, is called a monk who is free from underlying tendencies, who has cut off craving, who has turned away from the fetters, and who, through the right penetration of conceit, has made an end of suffering. These, monks,
are the five elements leading to escape.”
The tenth.
The fifth chapter on Brahmins.
Its summary verse:
Soṇo Doṇa, Saṅgārava,
Kāraṇapālī, and Piṅgiyānī;
Suppiyā, Vassa, and Vācā—
"And by means of that which leads out from the family.
The Fourth Fifty is completed.
Aṅguttara Nikāya 5.201
21. Kimila Chapter:
The Discourse to Kimila (AN 5.201, PTS AN iii 247)
On one occasion the Blessed One was dwelling at Kimilā in the Bamboo Grove.

Then the Venerable Kimila approached the Blessed One; having approached and paid homage to the Blessed One, he sat down to one side. As he was sitting there, the Venerable Kimila said this to the Blessed One:
“What, Bhante, is the cause, what is the reason, why the true Dhamma does not endure long after a Tathāgata has attained final Nibbāna?”
“Here, Kimila, when the Tathāgata has attained final Nibbāna, monks, nuns, laymen, and laywomen dwell without reverence and without deference toward the Teacher;
they dwell without reverence and without deference toward the Dhamma; they dwell without reverence and without deference toward the Saṅgha;
they dwell without reverence and without deference toward the training; and they dwell without reverence and without deference toward one another.”
“This, Kimila, is the cause, this is the reason why, after the Tathāgata has attained final Nibbāna, the true Dhamma does not endure for long.
“But what, Bhante, is the cause, what is the reason why, after the Tathāgata has attained final Nibbāna, the true Dhamma endures for long?
“Here, Kimila, after the Tathāgata has attained final Nibbāna, the bhikkhus, bhikkhunīs, male lay followers, and female lay followers [remain devoted] to the Teacher...”
They dwell with reverence and deference; they dwell with reverence and deference toward the Dhamma; they dwell with reverence and deference toward the Saṅgha;
they dwell with reverence and deference toward the training; they dwell with reverence and deference toward one another.
“This, Kīmila, is the cause, this is the condition, by which the true Dhamma endures for a long time after a Tathāgata has attained final Nibbāna. Thus it was said.
First.
Aṅguttara Nikāya 5.202

21. The Chapter on Kimila: Discourse on Hearing the Dhamma (AN 5.202, PTS AN iii 248) “Monks, there are these five benefits in hearing the Dhamma. What five? One hears the Dhamma that has not been heard before; one clarifies the Dhamma already heard; one gains confidence in the Dhamma that has not yet been gained; one’s doubts regarding the Dhamma already gained are dispelled; and one comes to delight in the Dhamma. These, monks, are the five benefits in hearing the Dhamma.”
“Bhikkhus, there are these five benefits in listening to the Dhamma.
What are the five?
One hears what has not been heard; one clarifies what has been heard; one overcomes doubt; one straightens one’s view; and one’s mind becomes serene.”
“Monks, these are the five benefits of listening to the Dhamma.
The second [sutta].
*Aṅguttara Nikāya* 5.203.
21. Kimila Chapter:
The Discourse on the Noble Steed (Assājānīyasutta) (AN 5.203, PTS AN iii 248)
“Bhikkhus, endowed with five factors, a king’s excellent thoroughbred horse is worthy of a king, an asset to a king, and is reckoned as a very limb of the king.
With which five?
With honesty, speed, gentleness, patience, and amiability.”
“Monks, possessed of these five factors, a king’s noble thoroughbred horse is worthy of a king, an asset to a king, and is reckoned as a very limb of the king.

In the same way, monks, possessed of five qualities, a monk is worthy of gifts, worthy of hospitality, worthy of offerings, worthy of reverential salutation, and is an unsurpassed field of merit for the world. What are the five? [The text continues with the list of qualities.]”
“By straightforwardness, by speediness, by gentleness, by patience, and by mildness—

it is through possessing these five qualities, monks, that a monk is worthy of offerings, worthy of hospitality, worthy of gifts, worthy of reverential salutation, and an unsurpassed field of merit for the world. Thus was the third [discourse].

Aṅguttara Nikāya 5.204 21. Kimilavagga Balasutta (The Discourse on Strength) “Monks, there are these five strengths. What five? The strength of faith, the strength of energy, the strength of mindfulness, the strength of concentration, and the strength of wisdom. These, monks, are the five strengths.”
“Bhikkhus, there are these five powers.
What are the five?
The power of faith, the power of moral shame, the power of moral dread, the power of energy, and the power of wisdom—
these, monks, are the five powers. Thus ends the fourth [sutta].
Aṅguttara Nikāya 5.205 21.
Kimila Chapter The Discourse on the Barrenness of Mind (Cetokhila Sutta)
“Bhikkhus, there are these five kinds of mental barrenness.
What are the five?
“Here, monks, a monk is doubtful, uncertain, undecided, and lacks confidence in the Teacher.
For that monk who is doubtful, uncertain, undecided, and lacks confidence in the Teacher, his mind does not incline toward ardor, devotion, perseverance, and striving.
That his mind does not incline toward ardor, devotion, perseverance, and striving—this is the first wilderness of the mind.”
Furthermore, monks, a monk is doubtful about the Dhamma …pe… he is doubtful about the Saṅgha …pe… he is doubtful about the training …pe…
He is angry with his fellow celibates, displeased, with a resentful mind, and harboring resentment.

Monks, for that monk who is angry with his fellow celibates, displeased, with a resentful mind, and harboring resentment, his mind does not incline toward ardor, commitment, perseverance, and striving.
For one whose mind does not incline toward ardor, commitment, perseverance, and striving—this is the fifth mental barrenness.
“Monks, these are the five mental barrennesses.
The fifth.
Aṅguttara Nikāya 5.206

21. The Chapter on Kimila: The Discourse on the Bond (Vinibandhasutta) “Bhikkhus, there are these five bonds. What five? The bond of lust, the bond of hatred, the bond of delusion, the bond of views, and the bond of ignorance. These, bhikkhus, are the five bonds. “Bhikkhus, there are these five higher fetters. What five? The bond of lust for form, the bond of lust for the formless, the bond of conceit, the bond of restlessness, and the bond of ignorance. These, bhikkhus, are the five higher fetters. “Bhikkhus, when a noble disciple has abandoned these five bonds and severed these five higher fetters, he is called a noble disciple who is a non-returner, one who has destroyed the taints and will not return to this world. Thus spoke the Blessed One. Having said this, the Sublime One rose from his seat and entered his dwelling. Then, not long after the Blessed One had left, the Venerable Ānanda addressed the bhikkhus: “Friends, bhikkhus! “Friend,” those bhikkhus replied to the Venerable Ānanda. The Venerable Ānanda said this: “Friends, the Blessed One taught the Dhamma to us in brief without expounding its meaning in detail: ‘Bhikkhus, there are these five bonds... [as above] ...he will not return to this world. Friends, it would be good if the Venerable ones could explain the detailed meaning of this statement spoken in brief by the Blessed One. “Then, friend Ānanda, let us go to the Blessed One and report this matter to him. As the Blessed One explains it to us, so we shall remember it. “Yes, friends,” the Venerable Ānanda replied to those bhikkhus. Then the Venerable Ānanda and those bhikkhus approached the Blessed One, paid homage to him, and sat down to one side. Sitting there, the Venerable Ānanda reported to the Blessed One everything that had occurred, adding: “It would be good, venerable sir, if the Blessed One would explain the detailed meaning of this statement spoken in brief by the Blessed One. “Ānanda, suppose a man were to throw a yoke with a single hole into the great ocean, and a cow’s hair with a single tip were to be blown across it by the wind. And suppose a second, third, fourth, fifth, sixth, and seventh cow’s hair were likewise to be blown across it by the wind. What do you think, Ānanda, would that yoke with a single hole eventually be struck by those seven cow’s hairs? “It might be so, venerable sir, if the ocean were to dry up and evaporate, or if the earth were to be destroyed; but that yoke with a single hole would certainly not be struck by those seven cow’s hairs.

“So too, Ānanda, for a noble disciple, when five things are present and five things are abandoned, it is impossible and inconceivable that he should not attain final knowledge before his time. What five things are present? Here, Ānanda, a noble disciple possesses confirmed confidence in the Buddha: ‘The Blessed One is an arahant, perfectly enlightened, accomplished in true knowledge and conduct, fortunate, knower of the world, unsurpassed leader of persons to be tamed, teacher of devas and humans, the Enlightened One, the Blessed One. He possesses confirmed confidence in the Dhamma: ‘The Dhamma is well-expounded by the Blessed One, directly visible, immediate, inviting one to come and see, applicable, to be personally experienced by the wise. He possesses confirmed confidence in the Saṅgha: ‘The Saṅgha of the Blessed One’s disciples is practicing the good way, practicing the straight way, practicing the true way, practicing the proper way; that is, the four pairs of persons, the eight types of individuals—this Saṅgha of the Blessed One’s disciples is worthy of gifts, worthy of hospitality, worthy of offerings, worthy of reverential salutation, the unsurpassed field of merit for the world. He possesses the virtues dear to the noble ones—untorn, unbroken, unspotted, unsplattered, liberating, praised by the wise, untarnished, leading to concentration. And what five things are abandoned? Lust for form is abandoned, lust for the formless is abandoned, conceit is abandoned, restlessness is abandoned, and ignorance is abandoned. For a noble disciple, Ānanda, when these five things are present and these five things are abandoned, it is impossible and inconceivable that he should not attain final knowledge before his time. When this was said, the Venerable Ānanda said to the Blessed One: “Venerable sir, it is wonderful, it is marvelous how well the Blessed One has stated this! Venerable sir, it is as if one were to set upright what had been overturned, or to reveal what was hidden, or to show the way to one who was lost, or to carry an oil lamp into the darkness so that those with eyes might see forms. Just so, the Blessed One has explained the Dhamma in various ways. Venerable sir, those bhikkhus who are learners, who have not yet attained their heart’s ideal, who dwell aspiring for the supreme security from bondage—they will understand this Dhamma through the Blessed One’s teaching. But those bhikkhus who are arahants, whose taints are destroyed, who have lived the holy life, done what had to be done, laid down the burden, reached their own goal, utterly destroyed the fetters of existence, and are completely liberated through final knowledge—they themselves have already understood this Dhamma. “Ānanda, those bhikkhus who are learners, who have not yet attained their heart’s ideal, who dwell aspiring for the supreme security from bondage—they will understand this Dhamma through the Blessed One’s teaching. But those bhikkhus who are arahants, whose taints are destroyed... and are completely liberated through final knowledge—they too will understand this Dhamma through the Blessed One’s teaching. This is what the Blessed One said. Elated, the Venerable Ānanda and those bhikkhus rejoiced in the Blessed One’s words. *The Book of the Fives, Chapter 21: The Chapter on Kimila.*
“Bhikkhus, there are these five mental shackles.
What are the five?

Here, bhikkhus, a bhikkhu is not free from lust for sensual pleasures; he is not devoid of desire, not devoid of affection, not devoid of thirst, not devoid of fever, and not devoid of craving for them.”
“Bhikkhus, when a bhikkhu is not free from lust for sensual pleasures, not free from desire, not free from affection, not free from thirst, not free from fever,

and not free from craving for them, his mind does not incline toward ardor, commitment, perseverance, and striving. When the mind does not incline toward ardor, commitment, perseverance, and striving, this is the first mental bondage.”
Furthermore, monks, a bhikkhu is not free from lust for the body … he is not free from lust for forms … having eaten as much as he desires until his belly is full,
he dwells addicted to the pleasure of sleep, the pleasure of reclining, and the pleasure of drowsiness … [and so forth].
He leads the holy life aspiring for one or another class of devas, thinking: “By means of this virtue, or observance, or austerity, or holy life, I shall become a deva or some other kind of deva.
Monks, that monk who leads the holy life aspiring for one or another class of devas, thinking:
“By means of this virtue, or observance, or austerity, or holy life, I shall become a deva or some other kind of deva,”
His mind does not incline toward ardor, devotion, perseverance, and striving.
When the mind does not incline toward ardor, devotion, perseverance, and striving, this is the fifth mental bond.
These, monks, are the five mental bonds.”
The Sixth.
Aṅguttara Nikāya 5.207 21. Kimila-vagga
Yāgusutta:

“Bhikkhus, there are these five benefits of rice gruel. What five? It settles the stomach; it allays hunger; it dispels thirst; it cleanses the bladder; it brings about ease in the digestion of what has been eaten, drunk, chewed, and tasted. These, bhikkhus, are the five benefits of rice gruel.”
“What five?
It wards off hunger, it allays thirst, it harmonizes the wind, it cleanses the bladder, and it digests any remaining undigested food.
These, monks, are the five benefits of rice porridge.”
Seventh.
Aṅguttara Nikāya 5.208 21. Kimilavagga
The Discourse on the Tooth-Stick (Dantakaṭṭhasutta): “Bhikkhus,
there are these five disadvantages in not chewing a tooth-stick.”
Which five?
The eyesight fails, the mouth becomes foul-smelling, the taste-buds do not become purified, bile and phlegm envelop the food, and food does not agree with him.
These, monks, are the five disadvantages of not chewing tooth-sticks.
“Monks, there are these five benefits from chewing a tooth-stick.
What are the five?
The eyes are clear, the mouth does not have a foul odor, the taste-carrying channels are purified, bile and phlegm do not coat the food, and it cleanses the food.”
“Monks, these are the five benefits of chewing tooth-sticks.
The eighth.
Aṅguttara Nikāya 5.209

21. The Chapter on Kimila: The Discourse on the Essence of Song (Gītassara Sutta) At Sāvatthī. “Bhikkhus, just as whatever is the essence of a song is found in its opening verse, so too, bhikkhus, whatever is the essence of the holy life is found in this: the destruction of craving, the removal of desire, the cessation, stilling, and extinguishment of craving. This, bhikkhus, is the essence of the holy life. Thus have I heard. At one time the Blessed One was dwelling at Sāvatthī in Jeta’s Grove, Anāthapiṇḍika’s Park. There the Venerable Kimila approached the Blessed One, paid homage to him, sat down to one side, and said to the Blessed One: “Venerable sir, it is said, ‘the essence of the holy life, the essence of the holy life. In what way, venerable sir, is there the essence of the holy life? “Kimila, just as whatever is the essence of a song is found in its opening verse, so too, Kimila, whatever is the essence of the holy life is found in this: the destruction of craving, the removal of desire, the cessation, stilling, and extinguishment of craving. This, Kimila, is the essence of the holy life. Then the Venerable Kimila, having delighted and rejoiced in the Blessed One’s words, rose from his seat, paid homage to the Blessed One, and keeping him on his right, departed. Not long after the Venerable Kimila had left, the Blessed One addressed the bhikkhus: “Bhikkhus, suppose a man were to say: ‘I will describe to you the essence of a song,’ he would be speaking correctly if he were to say: ‘Whatever is the essence of a song is found in its opening verse. Why is that? Because whatever is the essence of a song is indeed found in its opening verse. So too, bhikkhus, suppose a man were to say: ‘I will describe to you the essence of the holy life,’ he would be speaking correctly if he were to say: ‘The destruction of craving, the removal of desire, the cessation, stilling, and extinguishment of craving—this is the essence of the holy life. Why is that? Because, bhikkhus, whatever is the essence of the holy life is indeed found in this: the destruction of craving, the removal of desire, the cessation, stilling, and extinguishment of craving. This, bhikkhus, is the essence of the holy life. This is what the Blessed One said. Elated, those bhikkhus delighted in the Blessed One’s words. Thus have I heard. At one time the Blessed One was dwelling at Sāvatthī in Jeta’s Grove, Anāthapiṇḍika’s Park. There the Venerable Kimila approached the Blessed One, paid homage to him, sat down to one side, and said to the Blessed One: “Venerable sir, it is said, ‘the essence of the holy life, the essence of the holy life. In what way, venerable sir, is there the essence of the holy life? “Kimila, just as whatever is the essence of a song is found in its opening verse, so too, Kimila, whatever is the essence of the holy life is found in this: the destruction of craving, the removal of desire, the cessation, stilling, and extinguishment of craving. This, Kimila, is the essence of the holy life. Then the Venerable Kimila, having delighted and rejoiced in the Blessed One’s words, rose from his seat, paid homage to the Blessed One, and keeping him on his right, departed. Not long after the Venerable Kimila had left, the Blessed One addressed the bhikkhus: “Bhikkhus, suppose a man were to say: ‘I will describe to you the essence of a song,’ he would be speaking correctly if he were to say: ‘Whatever is the essence of a song is found in its opening verse. Why is that? Because whatever is the essence of a song is indeed found in its opening verse. So too, bhikkhus, suppose a man were to say: ‘I will describe to you the essence of the holy life,’ he would be speaking correctly if he were to say: ‘The destruction of craving, the removal of desire, the cessation, stilling, and extinguishment of craving—this is the essence of the holy life. Why is that? Because, bhikkhus, whatever is the essence of the holy life is indeed found in this: the destruction of craving, the removal of desire, the cessation, stilling, and extinguishment of craving. This, bhikkhus, is the essence of the holy life. This is what the Blessed One said. Elated, those bhikkhus delighted in the Blessed One’s words.

Aṅguttara Nikāya 5.210 21. Kimila Vagga Muṭṭhassati Sutta: On Lapse of Mindfulness “Bhikkhus, there are these five qualities that lead to the decline of a bhikkhu who is a trainee. What five? “Bhikkhus, there are these five dangers for one who falls asleep unmindful and lacking clear comprehension. What five? [The text continues with the enumeration of these five dangers.]”
One sleeps in suffering, one awakens in suffering, one sees evil dreams, the deities do not protect one, and one emits impurity.
Monks, these are the five dangers for one who falls asleep with unestablished mindfulness and without clear comprehension.

“What five?
One sleeps happily, one awakens happily, one does not see evil dreams, deities protect one, and no impurity is emitted.
These, monks, are the five benefits for one who falls asleep with mindfulness established and clear comprehension.”

22. Akkosakavagga Bahubhāṇisutta (AN 5.214, PTS AN iii 254) “Monks, there are these four types of persons found existing in the world. What four? The one who speaks much; the one who speaks little; the one who speaks at the right time; and the one who speaks what is beneficial. And how, monks, is one a person who speaks much? Here, monks, someone is a talkative fellow, one who talks excessively, one who talks at the wrong time, one who talks what is not fact, one who talks what is useless, and one who talks without mindfulness. This, monks, is called a person who speaks much. And how, monks, is one a person who speaks little? Here, monks, someone is not a talkative fellow, one who does not talk excessively, one who does not talk at the wrong time, one who does not talk what is not fact, one who does not talk what is useless, and one who does not talk without mindfulness. This, monks, is called a person who speaks little. And how, monks, is one a person who speaks at the right time? Here, monks, someone, when questioned, answers at the right time; when not questioned, he does not speak out of his own accord; he speaks what is true, what is factual, and what is connected with the goal. This, monks, is called a person who speaks at the right time. And how, monks, is one a person who speaks what is beneficial? Here, monks, someone speaks what is beneficial, not what is harmful; he speaks what is wholesome, not what is unwholesome; he speaks with a mind of loving-kindness, not with a mind of ill will. This, monks, is called a person who speaks what is beneficial. These, monks, are the four types of persons found existing in the world.”
“Bhikkhus, there are these five dangers for a person who talks too much. What are the five? He speaks falsehood;
he speaks maliciously; he speaks harshly; he speaks idle chatter; and with the breakup of the body, after death, he is reborn in a state of deprivation, a bad destination, a lower realm, or hell.”
“Monks, these are the five disadvantages in a person who speaks much.
Monks, there are these five advantages in a person who speaks with measured words.
What are the five?”

He speaks no falsehood, he speaks no slander, he speaks no harsh speech, and he speaks no idle chatter; with the breakup of the body, after death, he is reborn in a good destination, a heavenly world.
These, monks, are the five benefits for a person who speaks with deliberation. Thus the fourth [sutta].
Aṅguttara Nikāya 5.215 22. Akkosakavagga Paṭhamaakkhantisutta (The First Discourse on Intolerance) “Bhikkhus, there are these five dangers in intolerance.

What five? First, one who is intolerant incurs a bad reputation for being difficult to live with; this is the first danger in intolerance. Second, one who is intolerant provokes much resentment; this is the second danger in intolerance. Third, one who is intolerant does not find joy in the Dhamma; this is the third danger in intolerance. Fourth, one who is intolerant does not attain concentration; this is the fourth danger in intolerance. Fifth, one who is intolerant, upon the dissolution of the body, after death, reappears in a state of deprivation, in an unhappy destination, in perdition, even in hell; this is the fifth danger in intolerance. These, bhikkhus, are the five dangers in intolerance.”
“Bhikkhus, there are these five disadvantages in impatience.
What are the five?

One becomes disliked and unpleasant to many people, one becomes full of enmity and full of faults, one dies confused, and with the breakup of the body, after death, one is reborn in a state of deprivation, a bad destination, a lower realm, or hell.
These, monks, are the five disadvantages of impatience.
There are these five advantages of patience, monks.
“What are the five?

One is dear and pleasing to many people; one does not have much enmity; one does not have much fault; one dies unconfused; and with the breakup of the body, after death, one reappears in a happy destination, in a heavenly world.
These, monks, are the five benefits of patience.”

22. Akkosakavagga Paṭhama-apāsādikasutta (AN 5.217) [The Blessed One said: "Monks, there are these five qualities that make one untrustworthy. What five? Here, monks, a person is untrustworthy by nature; he does not speak as he has seen, nor as he has heard. He speaks contrary to what he has seen and contrary to what he has heard. And when he is asked, 'Have you seen this? or 'Have you heard this?', he says, 'I have not seen it' or 'I have not heard it,' even though he has actually seen or heard it. Furthermore, monks, a person is untrustworthy because of his greed. For the sake of gain, honor, or fame, he speaks falsely about what he has seen or heard. When asked, 'Have you seen this? or 'Have you heard this?', he says, 'I have not seen it' or 'I have not heard it,' even though he has actually seen or heard it. Furthermore, monks, a person is untrustworthy because of his hatred. Out of malice, he speaks falsely about what he has seen or heard. When asked, 'Have you seen this? or 'Have you heard this?', he says, 'I have not seen it' or 'I have not heard it,' even though he has actually seen or heard it. Furthermore, monks, a person is untrustworthy because of his delusion. Being confused, he speaks falsely about what he has seen or heard. When asked, 'Have you seen this? or 'Have you heard this?', he says, 'I have not seen it' or 'I have not heard it,' even though he has actually seen or heard it. Furthermore, monks, a person is untrustworthy because of his fear. Out of dread, he speaks falsely about what he has seen or heard. When asked, 'Have you seen this? or 'Have you heard this?', he says, 'I have not seen it' or 'I have not heard it,' even though he has actually seen or heard it. These, monks, are the five qualities that make one untrustworthy. Monks, there are these five qualities that make one trustworthy. What five? Here, monks, a person is trustworthy by nature; he speaks as he has seen and as he has heard. He does not speak contrary to what he has seen, nor contrary to what he has heard. And when he is asked, 'Have you seen this? or 'Have you heard this?', he says, 'I have seen it' or 'I have heard it,' provided that he has actually seen or heard it. Furthermore, monks, a person is trustworthy because he is free from greed. Without being motivated by gain, honor, or fame, he speaks truthfully about what he has seen or heard. When asked, 'Have you seen this? or 'Have you heard this?', he says, 'I have seen it' or 'I have heard it,' provided that he has actually seen or heard it. Furthermore, monks, a person is trustworthy because he is free from hatred. Without being motivated by malice, he speaks truthfully about what he has seen or heard. When asked, 'Have you seen this? or 'Have you heard this?', he says, 'I have seen it' or 'I have heard it,' provided that he has actually seen or heard it. Furthermore, monks, a person is trustworthy because he is free from delusion. Without being confused, he speaks truthfully about what he has seen or heard. When asked, 'Have you seen this? or 'Have you heard this?', he says, 'I have seen it' or 'I have heard it,' provided that he has actually seen or heard it. Furthermore, monks, a person is trustworthy because he is free from fear. Without being motivated by dread, he speaks truthfully about what he has seen or heard. When asked, 'Have you seen this? or 'Have you heard this?', he says, 'I have seen it' or 'I have heard it,' provided that he has actually seen or heard it. These, monks, are the five qualities that make one trustworthy."* *The full sutta continues with the Buddha's exposition on the benefits of trustworthiness and the consequences of being untrustworthy.*
“Bhikkhus, there are these five dangers in what is untrustworthy.
What five?
One reproaches oneself.”

22. Akkosakavagga The Second Discourse on Impoliteness (Dutiya-apāsādika-sutta) At Sāvatthī. “Monks, there are these five qualities of one who is impolite. What five? He speaks out of season; he speaks what is untrue; he speaks what is unbeneficial; he speaks with a mind of ill will; and he speaks at a time when his words are not welcome and are not pleasing to others. These, monks, are the five qualities of one who is impolite. Furthermore, monks, there are these five qualities of one who is polite. What five? He does not speak out of season; he does not speak what is untrue; he does not speak what is unbeneficial; he does not speak with a mind of ill will; and he speaks at a time when his words are welcome and pleasing to others. These, monks, are the five qualities of one who is polite.”

23. Dīghacārikavagga Atinivāsasutta (AN 5.223, PTS AN iii 258) “Monks, there are these four kinds of persons found existing in the world. What four? The person who dwells too long; the person who dwells too short; the person who dwells at the right time; and the person who does not dwell at all. And how, monks, is one a person who dwells too long? Here, monks, a bhikkhu dwells for too long in a certain village or town. Because he dwells there for too long, he becomes overly familiar with the families there. Being overly familiar, he becomes intimate. Being intimate, he becomes involved in their affairs. Being involved in their affairs, he comes to live off those families. Living off them, he becomes dependent on them. Being dependent, he becomes subject to their will. Thus, monks, this is called a person who dwells too long. And how, monks, is one a person who dwells too short? Here, monks, a bhikkhu dwells for too short a time in a certain village or town. Because he dwells there for too short a time, he does not become overly familiar with the families there. Not becoming overly familiar, he does not become intimate. Not becoming intimate, he does not become involved in their affairs. Not being involved in their affairs, he does not come to live off those families. Not living off them, he does not become dependent on them. Not being dependent, he does not become subject to their will. Thus, monks, this is called a person who dwells too short. And how, monks, is one a person who dwells at the right time? Here, monks, a bhikkhu dwells for the right length of time in a certain village or town. Because he dwells there for the right length of time, he becomes overly familiar with the families there. Being overly familiar, he becomes intimate. Being intimate, he becomes involved in their affairs. Being involved in their affairs, he does not come to live off those families. Not living off them, he does not become dependent on them. Not being dependent, he does not become subject to their will. Thus, monks, this is called a person who dwells at the right time. And how, monks, is one a person who does not dwell at all? Here, monks, a bhikkhu does not dwell in any village or town. Thus, monks, this is called a person who does not dwell at all. These, monks, are the four kinds of persons found existing in the world.”
“Monks, there are these five disadvantages in staying too long.
What are the five?
One possesses many goods and amasses many goods; one possesses many medicines and amasses many medicines; one has many duties...”
He becomes one who has much to do, being competent in his duties; he dwells in association with householders and renunciants through an improper intimacy with householders;
and when departing from that residence, he departs with longing for it.
These, monks, are the five disadvantages of staying too long.
“Monks, there are these five advantages in living in a common residence.
What are the five?
One does not have many belongings nor an accumulation of many belongings; one does not have many medicines nor an accumulation of many medicines.”

He is not burdened with many duties, nor does he have much to do; he is not preoccupied with what ought to be done. He dwells unattached to both householders and renunciants, avoiding inappropriate association with householders.
And when departing from that residence, he departs without looking back.
These, monks, are the five advantages of living in a balanced community.”
The Third.
Aṅguttara Nikāya 5.224.
Chapter 23: On Long Journeys (Dīghacārikavagga).
The Discourse on Stinginess (Maccharīsutta): “Bhikkhus,
there are these five dangers in staying too long.”
What are the five?
One is stingy regarding dwellings, stingy regarding families, stingy regarding gains, stingy regarding praise, and stingy regarding the Dhamma.
These, monks, are the five dangers in staying too long.
“Monks, there are these five advantages in living together with those of equal standing.

What are the five? One does not become stingy regarding dwellings; one does not become stingy regarding families; one does not become stingy regarding gains; one does not become stingy regarding praise; and one does not become stingy regarding the Dhamma.”
“Monks, these are the five advantages of living in a balanced community.
The fourth.
Aṅguttara Nikāya 5.225

23. Dīghacārikavagga Paṭhamakulūpakasutta (The Discourse on Visiting Families First) “Bhikkhus, there are these five dangers for a bhikkhu who visits families first. What five? (1) Whatever gain he obtains, it is not easy for him to enjoy it with a mind free from longing. (2) Whatever praise he receives, it is not easy for him to endure it with a mind free from aversion. (3) He does not easily attain concentration when he wishes to do so. (4) His mind does not easily incline toward seclusion. (5) He does not quickly reach the final goal of the holy life. These, bhikkhus, are the five dangers for a bhikkhu who visits families first.”
“Bhikkhus, there are these five dangers for one who associates with families. What are the five? One falls into an offense regarding unannounced wandering;

one falls into an offense regarding sitting in private; one falls into an offense regarding sitting on a concealed seat; one falls into an offense while teaching the Dhamma to a woman for more than five or six sentences; and one dwells full of sensual intentions.”
“Monks, these are the five dangers for one who frequents families.
The fifth.
Aṅguttara Nikāya 5.226
23. The Chapter on Long Journeys.
Discourse on the Second Family-Visiting Monk (AN 5.226, PTS AN iii 259).
“Bhikkhus, there are these five dangers for a bhikkhu who frequents families and dwells in excessive association with them.
What are the five?
Frequent sight of women;”
When there is seeing, there is association;
when there is association, there is intimacy;
when there is intimacy, there is an opportunity for attack.

"For one whose mind has become immersed [in sensual desires], this is to be expected: 'He will either lead the holy life without enthusiasm, or he will commit some defiled offense, or he will renounce the training and return to the lower life.
These, monks, are the five dangers for a monk who visits families and dwells excessively associated with them.
This is the sixth.
Aṅguttara Nikāya 5.227 23.

Dīghacārikavagga Bhogasutta “Monks, there are these five kinds of wealth. What five? The wealth of faith, the wealth of virtuous behavior, the wealth of learning, the wealth of generosity, and the wealth of wisdom. These, monks, are the five kinds of wealth.”
“Bhikkhus, there are these five dangers in wealth. What five? (AN 5.227, PTS AN iii 259)”
Wealth is shared with fire; wealth is shared with water; wealth is shared with kings; wealth is shared with thieves; wealth is shared with unloved heirs.
These, monks, are the five dangers in regard to wealth.
There are, monks, these five advantages in regard to wealth.
Which five?
Relying on wealth, he comforts himself, gladdens himself, and properly maintains his own well-being; he comforts his mother and father, gladdens them, and properly maintains their well-being;
he comforts his children, wife, slaves, laborers, and servants, gladdens them, and properly [maintains their well-being].
“He protects his happiness; he makes his friends and companions happy and satisfied, and he properly protects their happiness;
he establishes an uplifting offering among ascetics and brahmins that leads to heaven, has a pleasant result, and conduces to rebirth in heaven.
These, monks, are the five benefits in wealth.”
Seventh. Aṅguttara Nikāya 5.228. Chapter 23:
On Long Journeys (Dīghacārikavagga).
Ussūrabhattasutta: “Bhikkhus,
there are these five disadvantages in a family where meals are eaten late.”
Which five?
Those guests and visitors they do not honor at the proper time;
those deities who receive offerings they do not honor at the proper time;
Those ascetics and brahmins who eat but one meal a day, abstaining from food at night and refraining from eating at improper times—they do not honor [the meal] at the proper time;
their slaves, laborers, and servants perform their work with averted faces;
and that which is eaten out of season, even if it be only a little, lacks nutritive strength.
“Monks, there are these five disadvantages in a family where meals are served at irregular times.
Monks, there are these five advantages in a family where meals are served at regular times.
What are the five?”
Those guests and visitors they honor at the proper time;
those deities who accept offerings they honor at the proper time;
those ascetics and brahmins who eat but one meal a day, who abstain from food at night, and who refrain from eating at improper times—they honor them at the proper time.
"Slaves, laborers, and servants perform their work without turning away from them;
and for that same duration, whatever food they eat remains nutritious.
These, monks, are the five benefits for a family that provides meals at the proper time."
The Eighth. Aṅguttara Nikāya 5.229 23.
Dīghacārikavagga (The Chapter on Long Journeys)
The Discourse on the First Black Snake (Paṭhamakaṇhasappasutta). “Bhikkhus,
there are these five dangers in a black snake.”
Which five?
It is impure, foul-smelling, timid, fearful, and treacherous to friends.
These, monks, are the five dangers in a black snake.
In the same way, monks, there are these five disadvantages in women.
What are the five?
She is impure, she is foul-smelling, she is timid, she is fearful, and she is treacherous to friends.
“Monks, these are the five dangers in women.
Thus was the ninth [discourse]. Aṅguttara Nikāya 5.230.
23. The Chapter on Long Journeys:
The Second Discourse on the Black Snake (Dutiyakaṇhasappasutta) (AN 5.230, PTS AN iii 260)
“Bhikkhus, there are these five dangers in a black snake.
What are the five?
It is angry, it is vengeful, its venom is fierce, it has a forked tongue, and it betrays friends.”
“Monks, these are the five dangers of a black snake.
In the same way, monks, there are these five dangers in women.
What are the five?
"Angry, resentful, of terrible venom, double-tongued, and treacherous to friends.
In this regard, monks, this is the terrible venom of women:
for the most part, monks, women are possessed of intense passion."
In this regard, monks, this is the double-tonguedness of women:
for the most part, monks, women are speakers of divisive speech.
In this regard, monks, this is the treachery toward friends of women: [as follows].
“Monks, for the most part, women are unfaithful.
These, monks, are the five dangers regarding women.
The tenth.
The third chapter: The Chapter on Long Journeys.
Its summary verse:
Two long journeys have been described.
Excessive attachment to dwelling and stinginess;
two types of family patrons and wealth,
and two kinds of suitable food.
Aṅguttara Nikāya 5.231 24.
Āvāsikavagga Āvāsikasutta (The Resident Monk)
“Bhikkhus, a resident bhikkhu who possesses five qualities is not worthy of being cultivated. Which five? [Text follows].”
He is not perfect in deportment nor perfect in conduct;
he is not learned nor a retainer of what he has heard;
he is not one who practices effacement nor one who delights in seclusion.
He is not one of beautiful speech, nor is he one who speaks beautifully;
he is of poor wisdom, dull, and muddle-headed.
Possessing these five qualities, monks, a resident monk is unworthy of being cultivated.
“Bhikkhus, a resident bhikkhu endowed with five qualities is one who should be cultivated.
With which five?
He is perfect in deportment and perfect in conduct.”
He is learned and retains what he has heard;
he is one who practices self-effacement and delights in seclusion;
he is a speaker of noble words and possesses noble speech.
“He is wise, not dull-witted, and not deaf-mute.
Possessing these five qualities, monks, a resident monk is one who should be cultivated. Thus was the first [discourse].

Aṅguttara Nikāya 5.232 24. Āvāsikavagga Piyasutta (The Discourse on the Dear One) “Monks, there are these five things that are dear, beloved, and pleasing to a resident monk. What five? First, a resident monk is one who is well-conducted in his bodily conduct; he does not, for the sake of minor and trifling matters, engage in frivolous speech regarding the training rules. This is the first thing that is dear, beloved, and pleasing to a resident monk. Second, a resident monk is one who is well-conducted in his verbal conduct; he does not, for the sake of minor and trifling matters, engage in frivolous speech regarding the training rules. This is the second thing that is dear, beloved, and pleasing to a resident monk. Third, a resident monk is one who is well-conducted in his mental conduct; he does not, for the sake of minor and trifling matters, engage in frivolous speech regarding the training rules. This is the third thing that is dear, beloved, and pleasing to a resident monk. Fourth, a resident monk is one who is well-conducted in his livelihood; he does not, for the sake of minor and trifling matters, engage in frivolous speech regarding the training rules. This is the fourth thing that is dear, beloved, and pleasing to a resident monk. Fifth, a resident monk is one who is well-conducted in his observance of the Uposatha; he does not, for the sake of minor and trifling matters, engage in frivolous speech regarding the training rules. This is the fifth thing that is dear, beloved, and pleasing to a resident monk. These, monks, are the five things that are dear, beloved, and pleasing to a resident monk.”

“Bhikkhus, possessing five qualities, a resident bhikkhu is dear and agreeable to his fellow practitioners of the holy life, and is respected and esteemed by them. What are the five? [The Buddha said:]”

He is virtuous; he dwells restrained by the Pātimokkha, possessed of proper conduct and resort, seeing danger in even the slightest faults, and having undertaken them, he trains himself in the rules of training.

He is learned, a retainer of what he has heard, and a storehouse of what he has heard—those teachings that are good in the beginning, good in the middle, and good in the end, with the right meaning and phrasing, which proclaim the perfectly complete and pure holy life (*brahmacariya*)—such teachings as these he possesses.
They have become very learned regarding the teachings, having retained them in memory, mastered them through speech, examined them with the mind, and thoroughly penetrated them through right view.
They are a speaker of what is beautiful, possessing beautiful speech, endowed with polite language that is clear, flawless, and expressive of the meaning.
They are one who gains at will, without difficulty, and without trouble, the four jhānas that belong to the higher mind and provide a pleasant dwelling in this very life.
With the destruction of the taints, he dwells having realized for himself with direct knowledge, in this very life, the taintless liberation of mind and liberation by wisdom, having entered upon it.
Possessing these five qualities, monks, a resident monk is dear and agreeable to his fellow celibate practitioners, and is respected and esteemed.
This is the second [discourse].

Aṅguttara Nikāya 5.233 24. Āvāsikavagga Sobhanasutta “Bhikkhus, there are these five kinds of persons found existing in the world. What five? The person who is beautiful but not virtuous; the person who is virtuous but not beautiful; the person who is neither beautiful nor virtuous; and the person who is both beautiful and virtuous. And how, bhikkhus, is a person beautiful but not virtuous?

Here, someone is handsome, attractive, graceful, possessing supreme beauty of complexion, well-favored by fortune, and endowed with the marks of a great man; yet he destroys life, takes what is not given, engages in sexual misconduct, speaks falsely, and indulges in liquor, wine, and intoxicants, the basis for heedlessness. This is called a person who is beautiful but not virtuous. And how, bhikkhus, is a person virtuous but not beautiful? Here, someone is ugly, unattractive, ungainly, lacking beauty of complexion, unfavored by fortune, and devoid of the marks of a great man; yet he abstains from destroying life, from taking what is not given, from sexual misconduct, from false speech, and from liquor, wine, and intoxicants, the basis for heedlessness. This is called a person who is virtuous but not beautiful. And how, bhikkhus, is a person neither beautiful nor virtuous? Here, someone is ugly, unattractive, ungainly, lacking beauty of complexion, unfavored by fortune, and devoid of the marks of a great man; and he destroys life, takes what is not given, engages in sexual misconduct, speaks falsely, and indulges in liquor, wine, and intoxicants, the basis for heedlessness. This is called a person who is neither beautiful nor virtuous. And how, bhikkhus, is a person both beautiful and virtuous? Here, someone is handsome, attractive, graceful, possessing supreme beauty of complexion, well-favored by fortune, and endowed with the marks of a great man; and he abstains from destroying life, from taking what is not given, from sexual misconduct, from false speech, and from liquor, wine, and intoxicants, the basis for heedlessness. This is called a person who is both beautiful and virtuous. These, bhikkhus, are the five kinds of persons found existing in the world.”
“Bhikkhus, possessing five qualities, a resident bhikkhu beautifies his dwelling-place. Which five? [The Buddha said:]”
He is virtuous... having undertaken them, he trains in the rules of training;
he is learned... his view is well-penetrated;
he is a good speaker, possessed of a beautiful voice, endowed with speech that is polished, clear, articulate, and expressive of the meaning.
He is capable of instructing, exhorting, inspiring, and gladdening those who approach him with a discourse on the Dhamma;
he is one who gains at will, without difficulty, and without trouble, the four jhānas that belong to the higher mind and provide a pleasant dwelling in this very life.
Endowed with these five qualities, monks, a resident monk beautifies the monastery.”
The Third.
Aṅguttara Nikāya 5.234 24.
Āvāsikavagga (The Chapter on Resident Monks)
Bahūpakārasutta: “Bhikkhus,
endowed with five qualities, a resident bhikkhu is of great service to the monastery.
Which five? He is virtuous ...
[as above] ... he trains himself in the training precepts after having undertaken them;
he is learned ... [as above] ... his view is well-penetrated.
He repairs what is broken and dilapidated.
Now, a great community of monks has arrived—monks from various kingdoms—and they approach the householders and announce:
"Friends, a great community of monks has arrived—monks from various kingdoms. Perform meritorious deeds! This is the time to perform meritorious deeds."
He is one who obtains at will, without difficulty, and without hardship, the four jhānas that constitute higher mental states and provide a pleasant dwelling in this very life.
Possessing these five qualities, monks, a resident monk is of great benefit to the monastery. Thus was the fourth [discourse].
Aṅguttara Nikāya 5.235 24.

Āvāsikavagga Anukampasutta (The Discourse on Compassion) "Bhikkhus, possessing five qualities, a resident bhikkhu is worthy of gifts, worthy of hospitality, worthy of offerings, worthy of reverential salutation, an unsurpassed field of merit for the world. What five? Here, a resident bhikkhu is compassionate toward his fellow monks who are junior, of middle standing, and senior; he is one who encourages, inspires, and gladdens them with talk on the Dhamma. Possessing these five qualities, a resident bhikkhu is worthy of gifts, worthy of hospitality, worthy of offerings, worthy of reverential salutation, an unsurpassed field of merit for the world."
“Bhikkhus, possessing five qualities, a resident bhikkhu shows compassion toward householders. What are the five? [Text follows]”
He encourages others in higher virtue;
he establishes them in the vision of the Dhamma;
and having approached those who are ill, he arouses mindfulness in them.
"Venerable sirs, establish mindfulness directed toward the state of an arahant.
Now, a great assembly of monks had arrived—monks from various kingdoms—and they approached the householders and announced:
"Friends, a great assembly of monks has arrived, including monks from various kingdoms. Perform meritorious deeds; it is the right time to perform meritorious deeds."
Furthermore, whatever food they give him—whether coarse or refined—he eats it himself; he does not squander what has been given out of faith.
Endowed with these five qualities, monks, a resident monk shows compassion for householders.
Thus ends the fifth [discourse].
Aṅguttara Nikāya 5.236 24. Āvāsikavagga First Discourse on Those Deserving of Censure “Monks, there are these five qualities of one who deserves censure.

What five? Here, monks, a monk is immoral; he is one who dwells in a way that brings harm to his fellow monks; he is one who speaks in dispraise of others; he is one who is miserly with regard to the Dhamma; and he is one who does not apply himself to wakefulness. These, monks, are the five qualities of one who deserves censure. “Monks, there are these five qualities of one who is worthy of praise. What five? Here, monks, a monk is virtuous; he is one who dwells in a way that brings benefit to his fellow monks; he is one who speaks in praise of others; he is one who is not miserly with regard to the Dhamma; and he is one who applies himself to wakefulness. These, monks, are the five qualities of one who is worthy of praise.”
“Bhikkhus, possessing five qualities, a resident bhikkhu is deposited in hell as if carried there. What are the five? [The Sutta continues:]”
Without investigating and without scrutinizing, one speaks in praise of one who deserves dispraise;
without investigating and without scrutinizing, one speaks in dispraise of one who deserves praise;
without investigating and without scrutinizing, one conceives confidence in a matter that inspires lack of confidence.
Without investigating and without scrutinizing, he shows lack of confidence regarding matters that inspire confidence;
he squanders what has been given out of faith.
Possessing these five qualities, monks, a resident monk is placed in hell as if carried there.
“Monks, a resident monk endowed with five qualities is deposited in heaven as if carried there.
What are the five?
Having investigated and scrutinized, he speaks dispraise of one who deserves dispraise.”
Having investigated and scrutinized, he speaks praise of one who deserves praise;
having investigated and scrutinized, he expresses lack of confidence regarding a matter that inspires lack of confidence;
and having investigated and scrutinized, he expresses confidence regarding a matter that inspires confidence.
He does not squander what has been given out of faith.
Endowed with these five qualities, monks, a resident monk is placed in heaven as if carried there.
The sixth.
Aṅguttara Nikāya 5.237 24.
Āvāsikavagga Dutiya-avaṇṇārahasutta (The Second Discourse on Those Deserving of Censure)
“Bhikkhus, possessing five qualities, a resident bhikkhu is deposited in hell as if carried there. What are the five? [The Sutta continues:]”
Without investigating and without scrutinizing, one speaks in praise of one who deserves dispraise;
without investigating and without scrutinizing, one speaks in dispraise of one who deserves praise;
one is stingy regarding one's dwelling and greedy for one's dwelling.
He is stingy regarding families and greedy for families;
he squanders what has been given out of faith.
Endowed with these five qualities, monks, a resident monk is placed in hell as if carried there in a vessel.
“Monks, endowed with five qualities, a resident monk is deposited in heaven just as he was brought there.
What are the five?
Having investigated and scrutinized, he speaks dispraise of one who deserves dispraise.”
Having investigated and scrutinized, he speaks praise of one who deserves praise;
he is not stingy regarding his dwelling nor greedy for his dwelling;
he is not stingy regarding families nor greedy for families.
He does not squander what has been given out of faith.
Endowed with these five qualities, monks, a resident monk is placed in heaven as if carried there.
The seventh [sutta].
Aṅguttara Nikāya 5.238 24.
Āvāsikavagga Tatiyaavaṇṇārahasutta (The Third Discourse on Being Worthy of Censure)
“Bhikkhus, possessing five qualities, a resident bhikkhu is deposited in hell as if carried there. What are the five? [The Sutta continues with the list.]”
Without investigating and without scrutinizing, one speaks in praise of one who deserves dispraise;
without investigating and without scrutinizing, one speaks in dispraise of one who deserves praise;
and one is stingy regarding one's dwelling.
He is stingy regarding families;
he is stingy regarding gains.
Endowed with these five qualities, monks, a resident monk is placed in hell as if carried there.
“Monks, a resident monk endowed with five qualities is deposited in heaven as if carried there.
What are the five?
Having investigated and scrutinized, he speaks dispraise of one who deserves dispraise.”
Having investigated and scrutinized, one speaks praise of one who deserves praise;
one is not stingy regarding one's dwelling;
one is not stingy regarding families.
He is not stingy regarding gains.
Endowed with these five qualities, monks, a resident monk is deposited in heaven as if carried there.
Thus ends the eighth [discourse].
Aṅguttara Nikāya 5.239 24.
Āvāsikavagga First Discourse on Meanness (Paṭhamamacchariyasutta)
“Bhikkhus, possessing five qualities, a resident bhikkhu is deposited in hell as if brought there. What are the five? [Text follows].”
He is stingy regarding dwellings;
he is stingy regarding families;
he is stingy regarding gains.
He is envious of praise;
he misappropriates what has been given out of faith.
Endowed with these five qualities, monks, a resident monk is placed in hell as if carried there.
“Monks, a resident monk endowed with five qualities is deposited in heaven as if carried there.
What are the five?
He is not stingy regarding the dwelling;”
He is not stingy regarding family;
he is not stingy regarding gain;
he is not stingy regarding praise.
He does not squander what has been given out of faith.
Endowed with these five qualities, monks, a resident monk is placed in heaven as if carried there.
Thus ends the ninth [sutta].
Aṅguttara Nikāya 5.240 24.

Āvāsikavagga Dutiyamacchariyasutta (The Second Discourse on Stinginess) “Monks, there are these five kinds of stinginess. What five? Stinginess regarding dwellings, stinginess regarding families, stinginess regarding gains, stinginess regarding praise, and stinginess regarding the Dhamma. These, monks, are the five kinds of stinginess.”
“Bhikkhus, possessed of five qualities, a resident bhikkhu is deposited in hell as if carried there. What are the five? [The Sutta continues with the list.]”
He is stingy regarding dwellings;
he is stingy regarding families;
he is stingy regarding gains.
He is stingy with praise;
he is stingy with the Dhamma.
Possessing these five qualities, monks, a resident monk is deposited in hell as if carried there.
“Monks, a resident monk endowed with five qualities is placed in heaven as if carried there.
What are the five?
He is not miserly regarding his dwelling;”
He is not stingy regarding family;
he is not stingy regarding gain;
he is not stingy regarding praise.
“He is not stingy with the Dhamma.
Endowed with these five qualities, monks, a resident monk is placed in heaven as if carried there.
The tenth.
The fourth chapter: On Residents.
Its summary verse:
The resident, the beloved, and the handsome;
The very helpful one and the compassionate one;
the three who are unworthy of praise,
and the two types of stinginess.
Aṅguttara Nikāya 5.241 25.

Duccaritavagga Paṭhamaduccaritasutta (The First Discourse on Misconduct) “Monks, there are these five kinds of misconduct. What five? Misconduct by way of body, misconduct by way of speech, misconduct by way of mind, the result of misconduct by way of body, and the result of misconduct by way of speech and mind. These, monks, are the five kinds of misconduct.”
“Bhikkhus, there are these five dangers in misconduct.
What are the five?
One reproaches oneself;
the wise, having investigated, censure one;
and an evil reputation spreads abroad.
He dies confused;
with the breakup of the body, after death, he reappears in a state of deprivation, a bad destination, a lower realm, even in hell.
These, monks, are the five dangers in misconduct.
“Monks, there are these five benefits in well-conducted conduct.
What are the five?
One does not reproach oneself.”
The wise praise one after having investigated;
a good reputation spreads abroad;
and one passes away unconfused.
With the breakup of the body, after death, one is reborn in a happy destination, in a heavenly world.
These, monks, are the five benefits of good conduct. Thus was the first [discourse].
Aṅguttara Nikāya 5.242 25.

Duccaritavagga Paṭhamakāyaduccaritasutta (The First Discourse on Bodily Misconduct) “Bhikkhus, there are these five results of bodily misconduct. What five? First, one experiences pain and distress here and now; second, one creates a basis for the arising of demerit; third, one incurs the censure of the wise; fourth, with the breakup of the body, after death, one is reborn in a state of misery, in a bad destination, in a place of suffering, or in hell; fifth, one’s mind does not incline toward renunciation. These, bhikkhus, are the five results of bodily misconduct.”
“Bhikkhus, there are these five dangers in bodily misconduct … [as before] … and five advantages in bodily good conduct … [as before] …” The second.
Aṅguttara Nikāya 5.243 25.

Duccaritavagga Paṭhamavacīduccaritasutta (The First Discourse on Verbal Misconduct) “Monks, there are these five kinds of verbal misconduct. What five? (1) Speaking falsehood; (2) Speaking malicious speech; (3) Speaking harsh speech; (4) Speaking idle chatter; (5) Holding wrong view. These, monks, are the five kinds of verbal misconduct.”
“Bhikkhus, there are these five dangers in verbal misconduct … [as before] … there are these five advantages in verbal good conduct … [as before] …” The third.
*Aṅguttara Nikāya* 5.244.
25. The Chapter on Misconduct.
First Discourse on Mental Misconduct:
“Bhikkhus, there are these five dangers in mental misconduct … [and so on] … there are these five advantages in mental good conduct.”
Which five?
One does not reproach oneself;
the wise, having investigated, praise one.
A good reputation spreads abroad;
one dies unconfused;
and with the breakup of the body, after death, one reappears in a happy destination, in a heavenly world.
“Monks, these are the five benefits of mental good conduct.
Thus was the fourth [discourse]. Aṅguttara Nikāya 5.245
25. The Chapter on Misconduct The Second Discourse on Misconduct (AN 5.245, PTS AN iii 268)
“Bhikkhus, there are these five dangers in misconduct.
What five?
One reproaches oneself;”
The wise, having investigated, censure him;
an evil reputation spreads abroad;
he falls away from the true Dhamma.
One becomes established in what is not the true Dhamma.
Monks, these are the five dangers in misconduct.
Monks, there are these five benefits in good conduct.
Which five?
One does not reproach oneself;
the wise, having investigated, praise one.
A good reputation spreads abroad;
one emerges from what is not the true Dhamma and becomes established in the true Dhamma.
“Monks, these indeed are the five benefits of good conduct.
Thus was the fifth [discourse]. Aṅguttara Nikāya 5.246.
